docs.title: Evidence Hound
docs.text:
Sniffs out compliance evidence from your systems and fetches it into CISO Assistant, on schedule, every time.

Small businesses in the defence industry must reach and then keep cyber compliance, such as Essential Eight Maturity Level 2 (DISP, Australia) or NIST SP 800-171 (CMMC, US), usually without a CISO or a GRC team, and with a few hours a week for it. Evidence Hound makes that manageable with open-source tools:

  • CISO Assistant, self-hosted, is the system of record: audits, controls, evidence, suppliers, risks and tasks.
  • hound collects evidence from your systems on a schedule, maps it to each framework's requirements and keeps CISO Assistant's audits current, so compliance is continuous rather than a scramble before each assessment.
  • Your own coding agent (Claude Code or GitHub Copilot) drafts the decisions, supplier reviews and evidence proposals; you accept or challenge them in one guided review a week. No model collects evidence, and nothing is accepted without a person.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
New here? Getting started is one route from a trial on your laptop to your first weekly review. The rest of the site is reference that route links to.

You want to Read See it work on your laptop in an hour or two Getting started, then the local trial Run it for real next to CISO Assistant First deployment, then backups and hardening Move your registers in Onboarding and moving off spreadsheets Know what to do each week as the GRC member GRC member guide and the weekly review Report to the committee and the board Reporting, security committee, board Answer a prime's NIST SP 800-171 questions Answer a prime's questionnaire Govern your use of AI AI governance primer Connect a system Collectors, or write a profile for any REST API

Every command and its options are on the cheat sheet. What is in this release, its known limitations and how to upgrade are in the release notes.

Your organisation's configuration (systems, tenants, audits, evidence) lives in your own private compliance repo, never in this project. Evidence Hound is Apache-2.0; CISO Assistant is AGPL-3.0 and is used over its API only.

docs.title: AI governance for a cyber GRC team
docs.text:
This primer is for a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) team that knows cyber compliance but is new to AI governance. It takes about 15 minutes to read. It explains what AI governance asks of a small business, using the Australian Government's Guidance for AI Adoption (known as AI6), and shows each step with the fictional Example Pty Ltd.

You do not need to become an AI expert. Most of the work is the same work you already do for cyber: know what is in use, who owns it, what could go wrong, what was checked, and who can step in.

docs.title: AI governance in plain words
docs.text:
AI GRC is governance, risk and compliance applied to the AI tools your organisation uses or builds. For each one you want to be able to answer: what is it, who is responsible, what could go wrong, what did we check before relying on it, and who can step in when it gets something wrong.

An AI system is any tool that makes predictions, recommendations, content or decisions from data with some autonomy. Examples are a chat assistant staff use, an AI feature switched on inside a software-as-a-service product, or a model a developer built. For a small business most AI systems are third-party products, so most of the work is knowing they are there and who looks after them.

AI6 is voluntary guidance from the National AI Centre (October 2025). It is not a law or a certification. It does for AI what the Essential Eight does for cyber: a short list of practices to adopt and show you follow. There is no AI6 audit body. The AI6 audit in CISO Assistant is your own self-assessment, for the security committee and the board.

AI6 comes in two versions with the same six practices:

  • Foundations is for organisations starting out, or using AI in low-risk ways. It has the six practices, each with "Getting started" and "Next steps" actions. Start here.
  • Implementation is for organisations that build or customise AI, or use it for higher-risk decisions. It splits the practices into 21 sub-practices with detailed actions.

The example uses Foundations. In CISO Assistant the AI6 framework has both, as two groups: F for Foundations and I for Implementation. An audit for group F shows only the rows Foundations asks for.

docs.title: How the work fits the tools you already use
docs.text:
• CISO Assistant stays the system of record. Each AI system is an asset, labelled ai-system, with its owner. Its register entry (its screening outcome, how people oversee it, when it was screened, assessed and tested) is shown in the asset's labels and description. AI risks are risk scenarios linked to the asset. A third-party AI product is a solution of a supplier, as for any other supplier.
  • The register is CISO Assistant's asset list, filtered by the ai-system label. You export it with CISO Assistant's own Excel export. There is no separate spreadsheet.
  • Your repo holds what you decide: which AI systems exist, who owns them, their screening outcome, the National AI Centre register template's columns, oversight arrangement and dates, in an ai block on each system. Changes go through pull requests like the rest of your scope, and hound scope apply copies them to CISO Assistant.
  • hound checks the register on every run: a system with no owner, an elevated system with no approved impact assessment, a test date that has gone stale. Those checks fill the AI6 rows that can be checked; the rest are manual evidence with an owner and a reminder, as for the Essential Eight.

docs.title: The six practices, with Example Pty Ltd
docs.text: Example Pty Ltd has twelve staff. Its IT team is Alex Example, and Sam Example is the CEO. The GRC team is Alex, two to eight hours a week.

docs.title: 1. Decide who is accountable
docs.text:
Name one senior person accountable for AI overall, and an owner for each AI system. Make sure staff who use AI know enough to use it well, and that suppliers' responsibilities are clear.

Example Pty Ltd: Sam (the CEO) is accountable for AI. Staff start using a chat assistant, Example Chat, to draft emails and proposals. Alex registers it as an AI system in the repo with Alex as its owner, and adds a one-page AI policy to the documents of the AI6 audit. Sam approves the policy. A ten-minute briefing at the staff meeting covers what not to paste into the assistant.

docs.title: 2. Understand impacts and plan accordingly
docs.text:
Before using an AI system, think about who it affects and how. Give people a way to raise a concern or ask for a decision to be reviewed by a person.

Example Pty Ltd: Example Chat drafts text that a staff member always reads before sending, so it affects customers only through what staff choose to send. Alex records that in a short impact note on the system. The existing complaints address on the website is the feedback route; Alex adds a line saying a person reviews any complaint about AI-drafted content.

docs.title: 3. Measure and manage risks
docs.text:
Screen each AI system with the National AI Centre's seven yes-or-no screening questions. No to every question means normal: carry on with your usual steps. Yes to any question means elevated: senior leadership or a governance committee looks at it before it goes ahead, and its risks and the controls for them are recorded. The committee can also find a system unacceptable, and then it is not used.

Example Pty Ltd: Alex answers the screening questions for Example Chat. It makes no decisions about people, handles no sensitive personal data by design, and its output is always checked, but it is built on a general-purpose language model that takes open-ended instructions, so question 7 is a yes and it is elevated. That surprises Alex; it is common, and it means a short impact assessment the CTO approves, one risk scenario ("staff paste confidential client details into a prompt") and a test every 6 months. A few months later, the sales team asks to switch on an AI feature in the customer system that scores leads. It uses customer details (question 1) and a wrong score is hard to put right (question 6), so it is elevated too: Alex records a risk scenario in CISO Assistant ("leads from some regions are scored unfairly low") with its control (a monthly spot check of low-scored leads), and its impact assessment is approved before it goes live. A rules-based ticket router with no personal data would answer no to everything and be normal.

docs.title: 4. Share essential information
docs.text:
Keep a register of AI systems. Tell people when they are dealing with AI or with AI-generated content, and know what your suppliers tell you about their AI.

Example Pty Ltd: the register is the list of assets labelled ai-system in CISO Assistant, two entries by now. The proposal template gains a footer line saying drafts may be prepared with AI assistance and are reviewed by staff. The supplier of the customer system is already a third party in CISO Assistant; its assessment now includes a question about its AI feature.

docs.title: 5. Test and monitor
docs.text:
Check that an AI system works as intended before relying on it, and keep checking. The riskier the system, the more often.

Example Pty Ltd: before switching on lead scoring, the sales lead compares its scores with last quarter's actual sales for 50 leads and records the result as evidence; Alex sets the test date in the system's ai block. hound checks that date on every run: an elevated system tested more than 6 months ago (12 for a normal one) shows as a failing check, and the AI6 row for testing follows it.

docs.title: 6. Maintain human control
docs.text:
Make sure a person can oversee, override or switch off the system, and know how you would stop using it.

Example Pty Ltd: Example Chat is human in the loop: a person approves every output before it is used. Lead scoring is human on the loop: it runs by itself, and the sales lead watches the monthly spot check and can switch the feature off in the customer system's settings. Alex writes both arrangements in the oversight note of each system's ai block. hound fails the oversight check if an elevated system has nobody in or on the loop.

docs.title: What the committee sees
docs.text: The monthly security committee report gains an AI section: how many AI systems there are by screening outcome, which were added or retired this month, which fail a check, and the AI6 rows that are not yet met. The quarterly board report shows the AI6 self-assessment beside the Essential Eight. For Example Pty Ltd that is a few lines: two systems (both elevated), nothing failing, and the next step on the plan.

docs.title: What you do not need to do at Foundations
docs.text:
• You do not need the 21 sub-practices or their detailed actions. Those are Implementation, for organisations that build AI or use it for higher-risk decisions.
  • You do not need to test or audit a supplier's model. For a third-party product, check what the supplier tells you and how you use it.
  • You do not need a separate AI risk method. Use your existing risk register, with AI risks as risk scenarios.
  • You do not need an impact assessment for a normal system. Screening is enough, and you redo it when the use changes. (The National AI Centre's policy template asks for one for every system; if your policy keeps that, follow your policy.)
  • You do not need a certificate or an external audit. AI6 is a self-assessment.
  • You do not need a separate register spreadsheet. CISO Assistant's asset list is the register, with the National AI Centre register template's columns in each asset's description.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning AI system A tool that makes predictions, recommendations, content or decisions from data with some autonomy. AI6 The six practices of the Australian Government's Guidance for AI Adoption (National AI Centre, 2025). Foundations The short version of AI6, for organisations starting out or using AI in low-risk ways. Implementation The detailed version of AI6, with 21 sub-practices, for organisations that build AI or use it for higher-risk decisions. Screening The National AI Centre's seven yes-or-no questions about an AI system's use. Screening outcome Normal (no to every question), elevated (yes to any) or unacceptable (the committee's decision; not used). Impact assessment A fuller review of who an elevated system affects and how, approved before it goes live. Human in the loop A person approves each output before it is used. Human on the loop The system acts by itself while a person watches and can step in. Human out of the loop Nobody reviews the system's outputs as it works; only afterwards, if at all. Register The list of AI systems: the ai blocks in your repo's scope, shown in CISO Assistant as assets labelled ai-system. Third-party AI An AI product or feature you use but did not build, recorded with its supplier.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• The walkthrough in docs/tutorials/ai-governance.md registers an AI system on the local stack and follows it through screening, assessment, testing and the committee report. It is written once the AI register and its checks are built (sprint s11).
  • The guidance itself: Guidance for AI Adoption: Foundations and Implementation guidance, on ai.gov.au.

docs.title: AI governance (AI6) in Evidence Hound
docs.text: This is the reference for how Evidence Hound and CISO Assistant support AI governance with the Australian Government's Guidance for AI Adoption (AI6). New to AI governance? Read the primer first, then follow the walkthrough on the local stack; the training outline turns it into a 30-minute team session.

docs.title: What AI6 asks, and where each part lives
docs.text:
AI6 asks six things: decide who is accountable, understand the impacts, measure and manage the risks, share essential information, test and monitor, and keep people in control. Evidence Hound handles them with what CISO Assistant already has, plus your repo:

AI6 asks for Kept in How it is checked A register of AI systems, each with an owner The ai block of each AI system in scope/setup.yaml, shown in CISO Assistant as an asset labelled ai-system ai-register collector Screening with the National AI Centre's questions, and an approved impact assessment before an elevated system goes live The same ai block: screening, screening_yes, screened_on, impact_assessment, impact_assessed_on, in_use_from ai-register collector The risks of elevated systems Risk scenarios in CISO Assistant, linked to the system's asset ciso-assistant profile Human oversight oversight and oversight_note in the ai block ai-register collector Testing, and testing again in proportion to risk last_tested_on in the ai block, with the test result as evidence ai-register collector Suppliers of third-party AI The supplier's solution, entity assessment and contract in CISO Assistant (as for any supplier) ciso-assistant profile Policy, training, redress, disclosure, monitoring and incident reviews Records a person keeps and attests ai-governance (yearly) and ai-operations (quarterly) manual sources The self-assessment An audit of the AI6 framework, group F (Foundations) mappings/ai6.yaml turns every check into AI6 results

CISO Assistant's custom fields are an Enterprise feature, so the register entry lives in the repo and reaches CISO Assistant as filtering labels (ai-screening-elevated, ai-use-third-party, ai-oversight-on-the-loop, ai-retired) and as lines in the asset's description. Filtering the asset list by ai-system gives the register; CISO Assistant's own Excel export saves it.

docs.title: Who sets each field
docs.text:
Everything in the ai block is changed by pull request, so each change is reviewed. The scope guide lists the keys and what hound scope validate reports.

Field Set by When screening, screening_yes, screened_on The GRC team, from the screening runbook When a system is proposed, and again when its use changes registered_on The GRC team When the system is approved and added to the register version, use, purpose, intended_uses, limitations, misuse, data_sources, stakeholders The system's owner, reviewed by the GRC team At screening, and when the system or its use changes oversight, oversight_note The system's owner, reviewed by the GRC team At screening, and when the arrangement changes impact_assessment, impact_assessed_on The GRC team, once the assessment is approved Before an elevated system goes live in_use_from, retired_on The system's owner At go-live and when the system is switched off last_tested_on The system's owner, with the test result kept as evidence Before go-live, then at least every 12 months (6 for an elevated system)

A third-party AI system also names its supplier's solution, and its supplier is approved before the system is registered, as for any other system.

docs.title: The checks
docs.text: The collector guide lists each check and when it passes. In short: the ai-register collector checks the entries in your repo every night (owners, screening, impact assessments before use, oversight, test dates) and the ciso-assistant profile checks what only CISO Assistant holds (risk scenarios, supplier assessments and contracts). Every observation names the AI6 sub-practice in words and says what to do. Checks a person attests come from two manual sources, copied from examples/manual-sources/ai6/: ai-governance once a year and ai-operations each quarter.

docs.title: The National AI Centre's templates
docs.text:
The register, the screening and the AI policy follow the National AI Centre's own templates, so an assessor sees the government's terms.

Template Published How it is used AI register template (Word and Excel) ai.gov.au; the copies used here were last changed in June 2026 (Word) and May 2026 (Excel) Its 12 columns are the ai block's keys (traced below). Each run's ai-register.json holds every column for every AI system, ready to give an assessor. AI screening questions (PDF) ai.gov.au; last changed July 2026 Its seven questions are the screening runbook, and its outcome is screening. AI policy guide and template (Word) ai.gov.au; last changed June 2026 The source for your AI policy, which the AI6 audit lists as a document (AI6-1.4, AI6-3.1). See the AI policy.

None of the three states a licence or a version number, so this repo does not copy their text: the tables below summarise them in our own words. Download them from ai.gov.au and keep your filled-in copies with your own records.

docs.title: The National AI Centre's register template
docs.text:
Every column of the template, and where the register keeps it. ai. keys are in the system's ai block in scope/setup.yaml; they reach CISO Assistant in the asset's description, and ai.register_complete fails while one is empty.

Template column Kept as Notes Name and version The system's name, and ai.version version is optional, for systems that have one. Owner The system's owner The accountable person (AI6-1.1); checked by ai.owner_assigned. Status Worked out each run from ai.in_use_from and ai.retired_on Pilot until it goes live, operational while in use, decommissioned once retired; written to ai-register.json as status. Kept as dates so a status cannot be forgotten. Source ai.use, and for a supplier's product the system's solution built is the internal team; third_party names the supplier's solution, so the supplier is approved first. Purpose/business goals ai.purpose Intended use case(s) ai.intended_uses A list. Known limitations and prohibited use ai.limitations Any foreseeable misuse ai.misuse Write "None identified." when there is none. Data sources and type ai.data_sources A list, each with its type, such as "Past proposals (text)". Sensitive data is also recorded in the system's data (CUI, PII and so on). Registered date ai.registered_on Screening outcome ai.screening, with ai.screening_yes normal, elevated or unacceptable, as the template's drop-down; the answers show the reasoning. Key stakeholders affected ai.stakeholders A list.

docs.title: The National AI Centre's screening questions
docs.text:
The seven questions, in brief. A yes to any of them makes the outcome elevated; no to all of them makes it normal. Unacceptable is the AI governance committee's decision for a use the organisation will not accept, whatever the answers. hound scope validate reports ai.screening_disagrees when the outcome and the answers do not match.

Question In brief A yes means 1 It uses personal, sensitive or confidential information, in training, operation or prompts. Elevated: also record the data in the system's data 2 It talks directly to people with freedom to answer without a person checking. Elevated 3 It acts on its own at scale, or would be hard to stop or correct. Elevated: think about oversight 4 It makes or supports decisions about people in vulnerable or under-represented groups. Elevated 5 It works in a regulated area or can have legal effects on people. Elevated 6 Harm from a wrong decision would be hard to contest, reverse or put right. Elevated 7 It is general purpose, or easily used beyond what it was meant for. Elevated

An elevated system needs more before and after it goes live, and the checks enforce it: an approved impact assessment before in_use_from (ai.impact_assessment_before_use), its risks as risk scenarios in CISO Assistant (ai.risks_in_register), a person in or on the loop (ai.human_oversight_documented), and a test at least every 6 months instead of 12 (ai.test_results_current). The template says to consult senior leadership or the governance committee before planning an elevated system in detail; the runbook makes that the approval of the impact assessment. An unacceptable system in use fails ai.screening_recorded.

docs.title: The AI policy
docs.text:
The policy template sets out a policy's purpose and scope, what counts as an AI system, the policy statements (human-centred use, accountability, risk and impact assessment, testing, fairness, transparency and human oversight), the roles (policy owner, approvers, compliance monitor, governance committee, system owners and all staff), screening new use cases, incidents and yearly review.

Write your own policy from it, approve it, and list it under documents in your AI6 audit for AI6-1.4 and AI6-3.1, as the example's AI6 audit does with a placeholder (ex-ai6-2026.yaml). The yearly ai-governance source attests it was approved (ai.policy_approved). Two things to match up when you write it: the template's screening outcomes are normal, elevated and prohibited in one place and unacceptable in another (the register uses unacceptable); and it asks for a risk and impact assessment for every AI system, where the register asks for an approved one only for elevated systems. Choose one rule for your policy, and say so in it.

docs.title: Adopting at Foundations
docs.text:
1. Add the AI6 library to scope/setup.yaml (as examples/compliance-repo/scope/setup.yaml does), an audit for group F, and an ai6 programme with register: { of: ai_systems, by: [screening, use] }.
  2. Register each AI system you use with an ai block, after screening it.
  3. Add the ai-register collector, the ciso-assistant profile and the two manual sources to hound.yaml, and mappings/ai6.yaml as a target for the AI6 audit.
  4. Add evidence plan rows for the manual sources, so their owners are reminded.
  5. hound scope plan, review, hound scope apply, then hound run.

If your team uses its own coding agent with hound onboard or hound manual propose, that agent is AI use too: screen it and register it like any other AI system (a person approves every proposal, so it is human in the loop; it reads your repo, so expect question 1 to be yes).

The example compliance repo has all of this for two fictional AI systems; one is deliberately not tested yet, so a run shows AI6-4.1 (the register) met and AI6-5.1 (testing before use) not met.

docs.title: Moving to Implementation
docs.text: Change the audit's and the programme's group from F to I. AI6-4.4 (AI-generated content transparency) joins the audit; it is filled by ai.generated_content_labelled from the ai-governance manual source. Implementation expects more depth in each record a person attests: read the Implementation practices for each sub-practice and widen your runbooks.

docs.title: What Evidence Hound does not do
docs.text:
• It does not test, evaluate or monitor a model. last_tested_on records that a test was done; the test itself is yours.
  • It has no AI incident workflow. AI incidents go through your incident process; the ai-operations source attests they were reviewed.
  • It does not screen a system for you. Screening is a person's judgement, recorded in the repo and reviewed by pull request.
  • It has no model of its own. An agent may draft a register entry or a manual result; a person reviews it before it counts.

docs.title: The AI6 framework library
docs.text:
frameworks/ai6.yaml is a CISO Assistant library for AI6, and frameworks/ai6.json its snapshot.

  • Source. Guidance for AI Adoption: Foundations and Implementation practices, National AI Centre, v1.0, October 2025.
  • Text. The guidance states no licence, so the library carries the practice and sub-practice titles with short descriptions in our own words and a link to the guidance. It will carry the full text only if the guidance is published under CC BY 4.0.
  • Structure. The six practices are headings (AI6-1 to AI6-6, not assessed). The 21 Implementation sub-practices (AI6-1.1 to AI6-6.2) are the assessable rows.
  • Groups. I (Implementation) holds every sub-practice. F (Foundations) holds a sub-practice when at least one Foundations action falls under it (table below). An audit for group F shows only those rows. Only AI6-4.4 (AI-generated content transparency) has no Foundations action.
  • Versions. The library's version goes up with every content change, with a note at the top of the file. CISO Assistant keeps a framework loaded from an older library, and hound scope validate reports it rather than upgrading silently.

docs.title: Foundations actions traced to sub-practices
docs.text:
Foundations has no numbered sub-practices: each practice has "Getting started" and "Next steps" actions, 30 in all. Each is traced to the one Implementation sub-practice it falls under. The actions are summarised in our own words; the numbers (F1.1 to F6.4) are ours, in the order the guidance lists them.

Action Foundations part Action, in brief Sub-practice F1.1 Getting started Name a senior leader as the overall owner of AI governance. AI6-1.1 F1.2 Getting started Write an AI policy for responsible use, with advice to staff on the risks. AI6-1.4 F1.3 Next steps Make one named person accountable for each AI system in use. AI6-1.1 F1.4 Next steps Train the accountable people to decide well about AI risks. AI6-1.3 F1.5 Next steps Agree responsibilities with vendors, developers and integrators. AI6-1.2 F1.6 Next steps Grow the AI policy into a governance framework of policies and procedures. AI6-1.4 F2.1 Getting started Assess who an AI system affects, with care for vulnerable groups. AI6-2.1 F2.2 Getting started Give people a way to challenge AI decisions and have harms put right. AI6-2.2 F2.3 Next steps Engage the people affected through the system's life. AI6-2.1 F2.4 Next steps Watch feedback for patterns of unwanted impact. AI6-2.3 F3.1 Getting started Screen AI systems and uses to flag those that are unacceptable or need more governance. AI6-3.2 F3.2 Next steps Fit risk processes to the kind of AI: traditional IT, narrow, general-purpose or agentic. AI6-3.1 F3.3 Next steps Assess the risks of each use and plan how to reduce them. AI6-3.2 F3.4 Next steps Apply controls in proportion to each use's risk. AI6-3.3 F3.5 Next steps Investigate and learn from AI incidents. AI6-3.4 F4.1 Getting started Keep a register of every AI system, built or bought, including AI inside other tools. AI6-4.1 F4.2 Getting started Tell people when AI makes or influences decisions, or could be mistaken for a person. AI6-4.2 F4.3 Next steps Explain what each AI system can and cannot do. AI6-4.2 F4.4 Next steps Be open along the supply chain about components and data sources. AI6-4.3 F4.5 Next steps Explain AI outcomes to the people affected, in proportion to the stakes. AI6-4.2 F5.1 Getting started Ask suppliers for proof their AI system was tested. AI6-5.1 F5.2 Getting started Test before deployment. AI6-5.1 F5.3 Getting started Monitor after deployment in proportion to the risk. AI6-5.2 F5.4 Getting started Extend data governance and cyber security to cover AI. AI6-5.4 F5.5 Next steps Stress-test the system, including attempts to get around its controls. AI6-5.3 F5.6 Next steps Consider independent testing for uses that need more governance. AI6-5.3 F6.1 Getting started Give meaningful human oversight matched to the system's autonomy and stakes. AI6-6.1 F6.2 Getting started Build in points where a person can pause, override, roll back or shut down the system. AI6-6.1 F6.3 Next steps Train the people who oversee AI on when to step in. AI6-6.1 F6.4 Next steps Keep another way to do critical work if the AI fails or is retired. AI6-6.2

docs.title: Audit update plan
docs.text:
hound plan turns one run's results into the exact list of changes to send to a CISO Assistant audit. Publishing (s02) is then a plain loop over that list.

$ hound plan --dry-run --config examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml --checks tests/fixtures/checks-sample.json

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Config target (see examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml): the mapping file, the audit's ref_id (compliance_assessment) and a map from control keys to applied control ref_ids. IDs always come from config, never from code.
  • Check results file: checks (as for hound mapping apply), plus optional evidence (id, file_name, media_type, sha256, size_bytes, collected_at) and control_statuses (control key and status: to_do, in_progress, on_hold, active, deprecated).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A JSON array of CISO Assistant dispatcher messages, in this order:

  1. upload_attachment for each evidence item, by ID. Selector {name: file_name, ref_id: id}; values {file_content, file_name}. In a dry run file_content describes the file instead of holding its base64 content.
  2. update_requirement_assessment for each requirement result, in mapping order. Selector {compliance_assessment__ref_id, requirement__ref_id}; values {result, observation, evidences}, where evidences lists the ref_ids of evidence uploaded in step 1.
  3. update_applied_control for each control status, by key. Selector {ref_id}; values {status}.

The plan fails, with every problem listed and exit code 3, if a requirement cites evidence that is not in the file or a control key is not in the target.

docs.title: Business impact analysis
docs.text:
This guide is for a GRC team that records how long each system can be down, and what recovery has been proven, in CISO Assistant's business impact analysis (BIA), with the analysis written and reviewed in the compliance repo. The full file reference is in Scope files.

The example compliance repo has one: examples/compliance-repo/scope/bia/ex-bia-2026.yaml, with recovery objectives on its systems in examples/compliance-repo/scope/setup.yaml.

docs.title: 1. Set each system's objectives
docs.text:
In scope/setup.yaml, give a system its security objectives on CISO Assistant's 0 to 4 scale and its recovery objectives as durations:

      - name: Example 365
        objectives: {confidentiality: 3, availability: 2}
        recovery: {rto: 4h, rpo: 1d, mtd: 3d}

They are written only when the file declares them, so values set in CISO Assistant are otherwise kept.

docs.title: 2. Write the BIA
docs.text:
One file per BIA under scope/bia/, on one risk matrix's impact scale (see Risk studies). Each system gets one assessment: what it depends on, the controls that keep it running, its recovery flags, and escalation thresholds that say how bad an outage becomes over time:

  - system: Example 365
    dependencies: [Example laptops]
    controls: [AC-BACKUP]
    recovery: {documented: true, tested_by: [backup.restore_tested], targets_met: false}
    thresholds:
      - {after: 4h, impact: Minor, justification: Staff use phones.}
      - {after: 1d, impact: Major, justification: Customers notice missed replies.}

hound scope validate scope/ checks that thresholds ascend, that each impact is a level of the matrix, and that systems and controls exist. It warns when an impact falls after an earlier, higher one, because CISO Assistant carries the highest impact forward.

docs.title: 3. Let evidence set "recovery tested"
docs.text: A hand-ticked "tested" box says only that someone ticked it. Name the checks that prove it instead, with tested_by (or documented_by, targets_met_by). After collecting, each hound run sets the flag from every collector's latest results: true only when every named check passed. It writes only when the value changes, links the checks' evidence to the assessment, and lists what it set under recovery in its JSON. A flag cannot be both set by hand and named by checks (scope.result_conflict).

docs.title: 4. Plan, review and apply
docs.text:
$ hound scope plan scope/ --config hound.yaml
$ hound scope apply scope/ --config hound.yaml

The plan keys an assessment bia/system and a threshold bia/system/after, such as EX-BIA-2026/Example 365/1d. It leaves alone a flag that runs set from checks.

docs.title: What stays in CISO Assistant
docs.text:
• Computed impacts. CISO Assistant works out each assessment's impact over time from its thresholds, and carries the highest impact forward; the file holds only the thresholds.
  • Recovery flags named by checks. Each run sets them from the evidence, so neither the file nor hound scope apply writes them.
  • Approval. Moving a BIA to done is the team's decision after review; the file records its status, and CISO Assistant keeps who changed it and when.

docs.title: CISO Assistant as configuration
docs.text:
What in CISO Assistant is configuration that hound can declare in files, what is runtime data, and how each piece behaves through the REST API. Checked against CISO Assistant v4.3.4: its OpenAPI schema (/api/schema/, 1,805 paths), its source, and a probe script run against a local instance in CI.

  • Probe: scripts/ca-inventory.sh. HOUND_CA_TOKEN=… scripts/ca-inventory.sh <api-url> <out-dir> saves the full schema (openapi.json), a snapshot of the resources below (openapi-paths.json) and the answers (answers.json). It creates EX-PROBE-* objects and deletes them afterwards, except the probe library. Run it against a throwaway instance.
  • Snapshot: tests/fixtures/ciso-assistant/openapi-v4.3.4.json holds every operation on the resources hound calls or s06 configures (347 paths), plus the seven list endpoints the posture snapshot reads (s12-04: risk acceptances, security exceptions, findings, incidents, risk scenarios, task occurrences and entity assessments), added by hand and exercised by the functional tests. OpenApiSnapshotTests fails when an endpoint hound calls (ApiEndpoints.Used) is missing from it. To upgrade CISO Assistant, run the probe against the new release, replace the snapshot and fix what fails.

docs.title: Conventions that hold for every object
docs.text:
• Stable key. Most objects have a ref_id. CISO Assistant fills a blank ref_id automatically, so hound always sends its own and finds objects by it (list filter ?ref_id= or search). Library content (frameworks, requirement nodes, reference controls, risk matrices, threats) is keyed by URN instead.
  • Endpoints. Collections are /api/<resource>/ (GET list, POST create) and items are /api/<resource>/{id}/ (GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), with {id} the UUID. /api/<resource>/{id}/object/ returns the read serializer with names rather than IDs.
  • Writes hound is not allowed to make are not always errors. On a requirement assessment, a field that the audit's field_visibility makes read-only for the auditor is dropped from the write and the request still returns 200 (see Q4). hound must read back what it wrote rather than trust the status code.
  • Sized request bodies. Send JSON with a Content-Length. A chunked body reaches CISO Assistant empty, so a PATCH returns 200 and changes nothing.

docs.title: Managed in this sprint (s06)
docs.text:
Object Kind Endpoint Stable key Create Update Lock Delete Library (framework, mapping set, reference controls, risk matrix) Configuration /api/stored-libraries/upload/ (POST, raw file body), then /api/stored-libraries/{id}/import/; loaded ones under /api/loaded-libraries/ Library URN (and version) Upload stores it; import loads it A newer version is offered by /api/loaded-libraries/{id}/update/ None /api/stored-libraries/{id}/unload/, DELETE on the loaded library; refused while audits use it Framework Configuration (from a library) /api/frameworks/ URN Only through a library Only through a library update None With its library Domain (folder) Configuration /api/folders/ Name under its parent folder (no ref_id) POST with parent_folder and content_type: DO PATCH None DELETE deletes everything inside it Perimeter Configuration /api/perimeters/ ref_id POST with folder PATCH None DELETE Asset (system) Configuration /api/assets/ ref_id POST with folder, type PR or SP PATCH, including parent_assets None DELETE Applied control Configuration (status is runtime, set by collectors) /api/applied-controls/ ref_id POST PATCH Not frozen by an audit lock (Q1) DELETE Audit (compliance assessment) Configuration; its rows are runtime /api/compliance-assessments/ ref_id POST with framework, perimeter, selected_implementation_groups; baseline copies another audit's results (Q3) PATCH is_locked: true refuses every other change to the audit and its rows (Q1) DELETE Requirement assessment (row) Runtime, created with its audit /api/requirement-assessments/ Audit ref_id + requirement URN (or ref) Never: created with the audit PATCH result, observation, evidences, applied_controls; read-only fields dropped silently (Q4) Refused while the audit is locked With the audit Evidence Runtime (documents are configuration) /api/evidences/ ref_id POST PATCH; a new file is a new revision None DELETE Evidence revision Runtime /api/evidence-revisions/ Evidence + version POST with the file; CISO Assistant stores its SHA-256 (Q2) None None DELETE

Audit fields hound writes (from the ComplianceAssessmentWrite schema): ref_id, eta, due_date, authors, reviewers, field_visibility, is_locked, baseline, status. Audit status takes planned, in_progress, in_review, done and deprecated (Assessment.Status; the schema names its enum by a number, so read it from the source). There are no separate start and end date fields: eta is the planned completion and due_date the deadline, so an audit period's dates belong in hound's own files (s06-10).

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Workflows, quick forms, campaigns, EBIOS RM studies and quantitative risk studies. They are authored in CISO Assistant, or imported through libraries and the Data Wizard (/api/data-wizard/). hound neither writes nor exports them.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text: Each answer comes from answers.json, produced by scripts/ca-inventory.sh against v4.3.4 in the functional CI job (run 44906131552, step "Show the CISO Assistant inventory").

docs.title: Q1. Does locking an audit also freeze the applied controls linked to it? (s06-10)
docs.text:
No. With a locked audit (PATCH is_locked: true → 200):

  • PATCH of a linked applied control's status → 200, and the status changes to active.
  • PATCH of a row → 400 "Cannot modify the requirement when the audit is locked."
  • PATCH of another audit field → 400 "Cannot modify the audit attributes when it is locked. Only the 'Locked' field can be modified."

So closing a period must record the controls' state itself; the lock alone does not.

docs.title: Q2. Does replacing an evidence file create a revision with its SHA-256 hash, and can the API read it? (s06-04)
docs.text: Yes. Two uploads to one evidence item → 201, 201, and GET /api/evidence-revisions/?evidence=<id> lists versions 2 and 1, each with attachment_hash equal to the file's SHA-256 (97b413bc…). hound compares that hash before uploading.

docs.title: Q3. Which audit fields hold status, start and end dates, and how is an audit created from a baseline? (s06-10)
docs.text: The write fields are status, eta and due_date (plus ref_id, authors, reviewers, field_visibility, is_locked, baseline); there are no start or end date fields. POST /api/compliance-assessments/ with baseline: <audit id> → 201, and the compliant row of the baseline was copied to the new audit (1 of 1).

docs.title: Q4. Are writes to a field the service account's role can only read ignored silently? (s06-06)
docs.text: Yes. On an audit whose field_visibility makes observation read-only for the auditor, PATCH of a row with observation and result → 200; afterwards result is compliant (written) and observation is empty (dropped). The scope plan must warn about such fields rather than expect an error.

docs.title: Q5. Can the API upload a custom library, update the main entity, and set feature flags? (s06-09, s10-01)
docs.text:
• Feature flags: GET /api/settings/feature-flags/ → 200 and PATCH → 200. 62 flags, including tprm, metrology, bia, policy_documents and outgoing_webhooks.
  • Main entity: GET /api/entities/?builtin=true finds it, and PATCH → 200.
  • Custom library: the only upload path is POST /api/stored-libraries/upload/, which uses DRF's FileUploadParser: the body is the raw YAML file, named by a Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=… header. Sent that way, the probe library uploads → 201 and is returned as a stored library with its URN (run 44907514706). A multipart form is refused with 400 "Missing filename. Request should include a Content-Disposition header with a filename parameter."

docs.title: Q6. Do BIAs, entity assessments and metric instances have a ref_id, and can entity assessments be revised through the API? (s15-04, s10-02)
docs.text: All three have ref_id in both their read and write schemas (BusinessImpactAnalysis*, EntityAssessment*, MetricInstance*). No path in the schema matches an entity assessment revision, and the tprm models have no revision model, so a new assessment period is a new entity assessment with its own ref_id.

docs.title: Closed-loop feedback
docs.text: The public repo's automation is the reviewer that never sleeps. Every push to a sprint branch produces feedback, and the next task does not start until that feedback is clean.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text: Signal Source Where to read it Blocks merge Build, unit, contract tests ci.yml PR checks; test report artifact Yes Functional tests ci.yml (functional job) PR checks Yes Lint, format, analysers ci.yml PR checks Yes Organisation data check ci.yml (org-data job) PR checks Yes Code scanning CodeQL default setup Security tab; PR annotations Yes (high and above) Secrets Secret scanning with push protection Push is rejected; Security tab Yes Dependencies Dependabot alerts and the dependency review action Security tab; PR checks Yes (high and above) Supply chain posture OpenSSF Scorecard (weekly) Security tab No; reviewed monthly

docs.title: The loop for each task
docs.text:
1. Push the task's commits.
  2. Wait for checks: gh pr checks --watch.
  3. Read failures: gh run view --log-failed.
  4. Read new code scanning alerts on the branch: gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/alerts?ref=refs/heads/$(git branch --show-current)&state=open"
  5. Read Dependabot alerts: gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/dependabot/alerts?state=open"
  6. Fix with a new red-green cycle when the failure is behavioural; fix directly when it is lint or configuration.
  7. Record anything that needs a later task under "Discovered work" in the sprint file.

The /check-feedback Claude Code command runs steps 2 to 5 and summarises.

docs.title: Sprint-level review
docs.text: At sprint end, before merging: all checks green, zero open high or critical alerts introduced by the sprint, sprint file updated with functional check results, and a short "Sprint review" note at the bottom of the sprint file (what shipped, what slipped, what the feedback taught us).

docs.title: Deployment configuration
docs.text:
One YAML file per deployment says how to reach CISO Assistant, where evidence is stored, which collectors run and which audit they update. Nothing organisation-specific lives in code. The fictional examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml is a complete example, and schemas/config.schema.json describes every key for editors and other tools.

The config lives in your private compliance repo next to the scope files that say what CISO Assistant should hold; the template is examples/compliance-repo/ (its hound.yaml), and scope.md explains the scope files and the review workflow.

$ hound config validate examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml
valid

hound config validate reports every problem at once, each with its file and line, and exits 3 if there are any. It never prints a value that might be a secret.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Key Required Meaning ciso_assistant.url yes API address, for example http://localhost:8000/api/. The HOUND_CA_URL setting overrides it. ciso_assistant.token yes Secret reference to a CISO Assistant personal access token. ciso_assistant.transport no rest, the only transport. The Kafka transport was removed in release 3; kafka or kafka_bootstrap_servers gives config.transport_removed. evidence.root yes Evidence folder, relative to the config file. evidence.retention_days no Runs older than this many days are deleted; the latest successful run of each collector is always kept. evidence.period_retention_years no How many years the final run of each ended audit period is kept, however old (default 7). It is the evidence behind a closed record. scheduler.time_zone no IANA time zone the collectors' cron schedules are read in, for example Australia/Sydney (default UTC). "0 3 * * *" then means 03:00 there, across daylight saving changes. scheduler.jitter_seconds no The most each collector's scheduled runs are delayed by (default 300, at most 3600, 0 for none). Each collector gets its own stable delay, so collectors sharing a schedule do not call their APIs at the same moment. scope no The compliance repo's scope folder, relative to the config file. A target that names an audit with a cycle there publishes to the period open on the run's date (see scope.md), and those periods' final runs are kept as above. collectors[] yes (may be empty) name (unique, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens), type (a known collector type), schedule (five-field cron, read in scheduler.time_zone), settings (plain values) and secrets (references). targets[] yes, or target The audits results are published to. Each has the keys below. targets[].mapping yes Framework mapping file, relative to the config file. targets[].compliance_assessment yes The audit's ref_id in CISO Assistant, or the series ref_id of an audit with a cycle in scope. Each audit is targeted once. targets[].controls no Control key to applied control ref_id. targets[].health_control no Applied control ref_id that each collector's "collector health" evidence is linked to after every run (see running.md). targets[].no_evidence no non_compliant (default) or not_assessed: what a requirement whose check is missing or failed is published as. CISO Assistant leaves not-assessed rows out of its compliance percentage, so the default keeps it honest; see scope.md.

Paths are resolved against the config file's folder. Unknown keys are errors, so a typo never goes unnoticed.

docs.title: Several audits from one run
docs.text:
One collection run can feed several audits, for example the Essential Eight and the ASD Essentials during a migration, or the Essentials and NIST SP 800-171 later. List them under targets:

targets:
  - mapping: ../mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml
    compliance_assessment: EX-E8-2026
    health_control: AC-AUTO-EVIDENCE
  - mapping: ../mappings/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml
    compliance_assessment: EX-ESSENTIALS-2026
  • Each evidence file is uploaded once and linked from every audit whose requirements cite it.
  • An applied control configured by several targets is updated once.
  • A failure publishing to one audit does not stop the others. hound publish and hound run report sent, skipped and failed items for each audit under audits.
  • A single target: map is still accepted, and is read as a list of one. Use one form or the other, not both.

docs.title: Secrets are references
docs.text:
A secret in the config is always a reference, resolved when the tool runs:

Reference Resolves to env:NAME The environment variable NAME. file:/run/secrets/name The file's content with one trailing newline trimmed, for example a Docker secret.

hound config validate --check-secrets <file> also resolves every reference and reports each one that is missing, naming the reference but never a value. Resolved secrets are held in a type whose text form is ***.

A value that looks like a secret fails validation: ciso_assistant.token or a secrets entry that is not a reference, a setting whose name contains password, secret, token, api_key, private_key or credential (except a setting ending in _url that holds a web address, such as a profile's token_url, or one ending in _path that holds an absolute path), a setting holding a private key, and a setting holding a run of 32 or more letters and digits.

docs.title: Collector types
docs.text:
Type What it does fake Fixed, fictional results for tests, demos and dry runs. Optional setting tenant. manual Export files that an owner drops in a folder, for systems without an API. See Manual sources. m365 Microsoft 365 through Microsoft Graph, read-only: MFA, Conditional Access, privileged roles, Intune device compliance and Office hardening. See collectors/m365.md. vuln-scan Vulnerability scanner exports dropped in a folder: Nessus v2, or any CSV (such as Microsoft Defender vulnerability management) through a column map. See collectors/vuln-scan.md. ai-register The AI register entries (the ai blocks of systems) in the compliance repo's scope/setup.yaml: owners, screening, impact assessments, oversight and test dates. Setting scope, the scope folder. See collectors/ciso-assistant.md. rest Any HTTP API described by a profile in the profiles folder, such as sophos-central for Sophos Central. See collectors/rest.md, collectors/sophos.md and, for infrastructure drift from an IaC pipeline's plan, collectors/terraform-drift.md, and for hosting controls from its infrastructure tests, collectors/terraform-tests.md, and for CISO Assistant's AI risks and supplier records, collectors/ciso-assistant.md. The old sophos type is retired (config.collector_type_retired).

hound collectors list prints every registered type with the check IDs it reports and the settings and secrets it reads. A collector with a required setting or secret missing fails validation with config.setting_missing or config.secret_missing. Settings a collector describes as paths, such as drop_folder, are resolved against the config file's folder like every other path.

docs.title: Manual sources
docs.text:
A manual collector instance is one manual source. Its settings:

Setting Required Meaning drop_folder yes Folder the owner drops export files in. patterns no Comma-separated file patterns to accept, such as *.txt,*.cfg. Default: every file. checks yes Comma-separated check IDs this source supports. due_days yes Days after which fresh evidence is due, such as 30. owner yes Who owns the evidence and attests it. 
collectors:
  - name: example-firewall-config
    type: manual
    schedule: "0 6 * * *"
    settings:
      drop_folder: ../.dev/manual/example-firewall-config
      patterns: "*.txt,*.cfg"
      checks: network.firewall.rules_reviewed, network.firewall.config_exported
      due_days: 30
      owner: Alex Example

Each run reads the drop folder and emits every accepted file dated within the last due_days as evidence, with SHA-256 hashes like any other evidence. The same content dropped twice is emitted once, under its newest name. The newest file decides each configured check:

Newest file within the interval Check result Has an attestation with an outcome for the check That outcome (pass, fail, partial or not_applicable), naming who attested, when, and the note Has an attestation, and the file changed after it was attested partial: "evidence changed since it was attested" (when the attestation records the file's hash) Has an attestation without an outcome for the check partial: "evidence present, not attested for this check" Has no attestation (with or without an agent's proposal) partial: "evidence present, not attested" None, but an older file exists error: "evidence overdue since " None ever error: "no evidence uploaded yet"

A file is dated by its attestation's date, or by when it was written if nobody attested it. A missing drop folder or an invalid attestation fails the collector's run with manual.drop_folder_missing or manual.attestation_invalid.

An attestation is a sidecar next to the file, named <file>.attest.yaml:

who: Alex Example
date: 2026-11-20            # or 2026-11-20T09:30:00Z
note: Rules reviewed with the network team.
outcomes:
  network.firewall.rules_reviewed: pass
  network.firewall.config_exported: pass

hound manual upload copies a file into a source's drop folder and, for a person at a terminal, asks whether to attest it. Through a pipe or from an agent it copies the file without attesting it; a person attests it later with hound manual approve or in the weekly review. Prompts go to stderr; the copied file's path goes to stdout.

$ hound manual upload --config hound.yaml --source example-firewall-config firewall-export.txt
Attest this file now? [y/N]: y
Attested by [Alex Example]:
Outcome for network.firewall.rules_reviewed (pass, fail, partial, not_applicable) [pass]:
Outcome for network.firewall.config_exported (pass, fail, partial, not_applicable) [pass]:
Note (optional): Rules reviewed with the network team.

The command refuses a file that does not match the source's patterns, or whose name is already taken by different content (exit 3), and a non-attestable outcome answer (exit 2). A file whose content is already in the drop folder is not copied again.

docs.title: Proposals from an agent: hound manual propose and hound manual approve
docs.text:
No evidence without a person. A coding assistant set up with hound agent setup can read a manual evidence file and propose its result, but only a person attests it. Runs never use a model, and they publish attested results only.

$ hound manual propose example-backup-restore-test restore-test-2026-11.txt --config hound.yaml \
    --result pass --observation "Restore test of 18 November 2026: 3 files restored, hashes match." \
    --supports "Restored: 3 files to a scratch folder, hashes match" --json

The agent's command takes the source, the file (a path, or the name of a file already in the drop folder), --result pass|fail|partial for every check of the source, --check <check id>=<result> for a check that differs, --observation, and at least one --supports: an extract or a location in the file that shows the result. It copies the file into the drop folder if it is not there, and writes <file>.proposal.yaml beside it with proposed_by: agent, the file's SHA-256, the outcomes, the observation and the supporting extracts. A proposal is pending: it is not an attestation, a run does not publish it or store it as evidence, and the check stays "evidence present, not attested". Proposing again replaces a pending proposal. The command refuses a file a person already attested, a file the source's patterns do not accept, and a proposal without --supports (exit 3).

$ hound manual approve --config hound.yaml
Your name, recorded as the attester: Sam Example

[1/1] example-backup-restore-test restore-test-2026-11.txt
  File: /var/lib/evidence-hound/manual/example-backup-restore-test/restore-test-2026-11.txt
  Proposed by agent: pass
  Restore test of 18 November 2026: 3 files restored, hashes match.
  Supports: Restored: 3 files to a scratch folder, hashes match
  Attest (a), change (c), reject (r) or stop (s): a
Attested 1 of 1 proposals. The next 'hound run' publishes what you attested.

hound manual approve [--source <source>] walks a person through every pending proposal. Open the file and check it against what the agent quotes, then answer:

  • a attests the proposal as it stands.
  • c changes it: the outcome of each check (Enter keeps the proposed one), then the observation; what you enter is attested.
  • r rejects it, with a reason. The proposal keeps rejected_by, the date and the reason, and is not asked again; no attestation is written.
  • s stops; the rest wait.

Attesting writes <file>.attest.yaml with your name, the time, the outcomes, the observation as the note, proposed_by: agent and file_sha256, and removes the proposal. The next run publishes it as "Proposed by agent, attested pass by Sam Example on 2026-11-20: (sha256 )." with the file and the attestation attached. If the file changes after that, the check is partial until the file is attested again. An attestation entered without a proposal reads as before.

It needs a person at a terminal. When its input or output is redirected, as when an agent runs it or answers are piped in, hound manual approve refuses (exit 2) and changes nothing.

A collector is a class implementing ICollector from EvidenceHound.Collectors.Abstractions, registered with services.AddCollector<T>(). Two collectors with the same type stop the CLI at startup (collector.type_duplicate, exit 3).

docs.title: No language model here
docs.text: A deployment config never sets up a language model. An llm section, or any value that names a model key (llm_api_key), is refused with config.llm_in_runner. hound has no model of its own at all; model help comes from your coding assistant, see onboarding.md.

docs.title: Architecture: functional core, imperative shell
docs.text:
+-------------------------- composition root (CLI / runner) --------------------------+
            |                                                                                     |
 Collector  |  collect (I/O)  ->  evaluate (pure)  ->  map to framework (pure)  ->  plan (pure)   |  publish (I/O)
 adapters --+--> raw facts         CheckResult[]       RequirementResult[]         AuditUpdate[]  +--> CISO Assistant API
            |                                                                                     |
            +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
Layer Contents Rules Domain (core) Evidence, CheckResult, CheckId, RequirementResult, ControlStatus, AuditUpdate, RunRecord, FrameworkMapping Immutable records. No I/O. No framework or vendor names. Logic (core) evaluate, applyMapping, planUpdates, buildManifest, summariseRun Pure functions. Same input, same output. Property tests where useful. Ports (core) ICisoAssistantClient, IEvidenceStore, ISecretProvider, IClock; ICollector in EvidenceHound.Collectors.Abstractions, which references only the core Small interfaces, one purpose each. Adapters REST client, filesystem store, environment secrets, system clock, vendor collectors All side effects live here. Thin; tested with contract tests against fakes and recorded responses. Composition root CLI and scheduled runner Wires adapters to ports from configuration. The only place that knows concrete types.

Dependencies point inwards. Collectors reference the core; the core references nothing outside the standard library and its small approved dependency list.

docs.title: No model in collection, and no evidence without a person
docs.text:
hound run, hound serve and every collector are deterministic code: no language model is called while evidence is collected, assessed, mapped or published. A coding assistant works only before that, as an author of drafts and proposals in the config repo and the drop folders, and each one waits for a person:

  • Drafted configuration is approved with hound approve.
  • A proposed result for a manual evidence file (hound manual propose) is attested with hound manual approve. A proposal is not an attestation; the manual collector ignores it and publishes attested results only, naming who proposed and who attested.

Both commands refuse to run without a person at a terminal. Code that approves or attests takes the Terminal and checks Interactive first; do not add another path that writes approved_by or an attestation.

docs.title: Framework-neutral checks
docs.text:
Collectors emit stable check IDs such as identity.mfa.admins or backup.restore_tested with a result (pass, fail, partial, not_applicable, error), a short observation and evidence references. They never mention Essential Eight or NIST.

A mapping file per framework (mappings/<framework>.yaml) says which checks satisfy which requirement and how several checks roll into one result (for example: all must pass for compliant, any pass for partial). Adding a framework means adding a mapping file, not changing collectors.

docs.title: SOLID, applied
docs.text: Principle In this codebase Single responsibility A collector collects. Evaluation, mapping, planning and publishing are separate functions. Open/closed New systems are new collector packages registered as plugins; new frameworks are new mapping files. The core does not change. Liskov Every ICollector passes the shared collector contract test suite, CollectorContractTests<T>. ContractCoverageTests fails if a built-in collector has no contract test class. Interface segregation Ports are small: a collector never sees the CISO Assistant client; the publisher never sees vendor APIs. Dependency inversion Core defines ports; adapters implement them; the composition root wires them.

docs.title: Functional style
docs.text:
• Records are immutable; "changes" return new values.
  • Expected failures (API refused, bad config, missing evidence) are returned as Result<T> values carrying Problems (code and message), not thrown. Exceptions are for bugs.
  • No shared mutable state, no static singletons, no hidden clock or randomness: pass IClock and IDs in.
  • Small total functions composed into pipelines. Avoid boolean flags that switch behaviour; use separate functions.
  • Validate input at the edge (config, API responses) into domain types once; trust them inside.

docs.title: Errors and logging
docs.text:
One way, in every command:

What happened How it is handled Exit code Expected failure (bad config, invalid mapping, missing file) The function returns Result.Fail with Problems. The command passes them to Log.Problems, which logs each at Error with its Code as structured data. 3 Wrong arguments or unsupported mode Logged at Error through Log.Usage. 2 hound publish finished but some items failed Each failed item's problems go to Log.Problems; the JSON report on stdout lists every item. 4 Unexpected exception (a bug) Caught once, by the global handler in HoundCli.RunAsync. Logged at Critical with a one-line summary; the full exception is logged at Debug. 1 Cancellation (Ctrl+C) Logged at Warning. 130
  • Commands never catch exceptions themselves and never write errors to the console directly; they log through an ILogger from the one host built per run.
  • All log output goes to stderr as level: message (info, warn, error, crit, ...). Stdout carries only command output, so hound plan --dry-run > plan.json stays valid JSON.
  • Set the level with standard .NET configuration, for example Logging__LogLevel__Default=Debug for stack traces or Warning for quiet runs.
  • Log messages live in src/EvidenceHound.Cli/Log.cs as [LoggerMessage] methods with fixed event IDs.

docs.title: Adding a kind of scope object
docs.text:
hound scope plan and hound scope apply keep everything under scope/ in CISO Assistant through five stages, and each kind of object (risk studies, BIAs, metrics, suppliers and so on) has one file per stage. To add a kind, add one file to each, named after the kind:

Stage Where What it does Model src/EvidenceHound.Core/Scope/Scope<Kind>.cs Immutable records of the kind as the YAML declares it. Load src/EvidenceHound.Core.Yaml/ScopeLoader.<Kind>.cs Parses the YAML into the records, with a problem for every mistake and its line. Check src/EvidenceHound.Core/Scope/<Kind>Validator.cs Pure checks across files (names that must exist, dates, duplicates), called from ScopeValidator. Desired and read <Kind>Objects.cs in the core, ScopeStateReader.<Kind>.cs in EvidenceHound.CisoAssistant Both turn the kind into ScopeObjects with the same fields, so an unchanged object compares equal and ScopePlanner plans nothing for it. Add the kind to ScopeKind, and each list the reader fetches to RequestBudgetTests with its reason. Write src/EvidenceHound.CisoAssistant/ScopeWriter.<Kind>.cs Creates or updates the object in CISO Assistant when hound scope apply runs a plan.

The CLI needs no change: RepoScope loads and checks the whole folder, and the plan and apply commands work on every kind.

docs.title: Testing levels
docs.text:
Level Scope Runs Tooling Unit Pure functions and domain types Every commit, < 10 s xUnit v3 + FsCheck (property tests) + Shouldly Contract Adapters against recorded vendor responses and a fake CISO Assistant Every commit WireMock.Net Functional CLI end to end against a real CISO Assistant container Every PR in CI; on demand locally Testcontainers

Test names describe behaviour: given_all_admin_accounts_have_mfa_check_passes. Fixtures are synthetic and fictional. Coverage target: 90 % of core logic lines; adapters covered by contract tests.

docs.title: Commits and branches
docs.text:
• One branch per sprint: sprint/sNN-<slug>, opened as a draft PR by the Start sprint workflow.
  • Commit prefixes follow Conventional Commits with the task ID: test(s02-03): ... [red], feat(s02-03): ... [green], refactor(s02-03): ....
  • The sprint PR is merged (squash or merge commit) when every task is ticked and checks are green.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Evidence Hound has two parts: hound, a command line tool, and a reference deployment that runs CISO Assistant and hound side by side with Docker Compose. Start with the trial on your own machine, then deploy.

This page is the route from "what is this" to your first weekly review. Follow it in order; every other guide on the site is a reference one of these steps links to.

  1. Try it locally: the local trial, an hour or two.
  2. Install hound.
  3. Make your compliance repo: guided setup, then onboarding with your agent (the onboarding tutorial is a worked example).
  4. Deploy: the first deployment, then backups, hardening and updates.
  5. Run it each week: the GRC member guide and your first hound review.

The cheat sheet lists every command on two pages.

docs.title: 1. Try it locally
docs.text: You need Docker and an hour or two. The local trial starts a local CISO Assistant, sets up a fictional organisation with hound init, onboards its suppliers and systems with your coding agent, runs every collector against built-in dev servers (no real tenant needed) and walks you through a weekly review. make trial from a clone of this repository runs it step by step.

docs.title: 2. Install hound
docs.text:
Pick one:

  • The runner image, for scheduled runs next to CISO Assistant: ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:<version>. Check what you pull: gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:<version> --owner tnbozman.
  • The .NET tool, for your laptop and your agent (needs the .NET 10 SDK). Download the .nupkg files from the release into a folder, then install with the release's version:
$ dotnet tool install --global EvidenceHound.Cli --version 1.0.0 --add-source ~/hound-packages
$ hound --version

When the packages are on nuget.org, dotnet tool install --global EvidenceHound.Cli --version 1.0.0 is enough. Give the version either way: without it, dotnet tool install looks only for the newest version on nuget.org.

docs.title: 3. Make your compliance repo
docs.text:
Everything about your organisation lives in a private git repository of your own: the deployment config, the scope that becomes CISO Assistant's audits, mappings, supplier files and manual evidence runbooks. Make it once, in one of two ways:

  • Small and guided: hound init asks about your organisation and writes a repo you grow with hound add. Best for a first look, or with your agent driving.
  • The full template: the first deployment tutorial copies examples/compliance-repo, with access, settings, the deployment files and a pull request workflow already in place. Best when you deploy straight away.

The guided way:

$ hound init my-compliance --org "Example Pty Ltd"
$ cd my-compliance
$ git init -b main && git add . && git commit -m "Start from hound init"
$ hound agent setup --assistant claude

Push it to a private repository on your git host. When you deploy, copy the template's deploy/, scope/settings.yaml and .github/ into it, as the tutorial says.

Guided setup explains each question hound init asks, and onboarding how your agent drafts the rest for you to approve.

docs.title: 4. Deploy
docs.text:
Follow the first deployment tutorial from an empty VM, with the repo you made above: the Compose stack, the runner's token, your compliance repo mounted read-only, the first scope apply and the schedule. Then:

  1. Back it up and test a restore.
  2. Harden the host.
  3. Plan monthly updates.

docs.title: 5. Run it each week
docs.text: The GRC member guide is the weekly routine: your agent prepares the queue, you run hound review for one session, and the next run publishes what you accepted. Reports for the committee and board come from hound report each month and quarter.

docs.title: Guided setup: hound init and hound add
docs.text:
hound can write a compliance repo's files for you. hound init scaffolds a new organisation, and hound add adds a system, a control or a collector. Each asks only the questions it needs, shows the default in brackets (press Enter to take it), and checks the result the way hound config validate and hound scope validate do before it writes anything. A change that would not validate is not written: hound reports the problems, with exit code 3, and leaves the files as they were.

Every question has an option, so a wizard also runs unattended: give the answers as options and add --yes, and it asks nothing, taking the defaults for anything not given. Questions go to stderr, so the output stays clean.

The local trial uses these wizards from start to finish.

docs.title: hound init
docs.text:
hound init compliance

Writes a new compliance repo into the folder, which must be missing or empty:

Question Option Default Organisation name, also its domain in CISO Assistant --org Example Pty Ltd Short code for ref IDs, such as EX in EX-E8-Q2-2027FY --code from the name CISO Assistant API address --url https://ciso.example.com/api/ Time zone schedules run in --time-zone Australia/Sydney Essential Eight maturity level to assess, 1 to 3 --level 2 Audit interval: each quarter of the financial year (July to June), or each month --interval quarter Compliance owner's email --owner ceo@example.com

--evidence-root sets where the runner keeps evidence (default /var/lib/evidence-hound/evidence, outside the repo; only root or the runner container can write there, so for a trial as yourself use a folder in your home, such as --evidence-root ~/hound-evidence).

Audits are per system, so each shows its own gaps: hound init writes no organisation-wide audit. It names the series each system's audit joins (<CODE>-E8, so EX-E8-SOPHOS-NETWORK, by quarter or month) in scope/setup.yaml, and hound onboard <system> drafts the system's audit in it. --organisation-audit also writes one Essential Eight audit for the whole organisation: only when an organisation-wide source, such as policies, feeds it. --framework disp also writes a DISP membership readiness audit (DISP readiness), which is organisation-wide by nature. Neither is asked.

It writes:

File Holds hound.yaml The deployment config: CISO Assistant, evidence, the schedule's time zone, no collectors yet, and no targets until an audit is approved (hound approve adds a system's audit's target once the repo has that system's mapping, mappings/<system>-<framework>.yaml) scope/setup.yaml The root folder and the audit series (audit_series: its ref ID, maturity level and periods), the Essential Eight framework with its snapshot, and one domain with its perimeter scope/controls.yaml The health control, AC-AUTO-EVIDENCE scope/access.yaml The compliance owner as a user, and the GRC team they lead scope/evidence-plan.yaml, manual-sources/weekly-compliance-review.md The weekly review: a task for the GRC team every week, whose runbook says how to start hound review (the weekly review) scope/audits/README.md How audits are drafted: one per system and per shared platform. With --organisation-audit, also scope/audits/<code>-e8.yaml: the series <CODE>-E8 at that maturity level for the whole organisation, with its target and health control in hound.yaml. Each period is its own audit, such as EX-E8-Q2-2027FY (Audit periods) mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml, frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json The Essential Eight mapping and framework snapshot of this hound version With --framework disp: frameworks/disp.yaml, frameworks/disp.json, mappings/disp.yaml, scope/audits/<code>-disp.yaml The DISP library, its snapshot and mapping, and the audit series <CODE>-DISP, declared in scope/setup.yaml and added to targets in hound.yaml .devcontainer/ The GRC team's workspace: released hound, the .NET runtime and the Claude Code and GitHub Copilot extensions, so your machine needs only Docker and VS Code (work in the devcontainer) .gitignore, README.md What never goes in the repo, and the next steps

For more people, settings and a pull request workflow, copy them from the example compliance repo, as the first deployment tutorial describes.

At the end hound init asks whether to set up a coding assistant in the new repo (claude, copilot, both or none; --assistant answers it, and --yes takes none). With every answer given as an option nothing is asked, and --json answers with the organisation, the audits it wrote (audits, empty by default) and every file written, for an agent. It writes what hound agent setup writes.

docs.title: hound add system
docs.text:
hound add system --scope scope --audit EX-E8

Adds a system to a domain in scope/setup.yaml: its name, ref ID (default SYS- and the name), type (primary or supporting), owner, description and the systems it supports, by name (--name, --ref-id, --type, --owner, --description, --parents "Example 365"). The domain is asked only when the scope has more than one (--domain). Each --audit adds the system to that audit's systems.

docs.title: hound add control
docs.text:
hound add control --scope scope --audit EX-E8

Declares an applied control in scope/controls.yaml: its ref ID, name, owner, category (default technical) and the systems it covers (--ref-id, --name, --owner, --category, --systems), with status to_do until the first apply. With --audit, it asks which of that audit's requirements the control supports (--requirements ISM-1511,ISM-1515) and links them in the audit file. A requirement the framework does not have is refused.

docs.title: hound add collector
docs.text:
hound add collector manual --config hound.yaml
hound add collector rest --name sophos --set profile=sophos-central --config hound.yaml --secrets-dir /etc/evidence-hound/secrets

Adds a collector of any type hound collectors list lists. It asks for the collector's name (default: the type), its schedule (default 0 3 * * *) and each setting the collector requires, using the collector's own description of it. --set key=value gives any setting, optional ones included, without asking. For the rest collector, once it knows the profile (--set profile=<name>, and --set profiles_path=<folder> when the profiles folder is not the default), it also asks for each parameter the profile requires and has no default for, and takes the profile's secrets as the collector's.

For each secret the collector needs:

  • Without --secrets-dir, it asks for a reference, by default file:/run/secrets/<name>_<secret>, the path the runner container sees. Put the value in that file on the host yourself.
  • With --secrets-dir <folder>, it reads the value instead, without echo on a terminal, writes it to <folder>/<name>_<secret> (folder mode 700, file mode 600) and references that file. The value is never printed, logged or put on a command line.

hound add collector manual is how a manual evidence source is added: its drop folder, the checks it supports, how often fresh evidence is due and who owns it. See manual sources.

docs.title: How the files are changed
docs.text: An added entry goes at the end of its list, in the file's own indentation. Comments, blank lines and every other line stay as they were, so the change reads as a small diff in review. An empty [] list becomes a block list, and a missing list is added. Values are quoted only where YAML would read them as something else, such as "0 3 * * *" or "14".

docs.title: Incidents and reporting deadlines
docs.text:
This guide is for a GRC team that must report an incident to regulators and customers on their clocks: 72 hours to the DoD under DFARS 252.204-7012 when covered defence information is involved, 30 days to assess a data breach under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, and the reports to ASD's ACSC. You declare those obligations once, in the compliance repo; the incident itself is recorded in CISO Assistant; and hound incident obligations tells you which reports one incident owes and by when.

The example compliance repo has the obligations in examples/compliance-repo/scope/reporting.yaml and the plan's yearly test as a manual source (example-incident-response-plan in its hound.yaml, with the runbook examples/compliance-repo/manual-sources/incident-response-test.md).

docs.title: 1. Declare what you must report
docs.text:
scope/reporting.yaml lists each obligation: an id, who receives it (report_to), how long after the incident's discovery it is due (within, such as 72h or 30d), and what triggers it: when: {data: [cui]} for incidents on a system that handles those data kinds (the data of each system in scope/setup.yaml, see Scope files), or when: {always: true} for every incident.

obligations:
  - id: dfars-7012
    name: DFARS 252.204-7012 cyber incident report
    report_to: DoD, through the DIBNet portal (needs a medium assurance certificate)
    within: 72h
    when: {data: [cui]}
    reference: DFARS 252.204-7012(c)
  - id: reportcyber
    name: Report to ASD's ACSC through ReportCyber
    report_to: ASD's ACSC (cyber.gov.au/report)
    within: 1d
    when: {always: true}

Check each clock against its source, and add your customers' contract clauses the same way. hound scope validate checks the file.

docs.title: 2. Record the incident in CISO Assistant
docs.text: Under Operations, Incidents, record the incident with a reference ID (such as INC-2026-01) and the affected systems as its assets. Add a timeline entry of type detection at the time it was discovered: every clock starts there (without one, when the incident was reported).
