docs.title: 3. List the reports it owes
docs.text:
hound incident obligations INC-2026-01 --config hound.yaml

INC-2026-01 Malware on a laptop: discovered 2026-11-20 09:30 UTC, 2 report(s) owed
  reportcyber  due 2026-11-21 09:30 UTC  made 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC  to ASD's ACSC (every incident)
  dfars-7012  due 2026-11-23 09:30 UTC  due  to DoD, through the DIBNet portal (Example laptops handles cui)

--format json gives the same for an agent. The command reads CISO Assistant and writes nothing.

docs.title: The DFARS 252.204-7012 report
docs.text:
When the incident touches a system that handles CUI, the DFARS report is due 72 hours from discovery and is filed by a person on the DoD portal (DIBNet), with a medium assurance certificate. To gather what it asks for:

hound incident report-pack INC-2026-01 --dfars --config hound.yaml --out inc-2026-01-dfars.md

The pack lists the deadline, the affected systems that handle CUI with their data and CMMC asset category, the suppliers whose solutions provide them and their contracts, the customer contracts that carry the clause (the primes to tell, from scope/third-parties/), and the incident's timeline. It reminds you to keep images of the affected systems and the monitoring data for at least 90 days, and to send any malicious software you isolate to the DoD Cyber Crime Center as the portal directs. The portal asks for more than the pack holds, such as your CAGE code. hound reads only; keep the pack out of the repo.

docs.title: 4. Record each report you make
docs.text: Add a timeline entry to the incident that starts with Reported: and the obligation's id, then their reference: Reported: dfars-7012, DIBNet report 12345. The report then shows as made, and is never overdue.

docs.title: Where overdue reports show up
docs.text:
• The weekly review. With CISO Assistant configured (HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN), hound review lists each report an open incident has not made, due by its deadline, every week until the incident's timeline records it.
  • The committee report. hound report snapshot records the reports each incident owes; hound report committee lists the overdue ones in section 6 and proposes making each in section 8.

docs.title: Build the plan
docs.text:
hound irp build --programme essential-eight writes the incident response plan from what the repo already holds, so you write only the parts that need judgement. scope/irp.yaml names the programme, the plan's version, who holds each role and the Markdown file of each judgement section:

programme: essential-eight
version: "0.1"
roles:
  incident_manager: it@example.com    # leads a response
  deputy: IT team                     # stands in
  executive: ceo@example.com          # decides for the business, the only spokesperson
  legal_privacy: ceo@example.com      # law, contracts and privacy
  authorising_officer: ceo@example.com  # approves each version (ISM-0047)
sections:
  severity: irp/severity.md
  escalation: irp/escalation.md
  containment: irp/containment.md
  communication: irp/communication.md
  lessons_learned: irp/lessons-learned.md
  • Derived: the contacts from the roles, the systems with the sensitive data they handle and their recovery objectives (setup.yaml), the suppliers and customers with their contacts and contract clauses (third-parties/, including flowed-down clauses), and each report with its deadline and what triggers it (reporting.yaml). --json gives every value with its file and line.
  • Written by you: severity definitions, escalation decisions, containment priorities, communication approach and lessons learned. A missing role or section, or an empty file, is a gap listed first; --strict exits non-zero while any remain.
  • Layout: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3's functions (govern, identify, protect, detect, respond, recover), with the Australian reporting (ReportCyber, the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, DISP) and DFARS 252.204-7012 inside them, and a section for each of ISM-0043's eight items. It cites NIST SP 800-171 3.6.1 to 3.6.3 and the ACSC Cyber Incident Response Plan Guidance.

The plan holds names and contacts: keep the built plan out of a public repo, and store the approved copy as the evidence of the yearly check below. Raise version when you change the plan; the authorising officer approves each version.

docs.title: The plan and its yearly test
docs.text: The incident response plan is approved and tested once a year, for example with a one-hour tabletop exercise. Make it a manual source with the checks incident.response_plan_approved and incident.response_plan_tested, due every 366 days, with a runbook and an evidence plan row (see Manual evidence), as the example repo does.

docs.title: What stays in CISO Assistant
docs.text: The incidents, their timelines, severity and status are recorded in CISO Assistant, never in the repo. The repo holds only the obligations: who must be told, and how soon.

docs.title: Manual evidence
docs.text:
Some evidence has no API: a quarterly restore test, a privileged access review, the browser and Office policies on laptops nobody manages centrally. This guide shows how a small team gets that evidence on time without chasing people, and without giving system owners a CISO Assistant login. It uses CISO Assistant's own recurring tasks and email reminders; hound only writes them from the repo.

The flow:

  1. The evidence plan in the repo says, for each control, how its evidence arrives, who provides it and how often.
  2. hound scope apply turns each row a person provides into a recurring CISO Assistant task. CISO Assistant emails the owner the runbook before each due date.
  3. The owner exports what the runbook asks for and sends it to the GRC team. Their agent may read the export and propose a result (hound manual propose); a person in the GRC team attests it at a terminal (hound manual approve or the weekly review).
  4. The next hound run publishes the attested result to every requirement the source's checks are mapped to. The GRC team reviews it in CISO Assistant and marks the task done.
  5. A task still open at month end is an overdue item in the security committee's report. That is the escalation; nobody is emailed daily.

docs.title: The evidence plan
docs.text:
scope/evidence-plan.yaml has one row per control, or per group of requirements under a control:

grc_team: IT team                 # receives and reviews evidence, for rows that do not name their own
evidence:
  - ref_id: EV-MFA                # EV- then upper case letters, digits and hyphens
    control: AC-MFA               # an applied control from controls.yaml
    method: automated             # automated, manual or hybrid
    collector: example-m365       # a collector in hound.yaml (automated and hybrid rows)
  - ref_id: EV-BACKUP-RESTORE
    control: AC-BACKUP
    requirements: [ISM-1515]      # optional; every requirement of the control when left out
    method: manual
    collector: example-backup-restore-test
    owner: Backup owners          # a team in access.yaml (manual and hybrid rows)
    every: 3 months               # 1 week, 3 months, 6 months or 12 months
    runbook: manual-sources/backup-restore-test.md

hound scope validate scope/ --config hound.yaml checks it: a manual or hybrid row needs an owner, an interval and a runbook that is a file in the repo; an automated or hybrid row names a collector that hound.yaml configures; the control and the teams exist; an owner contact holds no role. The full reference is in scope.md and the scope schema.

hound scope apply writes, for every row, an evidence item named after the row and its control, labelled with its method (automated, manual or hybrid) and its collector's name so the GRC team can filter by them (CISO Assistant takes a label of letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, at most 36 long, so a longer collector name is left out). For each manual and hybrid row it also writes a recurring task: assigned to the owner and the GRC team, due every week, every 3 or 6 months, or yearly, with the runbook as its description, linked to the evidence item, the control and the requirements. The first due date is set when the task is created, one interval from that day; CISO Assistant moves it on after that.

docs.title: Owner contacts
docs.text:
Only the GRC team signs in to CISO Assistant. A system owner is an owner contact: a team in scope/access.yaml with an email and no members.

teams:
  - name: Backup owners
    description: Run the backup service and its quarterly restore test.
    email: backup-owners@example.com

CISO Assistant emails a task's reminders to its team's email, so the owner is reminded with no account. An owner contact never holds a role (evidence_plan.owner_contact_has_role): it has nobody to give it to. Use a shared mailbox or a distribution list, so the reminders survive a person leaving.

docs.title: Runbooks
docs.text:
A runbook is a Markdown file in the repo that tells the owner, in plain steps, what to do. CISO Assistant sends it as the task's description, so write it for someone who will read it in an email:

  • What to export: the export, report or settings page, from which console, as which file type. Ask for exports, not screenshots, where the product allows: an export can be read again and compared next time.
  • How often and who attests.
  • Send it to the GRC team: where to send it (a mailbox, or hound manual upload to the source's drop folder).
  • If something fails: a failed test is evidence too. Say so and send it.

examples/manual-sources/essential-eight/ has a runbook for each Essential Eight area no collector reads, with the collector to paste into hound.yaml beside it, and examples/manual-sources/essentials/ one for each ASD Essentials area the Essential Eight never asked about (index). Copy the ones you need into manual-sources/ in your repo, set the owner and the drop folder, and point an evidence plan row at the copy.

docs.title: Turning mail on
docs.text:
CISO Assistant sends no email until its mail server is set and mailing is turned on:

  1. Give the CISO Assistant backend its mail server through the EMAIL_* settings of its deployment (EMAIL_HOST, EMAIL_PORT, EMAIL_HOST_USER, EMAIL_USE_TLS, DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL, and the password as a secret, never in the repo).
  2. Turn mailing on and the daily overdue email off in scope/settings.yaml:
general:
  notifications_enable_mailing: true
  # Owners get the runbook 30, 7 and 1 days before each due date. Once a task is overdue, the committee report escalates it,
  # not a daily email.
  disabled_email_templates: [task_node_overdue]

Test it with a task due within 7 days and a mailbox you can read before you rely on it.

docs.title: The GRC team's steps
docs.text:
When an owner's evidence arrives:

  1. Check the file is complete and is what the runbook asked for.
  2. If it came by email, upload it: hound manual upload --config hound.yaml --source <source> <file>.
  3. Ask your agent to read it and propose a result for each check, with the extract that supports it: hound manual propose.
  4. A person attests the proposal at a terminal, in the weekly review with everything else that waits on them (hound review), or on its own with hound manual approve. An agent or a pipe is refused.
  5. After the next run, review the published results in CISO Assistant, attach the file to the task occurrence, and mark the occurrence done.

docs.title: The weekly review
docs.text:
The GRC team signs off everything that waits on a person in one session a week. The example evidence plan has a row for it: a weekly task assigned to the GRC team, whose runbook (weekly-compliance-review.md) says how to start.

  1. Before the session, the agent prepares the queue with the skill "weekly-review": hound review pending --json lists every item (manual evidence proposals, onboarding decisions, suppliers, supplier reviews, drafted audits and imported rows), and the agent records a recommendation for each with its reasons and sources (hound review recommend, kept in review/recommendations.json), and answers last week's challenges. hound review prepare --json does the preparation in one step: it refreshes the queue, lists the items still without a recommendation with the skill that drafts each, and saves the scope plan the session applies, in review/prepared.plan.json (never committed; *.plan.json is in .gitignore).
  2. The person runs hound review in their own terminal (--for 30m to stop after half an hour). Most urgent first, each item shows what it is, why it matters, the recommendation and what accepting it does. They accept, challenge (with a note the agent answers before the next session; the item stays queued) or skip. For a long queue, or decisions you want to understand before you accept them, go through them with your agent first (the agent hound-decisions, skill "work-through-pending-decisions"). hound review pending --json gives each item a risk (high for a not-applicable decision, a supplier, a finding, or an item whose recommendation is missing or has no source) and a summary by kind and recommendation, so the agent starts with the size of the job and the riskiest items. Then accept, challenge or skip each one by its key, hound review --only <key> (repeat --only for several): nothing else is asked or written. An unknown key is refused with the nearest keys, and it still needs you at a terminal. hound approve opens with the same count by kind and points here.
  3. Accepted items are written as hound approve and hound manual approve write them. A session records one sign-off under review/sign-offs/, naming the person, the time and every item, then shows the plan and applies it after a confirmation (--no-apply stops at the files). When the agent prepared a plan and no accepted item changed the scope files, the session applies that plan, and refuses it (scope.plan_stale) if CISO Assistant changed since it was made; otherwise it plans again. The session ends with one summary: what was accepted and challenged, what was applied to CISO Assistant, and how long it took.

Standing approvals. When a source's new export has the same checks and the same results as its last attestation, the session offers to accept that source's future unchanged exports for 12 months. The rule is written to review/standing-approvals.json, listed in every session's summary, and expires. Later unchanged exports from that source are accepted without being asked, and counted in the summary. A rule never covers a first attestation, a changed result, a not-applicable decision or any other kind of item.

docs.title: Attesting and publishing
docs.text: The Essential Eight mapping maps each template's checks to its requirements, so one attestation answers every requirement it covers, and the same checks can be mapped to another framework or a prime's questionnaire. A run publishes a requirement only when every one of its checks is reported. Until hound.yaml configures a requirement's manual source, no run writes it, and the GRC team may write its result by hand in the audit file. Once the source is configured, a hand-written result for the same requirement is reported as scope.result_conflict: remove it and let the attested source take over.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
These are accepted rather than built:

  • No timed escalation. The security committee's list of overdue tasks is the escalation.
  • CISO Assistant fixes the reminder days (30, 7 and 1 days before), so an owner gets the instructions and two warnings. Turning off task_node_due_soon would remove all three.
  • Disabling an email template applies to every task in the instance, the GRC team's own included.
  • Occurrences have no completion date; the period snapshots record who was overdue at each month end.
  • The email's link opens a CISO Assistant sign-in that owners cannot use. The runbook text in the email is what they act on.
  • hound never writes an occurrence's status, an evidence revision, a review or a result the GRC team sets in CISO Assistant.

docs.title: Framework mapping files
docs.text:
A mapping file says which framework-neutral checks satisfy each requirement of one framework, and how their outcomes combine. Adding a framework means adding a mapping file; collectors do not change.

Files live in mappings/ (your real ones belong in your private deployment repo). The JSON Schema is schemas/mapping.schema.json; add # yaml-language-server: $schema=../schemas/mapping.schema.json at the top of a file for editor help.

framework_urn: urn:example:risk:library:example-baseline   # library URN in CISO Assistant
description: Example baseline used in tests and docs.        # optional
requirements:
  - ref: "EX-1.1"            # requirement reference in the library
    rule: all_pass           # every check must pass
    checks: [identity.mfa.admins, identity.mfa.users]
  - ref: "EX-1.2"
    rule: any_pass           # at least one check must pass
    checks: [identity.mfa.phishing_resistant, identity.mfa.number_matching]
  - ref: "EX-2.1"
    rule: threshold          # at least `threshold` checks must pass
    threshold: 2
    checks: [patching.os.critical_48h, patching.apps.critical_48h, patching.os.supported]

Rules:

  • framework_urn starts with urn:. Each requirement is named once in a file.
  • Name each requirement with exactly one of ref (its ref_id) or urn (the URN of its requirement node).
  • Check IDs are lowercase dot-separated segments that start with a letter (identity.mfa.admins, backup.restore_tested), at most 128 characters, and are listed once per requirement.
  • threshold is required with rule: threshold, is between 1 and the number of checks, and is not allowed with the other rules.
  • draft: true marks a row hound mapping derive wrote and nobody has reviewed yet. Runs leave draft rows out and report each one as publish.draft_row; delete the line once a person has checked the row.
  • covers: part marks a row whose checks answer only part of the requirement, such as Essential Eight evidence for a NIST SP 800-171 requirement that is wider in scope. When every check passes, the row is partially compliant, not compliant, and its observation says a person must assess the rest. Leave it out, or write covers: whole, when the checks answer all of the requirement.
  • rest, on a row with covers: part, says what a person assesses to finish the requirement, such as "MFA on the VPN and on servers' local admin accounts". The published observation names it, so whoever reads the row in CISO Assistant knows what is left. Every shipped CMMC row has one.
  • Unknown keys are errors.

docs.title: Requirements a framework repeats
docs.text:
Some frameworks use the same ref_id in more than one place. The Essential Eight (November 2023) lists an ISM control under every mitigation strategy it applies to, and the ASD Essentials rates each action in every domain it applies to. Each place is its own row in a CISO Assistant audit.

  • urn: names exactly one row. Use it when each row needs its own result, as in the Essentials, where each domain is rated separately.
  • ref: with rows: all writes the same result to every row that has the ref. Use it when the rows really are the same requirement, as with an ISM control repeated across Essential Eight strategies.
  • ref: on its own must match one row. A ref that matches several is an error (mapping.ref_ambiguous) that lists the matching URNs.
framework_urn: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:asd-essentials-enterprise-it
requirements:
  - urn: urn:intuitem:risk:req_node:asd-essentials-enterprise-it:boundary-services:pro-01:it.pro-01.1
    rule: all_pass
    checks: [network.boundary.secure_design]
  - urn: urn:intuitem:risk:req_node:asd-essentials-enterprise-it:identity-services:pro-01:it.pro-01.1
    rule: all_pass
    checks: [identity.secure_design]
---
framework_urn: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:essential-eight-2023
requirements:
  - ref: ISM-0123          # listed under four strategies, same text in each
    rows: all
    rule: all_pass
    checks: [incident.reporting_to_ciso]

When publishing, rows outside the audit's selected implementation groups (such as ML3 rows in an ML2 audit) are left alone and reported as skipped with the note outside selected groups, not as errors.

docs.title: Requirements no check covers
docs.text:
A requirement that no collector can check is usually filled by a manual source: a person exports a record, attests a check with hound manual approve, and the next run publishes it (manual-evidence.md). Map the requirement to that check like any other. The Essential Eight and AI6 mappings work this way, with their manual sources in examples/manual-sources/.

When no manual source covers a requirement either, list it under manual_only, with the manual source you suggest for it:

manual_only:
  - ref: AI6-3.4
    source: incident register, reviewed by the AI governance owner

A manual_only entry names a requirement by ref or urn, as in requirements; hound mapping validate --framework checks that it exists in the framework, as for mapped requirements. hound writes nothing to its row: CISO Assistant keeps whatever the GRC team records there. manual_only: [] says none is left.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
hound mapping coverage shows how an audit's requirements are answered, per parent node (an Essential Eight strategy, an AI6 practice) and implementation group (a maturity level), so you can see that no row is left without an owner:

$ hound mapping coverage mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml --framework frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json --groups 1,2 \
    --manual examples/manual-sources/essential-eight --manual examples/example-essential-eight.yaml
| Parent | Group | Automated | Manual | Draft | Uncovered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pa | 1 | 7 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
...
Total: 46 automated, 109 manual, 0 draft, 0 uncovered (one per requirement row and group).
  • Automated: at least one of the requirement's checks comes from a collector.
  • Manual: every check is attested by a person through a manual source, or the requirement is under manual_only.
  • Draft: only draft: true rows answer it, and runs publish none of them until a person reviews the row.
  • Uncovered: nothing answers it. Map it to a check or a manual source.

A row marked covers: part counts as automated, but its checks answer only part of the requirement (every CMMC row is one), so a line under the total says how many, and --json gives them as part: a person assesses the rest of each in CISO Assistant.

For a framework with more than one level above its requirements, such as the ASD Essentials (domain, then principle, then action), a second table counts per top-level node, so you see each domain and priority phase:

$ hound mapping coverage mappings/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml --framework frameworks/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.json --groups 1 \
    --manual examples/manual-sources --manual examples/example-essential-eight.yaml
...
| Top level | Group | Automated | Manual | Draft | Uncovered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Governance and culture | 1 | 3 | 6 | 0 | 0 |
| Visibility and response | 1 | 1 | 11 | 0 | 0 |
| Boundary services | 1 | 11 | 26 | 0 | 0 |
| Identity services | 1 | 11 | 24 | 0 | 0 |

Total: 26 automated, 67 manual, 0 draft, 0 uncovered (one per requirement row and group).

--manual takes your hound config, a manual source template or a folder of them; the checks of every type: manual collector in them count as manual. Without --manual, every mapped requirement counts as automated, and a --manual path with no manual source in it is reported. In your own repo, pass --manual hound.yaml; the paths above are in the Evidence Hound repo. --groups is the audit's selected groups (default: all of the framework's), and --json prints the same counts for an agent.

docs.title: Deriving a mapping for a new framework
docs.text:
When a framework replaces another, such as the ASD Essentials replacing the Essential Eight, hound mapping derive drafts the new mapping from your existing one and a CISO Assistant transition mapping library (a library with a requirement_mapping_set). Each row of the new framework gets the union of the checks of the old rows the library links to it, with rule: all_pass, named by URN and marked draft: true:

$ hound mapping derive mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml --from frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json \
    --to frameworks/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.json \
    --links frameworks/mapping-essential-eight-2023-and-asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml --groups 1 --out draft.yaml
wrote 55 draft rows to draft.yaml; 38 rows got no checks and are listed at its end. Runs publish no draft row: review each one, then delete its 'draft: true' line.
  • Each row's comment names its source requirements. A link that only overlaps (intersect, as every Essential Eight to Essentials link is) may not cover the whole new requirement, so a person decides whether the checks are enough, adds checks where the new requirement asks for more, then deletes draft: true.
  • Rows the old mapping gives no checks are listed as comments at the end. Map each to a manual source's checks, or list it under manual_only.
  • --groups limits the draft to the new framework's implementation groups (for the Essentials, a priority phase). Without --out the draft is printed, and an existing --out file is never replaced unless you add --force.
  • hound carries the Essential Eight 2023 to Essentials library from CISO Assistant v4.3.4 in frameworks/, and a reviewed phase 1 mapping made this way in mappings/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml.

docs.title: Crosswalks to another framework
docs.text:
A crosswalk says which requirements of another framework your evidence for one programme already answers. hound carries one from the Essential Eight (ML1 and ML2) to NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2, for suppliers who hold CUI, in mappings/crosswalks/. It is advisory: it was drafted with AI from the requirement texts and nobody has reviewed it yet, and hound writes nothing to CISO Assistant from it. Full CMMC Level 2 comes later, with its own mapping and audit.

$ hound mapping crosswalk --from essential-eight --config hound.yaml
# Crosswalk: Essential Eight to urn:intuitem:risk:framework:nist-sp-800-171-rev2
...
Total: 1 answered, 30 partly answered, 79 open, of 110 requirements.

| Requirement | Status | Answered by: today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3.1.6 Use non-privileged accounts or roles for non-security functions | answered | ISM-0445 (equal, 1 check): compliant; ISM-1175 (subset, 1 check): compliant |
...
  • --from is a programme id from scope/setup.yaml. Its checks come from the config target for its audit; today's results from that audit in CISO Assistant. --offline skips CISO Assistant and shows only what would answer each requirement. --json prints the same for an agent.
  • Answered: an Essential Eight requirement that says the same (equal) or asks for more (superset) has checks behind it. Partly answered: only overlapping (intersect) or narrower (subset) requirements link to it, or the linked one has no checks. Open: nothing in the Essential Eight answers it; you need other evidence.
  • hound uses --file if you give one, else a crosswalk in mappings/crosswalks/ next to hound.yaml, else its own. Copy its file there to correct links, and once a person has checked every link, add reviewed: {by: <name or role>, on: YYYY-MM-DD}. The schema is schemas/crosswalk.schema.json.
  • CISO Assistant v4.3.4 has no API that lists a mapping library's links, so hound cannot read one yet; its file is used.

docs.title: Framework snapshots
docs.text:
A framework snapshot lets you check a mapping without CISO Assistant. It lists the framework's URN, version and implementation groups, and each assessable requirement's URN, ref_id, parent, groups and a short title, and the name of each parent node (an Essential Eight strategy), which reports show. Make one from a CISO Assistant library file and commit it under frameworks/:

$ hound framework snapshot essential-eight-2023.yaml --out frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json
wrote frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:essential-eight-2023 version 3, 152 assessable requirements

Library files ship with CISO Assistant under backend/library/libraries/ in its source repository. Snapshots of the Essential Eight (November 2023) and the ASD Essentials for enterprise IT, from CISO Assistant v4.3.4, are in frameworks/. Make a new snapshot when you upgrade CISO Assistant and the library version changes.

docs.title: How results are worked out
docs.text:
hound mapping apply <mapping> <checks.json> (and later the runner) turns check results into one result per requirement, in file order:

  1. Only the latest result of each check counts (by collected_at).
  2. If any mapped check has no result, or its result is error, the requirement is not_assessed.
  3. not_applicable checks are ignored. If every mapped check is not_applicable, so is the requirement.
  4. The rule decides the rest:
Rule compliant partially_compliant non_compliant all_pass every check passes no failures, some partial any check fails any_pass every check passes at least one pass or partial nothing passes or partly passes threshold at least threshold checks pass (capped at the number of applicable checks) fewer pass, but at least one pass or partial nothing passes or partly passes

The observation lists the rule and each check with its outcome and observation; the evidence is the sorted union of the checks' evidence.

docs.title: Validate a file
docs.text:
$ hound mapping validate mappings/example.yaml
valid: 4 requirements

Problems are printed with the file and line, and the command exits with code 3:

error: mappings/bad.yaml line 7: unknown rule 'most_pass'; use all_pass, any_pass or threshold.
error: mappings/bad.yaml line 6: requirement 'EX-1.1' is already used at line 3.

With --framework <snapshot>, it also checks every requirement against the framework: unknown URNs and refs, refs that match several rows without rows: all, and a mapping for a different framework.

$ hound mapping validate mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml --framework frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json
error: mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml line 12: ref 'ISM-0123' matches 4 rows: urn:intuitem:risk:req_node:essential-eight-2023:mfa:ism-0123, ... Name one row by 'urn', or add 'rows: all' to write the same result to every row.

docs.title: Metrics and dashboards
docs.text:
This guide is for a GRC team that wants the security committee to see trends, such as MFA coverage or how much of the Essential Eight is compliant, without anyone typing numbers each month. You declare what you measure in the compliance repo; hound scope apply writes it to CISO Assistant's metrology (metric definitions, metric instances, dashboards and widgets); each hound run fills in the values. The full file reference is in Scope files.

The example compliance repo has two metrics and a committee dashboard: examples/compliance-repo/scope/metrics.yaml.

Start with two or three metrics the committee will act on. Each one is a number someone must explain every month, so a long list costs more time than it saves.

docs.title: 1. Define what you measure
docs.text:
A definition says what is measured and how it reads: a number with a unit, which way is better, and the target. Add it to scope/metrics.yaml:

definitions:
  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA-CHECKS
    name: MFA checks passing
    unit: percentage
    direction: higher_is_better
    decimals: 0
    frequency: monthly
    target: 100

docs.title: 2. Measure it in a domain, from your runs
docs.text:
An instance measures a definition in one domain, with its owners and the controls it tells about. source: hound makes each run fill it in:

instances:
  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA-CHECKS-CORP
    name: MFA checks passing
    definition: EX-MET-MFA-CHECKS
    domain: Example Pty Ltd
    owners: [it@example.com]
    controls: [AC-MFA]
    source: hound
    measure: check_pass_rate
    checks: [identity.mfa.*]
Measure What it records each period check_pass_rate the share of the named checks that pass (checks: [identity.mfa.*]) requirements_compliant_pct the share of an audit's applicable requirements that are compliant (audit: EX-E8-2026); rows not assessed count against it evidence_freshness_pct the share of the checks (all, or the named ones) whose evidence is at most a week old collector_success_rate the share of the run's collectors that succeeded

docs.title: 3. Add a dashboard
docs.text:
A dashboard lays widgets on a 12-column grid. A widget shows a metric instance, a builtin metric CISO Assistant computes for an audit, risk study or domain, or text:

dashboards:
  - ref_id: EX-DASH-COMMITTEE
    name: Security committee
    domain: Example Pty Ltd
    widgets:
      - {title: MFA checks passing, metric: EX-MET-MFA-CHECKS-CORP, chart: line, time_range: last_year}
      - {title: Essential Eight progress, audit: EX-E8-2026, builtin: progress, x: 6}

docs.title: 4. Check, review and apply
docs.text:
$ hound scope validate scope/
$ hound scope plan scope/
$ hound scope apply scope/

validate checks the file offline: the codes it reports are listed in Scope files. plan shows the definitions, instances, dashboards and widgets it would create or change; review it in the pull request, then apply writes them.

docs.title: 5. Let the runs fill it in
docs.text:
After collecting, each hound run measures every instance with source: hound and records one value for the current period. A later run in the same period replaces it, and an unchanged value is not sent, so the chart shows one point a month. The run's JSON lists what it recorded under metrics. Two warnings name what it could not do: metric.not_applied (run hound scope apply first) and metric.nothing_measured (no check matched, or the audit has no applicable rows). See Metrics filled in by runs for the rules.

hound status --scope scope/ gives each programme's standing from the latest posture snapshot beside the collectors' runs, so the weekly look needs no dashboard at all; the dashboard is for the committee.

docs.title: Metrics people enter, and computed metrics
docs.text:
Not everything comes from a run. A qualitative metric lists its levels worst first, such as [Missing, Drafted, Approved, Reviewed], and someone enters its value in CISO Assistant each period; leave source out. A computed metric has a formula over other definitions, and CISO Assistant works it out from their instances in the same domain:

  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA
    name: MFA coverage
    unit: percentage
    formula:
      expression: covered / total * 100
      inputs:
        - {key: covered, definition: EX-MET-MFA-COVERED, combine: sum}
        - {key: total, definition: EX-MET-MFA-TOTAL, combine: sum}

A computed metric cannot also be filled in by runs (scope.result_conflict): CISO Assistant refuses values typed into it.

docs.title: The governance checks behind the numbers
docs.text: The ciso-assistant profile checks CISO Assistant itself on every run: suppliers' assessments and contracts current, risk studies reviewed within a year, approved security exceptions not past expiry, and critical systems' recovery tested. Name them in a check_pass_rate metric, for example checks: [risk.*, bia.*, supplier.*], to chart how well governance keeps up.

docs.title: What stays in CISO Assistant
docs.text:
• The values. Samples are never declared in the repo: runs record them, and people enter the ones runs cannot measure. CISO Assistant keeps their history, one value per period.
  • Computations. Formulas and builtin metrics (an audit's progress, a domain's open incidents) are worked out by CISO Assistant.
  • The charts. Dashboards are drawn and read in CISO Assistant; the repo holds only their layout.
  • Collection tasks. If someone enters a metric by hand, CISO Assistant's task for it reminds them each period.

docs.title: Onboarding
docs.text:
hound onboard takes a GRC team member through onboarding a system: the supplier first, then how each requirement of a framework is met for the system. The output is files for a pull request in the config repo; nothing is applied to CISO Assistant until a person reviews it and runs hound scope validate, plan and apply.

hound has no language model of its own. There is no API key, provider or token budget to manage. For model help, set up your coding assistant (Claude Code or GitHub Copilot) with hound agent setup: it reads your documents and API specifications, drafts through hound commands that check everything it writes, and you approve with hound approve in a terminal. Without an assistant, every step below works by answering hound's questions yourself. The design is in design/agent-driven-onboarding.md; it supersedes the earlier onboarding assistant design, in which hound called a model itself.

No model in evidence collection, and no evidence without a person. hound run, hound serve and every collector are deterministic code, and the runner refuses a deployment config (hound.yaml) that has an llm section (config.llm_in_runner). For manual evidence a coding assistant may read a file and propose its result with hound manual propose, but the result becomes evidence only when a person attests it with hound manual approve (manual sources).

Removed with the built-in model: hound onboard config, onboarding.yaml, and the options --no-model, --show-requests and (for the onboarding config) --config. hound onboard config now only says so. Since release 3 the options are refused like any unknown option; remove them from older scripts.

docs.title: Onboard a system
docs.text:
$ hound onboard EXAMPLE-ASSETS --framework frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json --group 1 --group 2 --spec ../specs/example-asset-api.openapi.yaml

Run it in the config repo (or pass --repo). The session goes in this order, and saves after every answer in onboarding/<system>/session.json. Run the same command again to carry on where it stopped.

  1. Who and what. Your name (recorded as who accepted each decision), the system owner, the product, and who supplies it: the supplier, the solution it provides and the contract covering it, each by ref_id and name.
  2. Supplier first. A supplier not yet under scope/third-parties/ is drafted there. Dependency, penetration, maturity and trust, and the solution's criticality, are each asked with their scale printed first (see What the terminal tells you); a level you leave empty stays in the file to decide (a coding assistant drafts them with their reasons through hound supplier draft). What the supplier provides, in your words, is kept in the session. Vendor documents you keep (an https URL or a file) are saved under documents/suppliers/<supplier>/ with their SHA-256 and retrieval date. The contract is drafted as status: draft, and the session stops: a system is onboarded only once its supplier is approved. Onboarding checks the scope files for an active contract covering the solution; hound scope plan then checks approval in CISO Assistant, where the GRC team concludes the supplier's assessment (see Supplier approval). A drafted supplier file includes that review (EA-<supplier>, due a month from today, then every 12 months, in the first domain and perimeter of scope/setup.yaml). So the order is: approve the contract in the file, apply the supplier, conclude its review as ok in CISO Assistant, then finish onboarding and apply the system.
  3. What the API offers. Each --spec (an OpenAPI 3 document, JSON or YAML) is read into a short summary: the endpoints that read, sign-in and paging.

  4. Applicability. Every requirement in the --group implementation groups (all of them without --group) gets one decision. Give the groups as your audits declare them, so the system's audit matches: for Essential Eight ML2 that is --group 1 --group 2. Each requirement gets one of api_check, manual, not_applicable or other_system, with its reasoning. For each, type c, m, n or o to decide (a accepts a proposal where a session has one, and l every remaining one that is not not_applicable), or s to save and stop. Not applicable always needs a justification and the name of who approves it; another system needs that system's name.

  5. Written for review. Once every requirement is decided, it asks for the domain and perimeter of the system's audit. These are names, not yes or no: the prompt lists the ones scope/setup.yaml declares, Enter takes the first, and any other answer is asked again. It then writes, into the working copy only:

  6. scope/audits/<system>-<framework>.yaml: the system's own audit. Not applicable rows are done with result not_applicable and the justification and approver in the observation; rows another system meets stay open (to_do, not_assessed) with provided_by naming that system, until its own audit shows the requirement met; manual rows are to do. Rows checked through the API are left to the collector (unlisted: not_assessed until its results are published). The audit lists the system. When the repo has an audit series, as hound init names it in scope/setup.yaml (audit_series, EX-E8 by quarter) or an organisation audit that runs in periods, the system's audit joins it: its ref ID is the series and the system's ref ID without SYS- (EX-E8-SOPHOS-NETWORK), on the same cycle, so a period reads EX-E8-Q2-2027FY-SOPHOS-NETWORK (Audit periods). Without a series it is <SYSTEM>-<FRAMEWORK>, with no cycle. Its target is added to hound.yaml when the repo has the system's own mapping (mappings/<system>-<framework>.yaml); the framework's general mapping maps every collector's checks, so another system's results would land in this system's audit.
  7. scope/setup.yaml: the system is declared in the audit's domain with solution: set to the supplier's solution, or, if it is already declared, solution: is added to it (a different solution already there stops the write). That is what lets hound scope plan hold the system back until its supplier is approved in CISO Assistant.
  8. mappings/<framework>.yaml: manual requirements the mapping does not name yet are added to manual_only, with your reasoning as the suggested source. Existing lines are never changed.
  9. onboarding/<system>-<framework>-<date>.md: the record for auditors: the system, the supplier and its levels, the documents kept with their hashes, and every decision with who drafted it and who accepted it.

Nothing is sent to CISO Assistant. Review the files in a pull request, then run hound scope validate scope, hound scope plan scope and hound scope apply scope. Running hound onboard again for the same system writes nothing; to onboard it against another framework, pass that framework's file and it writes a separate audit and record.

docs.title: What the terminal tells you
docs.text:
Before the first question, hound onboard prints the three steps ahead (the supplier, applicability, the files) and reminds you that nothing reaches CISO Assistant until hound scope apply. It refuses to start, before writing anything, in a folder with no scope/setup.yaml, because that is not a compliance repo. Without --spec it says that it cannot list what the system's API offers, so you can stop and add one.

Every opening question comes with a line that says what the answer is for and gives an example, such as The service, and what depends on it, e.g. "Perimeter firewall; all office internet traffic passes through it". A ref ID's prompt ends with its prefix (Supplier ref_id: SUP-), so you type only the rest; see Ref ID conventions.

After the vendor documents, each supplier level is asked with its scale printed first. Answer with a number and, when asked, a sentence saying why; the reason is written beside the level in the supplier file with your name. Leave a level empty to decide it later in the file. These are the scales, as the terminal prints them. Dependency, penetration, maturity and trust follow EBIOS Risk Manager's stakeholder criteria, which CISO Assistant's third-party records use.

dependency: how much the system relies on this supplier to keep working.

Value Meaning 0 None: nothing stops if the supplier does. 1 Low: the supplier is useful, and work carries on without it. 2 Moderate: work is harder without it, and another supplier could step in. 3 High: the supplier is needed, though it could be replaced with effort. 4 Total: the supplier is needed, and nothing could replace it in the short term.

penetration: how far the supplier can reach into your systems and data.

Value Meaning 0 None: no access to your systems or data. 1 Access as an ordinary user, or to user devices only. 2 Administrator access to user devices, or physical access to your premises. 3 Administrator access to business systems or servers. 4 Administrator access to core infrastructure, or physical access to server rooms.

maturity: how well the supplier manages its own cyber security.

Value Meaning 1 Security is handled case by case, with nothing written down. 2 Good practice and regulation are followed, without one overall policy. 3 An overall security policy is applied, and problems are mostly handled as they arise. 4 Risk is managed under an overall policy, ahead of problems.

trust: how sure you are that the supplier's intentions and interests line up with yours.

Value Meaning 1 Its intentions cannot be judged. 2 Its intentions are taken to be neutral. 3 Its intentions are known and probably good. 4 Its intentions are known and fully in line with yours.

criticality: how much the business depends on what the supplier provides (the solution).

Value Meaning 1 Low: the business carries on without it. 2 Medium: some work is slower or harder without it. 3 High: important work stops without it. 4 Critical: the business cannot run without it.

Maturity, trust and criticality have no 0: a level you leave empty is not yet assessed, and stays in the file as a comment to decide.

docs.title: Validate, sample and test the profile
docs.text:
Once applicability is decided, write the profile for the requirements you accepted as API checks: by hand (REST profiles), or ask your coding assistant, whose write-a-profile skill iterates with hound profile validate and hound profile test. Then check it against the real API yourself:

hound onboard profile EXAMPLE-ASSETS --name example-assets \
  --set client_id=00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001 --set base_url=https://api.example.com/ \
  --secret client_secret=env:EXAMPLE_ASSETS_SECRET
  • Checked as written. It reads profiles/<name>.yaml (--profiles, --name; by default the system's name in lower case), which must exist, and loads and validates it as hound profile validate does. It never changes the profile.
  • Sampled once, with your go-ahead. It asks before it calls the API (--sample answers yes). The profile's queries run once, read-only, with the instance settings (--set name=value) and secrets (--secret name=env:VAR or file:/path) you give. A query that fails is listed, such as a wrong path. Each answer is kept as a recording with the profile's identities fields hashed, tokens replaced and the API's address as {{api}}; an answer still holding a secret is refused.
  • You confirm each result. Each check's result on the sample is shown; type y if it is right, or the result it should give. Your answers and the recordings are saved as the profile test profiles/<name>.tests/onboarding.yaml, and the test runs.
  • What is still wrong is listed, and the command exits 1, as a failing hound profile test does. Fix the profile (or have your assistant fix it from the listed problems) and run it again.
  • Nothing is scheduled. Review the profile and its test in a pull request, run hound profile validate <name> and hound profile test <name>, then add a rest collector instance for it to hound.yaml.

docs.title: Onboard the environment first: which system provides each mitigation
docs.text:
Before onboarding systems one by one, decide once, for each mitigation of the framework, which product actually provides it. Then hound judges a requirement only on the audit of the system that provides it, and never fails an audit because it looked at the wrong system.

hound onboard environment --repo . --framework frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json --signals signals.json

hound onboard environment --repo . --graph example-m365      # read the signals live, as an m365 collector in hound.yaml
  • Signals suggest, you decide. --graph <collector> signs in as that m365 collector of the deployment config (--deployment, default hound.yaml in the repo), with its own settings and secrets, and makes two read-only Graph reads: subscribed licences (v1.0/subscribedSkus, enabled or in warning, needs Organization.Read.All) and the kinds of Intune configuration (v1.0/deviceManagement/deviceConfigurations, already granted to the collector). A tenant without Intune has no configuration kinds. Nothing is kept as evidence. Or give --signals, a JSON file of recorded answers (source, licences as SKU part numbers, configuration_types as Intune configuration types), not both. A licence such as Entra ID P2 suggests the Microsoft 365 system (--microsoft-system, by default the first system whose name has "365") for MFA; a system in scope/setup.yaml tagged capabilities: ac, rb is suggested for those mitigations first. Each suggestion shows the signal and its source, and is recorded with the decision, never as the decision.
  • One decision per mitigation. For each, type a to accept the suggestion, s to name the systems, m for manual evidence, g for a gap, or q to save and stop. It asks once for your name and the role that approves the decisions. A product not onboarded yet can be named; you are asked for its supplier.
  • What it writes, for review: scope/capabilities.yaml (see scope.md), and in each system's own audit, every requirement another system provides as an open row (not_assessed, provided_by: [<system>]), "Met by (audit ) ...; open until that audit shows it met", never as not applicable, so no gap shows as closed. hound scope plan lists these rows under "Open dependencies". A requirement the audit's mapping already computes (a target in hound.yaml, --deployment) is left to the mapping and listed, since a hand-written row would conflict with it (scope.result_conflict); take it out of that mapping if the system should not be judged on it. Nothing is merged into a combined audit, rows you wrote by hand are never changed, and running it again adds nothing.

  • What comes next: each named system not onboarded yet is listed with hound onboard "<system>", whose supplier goes through the supplier gate first; each gap is listed as requirements no system's audit answers.

  • With a coding assistant, the same decisions are drafted through hound onboard environment pending and decide (every kind of onboarding) and approved with hound approve.

  • Gaps in the plan. hound scope plan lists each mitigation decided as a gap under "Capability gaps" (and gaps in --json): the requirements no system's audit answers, never a fail on some system.

    • The default skill environment-capabilities describes how to tell which product is authoritative; organisation skills that apply to the environment step extend it. Both reach a coding assistant through its skill files and pending --json.

docs.title: Microsoft 365: which capabilities it provides
docs.text: Run it with --graph <m365 collector> to read the tenant's licences and Intune configuration kinds live, read-only, as that collector of hound.yaml. Microsoft 365 is then suggested for the mitigations they cover. An accepted suggestion is written with evidence: collector and route: <collector>, so the collector's checks for that capability run; a mitigation you give to another product (an application control or identity product, for example) is routed away from Microsoft 365, and its checks there answer not applicable, naming that product. See Capabilities. With --signals (recorded answers) nothing is routed, because no collector read them; set route by hand, or system on the collector.

docs.title: Set up your coding assistant: hound agent setup
docs.text:
$ hound agent setup --repo . --assistant both

hound agent setup writes the files a coding assistant reads in the compliance repo, so that it can onboard systems and suppliers, import an audit workbook, write a profile and review a plan before you apply it. Without --assistant it asks which one you use in VS Code: claude, copilot or both. hound init offers the same at its end (or takes --assistant).

Assistant Files Claude Code CLAUDE.md; .claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md; .claude/agents/hound-onboarding.md, hound-review.md, hound-decisions.md and hound-operations.md GitHub Copilot in VS Code .github/copilot-instructions.md; .github/agents/hound-onboarding.agent.md, hound-review.agent.md, hound-decisions.agent.md and hound-operations.agent.md; .github/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md

With both, the skills are written once, under .claude/skills/, which Copilot in VS Code reads too.

  • Twenty skills, from one source, covering every hound command. Onboarding: onboard the organisation, the environment, a third party, a system and an audit; assess a supplier; read an API specification; import an audit workbook; write a profile. Upkeep: process manual evidence, prepare the weekly review, work through pending decisions with you, review before apply, operate the collectors, keep frameworks, libraries, mappings, profiles and these files current. Documents and response: build the SSP and POA&M, respond to an incident and build the incident response plan, prepare the committee and board reports, answer a prime's questionnaire, move registers from spreadsheets. Each is the steps for driving hound, linking the guide it follows, and where hound has default guidance for that step (the same text hound skill list shows), that guidance too.
  • A command reference built from hound itself. The skill hound-commands lists every command and its options, generated from the hound that ran hound agent setup, so it matches what is installed. Every agent loads it. Run hound agent setup again after upgrading hound.
  • Four agents, with the least tools each needs. hound-onboarding reads, searches, edits and runs commands. hound-review reads, searches and runs commands; it cannot edit a file. hound-decisions takes you through the decisions waiting on you, one at a time, highest risk first, and gives you the hound review --only <key> to accept or challenge each; it records recommendations and edits no file. hound-operations runs the collectors, the SSP, incidents, frameworks and libraries, and the reports.
  • Every file opens with the same rules: organisation data stays in this private repo; never open secrets/; never approve on the person's behalf; nothing reaches CISO Assistant except through hound scope plan and hound scope apply. The rules guide the assistant; what enforces them is hound itself: hound approve refuses anything but a person at a terminal.
  • Your files are yours. Each file hound writes carries a comment naming hound and its version. Running the command again replaces those files (Updated), and leaves alone any file without the comment (Kept), including a CLAUDE.md you already had. To take a file over, delete the comment; to get hound's version back, delete the file and run the command again.

Your assistant's provider sees what the assistant reads in the repo. Keep secrets out of it, as the rules say.

docs.title: Drive it with an agent: pending, decide, supplier draft, approve
docs.text:
A coding agent (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot) can draft a whole onboarding without answering a prompt. Every command below takes options instead of questions and answers in JSON with --json; without --json the same facts print as text for a person. hound checks each step exactly as the interactive flow does. What an agent records is a draft: nothing is written to the scope's audits, and nothing is approved, until a person runs hound approve.

$ hound supplier draft --repo . --system EXAMPLE-ASSETS --ref SUP-EXAMPLE --name "Example Assets Ltd" \
    --solution-ref SOL-EXAMPLE-ASSETS --solution-name "Asset inventory" \
    --contract-ref CTR-EXAMPLE-ASSETS --contract-name "Asset inventory subscription" \
    --level "dependency=2:Holds the asset inventory only." --level "maturity=3:Holds an ISO 27001 certificate." --json
$ hound onboard EXAMPLE-ASSETS pending --json --repo . --group 1 --spec ../specs/example-asset-api.openapi.yaml \
    --owner it@example.com --product "Example Asset API" --solution SOL-EXAMPLE-ASSETS
$ hound onboard EXAMPLE-ASSETS decide urn:intuitem:risk:req_node:essential-eight-2023:pa:ism-1807 --repo . --json \
    --kind api_check --reasoning "GET /v1/devices lists every device, discovered daily." --source "GET /v1/devices"
$ hound onboard EXAMPLE-ASSETS pending --json --repo .
  • hound supplier draft writes scope/third-parties/<ref>.yaml with a draft contract and an open review. Each --level is <name>=<value>:<reason> (dependency and penetration 0 to 4; maturity, trust and criticality 1 to 4); a level outside its scale or without a reason is refused. It never overwrites a file.
  • hound onboard <system> pending starts the session when given --owner, --product and --solution (a solution a third-party file declares), then lists the requirements not yet decided with their text, the API summary from --spec, and the skills that apply (the defaults, plus the repo's own under skills/). Later calls need only the system and --repo.
  • hound onboard <system> decide <requirement> records one decision: --kind api_check|manual|not_applicable|other_system, --reasoning, any --source it rests on, --other-system <name> for another system, --justification <text> for not applicable. Name the requirement as pending lists it under requirement (its ref_id when that is unique in the framework, else its URN). It is marked drafted_by: agent in the session, with no one as its accepter or approver. Deciding a requirement again replaces the draft; a decision a person made is never replaced.
  • --json is also on hound scope validate, hound scope plan and hound explain (what code reads from a change: counts, objects, flags and topics; no model is asked).

docs.title: Every kind of onboarding, the same way
docs.text:
The agent drafts each kind through a command that asks nothing; hound checks it; a person approves with hound approve.

What Command Where the draft waits The organisation hound init <folder> --org ... --code ... --url ... --time-zone ... --level ... --interval ... --owner ... --assistant ... --json The new repo itself, for review The environment hound onboard environment pending --json, then hound onboard environment decide <mitigation> --provided-by system\|manual\|gap --reason ... [--system ...] scope/capabilities.yaml, with no approver A third party hound supplier draft --kind vendor\|reseller\|msp [--for <vendor>] ... [--document <path>]... scope/third-parties/<ref>.yaml, with a draft contract A system hound onboard <system> pending and decide onboarding/<SYSTEM>/session.json An audit hound audit draft --ref ... --name ... --framework ... --group ... --domain ... --perimeter ... --system ... --due ... onboarding/drafts/audits/<ref>.yaml An audit workbook hound scope import <workbook> --audit <ref> [--sheet ...] [--column <name>=<heading>]... Approved rows go to the audit; the rest wait in onboarding/drafts/imports/<audit>.json Manual evidence hound manual propose <source> <file> --result ... --observation ... --supports ... <file>.proposal.yaml beside the file in the drop folder, until hound manual approve
  • The environment. pending lists the mitigations not yet decided, the drafts waiting and the systems in scope. decide records one mitigation; deciding it again replaces the draft, and a decision a person approved is refused. Once every mitigation is decided and the decisions are approved, hound onboard environment asks nothing and writes the rows each system's audit leaves open for another system. While any mitigation is undecided it asks a person for each one, so an agent checks pending is empty first.
  • A reseller or managed service provider is a third party of its own. Draft the vendor first, then the reseller or provider with --kind and --for <vendor ref_id>; its description names the vendor it stands for. --document names a document kept in the repo that the draft rests on, and the file records it with its SHA-256. A system bought through one names it as supplied_through.
  • An audit is drafted per system, with a shared platform audited on its own (one audit per system). It is checked against the scope as it is drafted: its framework, domain, perimeter and systems must be in scope/setup.yaml. It stays out of the scope, and out of every plan, until hound approve moves it into scope/audits/.
  • An audit workbook (.xlsx or .csv) is read where it is; it is never copied into the repo. hound finds the columns by their headings (requirement, result, observation, evidence, approved by, approved on) or by --column. A row the workbook says someone approved is written to the audit's assessments with the workbook's own words, ending "Imported from <workbook>, row <n>, approved by <who> on <date>", so the provenance shows in hound scope plan and in CISO Assistant. A row with no approver is a draft: hound approve asks about it, and records the person who approves it, today. Rows not assessed are left out; rows whose requirement is not in the audit's framework are listed as unmatched and never guessed. Importing again adds nothing twice. Try it with examples/workbooks/example-audit-workbook.csv.

docs.title: Approve, in a terminal
docs.text:
$ hound approve --repo .

hound approve walks you through everything drafted in the repo that needs a person, one item at a time, in this order:

  1. Environment capabilities in scope/capabilities.yaml with no approved_by.
  2. Suppliers whose contract is a draft. Approving makes the contract active.
  3. Supplier reviews that are open, for suppliers with an active contract: conclude each as ok, warning or blocker, once the review is done.
  4. Not-applicable decisions an agent drafted, each with its reasoning and justification.
  5. Each system an agent drafted, with its decisions. Approving writes the system's audit, its entry in scope/setup.yaml and the onboarding record, as the interactive command does. A system waits while its supplier is not approved, a not-applicable decision is declined, or requirements are still undecided.
  6. Audits an agent drafted with hound audit draft. Approving moves the audit into scope/audits/, with your name and the date in its first line.
  7. Imported workbook rows with no approver. Approving writes the row to its audit, with you as its approver.

Answer y, n (leave it as a draft) or s (stop; nothing more is asked). Your name, asked once, and today's date are recorded on everything you approve: approved_by and approved_on on the capability and the contract, by and on on the review's conclusion, and the approver in the session and the onboarding record.

It needs a person at a terminal. When its input or output is redirected, as when an agent runs it or answers are piped in, hound approve refuses and changes nothing. hound manual approve is the same walk for manual evidence only: it shows each file an agent proposed a result for, and you attest, change or reject it (manual sources). Nothing is approved in CISO Assistant: review the changed files in a pull request, then hound scope plan and hound scope apply write the approved state, including each review's conclusion.

Or sign off once a week. hound review walks the same items, and manual evidence proposals, in one session: most urgent first, each with why it matters and the agent's recommendation, answered accept, challenge or skip. It records one sign-off and applies what you accepted. See the weekly review.

docs.title: Explain a change for review
docs.text:
hound explain writes a plain-English review summary of a plan or a config change, so you approve only what you understand. It reads the output of hound scope plan (Markdown or --json), hound plan, a diff (a file, or piped in: git diff | hound explain), or two versions of one file (hound explain before.yaml after.yaml).

  • Code reads it. The counts, the objects and what needs a careful look (requirements newly marked not applicable, deletions, removed checks in mappings or profiles, a check removed from a profile that a mapping in mappings/ still uses, a system without an owner, a supplier contract that is not active) come from code. The plan is the source of truth: the summary quotes its counts. No model is asked.
  • For an agent, --json gives the same facts (counts, objects, flags and topics); the review-before-apply skill has a coding assistant read them with the plan and the changed files before it proposes an apply.
  • Review only. It never edits config or applies a plan, and collection never uses it.

docs.title: Tutorial: onboard the example API
docs.text:
For a worked example of a whole stack, two systems and four suppliers, see the onboarding tutorial: Example Pty Ltd's privately hosted GRC platform on Oracle Cloud and its office firewall, onboarded, reviewed, validated and applied.

This walk-through onboards the fictional Example Asset API into a copy of the template config repo by answering hound's questions yourself: it needs no key and sends nothing anywhere. It takes about ten minutes. Run it from the root of this repository.

  1. A config repo to work in.
cp -R examples/compliance-repo /tmp/tutorial-repo
  1. Start onboarding. Group 1 keeps the list short (48 requirements); for Essential Eight ML2 you would give --group 1 --group 2.
hound onboard EXAMPLE-ASSETS --repo /tmp/tutorial-repo --group 1 \
  --spec examples/apis/example-asset-api.openapi.yaml

Answer the questions: your name, the system owner's email (owner@example.com), the product (Example Asset Service), the supplier (SUP-EXAMPLE, Example Vendor Pty Ltd), the solution (SOL-EXAMPLE-ASSETS, Example Asset Service), the contract (CTR-EXAMPLE-ASSETS, Example asset service subscription) and what the supplier provides. Press Enter when asked for a vendor document. The supplier is new, so hound drafts scope/third-parties/sup-example.yaml and stops:

SUP-EXAMPLE is not approved yet. Review scope/third-parties/sup-example.yaml; once the supplier is approved, make contract CTR-EXAMPLE-ASSETS active and run 'hound onboard EXAMPLE-ASSETS' again to decide applicability.

  1. Approve the supplier. Open the drafted file, fill in the levels it leaves to decide, and set the contract to status: active. In a real repo you would now apply the supplier and conclude its review EA-SUP-EXAMPLE as ok in CISO Assistant (see Supplier approval); the tutorial skips that, because onboarding itself checks only the contract.

  2. Decide applicability. Run the same command again. It shows what the API offers, then each requirement with "No proposal": the decisions are yours. Type c for ISM-1807 (the API lists devices and their last check-in) with a reason, and m with a reason for the rest. Type s at any point to stop; the next run carries on from there. At the end, accept the default domain and perimeter:

All 48 requirements decided: 1 API check(s), 47 manual, 0 not applicable, 0 for another system. The session is in onboarding/EXAMPLE-ASSETS/session.json.
Wrote scope/audits/example-assets-essential-eight-2023.yaml, scope/setup.yaml, onboarding/example-assets-essential-eight-2023-<date>.md. ...
  1. Review what it wrote. Read the audit, the system's new solution: line in scope/setup.yaml and the onboarding record, as a reviewer would in a pull request, then check the scope files offline:
cd /tmp/tutorial-repo && hound scope validate scope
  1. The profile. Copy the library's example profile and its tests, and run them offline (for your own system you would write the profile, or have your coding assistant write it, then validate, sample and test it):
mkdir -p profiles && cp -R <evidence-hound>/profiles/example.yaml <evidence-hound>/profiles/example.tests profiles/
hound profile test example --profiles profiles

To do the same with a coding assistant, run hound agent setup in the repo and ask it to onboard the system with hound.

docs.title: Skills: the assistant's guidance
docs.text:
A skill is a Markdown file with frontmatter that says how to approach a step. hound gives the skills for a step to a coding assistant with hound onboard <system> pending --json, and hound agent setup writes the defaults into the assistant's own skill files. Skills only guide: the named approver for not applicable, the supplier gate, hound approve and profile tests stay in code, and no skill can change them.

---
name: our-applicability
description: How we justify not applicable.
version: 1.0.0
applies_to: [applicability]          # supplier, system, applicability, profile, mapping, explain
frameworks: [essential-eight-2023]    # optional: only for these frameworks
overrides: applicability              # optional: replace this default on purpose
---
Guidance, in plain Markdown.
  • Defaults are built into hound, from this repository's skills/ folder: supplier assessment and tiering, supplier assurance documents, applicability and not-applicable justification, Essential Eight ML2 mapping, profile authoring, reading an API specification, and reviewing a config change (for hound explain).
  • Organisation skills live in the config repo's skills/ folder (skills_path, mounted read-only like profiles). They add to the defaults; one with a default's name is an error unless it says overrides:.
  • Choosing: a step gets every skill whose applies_to names the step and whose frameworks match, defaults first, within a size budget. Over the budget is an error naming the skills, never a silent cut.
Command Does hound skill list Every active skill: source, version, SHA-256, steps and override. hound skill new <name> Writes a skeleton to fill in. hound skill add <file> Validates the skill against the defaults and the folder, then copies it in. hound skill validate Checks every skill: frontmatter, steps, size and overrides. hound skill draft [--only <name>]... Writes the organisation's own skills (organisation-profile, risk-appetite, it-landscape, ai-landscape) as templates with their questions as headings, for you or your coding assistant to answer. A skill already in the folder is kept as it is. Templates go only into the skills folder, for you to review, edit and commit.

Each takes --skills <folder> (default HOUND_SKILLS_PATH, else ./skills).

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: This is the public, generic plan for the project. An adopting organisation keeps its own rollout plan (system list, owners, dates, committee) in a private repo.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A small defence-industry business has to reach and then sustain cyber compliance, for example Essential Eight Maturity Level 2 under DISP (Australia) or NIST SP 800-171 under CMMC (US). It typically has an IT team and some software developers but no CISO or GRC team, and its compliance evidence lives in spreadsheets that go stale between audits. Whoever looks after compliance has 2 to 8 hours a week for it.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
1. CISO Assistant is the system of record. Self-hosted Community Edition on Docker. Frameworks (Essential Eight, NIST SP 800-171 and others) come from its built-in library.
  2. Use CISO Assistant's standard integration paths. Spreadsheet registers move into the compliance repo's scope files, which hound scope apply writes to CISO Assistant over its REST API (move off spreadsheets). Collectors send updates in the same shape as its dispatcher messages, over its REST API with a service-account token.
  3. Build a base, not a collector for everything. The kit provides one standard way to update an audit. Each system gets a thin collector. Systems without a usable API use the manual-upload collector on a schedule.
  4. Stay framework-neutral. Collectors emit neutral check results; one mapping file per framework turns them into requirement results.
  5. AI-assisted build, automated upkeep. Claude Code implements sprint tasks by strict TDD inside a dev container; CI and GitHub Advanced Security close the loop. In operation, schedules, health records, backups and dependency updates keep it running with little manual effort.
  6. AI prepares, a person decides once a week. The person's own coding agent drafts every decision, proposal and plan through hound, and comes as close as it can to approving everything itself; every human review is gathered into one guided weekly session (read, understand, accept or challenge, apply), which is the single place a person signs off. No model collects evidence, and no evidence is accepted without a person or a standing approval they signed (design).

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Release Contents 1 Core, publisher, runner, collector SDK and test kit, manual-upload collector, the Microsoft 365 collector and the Sophos Central profile (Veeam was dropped in s09: backup evidence stays manual), CISO Assistant as configuration, a thin reference Docker deployment with scheduled runs (early, so evidence builds history), CISO Assistant users and settings as configuration, a tutorial for the private compliance repo, Essential Eight gap collectors (application control, vulnerability scan import, manual-upload templates), third parties as configuration, the evidence plan as recurring CISO Assistant tasks, one guided weekly review, an Essential Eight system security plan drafted from CISO Assistant records, AI governance on the Australian AI6 guidance, the completed Essential Eight mapping, a NIST SP 800-171 crosswalk, adoption guides, committee (operational) and board (governance) reporting, backups and hardening, NuGet packages, a signed release pipeline and a documentation site 2 ASD Essentials mapping, DISP membership readiness, risk, threats and BIA as configuration, incident reporting deadlines, supply-chain flow-down, CISO Assistant governance collector and metrics, CMMC Level 2 (NIST SP 800-171) mapping and its SSP and POA&M layout, SPRS score, annual affirmation and DFARS 7012 incident reporting, agent speed (one "what now" command, the week prepared in one step, skills for every feature, faster runs) 3 The first published release (1.0.0): a principal engineer's and a CISO's review of everything above, removals, refactoring and one route through the docs (release notes). The security document generators (s19b) move after release 3, reordered, with four cut.

Sprints are in docs/sprints/.

docs.title: Adoption path for an organisation
docs.text: Step What Code needed 1. Stand up Self-host CISO Assistant and the runner with deploy/compose No 2. Migrate Move spreadsheet compliance and third-party registers into the compliance repo (guide) No 3. Tier systems Automate the 3 or 4 highest-value systems; put every other system on the manual-upload collector with an owner and interval Config only 4. Operate Scheduled runs, collector health in CISO Assistant, manual uploads by owners No 5. Govern Monthly committee report, quarterly board report, authorising-official decisions recorded in CISO Assistant No 6. Extend Write a collector when a manual source becomes costly; add a framework mapping when a new obligation arrives Small

docs.title: People and governance (generic)
docs.text:
Role Responsibility Authorising official Accepts residual risk and signs off the compliance position; often the CTO when there is no CISO Capability owner Runs CISO Assistant, collectors and this kit System owners Manual evidence and remediation for their systems Supplier owners Third-party reviews and contract details Independent reviewer Periodic external assessment

Each role has a guide in docs/operate/, with training in docs/training/.

docs.title: Reporting: operation and governance
docs.text:
Reporting has two tiers with different audiences and questions. Both are generated from period snapshots of CISO Assistant data, so figures are reproducible and trends are reliable.

Security committee (operation) Board (governance) Cadence Monthly Quarterly Question answered What changed, what is failing, what is overdue, who does what next? Are we compliant and improving, what are the key risks, and what risk have we accepted? Content Collector health and evidence freshness; control status changes; exceptions and risk acceptances (new, expiring, expired); remediation (POA&M-style) progress; incidents; manual evidence and supplier reviews due; actions Compliance position statement; maturity posture per framework with four-quarter trend; top risks against appetite; risk-acceptance decisions and expiries; assurance coverage; decisions needed Length As long as needed, every figure linked to CISO Assistant Two pages plus appendix, no operational detail Owner Capability owner prepares; committee confirms actions Authorising official presents; board endorses risk appetite and acceptances Recorded in CISO Assistant Actions as tasks and applied controls; exceptions Risk-acceptance decisions; the report as evidence

The committee's monthly reports roll up into the board's quarter. Delivered in sprint s12 (tasks s12-04 to s12-07); release 2 adds the Essentials view (s14) and NIST SP 800-171 SSP and POA&M views (s17).

docs.title: Security of the project itself
docs.text:
• Public repo with secret scanning, push protection, CodeQL, Dependabot, dependency review and OpenSSF Scorecard.
  • An organisation-data deny-list check in CI blocks any adopter's real names or identifiers.
  • Collectors are read-only, use least-privilege credentials resolved at runtime, and never store secrets.
  • Releases are built from tags with provenance attestations and an SBOM.

docs.title: Publishing to CISO Assistant
docs.text:
hound publish plans a run's updates (the same plan as hound plan --dry-run) and sends them to CISO Assistant. It sends the whole plan; hound run sends only what changed (see Running collectors).

$ make ca-up                                    # local CISO Assistant, seeded; writes .dev/ca.env
$ set -a; . .dev/ca.env; set +a                 # HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN
$ make run ARGS="publish --config examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml \
    --checks tests/fixtures/publish/checks.json --evidence-dir tests/fixtures/publish/evidence"

Add --dry-run to print the report without calling CISO Assistant (no token needed).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Meaning HOUND_CA_URL The API root, for example http://localhost:8000/api/. HOUND_CA_TOKEN A CISO Assistant personal access token. Sent as Authorization: Token ...; never logged.

They are read through .NET configuration, so environment variables work everywhere.

docs.title: What happens, in order
docs.text:
1. Evidence uploads. For each evidence file the publisher finds the CISO Assistant evidence with ref_id equal to the evidence ID, creating it (named after the file) if there is none. If the latest revision's SHA-256 equals the file's, nothing is uploaded and the item is skipped. Otherwise the file is read from --evidence-dir, checked against the SHA-256 recorded at collection (evidence.hash_mismatch if it changed), and uploaded as a new revision.
  2. Requirement assessments. Each is found by compliance_assessment__ref_id and requirement__ref_id (the dispatcher's selector) and patched with result, observation and evidences. The plan cites evidence by ref_id; the publisher swaps in the CISO Assistant IDs from step 1. A requirement citing evidence whose upload failed fails with publish.evidence_unresolved.
