  3. Applied controls. Each is found by ref_id and its status set.

Every item is attempted: a failure is recorded and the rest go on. Running the same plan twice creates no duplicate evidence or revisions, and leaves results as they were.

docs.title: A requirement with no evidence
docs.text: When a check a requirement needs is missing from the run or ended in an error, the requirement has no evidence, and it is published as non_compliant with an observation that starts "No evidence yet:" and names each check and what happened to it. CISO Assistant leaves not-assessed rows out of its compliance percentage, so publishing them as not assessed would let a few passes read 100%. A target can opt out with no_evidence: not_assessed (configuration.md); see scope.md for the same rule on the rows the scope writes.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
Stdout is a JSON report; logs go to stderr.

{
  "planned": 0, "sent": 6, "skipped": 3, "failed": 0,
  "items": [
    { "update": "upload evidence ev-0001 (mfa-admins.json)", "outcome": "skipped", "problems": [] }
  ]
}
Exit code Meaning 0 Everything was sent or skipped. 3 Nothing was sent: bad config, check results, mapping, or missing URL, token or transport settings. 4 The run finished but at least one item failed. Each failure is logged at error with its code.

docs.title: Problem codes from CISO Assistant
docs.text:
Code Cause ciso_assistant.auth HTTP 401 or 403: bad or expired token, or missing permissions. ciso_assistant.not_found HTTP 404, or no object matches the selector (for example a requirement not in the audit's framework). ciso_assistant.ambiguous More than one object matches a selector that must match one. ciso_assistant.rejected Another 4xx; the message carries CISO Assistant's explanation. ciso_assistant.unavailable 5xx after retries, timeout, open circuit or no connection.

Requests retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 5xx, 408 and 429 (POST is never retried, so a create is never doubled), time out, and stop calling a failing server through a circuit breaker.

docs.title: Kafka transport (removed)
docs.text: Release 3 removed the Kafka transport. CISO Assistant's dispatcher cannot read what it holds, link evidence to controls or skip unchanged rows, and a small team would have to run Kafka for it. A config with transport: kafka or kafka_bootstrap_servers, or HOUND_TRANSPORT=kafka, stops with config.transport_removed: remove them and hound publishes over the REST API.

docs.title: Release 3 (1.0.0)
docs.text: Release 3 is the first published release of Evidence Hound, and the one the maintainer treats as the product. Releases 1 and 2 were built and tested but never tagged, so release 3 carries everything from sprints s00 to s19 under version 1.0.0. The changelog lists every feature and fix; this page says what a person adopting it needs to know.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text: A small business with one GRC member and two to eight hours a week, reaching and keeping Essential Eight Maturity Level 2, with CMMC Level 2, DISP readiness, the ASD Essentials and AI6 as further programmes from the same evidence. CISO Assistant is the system of record; hound writes its configuration from a git repository, collects evidence on a schedule, publishes the results, and puts everything that needs a person into one guided weekly review. Start with getting started.

docs.title: What changed in s19, the review before release
docs.text:
• Four mapping claims are narrower, so results are more honest (CISO review):
  • A vulnerability the vendor rates critical on an internet-facing service must be patched within 48 hours, as ISM-1876 and ISM-1877 say, not only one with a working exploit. Expect vuln.internet_facing.patched_in_window to fail sooner.
  • The Office attack surface reduction rules pass only when they block for all users or all devices. A policy assigned to some groups is partial.
  • ISM-1657 now also needs the yearly application control ruleset review (appcontrol.rulesets_validated), which attests compiled HTML, HTML applications and control panel applets.
  • Each CMMC row that covers part of its practice says what the person assesses (rest: in the mapping), and the observation in CISO Assistant names it.
  • hound next on a new repo lists onboarding as the first step instead of "nothing needs doing".
  • One route through the documentation, from the trial to the first weekly review; the onboarding tutorial moved to docs/tutorials/.
  • Simpler code behind the same behaviour: the command-line shell, the scope pipeline and the tests were refactored with the output of every command unchanged (engineering review).

docs.title: Removed, and what replaces it
docs.text: Removed Instead The Kafka transport (transport: kafka, kafka_bootstrap_servers, HOUND_TRANSPORT=kafka) The REST API, the default. A config that still names Kafka is refused with config.transport_removed. The evidence records in docs/evidence/ and examples/manual-exports/ Kept in git history; the guides that cited them link to the last commit that had them. The hidden options of the removed built-in model (--no-model, --show-requests, and the old --config on explain, onboard, onboard environment, onboard profile and skill draft) Nothing: each did nothing since the model was removed. A script that still passes one now stops with a usage error; delete the option. Model help comes from your coding assistant (hound agent setup). The onboarding assistant design (docs/design/onboarding-assistant.md) Agent-driven onboarding, which replaced it in s09.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
An assessor will ask for these, and hound does not give them:

  • CMMC assessment objectives. hound assesses the 110 practices of NIST SP 800-171; a C3PAO assesses its 320 objectives (SP 800-171A). Record each objective's answer in CISO Assistant. Every CMMC result is at most partially compliant until a person does.
  • Configuration, not tests. Collectors read how a control is configured. The ASD assessment process rates a test of the control (trying the macro, running the unapproved program) higher; keep those test results as manual evidence.
  • What the collectors see. Microsoft 365, Intune-managed Windows devices, firewalls managed in Sophos Central, and what your vulnerability scanner reaches. Servers, macOS and other services need a REST profile or a manual source, or a row that passes overstates. Decide each in the capability map (hound onboard environment).
  • ISM-1883 by counts. Few Global Administrators and roles activated only when needed show privileged access is limited, not that each account is required; the yearly privileged access review is where a person justifies each.
  • SPRS. hound sprs score computes the score and sprs affirmation-pack prepares the affirmation; the affirming official posts both in SPRS.
  • DFARS incident records. hound incident report-pack --dfars assembles the 72-hour report and reminds you to keep images of the affected systems for 90 days; keeping them is yours.

docs.title: Upgrade an existing compliance repo
docs.text:
For a repo made with a pre-release build:

  1. Pin the new version: the runner image ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:1.0.0 in deploy/deploy.env, and the .NET tool with dotnet tool update --global EvidenceHound.Cli --version 1.0.0.
  2. Remove --no-model and --show-requests from any script. Remove any transport: kafka or kafka_bootstrap_servers from hound.yaml, and HOUND_TRANSPORT from the runner's environment. hound config validate hound.yaml says what is left.
  3. Copy the shipped mappings you use over your copies, or make the same changes by hand: mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml (ISM-1657 adds appcontrol.rulesets_validated) and mappings/cmmc-2.0.yaml (a rest: on each row). If you map ISM-1657, add the application control review manual source when you do not have it yet.
  4. Run hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml, then hound run --config hound.yaml --dry-run, and read what changes: expect the attack surface reduction rows to turn partial where the policy is assigned to groups, and critical internet-facing findings to fail after 48 hours.
  5. Re-run hound agent setup so your agent's skills match this release.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: Releases are cut from a vX.Y.Z tag on main by the release workflow (release.yml). Nothing is published until a maintainer approves the release environment, and no long-lived token is needed except an optional NuGet key.

docs.title: What a release publishes
docs.text:
What Where Checked by Runner image ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:X.Y.Z (and X.Y), amd64 and arm64 GHCR image tests and a vulnerability scan before approval; build provenance and an SBOM attestation in the registry EvidenceHound.Cli (the hound .NET tool), EvidenceHound.Templates, EvidenceHound.Core, EvidenceHound.Collectors.* GitHub release assets, and NuGet when the key is set scripts/check-packages.sh (licence, repository and commit, README, symbols); hound installed from them as a test feed; build provenance CycloneDX SBOM of the CLI GitHub release asset Release notes GitHub release generated from the Conventional Commits since the last tag (scripts/changelog.sh --notes) Documentation site GitHub Pages (gh-pages branch) make docs: MkDocs in strict mode, on every pull request too

The version comes from the tag (MinVer). Between releases, builds are pre-releases of the next version, such as 1.0.1-alpha.0.3.

docs.title: Set up once
docs.text:
1. The release environment. In the repository's Settings > Environments, create release and add the maintainers as required reviewers. Allow deployments from tags matching v* only.
  2. GitHub Pages. In Settings > Pages, serve the site from the gh-pages branch, root folder. The release workflow writes that branch; the site is at https://tnbozman.github.io/evidence-hound/.
  3. NuGet (optional). To publish to nuget.org, create an API key there scoped to Push for the EvidenceHound.* glob, with an expiry, and add it to the release environment as the secret NUGET_API_KEY. Without it, the packages are attached to the GitHub release only. When nuget.org trusted publishing is set up for this repository, the key can be removed.

docs.title: Cut a release
docs.text:
1. On the sprint branch, write the changelog and commit it with the release's other changes: make changelog VERSION=1.0.0 (needs git-cliff: pip install --require-hashes -r tools/changelog/requirements.txt). In the same commit, move the deployments' pins to the new version with scripts/stamp-release.sh 1.0.0: it sets HOUND_RUNNER_IMAGE in deploy/compose/.env.example and examples/compliance-repo/deploy/deploy.env, EVIDENCE_HOUND_REF in the template's compliance.yml, and the image in the first deployment tutorial. A unit test checks that they agree.
  2. Merge the sprint's pull request into main when CI is green.
  3. Tag the merge commit and push the tag:
$ git switch main && git pull
$ git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1"
$ git push origin v1.0.0
  1. The release workflow's verify job first scans every commit in the history for organisation data (scripts/check-org-data.sh --history, with the ORG_DENYLIST secret), then builds and checks everything. Then approve the release environment in the run.
  2. Check the result:
$ gh release view v1.0.0
$ docker pull ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:1.0.0
$ gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:1.0.0 --owner tnbozman

A pull request that changes the release workflow, its scripts or the Dockerfile runs verify as a dry run on a local v1.0.0-dry-run tag: packages into a local test feed, hound installed from it, the SBOM and notes made, the image built, tested and scanned. Nothing is pushed.

docs.title: If a release goes wrong
docs.text: Before approval, cancel the run, delete the tag (git push origin :refs/tags/v1.0.0), fix, and tag again. After publishing, never move or reuse a tag: fix forward with the next patch version. A package pushed to NuGet can be unlisted but not deleted.

docs.title: Repository map
docs.text:
Every folder in this repository, why it is there, who uses it, and whether it stays. A test (RepoMapTests) fails when a folder is added without a row here, or a row names a folder that no longer exists, so add the row in the same change as the folder.

Users: person (a GRC team member or contributor reads or edits it), agent (the person's coding agent reads it), hound (the CLI reads or embeds it at run time), CI (a workflow or test runs it), release (it ships in a package or image).

Verdicts: keep; merge into the folder named; remove, with the reason. A verdict that removes something a person may rely on waits for the maintainer (s19-02).

Reviewed 2026-11-26 (s19-01).

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Folder Purpose Users Verdict .claude/ Slash commands for contributors' Claude Code (/start-sprint, /next-task, /check-feedback). agent keep .config/ .NET local tool manifest. docs.title: Reporting: snapshots, the committee and the board
docs.text:
hound reports in two tiers, built only from CISO Assistant and hound's own run store:

  • Monthly, to the security committee (operational): what changed, what is failing, what is overdue, and actions to confirm.
  • Quarterly, to the board (governance): one compliance position per programme, the trend over four quarters, key risks, the risks accepted on the board's behalf, and the decisions asked of it.

Both are plain Markdown. Every figure links back to its CISO Assistant object, and every report is a function of saved snapshots, so a past month's report can be produced again and says the same thing.

docs.title: 1. Take the month's snapshot
docs.text:
On the first working day of each month, for the month just ended:

$ hound report snapshot --period 2026-11 --config hound.yaml --control AC-REPORTING
wrote /var/lib/evidence-hound/evidence/reports/posture-2026-11.json: 2 programmes, 168 requirement rows
uploaded hound-report/posture-2026-11 to applied control AC-REPORTING
  • It reads each programme in scope/setup.yaml (framework, groups and audit of record), the requirement results of each audit, applied controls, risk acceptances and security exceptions, findings, incidents, risk scenarios, tasks and supplier reviews, and the latest run of each collector.
  • It writes the snapshot to reports/ in the evidence store. With --control, it also uploads it as evidence on that applied control, so the record of what you reported lives in CISO Assistant. Create the control once: hound add control --scope scope --yes --ref-id AC-REPORTING --name "Security reporting" --owner grc@example.com --category process, then hound scope apply.
  • When your audit runs in periods, the snapshot reads the period that holds the month's last day.

Your agent can run this for you; it only reads CISO Assistant, apart from the one upload.

docs.title: 2. The committee report
docs.text:
$ hound report committee --month 2026-11 --config hound.yaml --out committee-2026-11.md

It compares November's snapshot with October's. If October's is missing, it says so and reports November alone. Sections, in order:

  1. Summary: each programme's standing, then the few lines that need the committee's attention.
  2. Collector health: each collector's last run and outcome; a collector with no run in the last 7 days of the month is marked stale.
  3. Control status changes: per programme and parent (an Essential Eight strategy, an AI6 practice), and the register summary.
  4. Exceptions and risk acceptances: new, expiring within 60 days, and expired.
  5. Remediation: open items, completed this month and overdue, by owner and due date.
  6. Incidents opened and closed this month.
  7. Manual evidence and third parties: tasks due or overdue, owners overdue for a second month first.
  8. Actions: proposed, each with an owner and due date, for the committee to confirm. Every overdue item from section 7 is carried here until it is done, because the committee is the escalation after the reminder emails.

How to run the meeting is in the security committee guide.

docs.title: A programme's standing
docs.text:
Both reports give each programme's standing in one line, for example "Level met: none (level 0). Compliant 3 of 46 applicable (6%), counting rows not assessed as not met; assessed 64 of 107; not assessed: 43." A level (an Essential Eight maturity level, or any programme group) is met only when every row at it and below is compliant or not applicable, so one row not assessed holds it back. The percentage is rounded down, so it never reads 100% while a row is open.

Quote this line rather than CISO Assistant's compliance percentage. CISO Assistant leaves rows not assessed out of its percentage, so a few passing checks among many unassessed rows read 100%; hound applies a row with no evidence as non-compliant for that reason (scope.md).

docs.title: 3. The board report
docs.text:
$ hound report board --quarter 2026-Q4 --config hound.yaml --out board-2026-q4.md

It reads the snapshot of each quarter's last month (for 2026-Q4, December) for this quarter and the three before it. The body fits two printed pages; the operational detail goes in the appendix.

The compliance position it proposes for each programme follows fixed rules, so it never depends on a model:

Position When Off track A requirement got worse since last quarter, or more than 25% of the requirements assessed are non-compliant On track Nothing non-compliant, and at most 10% not assessed On track with conditions Anything in between

An exception or risk acceptance made this quarter that is valid for more than 12 months, or has no expiry, is marked for board endorsement. How the board uses the report is in the board reporting guide.

docs.title: 4. Schedule it
docs.text: When Who What First working day of the month Agent hound report snapshot for last month, then hound report committee Before the committee meets GRC member (30 minutes) Read the draft, check the summary and actions, refine the wording with AI help First working day of the quarter Agent hound report board for last quarter, after that month's snapshot Before the board meets Authorising official Confirm or change each compliance position

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Message What to do No snapshot for 2026-11 in ... Take that period's snapshot first: hound report snapshot --period <period> --config hound.yaml. '2026-13' is not a period ... Months are YYYY-MM, quarters YYYY-Qn. A programme has no coverage figures The config has no target for that programme's audit. Collector success rate is not shown hound keeps only each collector's latest run; the committee sees the last outcome and staleness.

docs.title: Risk studies and security exceptions
docs.text:
This guide is for a GRC team that keeps its risk register in CISO Assistant and wants each change proposed and reviewed in the compliance repo, like the rest of the scope. It shows the files, how hound checks them, how they reach CISO Assistant, and which decisions stay with a person in CISO Assistant. The full file reference is in Scope files.

The example compliance repo has all of it: examples/compliance-repo/scope/risks/ex-risk-2026.yaml, examples/compliance-repo/scope/exceptions.yaml and the matrix and threats in examples/compliance-repo/libraries/example-risk.yaml.

docs.title: 1. Choose a matrix and threats
docs.text:
A risk study is rated on one risk matrix. Use a built-in one (such as urn:intuitem:risk:library:critical_risk_matrix_5x5) or write your own in a library file, with the threats your scenarios name that no loaded catalogue has. List it in scope/setup.yaml and snapshot it, so hound can check level names and threats without CISO Assistant:

$ hound library validate libraries/example-risk.yaml
$ hound library snapshot libraries/example-risk.yaml --out libraries/example-risk.json

Raise the library's version whenever you change it: CISO Assistant takes only a new version, so hound stops with library.version_not_bumped otherwise. Give your threats and matrix their own ref_ids and names: CISO Assistant refuses a library whose threat reuses a ref_id or name already loaded in the same folder (HTTP 422, "already used in this scope").

docs.title: 2. Write the study and its scenarios
docs.text:
One file per study under scope/risks/. Each scenario names the systems it affects, its threats, the controls in place and planned, and its ratings by level name:

  - ref_id: R-01
    name: Ransomware encrypts the file shares
    systems: [Example 365]
    threats: [THR-02]
    existing_controls: [AC-BACKUP]
    current: {probability: Possible, impact: Major}
    residual: {probability: Unlikely, impact: Major}
    treatment: mitigate
    justification: Backups are restored and tested each month.

To add a scenario, copy one, give it a new ref_id, rate it, and run hound scope validate scope/. It names the line of any level the matrix does not have, any system, threat or control the scope does not declare, and a residual rating above the current one (treatment can only lower a risk).

docs.title: 3. Request a security exception
docs.text: A known gap you live with for a while, such as an application that cannot use single sign-on yet, goes in scope/exceptions.yaml with its expiry, owner, the systems, controls and scenarios it concerns, and the audit rows it covers. Write no status: only the approver decides, in CISO Assistant (scope.approval_not_configurable if you try).

docs.title: 4. Plan, review and apply
docs.text:
$ hound scope plan scope/ --config hound.yaml
$ hound scope apply scope/ --config hound.yaml

The plan shows rating changes by level name (such as current_probability: Likely → Possible), so a reviewer reads what changed without the matrix to hand. Its "Security exceptions and risk acceptances" section lists each request with the approver's decision, then what to renew or close: an approved exception that expires within 60 days, or one past its expiry that is still approved. Between plans, hound status --config hound.yaml --scope scope lists the exceptions whose declared expiry is near or past, offline.

A failing check on a row an approved, unexpired exception covers keeps its result, and hound run names the exception in the row's observation. An exception explains a gap; it does not close it.

docs.title: What stays in CISO Assistant
docs.text:
• Approvals. Accepting a risk and approving an exception are a person's decisions, made by the approver in CISO Assistant, so the decision keeps its separation of duties: the person who writes the request is not the one who approves it. A scenario with treatment: accept asks for a risk acceptance (ACC-<study>-<scenario>); hound never sets its state.
  • Computed levels. CISO Assistant computes each scenario's risk level from its probability and impact on the matrix, so the file holds only the ratings and hound never writes a level.
  • History. CISO Assistant keeps who changed what and when; the repo keeps why, in each reviewed pull request.

docs.title: Running collectors
docs.text:
hound run is the one command a schedule calls. For each collector in the deployment configuration it collects evidence into the local store, evaluates the checks, maps them to the audit's requirements, plans the updates and publishes them to CISO Assistant.

$ hound run --config examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml --dry-run
info: Collector example-fake: Succeeded
{
  "outcome": "succeeded",
  "run_id": "20261121T020000Z",
  "collectors": [
    {
      "name": "example-fake",
      "outcome": "succeeded",
      "problems": [],
      "publish": { "planned": 8, "sent": 0, "skipped": 0, "failed": 0, "audits": [ ... ] },
      "changes": [ { "compliance_assessment": "EXAMPLE-BASELINE-2026", "changed": 4, "unchanged": 0, "drift": 0 } ],
      "drift": []
    }
  ]
}

Without --dry-run the same report counts what was sent, skipped because CISO Assistant already had it, or failed. A dry run does not read CISO Assistant, so it plans every row.

docs.title: Only changes are sent
docs.text:
Before planning, hound run reads each target audit's rows, the evidence it cites and the applied controls it sets, and sends only what differs:

  • A row's state is its result, the outcome of each check behind it and the hashes of its evidence. Timestamps and observation wording are not part of it, so an unchanged row is never rewritten and its history in CISO Assistant shows only real changes.
  • Evidence whose latest revision has the same SHA-256 is neither uploaded nor looked up again; rows cite its existing ID. A changed file becomes a new revision of the same evidence item.
  • Every run has an ID, its start time in UTC (20261121T020000Z). Each row a run writes ends its observation with a marker such as [hound run 20261121T020000Z state 3f9c0a1b2c4d5e6f], which records the run and the state it wrote.
  • Drift. When a row still carries the marker of the state Evidence Hound would write, but its result or evidence was changed in the UI, the run writes the computed values back and reports publish.drift_corrected under drift, naming the audit, the row's URN and the old and new values. A row whose marker was removed is simply rewritten.
  • Rows outside the audit's selected implementation groups are neither sent nor counted.
  • History. Each published run appends one line per audit to <evidence root>/_history/<audit>.jsonl: date, run_id, changed, unchanged and drift. Lines are never rewritten. Dry runs and --no-publish runs add nothing.

hound plan without --dry-run does the same reading and planning and prints the run ID, the counts per audit, any drift and the dispatcher messages it would send, without changing anything. It needs HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN. hound plan --dry-run stays offline and prints every message.

Option Effect --only <name> Run one collector. An unknown name is a usage error (exit 2). --dry-run Collect and store evidence, then plan, but send nothing. --no-publish Collect and store evidence only. --parallel <n> How many collectors collect at once (default 4, at least 1). Each still plans and publishes in config order, reading what CISO Assistant holds for its audits once, so a later collector sees what an earlier one wrote.

Exit codes: 0 every collector succeeded, 1 any collector failed, 2 usage, 3 configuration or secrets.

docs.title: On a schedule
docs.text:
hound serve --config <file> runs each collector on its schedule until stopped; it is the runner container's default command in the reference deployment. Schedules are read in scheduler.time_zone and each collector's runs are delayed by its own jitter (see configuration). At start it logs each collector's next run:

info: example-m365: next run 2026-11-22 03:02:41 Australia/Sydney (2026-11-21 16:02:41 UTC)
  • Each scheduled run is hound run --only <name>: it reads the config file again, so a pull of the compliance repo applies to the next run. A changed schedule needs a restart of hound serve.
  • One collector never has two runs at once. An occurrence that falls due while its previous run is still going is skipped with a warning, not queued. Occurrences missed while the host was down run once, late, when it is back.
  • Runs happen one at a time, in name order when several fall due together. A run that fails is logged and the schedule carries on; hound status and the collector health evidence show it.
  • Stopping the container (SIGTERM) cancels the current run and exits 0.

Without hound serve. A host scheduler can call one-off runs instead. Set the runner's command to something harmless or remove the service's restart, then, for example with cron:

# /etc/cron.d/evidence-hound: every collector nightly at 03:00 host time
0 3 * * * root cd /opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose && docker compose run --rm runner run --config /config/hound.yaml >>/var/log/evidence-hound.log 2>&1

or a systemd timer:

# /etc/systemd/system/evidence-hound.service
[Service]
Type=oneshot
WorkingDirectory=/opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker compose run --rm runner run --config /config/hound.yaml

# /etc/systemd/system/evidence-hound.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00
RandomizedDelaySec=300
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

systemctl enable --now evidence-hound.timer. Use --only <name> and one timer per collector for different schedules. The host scheduler does not stop overlapping runs, so give each run time to finish before the next.

docs.title: One collector never stops another
docs.text:
Each collector runs on its own. If it crashes, cannot find a secret or CISO Assistant rejects one of its updates, that collector is reported as failed with its problems and the others carry on.

A collector updates the requirements its own checks answer. Each run also saves its latest results in _latest/ under the evidence root, so a requirement whose checks come from several collectors (say Microsoft 365 and a manual source) is filled by whichever of them runs once all of them have reported, using each check's newest result and citing every collector's evidence. A requirement some configured collector has not reported yet is left alone, so one collector never marks another's work as not assessed.

docs.title: Evidence in CISO Assistant
docs.text: Evidence IDs are scoped by collector (example-fake/mfa-users.json), and that ID is the evidence name in CISO Assistant, which needs names unique within a folder. Evidence from hound publish with other IDs is named file name (ID). Re-running with unchanged files uploads nothing new.

docs.title: Run status and collector health
docs.text:
Every run writes a run record (start, end, outcome, checks passed and failed, publish counts) to <evidence root>/_status/<collector>.json. hound status shows the latest one per collector:

$ hound status --config examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml
COLLECTOR     LAST RUN (UTC)       OUTCOME    PASSED  FAILED  PUBLISHED
example-fake  2026-11-21 05:21:21  succeeded  3       1       0 sent, 0 skipped, 0 failed

AUDIT                  LAST RUN (UTC)       RUN ID            CHANGED  UNCHANGED  DRIFT
EXAMPLE-BASELINE-2026  2026-11-21 05:21:21  20261121T052121Z  0        4          0

The audit table, from the history files, appears once any run has published.

With --scope scope/, status also gives each programme's standing from the newest posture snapshot in <evidence root>/reports/: the level met, compliant of applicable with rows not assessed counted as not met (rounded down, so a part never reads 100%), and how many rows are not assessed. It is the same line the committee report gives, so you see the real position without opening a report or trusting CISO Assistant's own percentage. With no snapshot yet it says so and how to take one (hound report snapshot). It then lists the security exceptions that expire within 60 days.

$ hound status --config hound.yaml --scope scope/
...
Standing from the 2026-11 snapshot taken 2026-11-28 02:00 UTC:
- Example Essential Eight: Level met: none (level 0). Compliant 2 of 3 applicable (66%), counting rows not assessed as not met; assessed 3 of 4; not assessed: 1.

--json gives the same figures for an agent: collectors (each latest run, with its problems), audits, and with --scope standing (the snapshot's period and each programme's level_met, compliant, applicable, compliant_pct, assessed, total and not_assessed, or snapshot: null with a hint) and exceptions_due.

--json also gives the health an agent needs without a console: each collector's latest checks (the check and its outcome only, never an observation or evidence) and publish_failed; ciso_assistant (reachable, token accepted or rejected after one read of the folder list, token_expiry, which CISO Assistant's API does not give so it is null, and rejected_publishes across the latest runs); and manual_sources, each with its owner, last_evidence, due and state (overdue, due_soon from 14 days before, or ok). Without a token the connection is not checked and reachable is null. hound next reads the same data.

With target.health_control set, each run also uploads the record as "collector health" evidence (hound-health/<collector>) and links it to that applied control, so the security committee sees in CISO Assistant when each collector last ran.

docs.title: Scope files
docs.text:
A compliance repo declares the organisation's structure in CISO Assistant as files, so it changes through reviewed pull requests rather than clicks. hound scope validate checks the files offline, hound scope plan shows what they would change in CISO Assistant, and hound scope apply writes them.

A complete fictional compliance repo is in examples/compliance-repo/: copy it to a new private repository to start your own (see The review workflow). The schema is schemas/scope.schema.json; add # yaml-language-server: $schema=… to the top of each file for editor help.

compliance-repo/
  hound.yaml            the deployment config (docs/configuration.md)
  scope/
    setup.yaml          organisation, frameworks, other libraries, domains with their perimeters and systems
    controls.yaml       applied controls, each declared once
    audits/
      ex-e8-2026.yaml   one file per audit (compliance assessment)
    access.yaml         users with their roles, and teams (optional)
    settings.yaml       feature flags and general settings (optional)
    third-parties/
      example-cloud.yaml  one file per supplier or other third party (optional)
    capabilities.yaml   which system provides each mitigation (optional)
    ssp.yaml            one system security plan per programme (optional)
    metrics.yaml        metric definitions, instances and dashboards (optional)
  mappings/             which checks satisfy which requirements (docs/mapping-files.md)
  frameworks/           framework snapshots and custom library files
  documents/            the files that documents name, relative to the compliance repo (the scope folder's parent)
  manual-sources/       the hand-exported sources; their exports go outside the repo
  CLAUDE.md             instructions for an AI assistant
  .github/workflows/compliance.yml

The local CISO Assistant (make ca-up, the dev container and the functional tests) is seeded by applying this example scope, so every pull request exercises hound scope apply.

docs.title: Ref ID conventions
docs.text:
Every ref ID reads the same way whoever wrote it: its kind's prefix, then upper case letters, digits and hyphens. hound keeps one table of these conventions, used by every prompt and by hound scope validate.

Kind Prefix Example third party SUP- SUP-EXAMPLE solution SOL- SOL-EXAMPLE-HOSTING contract CTR- CTR-EXAMPLE-2026 system SYS- SYS-FIREWALL control AC- AC-BACKUP perimeter PER- PER-CORP supplier assessment EA- EA-SUP-EXAMPLE evidence plan row EV- EV-BACKUP-RESTORE customer CUS- CUS-EXAMPLE-PRIME

An audit has no prefix. An audit that runs in periods, as hound init writes it, is a series <CODE>-<FRAMEWORK>, such as EX-E8, or <CODE>-<FRAMEWORK>-<SYSTEM> for one system; each period reads <CODE>-<FRAMEWORK>-<INTERVAL>-<YEAR>FY[-<SYSTEM>], such as EX-E8-Q2-2027FY (Audit periods). An audit without a cycle reads <CODE>-<FRAMEWORK>-<YEAR>, such as EX-E8-2026.

A prompt for a ref ID (hound add system, hound add control, hound onboard <system>) prints the prefix as part of the prompt, such as Supplier ref_id: SUP-, and takes only the rest. The answer is upper-cased, and an answer with a space or any other character is asked again with the rule. An option such as --ref-id is taken in full when it has its prefix and is given the prefix when it has not. hound scope validate reports any other ref ID as scope.ref_id_convention, naming the kind, the prefix and the ref ID to rename it to.

docs.title: setup.yaml
docs.text: Key Meaning organisation.root_folder The existing folder the domains sit under. Default Global. organisation.audit_series Optional. The series each system's audit joins when no organisation-wide audit carries it, as hound init writes it: {ref_id: EX-E8, groups: ["1", "2"], cycle: {period: quarter, starts: "2026-10-01"}}. hound onboard then writes a system's audit as EX-E8-<SYSTEM> on that cycle (Audit periods). organisation.entity Optional. The organisation's own entity, which CISO Assistant creates itself as its main entity: name, and optional description, mission, country, currency and identifiers, as for a third party. hound scope apply only ever updates it in place, never creates or deletes it, and it carries no [hound scope] marker. Left out, the main entity is not read or changed. frameworks Each framework to load: urn (the framework URN), and library (a library URN from CISO Assistant's stored libraries) or file (a custom library file). snapshot names the framework snapshot made by hound framework snapshot, so groups and requirements can be checked offline; Paths are relative to setup.yaml. libraries Other libraries to load. A URN loads one CISO Assistant already stores, such as the mapping set between the Essential Eight and the Essentials. A map with urn and file uploads your own library from the repo, such as a custom risk matrix or threat catalogue, and snapshot names the snapshot made by hound library snapshot. Raise the file's version whenever you change it: CISO Assistant only takes a new version, so hound stops with library.version_not_bumped otherwise, and uploads and updates the library when the version goes up. See Risk matrices and threats. domains Folders. Each has a name, a description, its perimeters (or a single perimeter) and its systems. perimeter name, optional ref_id and description. system name, type (primary or supporting), optional ref_id, description, owner, parents (other systems by name), tags (per-framework labels such as essentials_domain: identity or cui: "true"), solution (the third-party solution that provides it, by ref_id) supplied_through (a reseller or managed service provider, by the third party's ref_id) data (the sensitive data it handles) ai (its AI register entry, when it is an AI system), objectives (security objectives on CISO Assistant's 0 to 4 scale, such as {confidentiality: 3, availability: 2}) and recovery (recovery objectives rto, rpo and mtd as durations such as 4h or 2d; see Business impact analyses). Objectives and recovery objectives are written only when the file declares them, so values set in CISO Assistant are otherwise kept. A system with either supplier key is registered only once those suppliers are approved: see Supplier approval. programmes Optional. The compliance programmes the reports are organised by, such as the Essential Eight and later AI6. Each has id (a lowercase slug such as essential-eight, unique), name, framework (a framework URN declared above, with a snapshot), groups (the implementation groups reported against, which must exist in the snapshot), audit (the ref_id of the audit, or audit series, of record) and optional group_by (parent, the default: requirements are grouped under their parent node, such as the Essential Eight strategy), and optional register, the register its reports summarise: of (ai_systems, the AI systems, or systems, every system) and by (the fields to count by: screening, use and oversight for AI systems, type for systems), such as register: { of: ai_systems, by: [screening, use] }. An audit belongs to at most one programme. Programmes create nothing in CISO Assistant and never appear in hound scope plan. hound programme list shows each one with its requirement counts per group and per parent node, from the snapshot alone, and its register's counts from the scope.

docs.title: AI systems
docs.text:
An AI system is a system with an ai block: its entry in the AI register. The entry is reviewed by pull request like the rest of the scope, dates included, and is written to CISO Assistant as filtering labels and as lines added to the asset's description, because CISO Assistant's custom fields are an Enterprise feature. The register is CISO Assistant's asset list filtered by the ai-system label, which its own Excel export can save. The AI governance primer explains the terms.

systems:
  - name: Example lead scoring
    type: supporting
    owner: sales@example.com
    solution: SOL-EXCRM-SCORING          # needed for a third-party AI system
    ai:
      screening: elevated                # normal, elevated or unacceptable: the National AI Centre's screening outcome
      screening_yes: [1, 5]              # the screening questions answered yes, by number; [] for none
      screened_on: "2026-03-02"
      registered_on: "2026-03-04"        # the rest are the National AI Centre register template's columns
      version: "2026.1"
      purpose: Focus the sales team on the leads most likely to buy.
      intended_uses: [Rank new leads each morning]
      limitations: Not for decisions about credit or pricing.
      misuse: Using scores to drop leads from some regions.
      data_sources: [CRM lead records (structured)]
      stakeholders: [Prospective customers, Sales team]
      use: third_party                   # built, customised or third_party
      oversight: human_on_the_loop       # human_in_the_loop, human_on_the_loop or human_out_of_loop
      oversight_note: The sales lead reviews a monthly sample of low scores and can switch scoring off.
      impact_assessment: approved        # not_started, in_progress, approved or not_required
      impact_assessed_on: "2026-03-20"   # only with approved
      in_use_from: "2026-04-01"          # left out while it is a pilot
      last_tested_on: "2026-03-25"
      # retired_on: "2026-10-31"         # when it stopped being used

screening, screening_yes, screened_on, use, oversight and oversight_note are required. The register check ai.register_complete fails an entry without purpose, intended_uses, limitations, misuse, data_sources, stakeholders, registered_on or impact_assessment. The template's Status follows from the dates (pilot, operational, decommissioned). AI governance traces each template column to its key.

In CISO Assistant the asset gets the labels ai-system, ai-screening-elevated, ai-use-third-party and ai-oversight-on-the-loop (and ai-retired once retired), and its description gains the entry in words, starting "AI register: elevated screening (yes to questions 1, 5), third party, human on the loop." hound scope validate reports ai.screening_disagrees (normal with a yes, or elevated with none), ai.impact_date_without_approval, ai.retired_before_use, and ai.solution_missing for a third-party AI system with no solution.

docs.title: Risk matrices and threats
docs.text:
Risk studies are rated on a risk matrix and name threats from a threat catalogue. Both come from CISO Assistant libraries. Many arrive with a framework: CISO Assistant loads a library's declared dependencies with it, so loading the Essential Eight also loads intuitem's Common Catalog of threats (and its policy and reference controls catalogue). The ASD Essentials library declares none. hound scope plan shows what a framework brings in a brings line, read from its snapshot. Declare only what does not arrive with a framework.

A built-in matrix, such as urn:intuitem:risk:library:critical_risk_matrix_5x5, is a URN under libraries. Your own matrix or threats go in a library file under libraries/ in the repo, listed with its URN and file:

libraries:
  - urn: urn:intuitem:risk:library:critical_risk_matrix_5x5
  - urn: urn:example:risk:library:example-risk
    file: ../libraries/example-risk.yaml
    snapshot: ../libraries/example-risk.json

Check the file offline, then snapshot it so risk studies are checked by level name and threat without CISO Assistant:

$ hound library validate libraries/example-risk.yaml
valid: 1 risk matrix, 2 threats
$ hound library snapshot libraries/example-risk.yaml --out libraries/example-risk.json

hound library validate reports library.matrix_urn_invalid (a matrix URN not of the form urn:<packager>:risk:matrix:<id>), library.matrix_level_gap (an explicit level id that is not its position, counting from 0), library.matrix_grid_shape (not one grid row per probability level with one cell per impact level) and library.matrix_grid_unknown_risk (a cell that is not a risk level). hound scope validate runs the same checks on every library file the setup lists.

CISO Assistant only takes a changed library when its version goes up. If the file differs from the one it stores at the same version, hound scope plan and hound scope apply stop with library.version_not_bumped. Raise the version, and the apply uploads the file and updates the loaded library.

docs.title: controls.yaml
docs.text: controls lists each applied control once, because CISO Assistant treats an applied control as a reusable object serving many requirements across frameworks: ref_id (the stable key), name, and optionally description, domain (left out for the global domain), owner, status (to_do, in_progress, on_hold, active, degraded, deprecated), priority ("1" to "4"), category, eta, systems, reference_control (a URN), documents (ids of documents declared in audit files) and responsible_entity (consumer, shared, outsourced_service_provider, cloud_service_provider or not_applicable: who implements the control, for the SSP annex only; hound never writes it to CISO Assistant. Without it the annex infers Shared when the control covers a system a supplier's solution provides, and Consumer otherwise).

docs.title: access.yaml
docs.text:
Who can do what in CISO Assistant, so access changes are reviewed as pull requests and a rebuilt instance gets the same access. The file is optional; without it hound neither reads nor changes users.

  • users: email (the key, compared without case), first_name, last_name, active (default true), and service_account for an account that is not a person: publish (or true) for the collector runner, apply for an account that applies the scope.
  • teams: name, description, domain (left out for the root folder), leader and members by email, and email, the team's address for CISO Assistant's task reminders. A team with an email and no leader or members is an owner contact: it is reminded and has no login, so it holds no role (Manual evidence).
  • roles: a role on a domain (or the root folder, Global, for the whole organisation), for users and for every leader and member of teams. Built-in roles are administrator, domain_manager, analyst, approver, auditor (CISO Assistant calls it Reader) and baseline_reader; list user groups you created in CISO Assistant under custom_roles to use them as roles.

hound never sets or reads a password and never creates an API token: a key such as password or api_token anywhere in the file is an error (scope.secret_in_file) whose message never shows the value. A new user gets CISO Assistant's own invitation and sets their password there. Validation also reports duplicate or malformed emails, unknown roles, domains, users and teams, and any domain without an active user who can approve (an approver, domain manager or administrator on it or on Global), because risk acceptances and period sign-offs need one.

CISO Assistant gives a role on a domain through membership of that domain's built-in user group for the role ("Example Pty Ltd - Approver"); its API lets no one create role assignments directly. So each user's roles, given directly and through teams, become one field of the user, such as roles: BI-RL-ADM on Global, BI-RL-APP on Example Pty Ltd, and scope apply sets the user's groups to exactly those. A role removed from the file is taken away on the next apply, and the plan shows it as an update of the user (roles: … → …). A custom role is a user group you made in CISO Assistant on that domain, named as custom_roles lists it. A user removed from the file stays in CISO Assistant: scope apply --prune deactivates them (never deletes, so their history stays attributable) and leaves their groups as they were. Users the file does not list keep their groups.

scope plan ends with an Access review: active people who have not turned on multi-factor authentication, and each role a publish service account holds beyond analyst, however it was given (runner-token.sh starts the runner's account in the administrators group; declare it here to narrow it). CISO Assistant requires MFA for everyone or no one: set enforce_mfa: true in settings.yaml and each person turns it on at their next sign-in. Its API reports who has (has_mfa_enabled) but cannot turn it on for a person, so the access review lists anyone who has not yet.

docs.title: settings.yaml
docs.text:
CISO Assistant's feature flags (which modules people see) and general settings (instance-wide behaviour such as enforce_mfa), by name. The file is optional, and only the settings it names change: hound never resets a setting the file leaves out.

feature_flags:
  tprm: true       # third-party records
  dora: false      # an EU regulation the organisation is not subject to
general:
  enforce_mfa: true
  • feature_flags: each flag true or false.
  • general: each setting's value as CISO Assistant stores it: a boolean, a number, text or a list.

Names are checked offline against the settings snapshot of the CISO Assistant release the stack pins (ciso-assistant-settings.json, with each flag's default); an unknown name is an error (settings.flag_unknown, settings.setting_unknown) whose hint lists the valid ones. Two flags exist in the release but its API only offers them when a backend setting the stack leaves off is on: chat_mode (ENABLE_CHAT) and infra_config_management (ENABLE_INFRA_CONFIG_MANAGEMENT). Naming either is an error (settings.flag_gated). A secret setting such as openai_api_key is an error (scope.secret_in_file): set it in CISO Assistant itself. Turning off a module the scope still uses is an error too: compliance: false would hide the audits the scope declares (settings.feature_disabled_in_use). Upgrading CISO Assistant means refreshing the snapshot, and the functional tests compare it with the pinned release.

scope plan lists each named setting whose value differs (| Update | feature_flag | tprm | value: true → false |). scope plan --show-unmanaged adds an Unmanaged settings section: every flag and general setting the file does not name, with its current value, to help decide what to manage. Settings carry no marker and are never deleted, so --prune leaves them alone.

docs.title: third-parties/<entity>.yaml
docs.text:
The supplier register, one file per supplier or other third party, so a new supplier or a renewed contract is a reviewed pull request. How to move a supplier spreadsheet here with your agent, and keep it current: third-parties.md. Each file is a CISO Assistant entity with the solutions it provides to the organisation, the contracts covering them and, optionally, its representatives. The folder is optional; without it hound neither reads nor changes third parties.

ref_id: SUP-EXCLOUD
name: Example Cloud Pty Ltd
description: Hosts the customer portal.
mission: Managed cloud hosting.
country: AU                  # ISO 3166-1 alpha-2
currency: AUD                # ISO 4217
domain: Example Pty Ltd      # left out for the root folder
dependency: 3                # 0-4: how much we depend on it
penetration: 2               # 0-4: how far it reaches into our systems
maturity: 3                  # 1-4: its security maturity
trust: 3                     # 1-4: how far we trust it
identifiers:
  LEI: EXAMPLE0000000000000
solutions:
  - ref_id: SOL-EXCLOUD-HOST
    name: Managed hosting
    criticality: 3           # 1-4
contracts:
  - ref_id: CTR-EXCLOUD-2026
    name: Hosting agreement 2026
    status: active           # draft, active, expired or terminated
    start: "2026-01-01"
    end: "2026-12-31"
    annual_expense: 12000
    currency: AUD
    solutions: [SOL-EXCLOUD-HOST]
representatives:
  - email: account.manager@example.com
    first_name: Sam
    last_name: Example
    role: Account manager
  • The entity: ref_id and name, and optionally description, mission, country, currency, parent (another third party's ref_id, for a subsidiary), domain, the four levels CISO Assistant uses as defaults for its stakeholder assessments (dependency, penetration, maturity, trust), and identifiers (legal identifiers by kind, such as LEI, VAT or ABN). CISO Assistant keeps identifiers on the entity, not on its contracts.
  • solutions: what the entity provides, each with ref_id, name, and optionally description and criticality. A level or criticality the file leaves out is left as CISO Assistant holds it (its default on a new supplier), so a drafted supplier with levels still to decide plans no change after it is applied.
  • contracts: each with ref_id, name, status, and optionally description, start and end (yyyy-MM-dd), annual_expense, currency and solutions (the entity's own, by ref_id). A contract sits in the entity's domain.
  • representatives: people at the entity, by email, with optional first_name, last_name, role and phone. They are personal data, so keep them in CISO Assistant instead unless the compliance repo is private and access-controlled. hound never gives a representative a login.

Validation reports a country or currency code CISO Assistant does not accept (supplier.country_invalid, supplier.currency_invalid; the lists come from the pinned release), a level outside its range (supplier.level_invalid), a contract that ends before it starts (supplier.contract_dates_invalid), a contract covering a solution the entity does not provide (supplier.solution_unknown), a repeated ref_id or email, an unknown parent or domain, and an active contract whose end date has passed (supplier.contract_lapsed): renew it and record the new end date, or set it to expired or terminated. Turning off the tprm or contracts feature flag in settings.yaml while third parties or contracts are declared is an error. CISO Assistant ships with contracts off, so set contracts: true in settings.yaml to see contracts in its interface.

Objects are matched by ref_id (representatives by email), and the organisation's own entity, which CISO Assistant makes itself, is never touched. scope plan shows a renewed contract's new end date as a one-field update.

docs.title: Sensitive data
docs.text:
A solution and a system may list the sensitive data they handle, so a supplier handling data it is not approved for is reported and the list a prime or an auditor asks for comes from the repo. The list is framework-neutral:

solutions:
  - ref_id: SOL-EXCLOUD-HOST
    name: Managed hosting
    data:
      - kind: cui                       # cui, pii, export_controlled or classified
        detail: CUI//SP-CTI             # which: needed for export_controlled and classified
        role: stores                    # stores, processes, transmits or protects
        authority:                      # on a solution only: what approves it
          name: FedRAMP Moderate equivalent
          evidence: documents/suppliers/example-cloud-fedramp.pdf
          expires: "2027-06-30"
Kind Australian example US example cui Information a US prime marks as CUI under a subcontract Controlled technical information, CUI//SP-CTI pii Personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 Personal information under a state privacy law export_controlled Technology on the Defence and Strategic Goods List (DSGL) Technical data under ITAR or EAR classified Security-classified information under the PSPF (PROTECTED; OFFICIAL: Sensitive is not classified but can be recorded here) Classified national security information

Validation reports a system that handles a kind through its solution, or through supplied_through when it names no solution, whose data does not list that kind (data.supplier_not_authorised); an authority past expires (data.authority_expired); and export-controlled or classified data with no detail (data.detail_missing).

The first two are warnings: findings about the organisation, not mistakes in the files. They are printed by scope validate (and --json gives them "severity": "warning"), scope plan and scope apply, and listed in the weekly review (hound review) every week until they are fixed, but they block nothing. Record the truth while the data moves or the authority is renewed; never hide it to get a clean validate.

scope apply uses CISO Assistant's own features only: each kind is a filtering label data-<kind> (data-cui, data-export-controlled; CISO Assistant's labels take letters, digits, _ and -) on the solution's and the system's records, and each solution's description ends with its data and authorities. hound supplier list --data cui prints each supplier's solution handling a kind, with its role, authority, evidence, expiry and the systems that hold it, as Markdown for a prime or --json for an agent.

hound does not decide whether information is CUI, export controlled or classified: that is the owner's call with the prime, the contract and, where it applies, the export licence. It records what they decided and checks the suppliers against it.

docs.title: Supplier reviews and tiers
docs.text:
forced_tier:                 # optional: the tier the organisation decides, whatever CISO Assistant computes
  tier: critical             # critical, important, standard or low-impact
  reason: Holds staff personal data.
assessments:
  - ref_id: EA-EXCLOUD
    name: Example Cloud review
    solutions: [SOL-EXCLOUD-HOST]
    perimeter: Corporate IT    # a perimeter of setup.yaml, in the assessment's domain
    domain: Example Pty Ltd    # default: the entity's domain
    due_date: "2026-06-30"
    criticality: 3             # 1-4
    questionnaire: urn:example:risk:framework:example-baseline   # a framework of setup.yaml
    groups: ["1"]              # the questionnaire's implementation groups
    review_every: 12 months    # optional: "N months" or "N years"
  • assessments are CISO Assistant's entity assessments: hound sets up the review (its name, solutions, perimeter, due date and criticality) and, when it creates one with a questionnaire, CISO Assistant creates the questionnaire's audit with it. Answers, the expiry date and the tier stay CISO Assistant's. The conclusion is approved in this repo: hound approve records it under the assessment's conclusions, and hound scope apply writes it to CISO Assistant. A review with no conclusion in the file is left as CISO Assistant holds it, so one concluded there still counts.
  • conclusions lists the reviews a person concluded: review (the review's key, as below), result (ok, warning or blocker), by and on (who concluded it and the day). Write them with hound approve, in a terminal, not by hand:
    conclusions:
      - review: ENA-EXCLOUD-2026-03
        result: ok
        by: Sam Example
        on: "2026-04-02"
  • A contract can carry approved_by and approved_on: who approved the supplier by making the contract active with hound approve, and when. They are this repo's record and are not sent to CISO Assistant.
  • With review_every, each review is keyed <ref_id>-<yyyy-MM> by its due date, and once today reaches a review's due date the plan opens the next one, a cycle later. Without it, the review is the one object <ref_id>.
  • forced_tier needs a reason. hound never writes the tier; the plan lists a tier in CISO Assistant that differs from the forced one.

Validation reports an assessment naming a solution the entity does not provide (supplier.solution_unknown), an unknown perimeter, domain or questionnaire, a criticality outside 1 to 4, review_every without a due_date (supplier.review_without_due_date), a conclusion naming a review that is not one of the assessment's (supplier.conclusion_review_unknown) and a forced tier without a reason (supplier.forced_tier_reason_missing).

docs.title: Customer contracts and flow-down
docs.text:
A prime you supply is declared like a supplier, in its own file under scope/third-parties/, with CUS- in place of SUP- and customer: true on each of its contracts. The contract's obligations list the clauses it imposes:

ref_id: CUS-EXAMPLE-PRIME
name: Example Prime Pty Ltd
domain: Example Pty Ltd
contracts:
  - ref_id: CTR-PRIME-PARTS
    name: Machined parts subcontract
    status: active
    customer: true
    obligations:
      - clause: DFARS 252.204-7012
        framework: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:nist-sp-800-171-rev2
        level: "2"
        data: [cui]
        flow_down: true
      - clause: Essential Eight maturity level 2
        framework: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:essential-eight-2023
        level: "2"
  • clause is the clause as the contract names it. framework (a URN in setup.yaml) and level say what it requires; hound programme list then names, under each programme with that framework, the customer that requires it.
  • flow_down: true means your own suppliers must carry the clause. data limits it to suppliers whose solutions handle those kinds of sensitive data; with no data, every supplier contract must carry it.
  • A supplier contract lists the clauses it carries under its own obligations, by clause alone. hound scope validate warns with contract.flow_down_missing for each supplier contract that lacks one it owes (a finding that joins the weekly review and blocks nothing), also warns with contract.framework_unknown for a framework setup.yaml does not load (a requirement no programme tracks yet: add the framework and a programme for it), and reports contract.flow_down_invalid for flow_down on a supplier contract.
  • hound supplier list --data cui shows each supplier's flowed-down clauses as carried or missing: the answer to a prime's supply-chain questionnaire.

docs.title: Supplier approval
docs.text:
A supplier is approved when its latest concluded assessment is concluded ok, that conclusion has not expired, no later review is past its due date without a conclusion, and it has an active contract. A person approves in this repo with hound approve (in a terminal; an agent or a pipe is refused), which makes the contract active and records the review's conclusion in the supplier's file. What the file records counts before it is applied, and wins over what CISO Assistant holds for the same review, so one hound scope apply can write the supplier, its conclusion and the system together. scope plan and scope apply check this before planning:

  • A system not yet registered whose supplier (its solution's entity, or supplied_through) is not approved is refused with system.supplier_not_approved and the reason, such as "no concluded assessment", and nothing is applied. Approve the supplier and conclude its review as ok with hound approve, then plan again.
  • A registered system whose supplier is no longer approved stays registered; the plan lists it under Suppliers as supplier.approval_lapsed, for the security committee.
  • A tier that differs from forced_tier is listed under Suppliers as supplier.tier_differs. The JSON plan has both as suppliers.

docs.title: capabilities.yaml
docs.text:
Which system provides each mitigation of one framework, decided with hound onboard environment. Optional.

framework: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:essential-eight-2023
mitigations:
  - mitigation: ac              # the last part of the mitigation's node URN
    provided_by: system         # system, manual or gap
    systems: [Example app control]
    supplier: SUP-EXAPPCTL      # optional, a third party's ref_id
    owner: it@example.com       # optional
    evidence: profile           # optional: collector, profile or manual
    route: example-app-control  # optional: the collector or profile
    approved_by: GRC lead       # required: the role that approved it
    approved_on: "2026-11-23"
    reason: Application control is enforced by the third-party product, not Intune.
    signals:
      - "Microsoft Graph: licence SPE_E3 (Microsoft 365 E3) is subscribed"

The map only decides which system answers each requirement. Results stay in each system's own audit; in every other system's audit of the same framework, the mitigation's requirements stay open (not_assessed) with provided_by naming the providing system, and the observation names its audit; each closes when that system's audit shows the requirement met. Validation reports a framework setup.yaml does not load (capability.framework_unknown), a mitigation decided twice (scope.duplicate), not in the framework (capability.mitigation_unknown) or not decided at all (capability.decision_missing), a missing approver (capability.approver_missing), a system decision with no systems (capability.systems_missing) and an unknown supplier. A system named but not declared yet is not an error: it is waiting to be onboarded. hound scope plan lists each gap under "Capability gaps" (JSON gaps): the mitigation and the requirements no system's audit answers. It lists each requirement an audit leaves open for another system under "Open dependencies" (JSON dependencies): the audit, the requirement, the system that meets it, that system's audit if it has one, and the result there (as the scope declares it, "from collectors" when that audit's mapping computes it, or "no audit yet").

docs.title: evidence-plan.yaml
docs.text:
How each control's evidence arrives, from whom and how often. Optional. The guide is Manual evidence.

Key Meaning grc_team The team (in access.yaml) that receives and reviews evidence, for rows that do not name their own. evidence One row per control: ref_id (EV-), control, requirements (optional), method (automated, manual or hybrid), collector (a collector in hound.yaml, for automated and hybrid rows), owner (a team, for manual and hybrid rows), grc_team, every (3 months, 6 months or 12 months) and runbook (a Markdown file in the repo).

Each row becomes an evidence item labelled method: and collector:; each manual and hybrid row also becomes a recurring task for the owner and the GRC team, with the runbook as its description. Problems: evidence_plan.owner_missing, evidence_plan.every_missing, evidence_plan.runbook_missing, evidence_plan.runbook_file_missing, evidence_plan.collector_missing, evidence_plan.collector_unknown, evidence_plan.team_unknown, evidence_plan.control_unknown and evidence_plan.owner_contact_has_role.

docs.title: ssp.yaml
docs.text:
One system security plan (SSP) per programme. Optional. hound ssp build --programme <id> assembles the plan from one read of CISO Assistant and the repo, and writes nothing. It prints the plan in the layout of NIST SP 800-18 Rev 1 (ssp.md); --json gives every value with its source (ciso_assistant with the object, or repo with the file and line), so each one can be traced.

Key Meaning programme The programme's id from setup.yaml. One plan per programme. profile The controls annex: ism (ISM controls grouped by Essential Eight strategy) or nist-800-171 (CMMC, s17). The layout is always NIST SP 800-18 Rev 1, which also meets ISM-0041. system_name, version The system's name as the plan gives it, and the plan's version. classification, operational_status, system_type SP 800-18 sections 2, 7 and 8: the highest classification the system processes (such as OFFICIAL), whether it is operational, under development or being modified, and whether it is a major application or a general support system. Optional; shown as - when absent. perimeter The boundary: a perimeter in setup.yaml. The inventory is the systems the audits on that perimeter cover, as CISO Assistant holds them, with their owners. roles system_owner, authorising_official and security_contact, each a user's email or a team from access.yaml. All three are required. documents Boundary and network diagrams, data flows, policies and procedures, by document id from an audit. sections The parts that cannot be generated, as Markdown files in the repo (paths relative to the folder that holds scope/): purpose, environment, management and laws_and_policies, all required. See ssp.md for where each one goes in the plan.

Each requirement row gets a status from its result: compliant is Implemented, partially_compliant Partially implemented, not_applicable Not applicable, and non_compliant or not_assessed Planned when a linked control has an ETA, otherwise Not implemented. Its statement is the linked controls' descriptions in ref order, then the observation; the responsible party is the controls' owners. A row in place with no statement, a row in place or planned with no owner, and a row not applicable with no justification (its observation) are gaps: listed first, in --json, and fatal with --strict (exit 1). A row not yet implemented is not a gap: hound ssp poam --programme <id> lists it, one line per linked control with its owner, ETA and status.

External services are the solutions the scope links the boundary's systems to (solution: in setup.yaml), with their suppliers as CISO Assistant holds them. Controls and requirement rows come from the programme's audit of record. Problems: ssp.programme_unknown, ssp.perimeter_unknown, ssp.role_missing, ssp.role_unknown, ssp.document_unknown, ssp.section_missing, and scope.duplicate for a second plan for the same programme.

docs.title: risks/<study>.yaml
docs.text:
One file per risk study (CISO Assistant's risk assessment) and its scenarios. Ratings, treatment and justification are proposed and reviewed in a pull request like any other change; accepting a risk and approving it stays with the Approver in CISO Assistant. Ratings use the matrix's level names from its library snapshot. CISO Assistant computes the risk levels, so they are never written.

ref_id: EX-RISK-2026
name: Example Pty Ltd risk register 2026
domain: Example Pty Ltd
perimeter: Corporate IT                  # optional
matrix: urn:example:risk:matrix:example-4x4
status: in_progress                      # planned, in_progress, in_review, done or deprecated
authors: [it@example.com]
reviewers: [ceo@example.com]
eta: "2026-12-31"
scenarios:
  - ref_id: R-01
    name: Ransomware encrypts the file shares
    systems: [Example 365]               # impacted systems, by name
    threats: [THR-02]                    # by URN or ref_id, from a library snapshot
    existing_controls: [AC-BACKUP]       # by ref_id from controls.yaml
    planned_controls: [AC-MFA]
    current: {probability: Possible, impact: Major}
    residual: {probability: Unlikely, impact: Major}
    # inherent: {probability: Likely, impact: Severe}   # when CISO Assistant's inherent risk flag is on
    treatment: mitigate                  # open (the default), mitigate, accept, avoid or transfer
    justification: Backups are restored and tested each month.

-- (or leaving a rating out) means not rated. hound scope validate reports risk.matrix_unknown (no library snapshot holds the matrix), risk.level_unknown (a level name the matrix does not have, with its line), risk.residual_above_current (treatment can only lower a risk, as CISO Assistant's own consistency check says), risk.system_unknown, risk.threat_unknown, risk.control_unknown, risk.domain_unknown, risk.perimeter_unknown, duplicate ref_ids, and the warning risk.planned_control_active for a planned control that controls.yaml says is already active.

hound scope plan shows a rating change by level name, such as current_probability: Likely → Possible, so a reviewer reads what changed without the matrix to hand.

docs.title: Risk acceptances
docs.text: A scenario with treatment: accept asks CISO Assistant for a risk acceptance, under the ref_id ACC-<study>-<scenario> with the scenario's justification. hound never sets its state: the Approver accepts or rejects it in CISO Assistant, and hound scope plan shows what they decided.

docs.title: exceptions.yaml
docs.text:
Security exceptions: a known gap the organisation lives with for a time, such as an application that cannot use single sign-on until its upgrade. The request is written and reviewed in the repo; only an approver in CISO Assistant approves it, so the decision keeps its separation of duties.

exceptions:
  - ref_id: EXC-01
    name: Legacy finance app without MFA
    description: The finance app cannot use single sign-on until its upgrade.
    domain: Example Pty Ltd
    severity: medium                     # undefined, info, low, medium, high or critical
    owners: [it@example.com]
    expiration_date: "2027-03-31"
    observation: Sign-in is limited to the office network.
    systems: [Example 365]               # by name, from setup.yaml
    controls: [AC-MFA]                   # by ref_id, from controls.yaml
    scenarios: [EX-RISK-2026/R-01]       # <study ref_id>/<scenario ref_id>
    requirements:                        # audit rows the exception covers
      - audit: EXAMPLE-BASELINE-2026
        requirement: EX-1.1
  • A status in the file is an error (scope.approval_not_configurable). Apply the exception as a request; its approver decides in CISO Assistant.
  • hound scope validate reports exception.domain_unknown, exception.system_unknown, exception.control_unknown, exception.scenario_unknown, exception.audit_unknown and duplicate ref_ids.
  • hound scope plan lists each exception and risk acceptance with its CISO Assistant status (draft, in_review, approved, rejected, resolved, expired or deprecated), then what to renew or close: exception.expiring (an approved one that expires within 60 days) and exception.expired_but_approved.
  • hound status --config hound.yaml --scope scope lists, offline, the exceptions whose declared expiry is within 60 days or past.
  • When a check fails on a row an approved, unexpired exception covers, hound run names the exception in the row's observation, such as "Covered by security exception EXC-01 (Legacy finance app without MFA), approved until 2027-03-31." The result itself stays non-compliant: an exception explains a gap, it does not close it.

docs.title: bia/<bia>.yaml
docs.text:
One file per business impact analysis (BIA): how long each system can be down before the impact grows, on a risk matrix's impact scale. The continuity owner proposes it in a pull request; hound scope apply writes it to CISO Assistant's BIA, its asset assessments and their escalation thresholds, and CISO Assistant draws the impact-over-time chart.

ref_id: EX-BIA-2026
name: Example Pty Ltd business impact analysis 2026
domain: Example Pty Ltd
perimeter: Corporate IT                  # optional
matrix: urn:example:risk:matrix:example-4x4
version: "1.0"
status: in_progress                      # planned, in_progress, in_review, done or deprecated
authors: [it@example.com]
due_date: "2026-12-31"
assessments:
  - system: Example 365                  # one assessment per system, by name
    dependencies: [Example laptops]      # systems it needs to run
    controls: [AC-BACKUP]                # controls that keep it running, by ref_id
    recovery: {documented: true, tested: false, targets_met: false}
    observation: Mail and files stop when Example 365 is down.
    thresholds:                          # in ascending time
      - {after: 4h, impact: Minor, justification: Staff use phones.}
      - {after: 1d, impact: Major, qualifications: [Reputation], justification: Customers notice.}
      - {after: 3d, impact: Severe}

Durations are a whole number and a unit: m, h, d or w. impact is an impact level name from the matrix's library snapshot; qualifications are CISO Assistant's qualification terms by name, such as Reputation. hound scope validate reports bia.system_duplicate (one assessment per system), bia.threshold_order (thresholds must be unique and ascend), bia.impact_unknown, bia.system_unknown, bia.control_unknown, bia.matrix_unknown, bia.domain_unknown, bia.perimeter_unknown, scope.duration_invalid, and the warning bia.impact_falls for an impact lower than an earlier one, because CISO Assistant carries the highest impact forward. In a plan, an assessment is keyed bia/system and a threshold bia/system/after, such as EX-BIA-2026/Example 365/1d.

docs.title: Recovery flags from checks
docs.text:
A recovery flag can come from evidence instead of a hand-set value: name the checks that prove it with documented_by, tested_by or targets_met_by.

    recovery: {documented: true, tested_by: [backup.restore_tested]}

After collecting, each hound run sets the flag from every collector's latest results: true only when every named check passed, false when any failed or has no result. It writes only when the value changes, and links the checks' evidence to the asset assessment when CISO Assistant already holds it (evidence a run published for a requirement); evidence it does not hold is named in a recovery.evidence_not_published warning, and the flag is still set. The run's JSON lists each flag it set under recovery, with why. hound scope plan leaves such a flag alone, and an asset assessment that hound scope apply has not created yet waits for it. A flag cannot be both set by hand and named by checks (scope.result_conflict), and a check is named by its id (scope.value_invalid if it is not one).

docs.title: metrics.yaml
docs.text:
What the organisation measures, its targets and owners, and the dashboards that show it, written to CISO Assistant's metrology (metric definitions, metric instances, dashboards and widgets). A definition says what is measured; an instance measures it in one domain, how often, against what target and for whom; a dashboard lays widgets on a 12-column grid. Values are never declared here: runs or people enter them.

definitions:
  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA-COVERED
    name: Accounts with MFA
    unit: users                          # count, users, bytes, percentage, score, days, hours or events per second
    direction: higher_is_better          # higher_is_better, lower_is_better or none (the default for a number)
  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA-TOTAL
    name: Staff accounts
    unit: users
  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA
    name: MFA coverage
    unit: percentage
    direction: higher_is_better
    decimals: 1                          # 0 to 6
    frequency: monthly                   # 15min, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly or yearly
    target: 95
    formula:                             # computed each period from other definitions' instances in the same domain
      expression: covered / total * 100  # CEL
      inputs:
        - {key: covered, definition: EX-MET-MFA-COVERED, combine: sum}   # one, sum, avg, min, max or count
        - {key: total, definition: EX-MET-MFA-TOTAL, combine: sum}
  - ref_id: EX-MET-POLICY
    name: Policy maturity
    levels: [Missing, Drafted, Approved, Reviewed]   # qualitative: worst first
    target: Approved
instances:
  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA-CORP
    name: MFA coverage
    definition: EX-MET-MFA               # by ref_id, or a library definition by URN
    domain: Example Pty Ltd              # the root folder when left out
    grace_days: 5                        # days after a period ends before the value is late
    owners: [it@example.com]
    controls: [AC-MFA]                   # the applied controls it tells about
dashboards:
  - ref_id: EX-DASH-COMMITTEE
    name: Security committee
    domain: Example Pty Ltd
    widgets:                             # each found again by its title
      - {title: MFA coverage, metric: EX-MET-MFA-CORP, chart: line, time_range: last_year}
      - {title: Baseline progress, audit: EXAMPLE-BASELINE-2026, builtin: progress, x: 6}
      - {title: How to read this, text: Each figure is collected monthly., y: 2, width: 12, height: 1}

A definition is quantitative with a unit or qualitative with levels, never both. An instance's frequency and target fall back to its definition's, as CISO Assistant copies them.
