A widget shows one thing: a metric instance, a builtin metric of one audit, risk_study or domain (such as progress, total_scenarios or total_controls), or text. chart is kpi_card (the default), donut, pie, bar, line, area, gauge, sparkline, small_multiples, table or text; time_range defaults to last_30_days and aggregation to none; x, y, width and height default to 0, 0, 6 and 2, and x + width is at most 12.

hound scope validate reports metric.duplicate, dashboard.duplicate, metric.kind_ambiguous (a unit and levels), metric.unit_unknown (a warning: add another unit to CISO Assistant's terminologies first), metric.levels_unordered, metric.decimals_invalid, metric.target_invalid, metric.input_unknown, metric.input_invalid, metric.input_outside_domain (an input with no instance in the formula's domain), metric.definition_unknown, metric.control_unknown, metric.domain_unknown, dashboard.widget_invalid, dashboard.widget_duplicate, dashboard.metric_unknown, dashboard.builtin_unknown, dashboard.object_unknown and dashboard.widget_outside_grid. In a plan, a widget is keyed dashboard/title, such as EX-DASH-COMMITTEE/MFA coverage. The Metrics and dashboards guide walks through adding one; the example is examples/compliance-repo/scope/metrics.yaml.

docs.title: Metrics filled in by runs
docs.text:
An instance with source: hound is filled in by each hound run, so a trend is measured every period without anyone typing numbers.

  - ref_id: EX-MET-MFA-PASS-CORP
    name: MFA checks passing
    definition: EX-MET-PASS                # a definition with a unit, usually percentage, and no formula
    domain: Example Pty Ltd
    frequency: monthly
    source: hound
    measure: check_pass_rate               # see the table below
    checks: [identity.mfa.*]               # check ids, or every check below one
measure The percentage it records check_pass_rate Of the checks' latest results, the share that pass. Not applicable results are left out; partial and error do not pass. requirements_compliant_pct Of the requirements of the audit (by ref_id) in CISO Assistant, the share that are compliant. Not applicable rows are left out; not assessed rows count against it. evidence_freshness_pct Of the latest results of the checks (every check when none are named), the share collected in the last 7 days. collector_success_rate Of the collectors the run ran, the share that succeeded.

After collecting, each run measures every such instance from every collector's latest results and records one value for the instance's current period (its frequency's calendar period in UTC, as CISO Assistant counts it). A later run in the same period replaces that value; a value equal to the one CISO Assistant holds, to two decimals, is not sent. The run's JSON lists each value it recorded under metrics, with why. An instance hound scope apply has not created yet is named in a metric.not_applied warning, and a measure with nothing to count (no matching results) in metric.nothing_measured; neither records a value. --dry-run and --no-publish measure nothing.

hound scope validate reports metric.measure_invalid (a measure without the checks or audit it reads, a check pattern that is not one, a measure on a definition with levels, or a measure without source: hound), metric.audit_unknown, and scope.result_conflict for source: hound on a definition with a formula, because CISO Assistant computes those itself and refuses values typed in.

docs.title: One audit per system, and one per shared platform
docs.text:
Give each system its own audit, rather than one audit for the whole organisation. Each audit then shows that system's gaps, and what has and has not been assessed is plain to see. Name it after the system and the framework, such as EX-LAPTOPS-E8, and list the one system under systems.

  • A shared platform gets its own audit. A cloud tenancy or hosting platform that other systems run on is audited once, as a system of its own. A system that relies on it for a requirement names it in that row's provided_by: the row stays open, and hound scope plan lists it under "Open dependencies" until the platform's audit shows the requirement met.
  • Answer each piece of evidence once. A document is declared in one audit and linked in every audit of the same framework that shares one of its systems. A collector's run feeds every audit that a targets entry in hound.yaml names, so one backup test or admin review reaches several audits. A manual source is attested once and its checks reach each audit whose mapping uses them. Prefer a specific source per check (the restore test, the privileged-account review) over one blanket attestation.
  • An organisation-wide audit only when organisation-wide sources feed it, such as governance documents and policies. It is not a summary of the system audits.
Key Meaning ref_id, name The audit's stable key and title. framework, groups The framework URN and the implementation groups it assesses, such as ["1", "2"] for Essential Eight ML2. domain, perimeter Where the audit sits. eta, due_date, authors, reviewers Optional audit fields (dates as YYYY-MM-DD). field_visibility Optional, per field: {auditor: edit\|read\|hidden, respondent: …}.result,observation and evidences must stay edit for the auditor, because CISO Assistant silently ignores writes to fields the writer can only read. systems The systems in scope, by name. They are written to the audit's assets in CISO Assistant; systems added there by hand are kept until the scope names some. documents Static evidence such as policies and reports: id, name, files (paths or globs, relative to the compliance repo, the scope folder's parent), systems and requirements it supports. A document is linked to the rows it cites in its own audit, and in every other audit of the same framework that shares one of its systems. controls The applied controls this audit relies on, by ref_id, each with the requirements it supports in this framework. assessments Hand-written results for requirements no check covers: ref (or urn), status (to_do, in_progress, in_review, done), result, observation, and provided_by (the systems that meet it, when another system does: the row stays open, never not_applicable, and hound scope plan lists it under "Open dependencies" with that system's audit and its result there). cycle, sign_offs Optional, for an audit that runs in periods: cycle: {period: month\|quarter, starts: YYYY-MM-DD, close: sign_off\|auto} and sign_offs: [{period, by, date}]. See Audit periods. unlisted Required. What happens to in-group requirements the file does not list: {result: not_assessed}, or {result: not_applicable, reason: …} for an audit scoped to one system. Nothing is marked not applicable silently. It is applied only with --config, because the deployment's mappings say which rows a run computes, and those are left alone. no_evidence Optional. What a row the file leaves not_assessed (a hand-written row still to do, or the unlisted rule) is applied as: non_compliant (the default), with the observation "No evidence yet: …", or not_assessed to opt out. See No evidence is not compliance.

A requirement is named by its ref_id, or by its URN when the value starts with urn: (needed when a framework repeats a ref).

docs.title: No evidence is not compliance
docs.text:
CISO Assistant's compliance percentage, on an audit's page and in Compliance > Overview, counts compliant rows (and half of each partially compliant row) over the compliant, partially compliant and non-compliant rows. Rows not applicable and rows not assessed are both left out. An audit whose only results are a few passing automated checks, with every manual row still waiting, therefore reads 100% compliant, however many rows nobody has assessed.

So hound applies a row that waits for evidence as non_compliant, with an observation that starts "No evidence yet:" and keeps the file's own note (such as which manual source answers it). This covers a hand-written row still not_assessed, the unlisted rule's rows, and a row a run computes whose check is missing or failed to run (see publishing.md). The row's status stays as the file says, so it is still open work, and the percentage now counts it as a gap. When the evidence arrives the row takes its real result. hound scope export gives such a row back as the not_assessed row the file declared.

To keep CISO Assistant's behaviour for an audit, set no_evidence: not_assessed in its file (and on its target in hound.yaml for the rows a run computes). hound's own committee and board reports never leave unassessed rows out: each programme's standing gives the level met, compliant of applicable with rows not assessed counted as not met, and "not assessed: N" (reporting.md).

Start an audit file with every in-group requirement listed, titled in a comment, to do and not assessed:

hound scope new-audit --framework frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json --groups 1,2 --ref-id EX-E8-2026 --out scope/audits/ex-e8-2026.yaml

docs.title: Audit periods
docs.text:
An audit file with a cycle describes a series rather than one audit. The series' ref_id is <ORG>-<FRAMEWORK>, or <ORG>-<FRAMEWORK>-<SYSTEM> for one system's audit, where <SYSTEM> is the system's ref ID without SYS-. Each period is its own audit, and its label goes after the organisation and framework: <ORG>-<FRAMEWORK>-<INTERVAL>-<YEAR>FY[-<SYSTEM>].

ref_id: EX-E8-BACKUP
name: Backups
cycle: {period: quarter, starts: "2026-07-01"}   # close: sign_off (the default) or auto
sign_offs:
  - {period: Q1-2027FY, by: ceo@example.com, date: "2026-10-14"}

The year is the financial year, 1 July to 30 June, named by the year it ends: 2027FY runs from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027.

period Interval Example ref_id quarter Q1 to Q4, the quarter of the financial year (Q1 is July to September) EX-E8-Q2-2027FY-BACKUP (October to December 2026) month M01 to M12, the calendar month EX-E8-M07-2027FY-BACKUP (July 2026), EX-E8-M02-2027FY-BACKUP (February 2027)

starts must be the first day of a month, and for a quarterly cycle the first day of a financial-year quarter (1 July, 1 October, 1 January or 1 April); otherwise scope.cycle_start_invalid. Periods follow on from it, each labelled by the quarter or month it starts in. hound works out the periods from the date it runs on (UTC), and each scope plan and scope apply brings CISO Assistant up to that date:

  • The open period (the one holding today) is in progress. It is created from the previous period's audit as its baseline, so CISO Assistant copies its results, evidence links and hand-written assessments over, and its ETA is the period's last day. Its documents, controls, hand-written assessments and unlisted rule are written to it only.
  • An ended period moves to in review and is never written again, by scope apply or by runs.
  • With close: sign_off, an ended period stays in review until the file records its sign-off in sign_offs; the next scope apply sets it to done and locks it, so the approval is itself a reviewed commit. With close: auto it is done and locked as soon as it ends.
  • A missed boundary is caught up once: an apply after several periods have ended creates or closes each of them in turn.

A deployment target may name the series (compliance_assessment: EX-E8-BACKUP): with the config's scope: key pointing at this folder, each run publishes to the period open on the run's date. A run never writes to an audit that is in review, done or locked; it reports plan.audit_closed instead. Set HOUND_TODAY=YYYY-MM-DD to run any command as of another date, for example to check a boundary; a run then also records metrics filled in by runs for that date's period, as long as it is not in the future.

The plan lists what happens to each period under Audit periods: opens (with its baseline), closes (in review, awaiting sign-off), awaiting sign-off (still in review from an earlier period), or signed off (done and locked). In JSON these are periods[], each {audit, event, baseline}.

CISO Assistant v4.3.4 audits have no start or end dates, so the period shows in the ref_id, the name (Backups Q2-2027FY) and the ETA. Locking an audit does not freeze the applied controls it links to, so a locked period never blocks the open one.

docs.title: The review workflow
docs.text:
Every change to CISO Assistant's structure goes in as a pull request to the compliance repo:

  1. Copy the template. Copy examples/compliance-repo/ to a new private repository, replace Example Pty Ltd with your own organisation, and point hound.yaml at your CISO Assistant. If CISO Assistant is already set up, start from an export instead.
  2. Change the files. By hand, or with an assistant: the repo's CLAUDE.md tells it the layout, to validate after every change, never to write secrets or evidence into the repo, and to use the plan as the pull request's summary.
  3. Validate. hound scope validate scope/ --config hound.yaml and hound mapping validate mappings/<file>.yaml report every problem with its file and line.
  4. Review the plan. The pull request's workflow validates again and comments hound scope plan as Markdown: every create, field-by-field update, delete (only with --prune) and drift. Reviewers approve the change in CISO Assistant terms, not just the YAML diff.
  5. Apply on merge. Merging runs the apply job in a protected environment with required reviewers, so a second person approves the write itself. Once approved, it saves a plan with hound scope plan --out (shown in the job summary) and applies exactly that file with hound scope apply <file> (Saved plans). Apply is safe to run again; drift found later is written back the same way.

For example, to change who owns a system: edit its owner in scope/setup.yaml, run hound scope validate scope/ --config hound.yaml (it passes), and hound scope plan scope/ --config hound.yaml lists one update, | Update | system | Example laptops | owner: it@example.com → ceo@example.com |. hound scope apply scope/ --config hound.yaml writes it and reports "written": 1.

The workflow in the template, .github/workflows/compliance.yml, needs a self-hosted runner that can reach CISO Assistant, the HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN secrets, and an environment named ciso-assistant with required reviewers. Audit periods are closed the same way: a period's sign-off is a line in its audit file, reviewed and merged like any other change (Audit periods).

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
hound scope validate scope/ [--config hound.yaml] [--format json]

Every problem is reported at once with its file, line, code and a hint, and the exit code is 3 when there are any. --format json prints them as a list of {code, file, line, message, hint} for tools. With --config, each deployment target must name an audit and controls the scope declares.

Code Problem scope.yaml_invalid, scope.document_not_a_map The file is not a YAML map. scope.key_unknown, scope.key_duplicate, scope.key_missing, scope.value_invalid A key is not known, appears twice, is missing, or has a value of the wrong shape. scope.file_missing The scope folder has no setup.yaml. scope.duplicate Two domains, systems, perimeters of one domain, controls, audits, or documents of one audit share a name. scope.ref_id_convention A ref ID without its kind's prefix, or with characters other than upper case letters, digits and hyphens. See Ref ID conventions. scope.reference_unknown A domain, perimeter, system, framework, document or control is used but not declared. scope.framework_snapshot_missing, scope.framework_file_missing, scope.framework_snapshot_mismatch A framework cannot be checked offline: no snapshot, a missing file, or a snapshot of another framework. scope.group_unknown An audit selects a group its framework does not define. scope.requirement_unknown A requirement is not in the framework. scope.requirement_not_assessed A document, control or assessment cites a requirement outside the audit's groups. scope.result_conflict A hand-written result for a requirement a target's mapping also computes, so a person and a collector would write the same row. scope.other_system_as_not_applicable A requirement marked not_applicable because another system meets it (provided_by, or an observation starting "Provided by"): it would show as closed while nothing proves it met. Keep it open with provided_by. scope.field_not_writable field_visibility leaves result, observation or evidences below edit for the auditor. scope.unlisted_missing, scope.unlisted_reason_missing unlisted is missing, or marks requirements not applicable without a reason. scope.cycle_start_invalid A cycle's starts is not the first day of a month. scope.sign_off_without_cycle, scope.sign_off_date_invalid, scope.sign_off_unknown_period, scope.sign_off_early A sign-off in an audit without a cycle, with a date that is not YYYY-MM-DD, for a period the cycle does not have, or dated before its period ends. config.target_not_in_scope A deployment target names an audit or control the scope does not declare.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
HOUND_CA_URL=http://localhost:8000/api/ HOUND_CA_TOKEN=… hound scope plan scope/ [--config hound.yaml] [--format markdown|json] [--prune] [--detailed-exitcode] [--out plan.json]

With --config, the plan reaches CISO Assistant at the config's ciso_assistant.url with the token its ciso_assistant.token reference resolves to, so hound scope plan scope/ --config hound.yaml needs no variables when the token reference does (for example env:HOUND_CA_TOKEN). HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN override them when set, and are needed without --config. hound scope apply reads them the same way.

With --detailed-exitcode, as with Terraform, the plan exits 0 when there is nothing to change and no drift, 2 when there is, and 1 on any error, a usage error included, so that a pipeline can gate on 2. Without it, the exit codes are hound's usual ones. --out also saves the plan to a file, for Saved plans.

The plan validates the scope first and stops, reading nothing, when there are problems. Otherwise it reads CISO Assistant (GET requests only) and prints what applying the scope would do, as Markdown for a pull request comment or as JSON for tools. It writes nothing.

  • Create: objects the scope declares that CISO Assistant does not hold, with their fields.
  • Update: objects whose fields differ, field by field (old → new). An object that exists but was not made by hound is taken over: "mark as managed".
  • Delete, only with --prune: objects hound manages that the scope no longer declares. Objects made by hand are never deleted.
  • Suppliers: lapsed supplier approvals and tiers that differ from the forced one (see Supplier approval). A system whose supplier is not approved stops the plan.
  • Drift: objects changed in CISO Assistant since hound last wrote them (they are written back), objects under the root folder that the scope does not declare, an audit that is locked in CISO Assistant (it and its rows are never changed), and a framework whose loaded library is older than the snapshot's (it is reported, not upgraded).

docs.title: Changes to compliance
docs.text:
Below the change table, the plan shows what the change does to each audit's results, the way Terraform shows changes to outputs below the resource diff, so a reviewer approves the compliance effect and not only the objects. For each audit with a row whose result changes, it reads every row of the audit (GET only) and, from the framework snapshot, gives:

  • one line per selected implementation group (for the Essential Eight, each maturity level): requirements compliant before and after, out of the group's total;
  • each row whose result changes: the requirement and its title, its strategy or domain, the old and new result, and why (a hand-written assessment in the audit file, or the unlisted rule);
  • results that go backwards (from compliant or partially compliant to anything lower, or to not assessed) first, marked ⚠, and counted on the audit's line.
### Changes to compliance

**EX-E8-2026**: 2 result changes, 1 regression ⚠.

- Maturity Level One: 30 → 30 compliant of 48
- Maturity Level Two: 41 → 41 compliant of 107

|  | Requirement | Title | Strategy | Result | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ⚠ | ISM-1515 | Restoration of systems, applications and data from backups is tested… | RB | compliant → not_assessed | the unlisted rule |
|  | ISM-1486 | Web browsers do not process Java from the internet. | UAH | not_assessed → compliant | hand-written in the audit file |

Rows that collector runs own are never changed by the scope, so they are left out; hound plan shows their effect. A plan with no result changes has no such section. JSON plans have the same as compliance[], each {audit, groups[{group, name, before, after, total}], rows[{requirement, title, parent, old, new, why, regresses}]}, and scope apply puts it in its report, so the record of each apply carries the effect it had.

Changes come in dependency order: frameworks, domains, perimeters, users and teams, systems, audits, documents, controls, then assessments. Deletes come last, in reverse.

How objects are matched: a framework by URN, a domain and a system by name, a perimeter by domain and name, an audit and a control by ref_id, a document by its id (the evidence's ref_id), and a hand-written assessment by audit and requirement. Only objects in the root folder and the domains directly under it are read.

hound marks the objects it manages by ending their description with [hound scope <state>], a fingerprint of the fields it wrote, other than links and an audit's status and lock. Those are compared one by one instead, because runs add their own, such as a collector's health evidence on a control. That is how the plan tells an object edited in CISO Assistant (drift) from one the scope changed (an update). Frameworks and assessments carry no marker.

What the plan compares: a domain's description; a perimeter's name, ref_id, description and domain; a system's ref_id, type, description, owner, domain and parents; an audit's name, framework, groups, domain, perimeter, ETA, due date, authors and reviewers; a document's name, domain and file hashes; a control's name, description, domain, owner, priority, category, ETA, systems and documents; an assessment's status, result and observation; a row's applied controls and documents. A control's status and reference_control and a framework's library are written only when the object is created, because collectors and CISO Assistant own them afterwards.

Links are added, never removed: a control's systems and documents, an audit row's applied controls and documents, and a document's files keep what CISO Assistant already holds, unless --prune is given.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
HOUND_CA_URL=http://localhost:8000/api/ HOUND_CA_TOKEN=… hound scope apply scope/ [--config hound.yaml] [--dry-run] [--prune]

Apply validates the scope, plans it as above, and writes the changes in order. It is safe to run again: a second apply with nothing changed writes nothing. With --dry-run it prints the plan and writes nothing. When the scope has problems, it reports them and writes nothing.

It writes every kind:

  • Frameworks: a library from CISO Assistant's stored libraries is imported by URN; a custom library file is uploaded first. libraries are imported the same way.
  • Domains as folders under the root folder, perimeters, and systems as assets.
  • Audits as compliance assessments, by ref_id, with their framework, perimeter, selected groups, dates, authors and reviewers. Renaming an audit in the file renames it.
  • Documents as evidence in the audit's domain. Each file is uploaded as a revision only when no revision holds its SHA-256, so an unchanged file is never uploaded twice.
  • Controls as applied controls, once each, with their systems and documents.
  • Rows: each audit row the scope cites gets its controls and documents linked, hand-written assessments get their status, result and observation, and with --config the unlisted result goes to the in-group rows that neither the file lists nor a mapping computes.

hound run keeps the documents the scope linked to a row when it writes that row's evidence.

The report is JSON: how many changes were written, failed and skipped, and each change with its outcome. A change that depends on one that failed is skipped, such as a domain's perimeters and systems when the domain could not be written, or a system whose parent could not be; other changes go on. The exit code is 4 when any write failed.

Names are turned into IDs before anything is sent: the domain's folder, parent systems by name, frameworks and perimeters, and owners, authors and reviewers by user email (as CISO Assistant actors). A name that cannot be found fails that write and sends nothing for it.

docs.title: Saved plans
docs.text:
hound scope plan scope/ --config hound.yaml --out plan.json   # review the printed plan
hound scope apply plan.json                                    # writes exactly that plan

hound scope apply <file> applies a plan saved with --out without planning again, so what is written is what was reviewed. The file holds the changes and drift, the compliance impact, the CISO Assistant URL, the day the plan was made for, the scope folder and config it was made from with a SHA-256 of their files and of the documents they name, and, for each object the plan writes or deletes, a fingerprint of the state it read in CISO Assistant (none when it creates it).

Apply refuses the plan, writes nothing and exits 3 with scope.plan_stale, as Terraform refuses a stale saved plan, when:

  • HOUND_CA_URL names another CISO Assistant;
  • a scope file, the config or a document file changed since the plan was made;
  • an object the plan writes or deletes changed in CISO Assistant since, or one it creates now exists. The problem names each one.

Plan again, review it and apply the new file. A file that is not a saved plan from this version is scope.plan_invalid. Run apply from the folder the plan was made in: the file names the scope folder and config as they were given.

Do not commit a saved plan. It holds no token and no document's content (only hashes), but it does hold the URL and every value the plan writes. Keep it outside the repo, as the template's workflow does with $RUNNER_TEMP, and delete it once applied.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
HOUND_CA_URL=http://localhost:8000/api/ HOUND_CA_TOKEN=… hound scope export --out compliance-repo/scope [--root-folder Global] [--with-files]

Export is the way in for an organisation that set up CISO Assistant by hand. It reads CISO Assistant (GET requests only) and writes the scope folder from what it holds under the root folder:

  • setup.yaml: the root folder, each framework an audit uses (with its library and a snapshot under frameworks/, made from CISO Assistant's own copy so the files validate offline), and each domain with its perimeters and systems.
  • controls.yaml: every applied control, with its systems and documents.
  • audits/<ref_id>.yaml: each compliance assessment, with the documents and controls its rows link (each with the requirements it is linked to), and its hand-written results as assessments. unlisted is not_assessed, which changes nothing until you give --config.

What is left out, because collectors and manual sources rebuild it: rows a run computed (their observation ends with a run marker), rows still to do and not assessed, and evidence in the root folder, which is where runs put theirs. A control's status and reference control, a system's tags and an audit's field visibility are not exported; add them by hand if you want the files to set them. Libraries CISO Assistant loaded that no audit uses, such as mapping sets, are not listed either.

Everything is sorted and written the same way each time, so exporting an unchanged instance again gives no diff. With --with-files, each document's latest file is downloaded to documents/<id>/ next to the scope folder and listed in the audit file; without it, documents list no files and CISO Assistant keeps the ones it has.

An audit, control or document without a ref_id is given one made from its name (Essential Eight review 2026 becomes ESSENTIAL-EIGHT-REVIEW-2026; a document's is lower case). scope plan matches the object by that name until the next scope apply writes the ref_id to it.

Planning a fresh export of an instance hound manages lists no changes. Objects made by hand carry no marker yet, so the first plan lists each as "mark as managed"; the first apply marks them and writes any missing ref_id, and nothing else changes.

docs.title: System security plans
docs.text:
For a walkthrough, see Your system security plan.

hound ssp build --programme <id> prints a programme's system security plan (SSP). It uses one layout for every framework: NIST SP 800-18 Rev 1, Appendix A (Guide for Developing Security Plans for Federal Information Systems). The only part that changes with the framework is the controls annex (section 13):

profile in ssp.yaml Annex ism ISM controls for the Essential Eight, each listed once with the strategies it serves (for example ISM-1815 under mfa, rap, ac, uah). nist-800-171 NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2 requirements for CMMC Level 2, grouped by family, with each system's CMMC asset category in the inventory and the requirements CMMC does not allow on a POA&M flagged (32 CFR 170.21). See NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC Level 2.

Assessors and primes recognise this layout. hound does not use a separate layout per framework, such as the ASD Blueprint SSP template.

docs.title: How the plan meets ISM-0041
docs.text:
ISM-0041 asks for "an overview of the system (covering the system's purpose, the system boundary and how the system is managed) as well as an annex that covers applicable security controls".

ISM-0041 asks for Section of the plan Comes from The system's purpose 9. General description and purpose sections.purpose (you write it) The system boundary 1. System name and identifier (perimeter), 10. System environment (inventory), 11. Interconnections and external service providers perimeter in ssp.yaml; systems, solutions and suppliers in CISO Assistant; sections.environment How the system is managed 3 to 6 (owner, authorising official, contacts, assignment of security responsibility) roles in ssp.yaml; sections.management An annex of applicable controls 13. Security controls (annex) The programme's framework snapshot and its audit in CISO Assistant

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section Content Gaps Anything an assessor would not accept yet. Listed first; --strict exits 1 while any remain. 1. System name and identifier Name, boundary (perimeter) and audit of record. 2. System categorisation classification. 3. System owner roles.system_owner. 4. Authorising official roles.authorising_official. 5. Other designated contacts roles.security_contact. 6. Assignment of security responsibility sections.management. 7. System operational status operational_status. 8. System type system_type. 9. General description and purpose sections.purpose. 10. System environment sections.environment, then the inventory from CISO Assistant. 11. Interconnections and external service providers Solutions and suppliers from CISO Assistant. 12. Applicable laws, regulations and policies sections.laws_and_policies, then the documents. 13. Security controls (annex) One row per control in the programme's groups: applicability, status, statement, responsible party and the POA&M item that carries it. A control with no row in the audit reads Not implemented. 14. Completion and approval dates The version; the authorising official approves the plan in CISO Assistant. 15. Ongoing system security plan maintenance Rebuild with hound ssp build; review at least once a year and after significant change. Appendix: plan of action and milestones The same items as hound ssp poam.

docs.title: The ISM annex's columns
docs.text:
The ism annex follows the columns of ASD's Blueprint System Security Plan Annex Template (the template the ISM's documentation guideline points to), next to the SP 800-18 status the plan and POA&M use:

Column Comes from Control, Description The framework snapshot (hound framework snapshot keeps each requirement's full text). Strategies The parent nodes the control is listed under. An ISM control that serves several strategies appears once. Maturity levels The implementation groups the control is in. Control type Policy, Procedure, Technical or Documentation, from the reference controls CISO Assistant's library links the requirement to (ids starting pol., proc., tech. and doc.). Responsible entity responsible_entity on a linked control in controls.yaml, if set. Otherwise Shared when a linked control covers a system a supplier's solution provides, else Consumer. Implementation status The ASD template's terms, from the requirement's result in CISO Assistant (see below). SP 800-18 status, Statement, Responsible, POA&M As described above. Result in CISO Assistant Implementation status (ASD) SP 800-18 status compliant Effective Implemented partially_compliant Ineffective Partially implemented non_compliant Not implemented Planned or Not implemented not_applicable Not applicable Not applicable not_assessed, or no row Not assessed Planned or Not implemented

Partially compliant maps to Ineffective, the template's nearest term; the maintainer reviews this choice. The template's Alternate control and No visibility have no CISO Assistant result, so hound does not use them yet.

A section file that does not exist yet prints as "Section name is not written yet.", so a draft still builds.

--json gives the same plan with every value and its source, including the annex (annex[], with poam linking each unmet row to its POA&M item).

docs.title: Versions, sign-off and publishing
docs.text:
The plan is a controlled document. Until the authorising official signs a version, every copy says so: the title ends in "(DRAFT)", a banner under the title and the last line say it is not approved, and the Word file carries a "DRAFT: not approved" header on every page.

  1. Build the draft and keep its snapshot. hound ssp build --programme <id> --snapshot-out ssp-<id>-<version>.json prints the draft and writes the snapshot: everything the plan was built from (the model, each value with its source, and the section texts). The log gives the draft's SHA-256 and the snapshot's. The version is version: in scope/ssp.yaml. Keep the snapshot and any generated plan out of the repo: they hold the organisation's system details.
  2. Review. For a new version, hound ssp diff <old snapshot> <new snapshot> lists only what changed: boundary and inventory first (they usually need a new major version), then suppliers, statuses, statements and sections.
  3. Sign. The authorising official records the sign-off under the plan in scope/ssp.yaml, by pull request like an audit period:
sign_offs:
  - {version: "1.0", by: ao@example.com, date: "2026-11-24", sha256: <draft SHA-256>, snapshot: <snapshot SHA-256>}

by must be the plan's authorising_official (ISM-0047); both hashes are 64 lower-case hex digits, as the log printed them. 4. Rebuild the signed version. hound ssp build --programme <id> --from-snapshot ssp-<id>-1.0.json rebuilds the plan from the snapshot without contacting CISO Assistant. When the snapshot still gives the reviewed draft, it prints the approved plan: no draft marks, and "Approved by … SHA-256 of the reviewed draft: …". When it does not, it stops with ssp.signoff_hash_mismatch. A live build of a signed version whose data has since changed prints a draft and warns. 5. Publish. hound ssp publish --programme <id> --snapshot ssp-<id>-1.0.json uploads ssp-<id>-1.0.zip (the signed plan, its POA&M, the snapshot, and CISO Assistant's own Word audit report for the programme's audit) as a new revision of the evidence SSP-<ID>, "System security plan: ". It refuses a version with no sign-off (ssp.not_signed). If the audit report cannot be downloaded, the package goes without it and the log says why.

--format docx --out <file> also writes the plan as a Word file (headings, lists and tables from the same text). The same plan gives the same file.

docs.title: Control descriptions drafted by your own agent
docs.text:
A requirement that is implemented but has no implementation statement is a gap, usually because its controls have no description. hound has no model, but your own coding agent can draft the descriptions:

  1. hound ssp suggest --programme <id> prints a JSON brief: each control with no description behind such a gap, with its name, owner and systems, and the requirements it serves (description, status and evidence names). It holds names only, never evidence content, and sends nothing anywhere. --from-snapshot reads a snapshot instead of CISO Assistant.
  2. The agent drafts each description and writes it with hound ssp describe --control <ref> --text "<description>". That puts the text in scope/controls.yaml under a # drafted with AI: review before merging comment. Nothing goes to CISO Assistant.
  3. A person accepts, edits or rejects each description in the pull request. Once merged, hound scope apply sends the accepted text to CISO Assistant, and the next ssp build uses it as the statement.

Neither command runs on a schedule.

docs.title: Third parties
docs.text:
Your supplier register lives in the compliance repo, one file per supplier, and hound applies it to CISO Assistant. It replaces the supplier spreadsheet: a new supplier, a renewed contract or a concluded review is a small change a person reviews, and CISO Assistant's third-party features (entities, solutions, contracts, entity assessments, tiers) show the result.

This guide is the how-to. The file format, every field and every validation code are in the scope reference: third-parties/<entity>.yaml, Supplier reviews and tiers and Supplier approval.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Frameworks ask the same questions about suppliers in different words: the Essential Eight and the ASD Essential Series through the systems a supplier runs for you, CMMC through the service providers that handle or protect your controlled information, and every prime contractor's supplier questionnaire through who you depend on. A small team cannot keep three registers. One register in the repo, with each supplier's reasons and evidence beside it, answers all of them, and the systems a supplier provides are registered only once a person has approved it.

docs.title: Moving the supplier spreadsheet with your agent
docs.text:
A small team does not need to type this up. hound agent setup gives your coding agent (Claude Code or GitHub Copilot) the skills onboard-a-third-party and assess-a-supplier; it drafts, you decide.

  1. Give the agent what you have. The spreadsheet exported as CSV, each supplier's contract or order form, and what the supplier publishes about its security: its trust centre page, certificates (such as ISO 27001), independent audit reports and its security contact. Text, PDF and web pages all work; nothing has to be retyped.
  2. The agent drafts each supplier with hound supplier draft: the entity, the solution you buy, the contract as a draft, and an open review. Each level (dependency, penetration, maturity, trust, criticality) carries its reason, and the agent leaves maturity and trust undecided when no document backs them. A document you agree to keep goes under documents/suppliers/<supplier>/, so the reason can point at it. The contract's dates and cost come from the spreadsheet as options (--start, --end, --annual-expense, --currency), and --description says what the supplier does for you. A managed service provider that runs your own laptops and network is drafted with --kind msp and no --for.
  3. Check the draft. hound scope validate scope --config hound.yaml reports any problem with a file, a line and a hint; the agent fixes them.
  4. You approve. hound approve, in your own terminal, shows each supplier's levels and reasons, then asks you to make its contract active and conclude its review (ok, warning or blocker). An agent or a pipe is refused: approval is a person's step.
  5. Plan and apply. hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml shows what CISO Assistant will gain, and hound scope apply writes exactly that plan. Commit the change as a pull request, with the plan as its summary.

For worked examples, see the onboarding tutorial's four fictional suppliers in examples/onboarding-tutorial/scope/third-parties/ (in the Evidence Hound repo): a cloud host, a firewall vendor and two open-source projects, each with its levels, reasons, contract and review. The onboarding tutorial shows them being drafted and approved.

For CMMC Level 2, the register is where you show a prime which service providers handle or protect your controlled unclassified information (CUI). Record it in each solution's data with the authority that allows it, such as a FedRAMP Moderate equivalent, its evidence under documents/suppliers/ and its expiry (Sensitive data). hound supplier list --data cui then answers the prime, and the CMMC Level 2 audit (CMMC Level 2) assesses the practices.

docs.title: Keeping it current
docs.text:
• Reviews come due. With review_every, the plan opens the next review a cycle after the last one's due date, and a review past due without a conclusion means the supplier is no longer approved: the plan lists its systems under Suppliers for the security committee. Ask your agent to re-read the supplier's trust centre and documents before the due date and update the reasons; you conclude the review with hound approve.
  • Contracts renew. An active contract whose end date has passed is reported (supplier.contract_lapsed). Record the new end date, or mark it expired or terminated.
  • Tiers. CISO Assistant computes each supplier's tier from its levels. If you decide a tier yourself, set forced_tier with a reason, and the plan tells you when CISO Assistant's tier differs.

docs.title: Sensitive data and who may hold it
docs.text:
A prime, an auditor or the security committee will ask which suppliers handle CUI, personal information, export-controlled data or classified information, and on what authority. Record it on each solution's data (and on each system that holds it), with the authority and its expiry, and hound scope validate warns of a system holding data through a supplier that is not approved for it, and of an authority that has lapsed: a warning blocks nothing, and the weekly review lists it until it is fixed. hound supplier list --data <kind> prints the list to send. The keys, the four kinds with an Australian and a US example of each, and what hound leaves to the owner and the prime are in scope.md.

An agent drafting a supplier records the kinds a trust centre or contract names with hound supplier draft --data <kind>:<role>[:<detail>] and leaves the authority empty: a person adds it once the certificate, assessment or licence is in the repo.

docs.title: Representatives are personal data
docs.text: representatives (people at the supplier, by email) are optional. They are personal data, so keep them in CISO Assistant instead unless the compliance repo is private and only the GRC team can read it. Never add a representative from a public source without a reason to contact them, and remove one who leaves the supplier. hound never gives a representative a login.

docs.title: What stays in CISO Assistant
docs.text:
hound sets up the register and the reviews; the assessment work happens in CISO Assistant, and hound never writes it:

  • questionnaire answers and the audit CISO Assistant creates for a review with a questionnaire;
  • tiering results, the tier itself and its history;
  • campaigns sent to suppliers;
  • the expiry date of a review's result.

A review's conclusion is the exception: you record it in the repo with hound approve, so the reason a supplier is approved sits beside the supplier, and hound scope apply writes it to CISO Assistant.

docs.title: Answer a prime's questionnaire from the evidence you already have
docs.text: Primes and customers send security questionnaires, often several a year, each asking about the same controls in different words. A US prime may ask about NIST SP 800-171 even though you are assessed against the Essential Eight. Answer them all from one evidence set: your audit of record in CISO Assistant.

docs.title: 1. See what your Essential Eight evidence already answers
docs.text:
$ hound mapping crosswalk --from essential-eight --config hound.yaml > crosswalk.md

Add --offline when CISO Assistant is not reachable from where you run it: you get the same rows without today's results. The command, explained in mapping files, lists every NIST SP 800-171 requirement with the Essential Eight requirements that answer it and today's result of each, from your audit of record:

  • Answered: point the prime at the Essential Eight evidence named.
  • Partly answered: the Essential Eight covers part of it (for example workstations but not every system holding CUI). Answer with what it covers, and add what else you do.
  • Open: the Essential Eight does not cover it (for example physical security or personnel screening). You need other evidence, or the honest answer "not yet".

The crosswalk is advisory: it was drafted with AI from the requirement texts and nobody has reviewed it yet. Check the links you rely on before you send anything.

docs.title: 2. Answer the questionnaire with your agent
docs.text:
Give your agent the questionnaire (a spreadsheet or a PDF) and the crosswalk, and ask:

For each question in questionnaire.xlsx, find the NIST SP 800-171 requirement it asks about, if any, in crosswalk.md. Draft an answer from the Essential Eight evidence and today's result named there, and say which requirement and result each answer rests on. Where the crosswalk says open, or the result is not compliant, say so plainly and do not claim more. Mark every answer you are unsure of.

Then read every answer yourself. Change any that claims more than the evidence shows.

docs.title: 3. Give verifiable proof, not screenshots
docs.text:
Instead of a screenshot per question, offer the prime the same records your committee sees:

  • the audit of record's export from CISO Assistant (the requirement results with their observations and evidence names);
  • the month's posture snapshot from hound report snapshot, which lists each result and when it was collected;
  • for a requirement they care about, the evidence revision in CISO Assistant, with its date and hash;
  • which of your suppliers handle CUI, and on what authority: hound supplier list --data cui (third parties).

Every result names the check or the person that produced it and when, so the prime can see it is current. Agree with the prime how often they need it refreshed, and send the next month's snapshot rather than answering again.

docs.title: 4. Keep the answers
docs.text: Save the completed questionnaire as evidence in CISO Assistant (on your "Security reporting" applied control, or a control for customer assurance), so the next prime's questionnaire starts from it.

docs.title: CMMC Level 2 and the SPRS score
docs.text: This guide is for a small defence supplier that holds controlled unclassified information (CUI) and must self-assess against CMMC Level 2, which is the 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2, and keep its score current in the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS). It uses the same collectors and evidence as the Essential Eight: no collector changes.

docs.title: 1. Add the CMMC Level 2 audit
docs.text:
CISO Assistant ships the CMMC 2.0 library. Declare it in scope/setup.yaml and add an audit that selects both groups, because the library tags its 17 Level 1 practices L1 only:

frameworks:
  - urn: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:cmmc-2.0
    library: urn:intuitem:risk:library:cmmc-2.0
    snapshot: ../frameworks/cmmc-2.0.json

# scope/audits/ex-cmmc-2026.yaml
ref_id: EX-CMMC-2026
name: CMMC Level 2 2026
framework: urn:intuitem:risk:framework:cmmc-2.0
groups: [L1, L2]
domain: Example Pty Ltd
perimeter: Corporate IT

Then add a target to hound.yaml, so each run fills it beside the Essential Eight audit:

targets:
  - mapping: mappings/cmmc-2.0.yaml
    compliance_assessment: EX-CMMC-2026

The example compliance repo has all three: examples/compliance-repo/.

docs.title: 2. What runs fill, and what people assess
docs.text:
mappings/cmmc-2.0.yaml gives 32 practices the checks of the Essential Eight requirements that the crosswalk links to them. Every row is covers: part: the Essential Eight is narrower than 800-171, and the collectors see only Microsoft 365, Intune devices, Sophos Central firewalls and the vulnerability scanner, while a CMMC practice applies to every system that holds CUI. So when every check passes, the practice is partially compliant, never compliant, and its observation says a person must assess the rest (mapping files). The other 78 practices are listed under manual_only with the record each family keeps.

Before you rely on the mapping, read each row against your CMMC scope. Remove covers: part from a row only when its checks answer the whole practice for every system in that scope.

docs.title: 3. Work out the SPRS score
docs.text:
$ hound sprs score --audit EX-CMMC-2026 --config hound.yaml
SPRS score for EX-CMMC-2026 on 2026-12-02: 71 (from 110, NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology 1.2.1)
Deductions (12, 39 points):
  -5  3.1.12  AC.L2-3.1.12  non_compliant
  -5  3.5.3  IA.L2-3.5.3  partially_compliant  3 points instead of 5 if MFA is implemented for remote and privileged users, ...
  ...

The score starts at 110 and takes off each requirement's points (5, 3 or 1) unless its row is compliant or not applicable. The weights are in frameworks/sprs/dod-assessment-methodology-1.2.1.yaml, copied from the methodology's Annex A with its source cited, not in code.

  • A row that is partially compliant, not assessed or missing from the audit counts as not implemented, as the methodology has no partial credit except two cases. For those two, 3.5.3 (MFA) and 3.13.11 (FIPS-validated cryptography), hound takes the full 5 points off and names the 3-point case, because only a person can say which applies.
  • Where the methodology says not to subtract points because a capability is not permitted (remote access, wireless, mobile devices), record the practice as not applicable in CISO Assistant, with the policy that keeps it disabled.
  • Without a compliant system security plan (3.12.4), the score says an assessment could not be completed.

--format json gives the same for an agent. --control AC-SPRS uploads the score as evidence on the applied control you keep for it, so its history stays in CISO Assistant. A person reviews each deduction and enters the score in SPRS; hound never does.

docs.title: 4. Affirm each year
docs.text:
CMMC asks the affirming official to affirm continuing compliance every year (32 CFR 170.22). The evidence plan reminds them: a manual row with every: 12 months and first_due set a little before the anniversary of the last assessment, so the reminder lands on time whenever the plan is applied (a past date rolls forward a year at a time).

# scope/evidence-plan.yaml
  - ref_id: EV-CMMC-AFFIRMATION
    control: AC-SPRS
    method: manual
    owner: Affirming official
    every: 12 months
    first_due: "2026-12-15"
    runbook: manual-sources/cmmc-affirmation.md

Before they affirm, give them the pack. It needs the month's posture snapshot and the CMMC plan in scope/ssp.yaml (system security plan):

hound report snapshot --period 2026-11 --config hound.yaml
hound sprs affirmation-pack --programme cmmc-level-2 --period 2026-11 --config hound.yaml --out affirmation-2026.md

The pack lists the SPRS score, every open POA&M item with its owner and ETA (marking those past their date and those CMMC does not allow on a POA&M), each collector's freshness, and the manual sources past their due date. It decides nothing. The official affirms in SPRS themselves; the GRC team attaches the pack and the date to the yearly task at the weekly review. Keep the pack out of the repo.

docs.title: DISP membership readiness
docs.text:
Defence checks more than cyber security when a business applies for or keeps membership of the Defence Industry Security Program (DISP): it looks at governance, personnel and physical security too. Evidence Hound holds those expectations as one more audit in CISO Assistant, beside the Essential Eight, so one place shows what Defence will look at and what evidence answers it.

This is a readiness self-assessment, not the Defence Security Principles Framework (DSPF) itself. The library's requirements are short paraphrases of the DSPF control areas, each citing its area. Read the DSPF and Defence's DISP guidance for the authoritative text and for what your membership level asks, and check with your DISP contact.

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text:
Area Requirements Answered by Governance DISP-GOV-01 to 06: security officers, policy and plan, foreign ownership, control or influence, annual security report, supply chain, risk method DISP manual sources; supplier records (s10); the Essentials cyber governance source for the risk method Personnel security DISP-PER-01 to 05: clearances, pre-employment screening, separation, awareness training, contact reporting The clearances register source; the security awareness training source (shared with the ASD Essentials) Physical security DISP-PHY-01 to 03: visitors, access, facility security plan The facility security source Information security DISP-INF-01 to 03: classification and handling, incident reporting, incident records An incident register manual source with incident.reported_to_asd (the example compliance repo's example-incident-register); the annual security report source; handling is recorded by hand Cyber security DISP-CYB-01 to 08: one per Essential Eight strategy Every check the Essential Eight mapping gives that strategy at maturity levels 1 and 2

Files: the library frameworks/disp.yaml and its snapshot, the mapping mappings/disp.yaml, and the manual sources in examples/manual-sources/disp/ (index).

docs.title: Add it to a new compliance repo
docs.text:
$ hound init compliance --framework disp
Wrote Example Pty Ltd's compliance repo to /home/you/compliance: 15 files, audits EX-E8, EX-DISP.

--framework disp writes the library, its snapshot and mapping, declares the library in scope/setup.yaml (so hound scope apply uploads and loads it like any custom library), writes the audit scope/audits/<code>-disp.yaml in the same periods as the Essential Eight one, and adds it to targets in hound.yaml. One hound run then fills both audits from the same evidence.

docs.title: Add it to an existing repo
docs.text:
1. Copy frameworks/disp.yaml, frameworks/disp.json and mappings/disp.yaml into your repo.
  2. Declare the library in scope/setup.yaml, as the example compliance repo does (the example repo has steps 1 to 3 done, and stops there):
frameworks:
  - urn: urn:evidence-hound:risk:framework:disp-membership
    library: urn:evidence-hound:risk:library:disp-membership
    file: ../frameworks/disp.yaml
    snapshot: ../frameworks/disp.json
  1. Add an audit file with framework: urn:evidence-hound:risk:framework:disp-membership and groups: ["M"] (see examples/compliance-repo/scope/audits/ex-disp-2026.yaml), and a targets entry with mapping: mappings/disp.yaml.
  2. Copy the manual sources you need from examples/manual-sources/disp/ and examples/manual-sources/essentials/security-awareness-training/ under collectors: in hound.yaml (a repo from hound init has collectors: []: replace it with collectors: first), set their owners, and point evidence plan rows at their runbooks.
  3. hound scope plan, then hound scope apply, then hound run. hound mapping coverage mappings/disp.yaml --framework frameworks/disp.json --manual hound.yaml shows what each area still needs. Until the manual sources are in hound.yaml, coverage counts their checks as automated and warns if it finds no manual source at all.

docs.title: Keep personal details out
docs.text: Clearance and screening records are sensitive. The runbooks ask for names, levels, dates and outcomes only: never clearance case details, security questionnaires or identity documents. Evidence Hound stores what people send as evidence, so send summaries.

docs.title: Move your registers out of spreadsheets
docs.text:
This guide moves a small team's spreadsheet registers into a compliance repo, so that CISO Assistant is filled from configuration you can review, and the spreadsheets can be retired. Your AI agent does the typing, row by row; you read what it proposes and approve it. Plan on two to three hours of your time spread over a week, plus one month of running both side by side.

It uses the fictional registers in examples/migration/ and the example compliance repo. Try it there first.

docs.title: What moves where
docs.text:
Your spreadsheet Moves into With Systems and assets scope/setup.yaml, under the domain hound add system Security controls scope/controls.yaml, linked to the requirements each supports hound add control Suppliers and contracts scope/third-parties/, drafted, then approved by you hound supplier draft, then hound approve Audit results (an Essential Eight assessment workbook) The audit in scope/audits/ hound scope import (details) Evidence you collected by hand A manual source, attested by you each period manual evidence Risks, exceptions and incidents CISO Assistant itself, for now its own forms or its Data Wizard import (CISO Assistant docs)

Risks, exceptions and incidents stay in CISO Assistant until release 2 brings them into configuration. The reports read them from there either way.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Make a compliance repo with hound init and set up your agent with hound agent setup (first deployment).
  2. Export each register to CSV, one file per register, with a heading row. Keep the exports outside the repo if they hold anything you would not commit. Your agent reads CSV directly.
  3. Tidy the headings so each column says one thing. The sample files show the columns each command needs:
Register Columns Systems (systems.csv) name, ref_id, type (primary holds the data or business process, supporting does not), owner (an email), description, parents (the systems it supports, comma separated) Controls (controls.csv) ref_id, name, owner, category (policy, process, technical, physical or procedure), systems, requirements (such as ISM-1511,ISM-1515) Suppliers (suppliers.csv) ref (SUP-...), name, kind (vendor, reseller or msp), solution_ref, solution_name, contract_ref, contract_name, description, contract_end, data (sensitive data the solution handles, as kind:role:detail, such as cui:transmits:VPN traffic; empty if none)

If a control in your spreadsheet does not say which Essential Eight requirement it supports, ask your agent to suggest one from the requirement texts in frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json, and check each suggestion yourself.

docs.title: Move them in
docs.text:
Ask your agent: "Move the registers in <folder> into this repo with the commands in https://github.com/tnbozman/evidence-hound/blob/main/docs/adopt/migrate-from-spreadsheets.md. One command per row, systems first, then controls, then suppliers. Stop at the first error and tell me." For the sample files it runs:

$ hound add system --scope scope --yes --domain "Example Pty Ltd" --name "Example engineering file share" --ref-id SYS-ENG-FILES \
    --type primary --owner eng@example.com --description "Drawings and specifications for customer contracts, some marked CUI." \
    --audit EX-E8-2026
$ hound add control --scope scope --yes --domain "Example Pty Ltd" --ref-id AC-ENG-BACKUP --name "Back up the engineering file share daily" \
    --owner eng@example.com --category technical --systems "Example engineering file share" --audit EX-E8-2026 --requirements ISM-1511,ISM-1515
$ hound supplier draft --ref SUP-EXAMPLE-CAD --name "Example CAD Software Ltd" --kind vendor --solution-ref SOL-EXAMPLE-CAD \
    --solution-name "Example CAD" --contract-ref CTR-EXAMPLE-CAD --contract-name "Example CAD subscription" \
    --description "Makes the CAD software the engineers use." --end 2027-06-30 --json
$ hound supplier draft --ref SUP-EXAMPLE-NETOPS --name "Example Network Services Pty Ltd" --kind msp --solution-ref SOL-EXAMPLE-NETOPS \
    --solution-name "Managed firewall" --contract-ref CTR-EXAMPLE-NETOPS --contract-name "Managed firewall agreement" \
    --description "Manages the office firewall and VPN for us." --end 2026-12-31 --data "cui:transmits:VPN traffic to the engineering file share" --json

Systems go first because controls name them. Suppliers come last here only because their drafts wait for your approval; when you later onboard a new system, its supplier is approved first (onboarding). A system that holds CUI is the start of your CUI boundary: keep it small, and record which suppliers handle the data with --data (third parties). After the approval, hound supplier list --data cui lists them, which is what a prime asks first.

Then you approve the supplier drafts, yourself, in a terminal: hound approve. Your agent cannot do this for you.

docs.title: Reconcile
docs.text:
Before anything reaches CISO Assistant, check that every row arrived. For the sample registers the counts are:

Register Rows Check Systems 4 each ref_id appears in scope/setup.yaml Applied controls 4 each ref_id appears in scope/controls.yaml Suppliers 3 each ref has an approved file in scope/third-parties/

Then:

  1. hound scope validate scope --config hound.yaml reports no problems.
  2. hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml --out plan.json lists one create per row, and nothing you did not expect.
  3. hound explain plan.json reads the plan back in plain English. Steps 2 and 3 need CISO Assistant; without it, git diff | hound explain reads the change to the repo instead, but says less about systems and controls than the plan does. Read it, and compare it with the spreadsheet: same names, owners and requirements.
  4. hound scope apply scope --config hound.yaml writes it to CISO Assistant.
  5. In CISO Assistant, open the audit and check that the controls appear against the requirements you expected.

Ask your agent to do steps 1 to 3 and give you a table of spreadsheet rows against plan lines; you check the table, then run step 4.

docs.title: Run both for one month
docs.text:
Keep the spreadsheets for one reporting month, read only, so nobody edits both:

  • Make every change in the repo, by pull request, and let hound scope apply carry it to CISO Assistant.
  • At the month's end, take a snapshot and the committee report (reporting) and compare it with what the spreadsheet would have said. Note every difference and its cause.
  • When the differences are explained, the compliance owner signs off: record the decision on the "Security reporting" applied control in CISO Assistant (an evidence revision with the month's report and the note "spreadsheets retired"), then archive the spreadsheets.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text: Problem What to do hound add system says the file has nothing at 'domains[name=...].systems' The domain is unknown: name it exactly as in scope/setup.yaml, or add it there first. hound add control says a requirement is unknown Use the requirement's ref_id from the framework snapshot, such as ISM-1511, not a description. A supplier draft fails on --ref Ref IDs start with SUP- and use capitals, digits and dashes. hound scope plan wants to change something you did not touch Someone edited CISO Assistant directly. Run hound scope export to see it, then decide which copy is right.

docs.title: Collectors
docs.text:
A collector reads one kind of system, read-only, and reports framework-neutral checks with the evidence behind each. The mapping files turn checks into requirement results. Each guide lists the read-only permissions the collector needs.

Collector Type Reads Guide Microsoft 365 m365 Entra ID, Intune, Defender and Office settings through Microsoft Graph Microsoft 365 Any REST API rest A YAML profile from your compliance repo REST profiles Sophos Central rest, profile sophos-central Endpoints, policies and firewalls Sophos Central Terraform tests rest, profile terraform-tests Your IaC pipeline's control test results Terraform tests Terraform drift rest, profiles terraform-drift and terraform-drift-trigger Your IaC pipeline's drift plan Terraform drift CISO Assistant ai-register and rest, profile ciso-assistant The AI register, suppliers and risks CISO Assistant Vulnerability scans vuln-scan Nessus or CSV exports dropped in a folder Vulnerability scans Manual evidence manual Files people export, attested by a person Manual evidence, templates

No collector here for your system? Write a profile for its REST API, or, rarely, a collector.

docs.title: Governance checked on every run: the AI register, suppliers, risk and recovery
docs.text:
Two collectors check the AI register and your suppliers. Each reads the place where the facts are kept.

Collector Reads Checks ai-register (built in) The ai block of each system in your compliance repo's scope/setup.yaml: the AI register entry your team reviews by pull request. The seven checks on the entries themselves. rest with the ciso-assistant profile CISO Assistant, with a read-only API token: assets and their labels, risk scenarios, suppliers' solutions, entity assessments and contracts. Risks of the AI systems, and suppliers' assessments and contracts.

The AI governance primer explains the terms. Each check's observation starts with the AI6 sub-practice it serves, in words, and ends with what to do. mappings/ai6.yaml turns them into AI6 results.

docs.title: The ai-register collector
docs.text:
collectors:
  - name: ai-register
    type: ai-register
    schedule: "0 6 * * *"
    settings:
      scope: ../scope            # the scope folder, relative to this config file

An AI system is in use when its in_use_from date has come and it is not retired. Checks over systems in use are not applicable when there are none.

Check Passes when ai.register_complete every AI system has the National AI Centre register template's columns and an impact assessment status (not_required for a normal system) ai.owner_assigned every AI system has an owner ai.screening_recorded no system in use is prohibited, and each was screened before it went into use ai.impact_assessment_before_use each elevated system in use had its impact assessment approved on or before going into use ai.human_oversight_documented no elevated system in use is human_out_of_loop ai.tested_before_use each system in use has a last_tested_on date ai.test_results_current each system in use was tested within 6 months (elevated) or 12 months (normal)

Each run saves ai-register.json: every AI system's entry, whether it is in use, and the SHA-256 of scope/setup.yaml, so a result can be traced to the reviewed file. A setup.yaml that does not load is an error (ai_register.scope_invalid), never a fail: run hound scope validate and fix it.

docs.title: The ciso-assistant profile
docs.text:
Copy profiles/ciso-assistant.yaml into your profiles folder, then:

collectors:
  - name: ciso-assistant
    type: rest
    schedule: "0 6 * * *"
    settings:
      profile: ciso-assistant
      base_url: https://ciso.example.com/api/
    secrets:
      token: env:HOUND_CA_READ_TOKEN

The token is a CISO Assistant API token of a user whose role can only read, such as the built-in Reader role, on the domains you check. It is not the token hound publishes with.

Check Passes when ai.risks_in_register every asset labelled ai-screening-elevated is linked to at least one risk scenario ai.suppliers_assessed every solution providing an asset labelled ai-use-third-party comes from a supplier with an entity assessment concluded ok whose expiry date has not passed ai.supplier_contracts_current each of those solutions has an active contract not past its end date supplier.assessments_current the same, for every supplier's solution supplier.contracts_current the same, for every supplier's solution risk.studies_reviewed every risk study (risk assessment) not deprecated was updated within risk_review_interval (default P365D, a year). No risk study at all fails risk.exceptions_current no approved security exception is past its expiry date (one with no expiry date counts as current) bia.recovery_tested every business impact analysis assessment of a critical system has recovery tested ticked. A critical system is one with a recovery time objective (recovery: {rto: ...} on the system in your scope)

To review risk studies more often, set the interval in the collector's settings, for example risk_review_interval: P180D.

The labels come from your scope: hound scope apply writes them. A list the token cannot read makes the checks over it unable to assess, never a fail; the other checks still run. The profile's recorded test cases are in profiles/ciso-assistant.tests/; run them with hound profile test ciso-assistant.

docs.title: Microsoft 365 collector
docs.text:
The built-in m365 collector reads a Microsoft 365 tenant through Microsoft Graph, read-only, and reports framework-neutral checks for identity, privileged access, device compliance and Office hardening. Every Graph collection it reads is saved as JSON evidence, with personal data hashed.

It signs in as an Entra app registration with application permissions (client credentials). It never signs in as a person, and it never writes to the tenant.

To try it on a test tenant first, follow the local trial: it registers this collector with hound add collector m365 and runs it next to a local CISO Assistant.

docs.title: 1. Register the app
docs.text:
In the Microsoft Entra admin center, as a Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator:

  1. Identity > Applications > App registrations > New registration. Name it, for example Evidence Hound collector. Supported account types: Accounts in this organizational directory only. No redirect URI.
  2. Note the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID from the Overview page. They become the client_id and tenant_id settings.
  3. API permissions > Add a permission > Microsoft Graph > Application permissions. Add the six permissions below, then Grant admin consent. Remove the default delegated User.Read; the collector does not use it.
  4. Certificates & secrets. Upload a certificate (preferred, see below) or create a client secret.
  5. Optional but recommended: in Enterprise applications, open the app and set Assignment required to Yes, and in Conditional Access restrict the app's sign-ins to the host that runs the collector (a workload identity policy, if licensed).

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
All are read-only application permissions. Nothing else is needed.

Permission Used for Graph requests User.Read.All Which accounts are enabled members, and which are synchronised from on-premises. v1.0/users AuditLog.Read.All Which users are MFA-capable, from the authentication methods registration report. v1.0/reports/authenticationMethods/userRegistrationDetails Policy.Read.All Conditional Access policies: MFA, legacy authentication, authentication strengths. v1.0/identity/conditionalAccess/policies RoleManagement.Read.Directory Who holds directory roles, and whether they are eligible (PIM) or permanent. v1.0/roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments, roleEligibilitySchedules, roleAssignmentScheduleInstances DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All Intune-managed devices: operating system, build and compliance state. v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All Intune policies: Office macro settings, attack surface reduction rules, App Control for Business policies and AppLocker custom profiles. v1.0/deviceManagement/deviceConfigurations, beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies ThreatHunting.Read.All Microsoft Defender for Endpoint advanced hunting: application control events, the most-blocked files, and which Windows devices are onboarded. Three fixed queries, each sent as a POST with a // evidence-hound: <name> first line so the tenant's audit log shows which query ran. POST v1.0/security/runHuntingQuery

Only for hound onboard environment --graph (see onboarding): Organization.Read.All, to read the subscribed licences (v1.0/subscribedSkus). Collection never uses it; leave it out if you record the signals another way.

The sprint plan listed Reports.Read.All; the registration report actually needs AuditLog.Read.All, and Reports.Read.All is not used.

Licences: Conditional Access and the registration report need Microsoft Entra ID P1. Privileged Identity Management needs Entra ID P2 or ID Governance; without it the PIM collections are skipped and the PIM check reports not_applicable. The Intune checks need Intune. The application control events check needs Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 (or Microsoft 365 E5 or Defender for Business), which brings advanced hunting; without it, or without ThreatHunting.Read.All, the run still succeeds and only that check says why (not_applicable for the licence, error for the permission).

docs.title: Certificate (preferred)
docs.text:
A certificate cannot be phished or pasted into the wrong place as easily as a secret, and its private key never leaves the collector host. Create one on that host (or wherever you keep keys):

$ openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:3072 -sha256 -days 365 -nodes \
    -keyout hound-m365-private.pem -out hound-m365.crt -subj "/CN=Evidence Hound collector"
$ cat hound-m365.crt hound-m365-private.pem > hound-m365.pem
$ chmod 600 hound-m365-private.pem hound-m365.pem
  1. Upload hound-m365.crt (the public certificate only) under Certificates & secrets > Certificates.
  2. Give the collector hound-m365.pem (certificate followed by its unencrypted private key) as the client_certificate secret, for example as a Docker secret: client_certificate: file:/run/secrets/hound_m365_pem.
  3. Delete hound-m365-private.pem once the PEM is stored. Put a reminder in CISO Assistant (a recurring task) to renew the certificate before it expires.

docs.title: Client secret
docs.text: If a certificate is not practical, create a client secret under Certificates & secrets > Client secrets with the shortest expiry you can manage, and give it as the client_secret secret, for example client_secret: env:HOUND_M365_CLIENT_SECRET. When both secrets are set, the certificate is used.

docs.title: 2. Configure the collector
docs.text:
collectors:
  - name: example-m365
    type: m365
    schedule: "0 3 * * *"                     # daily, 03:00 UTC
    settings:
      tenant_id: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000e001
      client_id: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-00000000c001
      break_glass_accounts: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000b1, 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000b2
      supported_windows_builds: 10.0.22631, 10.0.26100
    secrets:
      client_certificate: file:/run/secrets/hound_m365_pem

The IDs above are made up. Keep your real tenant and client IDs in your private deployment config, never in this repo.

Setting Required Meaning tenant_id yes Directory (tenant) ID. client_id yes Application (client) ID of the app registration. supported_windows_builds yes Comma-separated Windows builds still in support, as the first three parts of the version (10.0.26100 is Windows 11 24H2). Review it when Microsoft ends support for a release. break_glass_accounts no Comma-separated object IDs of break-glass (emergency access) accounts. Conditional Access policies may exclude these and nothing else. graph_url no Microsoft Graph address. Default https://graph.microsoft.com/. Next pages are only followed on this host. sign_in no app (the default) signs in as the app registration, with its certificate or secret. none sends no credential, for the Microsoft 365 dev server only: it is accepted only when graph_url is on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], and refused otherwise (m365.sign_in_not_loopback). system no The system in scope/setup.yaml this instance collects from, such as Example 365. With it, scope/capabilities.yaml can say which capabilities Microsoft 365 provides (see Capabilities). include_identities no true keeps user principal names, mail addresses, people's names and device names in evidence. Default false: they are hashed. mfa_partial_percent no MFA-capable share of members at or above which MFA registration is partial rather than fail. Default 90. privileged_roles no Comma-separated role template IDs treated as privileged. Default: the 14 built-in roles listed under the checks below. global_admin_min no Fewest Global Administrators expected, break-glass accounts included. Default 2. global_admin_max no Most Global Administrators expected, break-glass accounts included. Default 4. compliant_pass_percent no Compliant share of managed Windows devices needed to pass. Default 95. compliant_partial_percent no Compliant share needed for partial. Default 80. application_control_window_days no Days of application control events the events check reads, 1 to 30 (advanced hunting keeps 30). Default 30. defender_onboarded_percent no Share of Intune-managed Windows devices onboarded to Defender for Endpoint needed for the events check to pass. Default 95. application_control_groups no Comma-separated group IDs an enforced application control policy must be assigned to, when none is assigned to all devices. Without it, application control assigned only to groups is partial. Secret Meaning client_certificate PEM certificate and private key of the app registration (preferred). client_secret Client secret, if no certificate is used.

hound config validate checks the required settings; hound config validate --check-secrets also resolves the secret references. The collector itself reports every bad setting at once (m365.setting_missing, m365.setting_invalid) before it makes any request.

docs.title: 3. Dry run
docs.text:
$ hound config validate --check-secrets hound.yaml
valid
$ hound collect --config hound.yaml --dry-run

A first run that fails with m365.graph_forbidden names the permission that is missing or not consented. m365.auth_failed means the tenant, client ID or credential is wrong, or the certificate has expired.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check ID Measures Outcomes Limits identity.mfa.registered_all_users Enabled member accounts that the registration report marks MFA-capable. Guests and disabled accounts are not counted. pass at 100 %; partial at or above mfa_partial_percent; else fail. An account missing from the report counts as not capable. The report can lag changes by up to a day. identity.mfa.enforced_conditional_access An enabled Conditional Access policy for all users and all cloud apps that requires MFA (the MFA control or an authentication strength, alone or combined with AND). pass when such a policy excludes only break_glass_accounts; fail naming any other excluded user, group or role; fail when there is none. Report-only policies do not count. Exclusions of guests or external users are not read yet. Conditions such as locations or platforms are not assessed. identity.legacy_auth_blocked An enabled policy for all users and all cloud apps that blocks the Exchange ActiveSync and "other" client app types. As above. Same as above. identity.mfa.phishing_resistant_admins Enabled policies requiring the built-in Phishing-resistant MFA authentication strength, and which privileged roles they cover. pass for every privileged role; partial naming roles not covered; fail for none.
