Custom authentication strengths are not recognised, even if phishing-resistant. identity.privileged.global_admin_count Accounts holding Global Administrator, active or eligible. pass within global_admin_min to global_admin_max; else fail. A group assigned the role counts as one holder. identity.privileged.admins_cloud_only Whether user accounts holding privileged roles (active or eligible) are cloud-only rather than synchronised from on-premises. pass when none is synchronised (groups and apps holding roles are noted, not assessed); fail naming synchronised accounts. Members of role-assignable groups are not expanded. identity.privileged.pim_eligible_not_permanent Whether privileged roles are held as eligible (activated just in time) rather than permanently assigned. pass when no permanent privileged assignment exists apart from break-glass accounts; fail naming them; not_applicable without PIM. Time-bound active assignments count as not permanent. endpoint.managed.compliant_ratio Share of Intune-managed Windows devices whose compliance state is compliant. pass at compliant_pass_percent; partial at compliant_partial_percent; else fail. No managed Windows devices fails. Devices in grace period count as not compliant. Devices not enrolled in Intune are not seen. endpoint.os.supported_versions Every managed Windows device runs a build in supported_windows_builds. pass, or fail listing unsupported builds with counts. No managed Windows devices fails. Checks the build, not the monthly patch level. apps.office.macros_blocked_from_internet An assigned Intune settings catalog policy enables Block macros from running in Office files from the Internet for Word, Excel and PowerPoint. pass when all three are assigned to all users; partial when only some apps are, or only through groups; else fail. Group Policy, the Cloud Policy service and Administrative Templates profiles are not read. Exclusion groups are not subtracted from "all users". endpoint.asr.office_rules_enabled The four Office attack surface reduction rules (Office child processes, executable content, code injection, Win32 API calls from macros) in block mode, in a settings catalog policy or endpoint protection profile assigned to all users or all devices. pass when all four block for all users or devices; partial when some block, are in audit or warn mode, or block only for some groups; fail when none is configured. Rules set by Group Policy or Defender for Endpoint security settings management are not seen. Per-device rule state is not read. endpoint.application_control.enforced An assigned App Control for Business policy (Intune endpoint security, found by its template family endpointSecurityApplicationControl) or AppLocker custom profile (OMA-URI ./Vendor/MSFT/AppLocker/ApplicationLaunchRestrictions/{Grouping}/{EXE,DLL,Script,MSI}/Policy) in enforced mode. pass when an enforced policy is assigned to all devices or to every group in application_control_groups; partial when policies are only in audit mode, their AppLocker values come back encrypted, or they cover only some groups; fail when none is assigned. Policies set by Group Policy, or by a custom profile using the ApplicationControl CSP, are not seen. App Control for Business mode is read from its built-in controls choice (..._enable_app_control_0 enforce, _1 audit) or Enabled:Audit Mode in uploaded XML: these IDs are still to be confirmed against a real export. Exclusion groups are not subtracted. endpoint.application_control.events_centrally_logged Defender for Endpoint advanced hunting: DeviceEvents with an AppControl… or AppLocker… action type over application_control_window_days, counted by device and action, the 20 most-blocked files, and the latest OnboardingStatus of each Windows device from DeviceInfo. pass when events arrived and at least defender_onboarded_percent of Intune-managed Windows devices are onboarded; partial when events arrived but fewer devices are onboarded; fail when no events arrived; not_applicable without an advanced hunting licence; error when the permission is missing. Events sent only to a SIEM or Windows Event Forwarding, not Defender, are not seen: record those with the manual application control event log template. Whether the events are reviewed is not judged. endpoint.application_control.file_types_covered Which file types enforced policies control: executables, software libraries, scripts and installers. App Control for Business covers all four by design; AppLocker needs the EXE, DLL, Script and MSI rule collections with EnforcementMode="Enabled". pass when all four are covered; fail naming the missing types. As above. An AppLocker collection whose value Graph returns encrypted counts as not covered.

Default privileged roles: Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, Privileged Authentication Administrator, Security Administrator, Conditional Access Administrator, Exchange Administrator, SharePoint Administrator, User Administrator, Authentication Administrator, Application Administrator, Cloud Application Administrator, Intune Administrator, Helpdesk Administrator and Billing Administrator.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
The checks are grouped by the capability they judge, using the Essential Eight mitigation codes that scope/capabilities.yaml uses:

Capability Checks mfa multi-factor authentication identity.mfa.registered_all_users, identity.mfa.enforced_conditional_access, identity.legacy_auth_blocked, identity.mfa.phishing_resistant_admins rap restrict administrative privileges identity.privileged.global_admin_count, identity.privileged.admins_cloud_only, identity.privileged.pim_eligible_not_permanent pos patch operating systems endpoint.managed.compliant_ratio, endpoint.os.supported_versions rmom restrict Microsoft Office macros apps.office.macros_blocked_from_internet, endpoint.asr.office_rules_enabled uah user application hardening endpoint.asr.office_rules_enabled ac application control endpoint.application_control.enforced, endpoint.application_control.file_types_covered, endpoint.application_control.events_centrally_logged

When the deployment names its scope folder (scope: in hound.yaml) and that folder has a capabilities.yaml, each run tells the collector which capabilities another product provides. A check whose every capability is provided elsewhere reports not_applicable, and its observation names the product and its audit, such as "Not judged on Microsoft 365: scope/capabilities.yaml records mfa as provided by Example identity provider (audit EX-IDP-E8-2026)." So a third-party product, such as an application control or identity product, is never reported as a Microsoft 365 failure. A check that serves two capabilities, such as the ASR Office rules, runs while Microsoft 365 provides either.

A mitigation is this instance's when its route names the instance, or its systems include the instance's system setting. Manual evidence and gaps are never the collector's. A system decision with no route counts as another product's only when the instance's system is set, so without a map, or without system and routes, every check runs as before.

hound onboard environment --graph <this collector> reads the tenant's licences and Intune configuration kinds read-only, as this instance, and suggests Microsoft 365 for the mitigations they cover. Nothing is enabled until you accept: an accepted suggestion is written with evidence: collector and route: <this collector>; naming another product instead routes that mitigation away from Microsoft 365.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Each run writes one JSON file per Graph collection, with the request, the number of pages read, and every item. Check results cite the files they read.

File Contents users.json Users: ID, enabled, member or guest, synchronised or cloud-only. mfa-registration.json Registration details: MFA-capable, registered methods. conditional-access-policies.json Conditional Access policies. role-assignments.json Active directory role assignments. role-eligibility-schedules.json PIM eligible assignments (only with PIM). role-assignment-schedule-instances.json PIM active assignment instances, permanent or activated (only with PIM). managed-devices.json Intune-managed devices: operating system, build, compliance state. device-configurations.json Intune device configuration profiles (AppLocker custom profiles included) and their assignments. configuration-policies.json Intune settings catalog policies (App Control for Business included), their settings and assignments. hunting-app-control-events.json Application control event counts by device ID and action type, with the last time seen. Advanced hunting: missing when the tenant refuses it. hunting-app-control-blocked-files.json The 20 most-blocked files: file name, SHA-256, publisher, block and device counts. hunting-defender-onboarding.json Windows devices by Defender for Endpoint onboarding status, as counts.

Unless include_identities is true, user principal names, mail addresses, people's display names and device names are replaced by sha256: and the first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the lower-cased value. The same person gets the same value in every file and run, so findings can still be traced, and object IDs are kept. A hash of a known address can be confirmed by anyone who has the address, so treat the evidence as internal.

Graph is read with paging (@odata.nextLink) and throttling handled: on 429 or 503 the collector waits as long as Retry-After says (at most five minutes) and gives up after five attempts with m365.graph_throttled.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
Code Meaning m365.setting_missing, m365.setting_invalid A setting is missing or has a value the collector cannot use. m365.credentials_missing Neither client_certificate nor client_secret is set. m365.certificate_invalid client_certificate is not a PEM certificate followed by its private key. m365.auth_failed Entra ID refused the sign-in (wrong IDs, wrong or expired credential). m365.graph_unauthorized Graph refused the token. m365.graph_forbidden A permission is missing or not consented; the message names it. m365.graph_not_licensed The tenant lacks a licence for a required collection. PIM collections are skipped instead. m365.graph_throttled Graph kept throttling after five attempts. m365.graph_next_link_foreign Graph returned a next page on another host; it was not followed. m365.graph_failed, m365.graph_invalid_response Any other Graph error, or a response that is not JSON.

The collector uses the Graph beta API for one request, the Intune settings catalog (configuration-policies.json), because it exists nowhere else. Beta APIs can change without notice. If that request starts failing, the run fails with m365.graph_failed (and the collector's health evidence shows it) until a release adapts to the change.

docs.title: REST collector and profiles
docs.text:
The built-in rest collector reads any HTTP API described by a profile: a YAML file that says how to sign in, which lists to read, and which checks to run over them. A new system, or a new check on a system, is a profile change, not a code change or a release. Sophos Central is read this way (profiles/sophos-central.yaml, guide), infrastructure drift from an IaC pipeline's plan artefact (profiles/terraform-drift.yaml, guide), hosting controls from the pipeline's infrastructure tests (profiles/terraform-tests.yaml, guide), and CISO Assistant's own AI risks and supplier records (profiles/ciso-assistant.yaml, guide).

Each run has three phases, and each is kept apart from the others:

  1. Collect. Sign in, run the bootstrap queries (such as whoami), then read each query once, following its pages. Each query is saved as one evidence file, <query>.json, with identities hashed.
  2. Extract. Build the datasets: join, flatten, filter and pick fields from the queries' items. Each dataset is saved as dataset.<name>.json, naming the query files it was built from and their SHA-256.
  3. Assess. Run each check over a query or a dataset. A check's result names the evidence it read.

Nothing in a run calls a language model. The profile is the whole definition; the engine only follows it.

To write your first profile, follow the tutorial Write a profile. The design and the decisions behind it are in the design note.

docs.title: The profiles folder and the library
docs.text:
hound has no profiles built in. Every profile loads from the organisation's profiles folder, by default /config/profiles, mounted read-only into the runner. Keep the folder in your private compliance repo, next to hound.yaml. Each profile is <name>.yaml, and its tests are in <name>.tests/ beside it.

This repository keeps a public library of tested profiles in profiles/: example (the fictional Example Asset API) and sophos-central. To use one, copy the profile and its tests into your profiles folder:

$ cp -R evidence-hound/profiles/sophos-central.yaml evidence-hound/profiles/sophos-central.tests /srv/compliance/profiles/
$ hound profile validate sophos-central --profiles /srv/compliance/profiles
$ hound profile test sophos-central --profiles /srv/compliance/profiles

A copied profile keeps its source and version. After you update your checkout of this repository, hound profile diff sophos-central --library <checkout> shows how your copy differs from the library version, so you can take the library's fixes without losing your own changes. Set HOUND_PROFILES_PATH and HOUND_LIBRARY_PATH to skip the options.

Command Does hound profile validate <name> Parses and checks the profile, listing every problem with its code. hound profile test <name> Runs each test case in <name>.tests/ offline, against its recorded answers, and compares each check's result with the expected one. Exits 1 if any case fails. hound profile diff <name> --library <checkout> Shows the lines that differ from the library version named in source.

make test-profiles runs hound profile test for every library profile; CI runs it on every push.

docs.title: Using a profile
docs.text:
collectors:
  - name: example-assets
    type: rest
    schedule: "0 5 * * *"
    settings:
      profile: example
      client_id: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000c1
      supported_os: "14, 15"
    secrets:
      client_secret: file:/run/secrets/example-assets_client_secret
Setting Required Meaning profile yes The profile's name, its file name without .yaml. profiles_path no The profiles folder. Default /config/profiles. include_identities no true keeps the identities the profile lists in evidence. Default false: they are hashed. allow_writes no true lets the profile's write: true queries run, such as the opt-in pipeline trigger of terraform-drift-trigger. Default false: they are refused and nothing is sent. Give the instance a token that can do only that one write. require_profile_tests no true makes a profile without tests unable to assess. Default false: a warning in the log.

Every other setting is one of the profile's parameters, and every secret one of its secrets. hound add collector rest --set profile=<name> asks for the ones the profile requires. hound config validate checks each instance against its profile: unknown settings, missing parameters, values of the wrong type and missing secrets are all reported before anything is called.

docs.title: Profile reference
docs.text:
A profile has these top-level keys. Anything else is refused (profile.key_unknown).

profile: example                 # the name; must match the file name
version: "1.0.0"                 # your version of this profile
source: evidence-hound/profiles/example.yaml   # where it was copied from, for hound profile diff
description: One line on what it reads.
requires:
  hound: ">=0.1"                 # the oldest hound that can run it
parameters: { ... }
secrets: { ... }
connection: { ... }
bootstrap: { ... }               # optional
queries: { ... }
datasets: { ... }                # optional
checks: [ ... ]

docs.title: Parameters and secrets
docs.text:
parameters:
  client_id:
    type: string
    required: true
    description: Client ID of the read-only API client.
  stale_after:
    type: duration
    default: P30D
    description: A device not seen for longer than this is stale.
secrets:
  client_secret:
    required: true
    description: Client secret of the read-only API client.
Type Holds string Any text. int A whole number. number A number, such as 0.95. bool true or false. list Comma-separated values, such as 14, 15. duration An ISO 8601 duration, such as P30D or PT12H. url An absolute http or https address.

A parameter is required when it says so and has no default. Text anywhere in the profile can use placeholders:

Placeholder Is ${name} A parameter, or a variable a query set with vars. ${secrets.name} A secret the profile declares. Evidence records the request with the placeholder, never the value. ${item.path} A field of the item a for_each query is called for, such as ${item.id}.

A placeholder with no value is a problem (rest.value_missing), never an empty string.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
connection:
  base_url: ${base_url}
  allowed_hosts: [api.example.com, login.example.com, "${base_url}", "${token_url}"]
  auth:
    type: oauth2_client_credentials
    token_url: ${token_url}
    client_id: ${client_id}
    client_secret: ${secrets.client_secret}
    scope: read
  rate_limit:
    per_second: 5
    max_retries: 3
  tls:
    pinned_thumbprint: ""        # optional: accept a self-signed certificate only with this SHA-256 thumbprint

Relative query paths are resolved against base_url.

Auth type Keys Sends none Nothing. oauth2_client_credentials token_url, client_id, client_secret or client_certificate, scope A bearer token from the token endpoint, renewed when it expires. With client_certificate (PEM with its key), a signed client assertion instead of a secret. api_key in (header or query), name, value A static key. bearer token A static bearer token. basic username, password HTTP basic authentication. mutual_tls certificate A client certificate (PEM with its key) as the only credential.

rate_limit defaults to 5 requests a second and 3 retries. A 429 or 503 answer is retried after its Retry-After. Redirects are followed at most 5 times, and only on the same host; any other redirect is refused (rest.redirect_refused) and nothing is sent.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
bootstrap:
  whoami:
    get: v1/whoami
    vars:
      org_id: $.organisation.id

queries:
  devices:
    get: v1/orgs/${org_id}/devices
    paging: { style: next_link, next: $.next }
    items: $.items
    identities: [hostname, serial, owner]

A bootstrap query runs before the others, is not saved as evidence and cannot be checked; it sets variables with vars (name to path). A query may also set vars for queries after it; hound orders queries by what they use and refuses a cycle (profile.dependency_cycle).

Key Meaning get or post The path or address. headers, query, body Request headers, query parameters and (for post) a JSON body. items Where the list is in each answer. Default $, the answer itself. paging How to follow pages (below). identities Property names, at any depth, that identify a person, device or network. Hashed in evidence and in datasets unless include_identities is true. vars Values later queries can use as ${name}. for_each Another query: this one is called once per item of it, with ${item.path}. At most max_calls calls (default 100). optional_on Status codes that mean "not available here", such as a missing licence: [403, 404]. Checks over it become not applicable, with the reason. async A report run as a job: status_url (path in the first answer), done (a test on the status answer), result_url, poll_seconds and timeout_seconds. format auto (from the content type), json, xml, csv or zip. arrays names XML paths that are always lists. write true marks a query that changes something, such as starting a pipeline run (terraform-drift-trigger). It runs only when the collector instance also sets allow_writes: true; otherwise nothing is sent and checks over it are unable to assess. Every other query only reads. redirect_hosts Hosts other than the API's that a redirect from this query's GET may lead to, such as the signed storage a pipeline artefact downloads from. They get a plain GET with no sign-in and no headers, so they never receive credentials. Any other redirect off the API's host is refused (rest.redirect_refused). member With format: zip (a pipeline artefact, for example), the file in the archive to read, as JSON, XML or CSV by its extension. Required with zip, refused without it. The archive and the unzipped member both count towards max_bytes, so a member that unzips past the cap is refused. keep Keep only these properties of each item, in memory and in evidence, for very large lists. max_items, max_bytes, max_pages Caps. Defaults 50,000 items, 50 MB and 1,000 pages. Over a cap, checks over the query are unable to assess, naming the cap. Paging style Keys Follows next_link next The next page's address at a path in the answer, until it is absent. page_number page, size_param, size, total_pages Page numbers from 1 until total_pages (a path in the answer). cursor cursor, param A cursor at a path, sent back as query parameter param, until there is none. offset offset_param, limit_param, limit, total Offset and limit, until total items, or a short page when there is no total. link_header The Link header's rel="next".

Paths are a small, fixed language so every path can be checked before a run: $, then .name, ['any name'], [2] or [*] (every element of a list).

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
A dataset shapes one query's items into the rows a check needs.

datasets:
  user_roles:
    from: users
    join:
      - with: roles
        on: { left: "$.roleIds[*]", right: $.id }
        as: roles
        optional: true
    where: { field: $.status, equals: active }
    fields:
      id: $.id
      mfa: $.mfa.enabled
      role_names: $.roles[*].name
Key Meaning from A query or another dataset. join Attach the rows of with whose right value equals a left value of the row, as a list under as. A join that is not optional counts rows that match nothing, and checks over the dataset report them. flatten A path to a list in each row: one row per element, with the original row under parent (a plain value goes under value). where Tests (as in checks) a row must pass to stay. fields Output name to path. Without it, whole rows are kept. A path that finds nothing leaves the field out.

A dataset built from a query that failed, or is not available, fails or is not available with it, and says which.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
checks:
  - id: example.device.os_supported
    title: Devices run a supported operating system
    over: devices
    each: { field: $.os.version, version_in: "${supported_os}" }
    require: all
    when_empty: not_applicable
    describe: "{passed} of {total} devices run a supported operating system. Supported: ${supported_os}."
Key Meaning id The framework-neutral check ID that mappings use, such as network.firewall.firmware_supported. Unique in the profile. over The query or dataset it reads. A code check may read several: [admins, roles]. where Tests that put a row in scope. Rows out of scope are not tested. each The test every row in scope is put to. require How row results become the check's result (below). when_empty What no rows in scope means: not_applicable, fail or unable_to_assess. Required: there is no default, because an empty list means different things for different checks. describe The observation. {passed}, {failed}, {total} (rows read) and {matched} (rows in scope) are filled in, as are ${...} placeholders. Failing rows are listed after it, by id or name, up to 20. code, with A built-in code check instead of each and require, with its own settings. history For a code check only: a query it is over whose items from the instance's earlier runs it is also given, oldest first, as the evidence store still keeps them. The run saves them as <query>.history.json, which the result cites, so it can be reproduced from this run's evidence. For things an API gives no date for, such as how long a firmware upgrade has been offered.

A test is a map with field, one operator, and optionally missing and negate:

Operator Passes when the field equals Equals the value (text, number or true/false). not_equals Does not equal the value. in Equals one of a list, such as "enabled, enforced" or a list parameter. matches Matches a regular expression. any_matches Is a list with at least one element matching a regular expression. exists Is present and not null (exists: true). For "is absent", add negate: true. version_in Is a version within one of a list: 21.0.1 is within 21.0 and 21, not within 21.5. version_at_least Is a version at least this one. within Is a date no older than a duration, such as P30D. older_than Is a date older than a duration. at_least Is a number at least this one. at_most Is a number at most this one.

missing says what a missing field means: unable_to_assess (the default), pass or fail. negate: true turns a pass into a fail and a fail into a pass; it does not change missing. A test that cannot be decided (a field that is not a date for within, say) makes the check unable to assess, naming the row.

require Pass when all Every row in scope passes each. any At least one does. none None does. count_at_most, as { count_at_most: N } At most N rows are in scope (N may be a placeholder). count_at_least, as { count_at_least: N } At least N rows are in scope. { ratio_at_least: 0.95, partial_at: 0.8 } At least 95% pass. From partial_at up to it, the result is partial; below it, fail.

Code checks are for what the operators cannot say. They are built into hound, named and tested; a profile names one with code. Today they are sophos.super_admin_count (Sophos Central admins and roles, with: { max: ... }), sophos.firmware_upgrade_age (firewalls and the firmware upgrade check, history of the upgrade check, with: { days: ... }), terraform.no_drift and terraform.tests_pass. There are no runtime code plugins.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every check gives one of these, which the mapping turns into CISO Assistant results:

Result Means pass The requirement holds on the evidence read. fail It does not. The observation names the rows that fail. partial Only for ratio_at_least with partial_at: between the two. not applicable Nothing to assess: no rows (with when_empty: not_applicable), or the API said the list is not available here (optional_on). unable to assess The evidence could not be read or decided: a failed query, a cap reached, a missing field, a join with unmatched rows. It never counts as a pass or a fail.

A broken query only affects the checks that read it. The run's _manifest.json names the profile, its version, its source and the SHA-256 of the file that ran.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Limit Default Change it with Items per query 50,000 max_items Bytes per query 50 MB max_bytes Pages per query 1,000 max_pages Calls per for_each query 100 max_calls Requests per second 5 rate_limit.per_second Retries after 429 or 503 3 rate_limit.max_retries Redirects 5 Fixed

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Allowed hosts. Credentials, tokens and requests only go to hosts in connection.allowed_hosts: a host name, a wildcard for its sub-domains (*.central.sophos.com), or an address (an entry with a port matches only that port). Anything else, including a data region named by the API, is refused with rest.host_not_allowed and nothing is sent. Credentials go only over https, except to this machine for recorded tests (profile.host_insecure).
  • Secrets. Secrets come only from the instance's secrets, which reference files or environment variables, and a profile can only use the secrets it declares. Before evidence is written, it is searched for every secret value; a file holding one is refused (rest.secret_in_evidence) and its checks are unable to assess.
  • Identities. The properties a query lists in identities are replaced by sha256: and the first 16 hex characters of a SHA-256 hash, before datasets and checks see them, unless the instance sets include_identities: true. The same value gets the same hash in every run, so findings can be followed over time.
  • Read only. A profile can post (some APIs search with a POST), but it is meant for reading. Give the API credential the least role that can read the lists.
  • No language model. Collection and assessment are the profile and the engine only.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
Profile problems start with profile. and are listed by hound profile validate, with the line they are on. Run problems start with rest.:

Code Meaning rest.auth_failed The token endpoint or API refused the credential. rest.host_not_allowed A request or token would have gone to a host not in allowed_hosts. Nothing was sent. rest.redirect_refused The API redirected to another host. Nothing was sent there. rest.value_missing A placeholder has no value: a missing parameter, or a variable a query did not set. rest.rate_limited Still 429 or 503 after every retry. rest.response_invalid An answer that is not the format expected, or has no items where items says. rest.zip_member_missing A zip answer without the member the query names; the message lists what the archive holds. rest.response_too_large A zip member that unzips past max_bytes. rest.job_failed, rest.job_timeout An async report failed or did not finish in time. rest.secret_in_evidence Evidence held a secret value; it was not written. rest.unreachable The API could not be reached (network, DNS or proxy). profile.tests_missing require_profile_tests is true and the profile has no tests.

docs.title: Sophos Central
docs.text:
Sophos Central is read by the rest collector with the sophos-central library profile (profiles/sophos-central.yaml). It reads the network devices a Sophos Central tenant manages through the Sophos Central APIs, read-only, and reports framework-neutral checks on them. Today that is the firewalls and their firmware, and the admins of Sophos Central itself, who can change every one of those devices. It saves each list it read as JSON evidence, with host names, addresses, serial numbers and people's names and email addresses hashed.

It does not read endpoint protection. Evidence about endpoints, such as antivirus scanning of Office macros (ISM-1672), comes from the endpoint's own tools or a manual source, not from Sophos Central.

It signs in with a Sophos Central API credential (OAuth client credentials). It never signs in as a person, and it never writes to the tenant.

Until s09 this was a built-in sophos collector. The profile gives the same checks and outcomes on the same recordings, so the coded collector was removed. A config that still says type: sophos fails validation with config.collector_type_retired and the replacement below: client_id, supported_firewall_firmware, super_admin_max and the client_secret secret keep their names, and tenant_id is no longer used.

docs.title: 1. Create the API credential
docs.text:
In Sophos Central, as a Super Admin:

  1. Go to Global Settings > API Credentials Management (in the Administration section) and choose Add Credential.
  2. Name it, for example Evidence Hound collector, and give it a short description such as "Read-only compliance evidence".
  3. Choose the role Service Principal Read-Only. It can read firewalls, admins and roles, and change nothing. The collector needs no more, so do not choose Service Principal Management, Forensics or Super Admin.
  4. Choose Add. Sophos Central shows the client ID and the client secret. Copy the secret now: it is shown only once. If you lose it, choose Renew on the credential to get a new one.
  5. Note the credential's expiry date, and put a reminder in CISO Assistant (a recurring task) to renew it before it expires.

Store the client secret only as a secret on the host that runs the collector, for example as a Docker secrets file:

$ install -m 600 /dev/null /srv/compliance/secrets/sophos_client_secret
$ cat > /srv/compliance/secrets/sophos_client_secret     # paste the secret, then Ctrl-D

Never put the secret in the compliance repo, in chat or in a ticket. The client ID is not a password, but it identifies your credential: keep it in your private deployment config only.

docs.title: Which credential
docs.text:
Create the credential in the tenant's own Sophos Central (most organisations do). A Sophos Central Partner or Enterprise Dashboard (organisation) credential is not supported: Sophos Central gives it no data region, so both checks are unable to assess with rest.value_missing for data_region. Create a tenant credential instead.

After signing in, the profile asks whoami for the tenant's ID and where its data lives (its data region, for example https://api-eu01.central.sophos.com). The profile's allowed_hosts are Sophos ID, the global API and *.central.sophos.com, so the token is only ever sent there. A data region on any other host is refused with rest.host_not_allowed, and nothing is sent to it.

docs.title: 2. Configure the collector
docs.text:
Copy the profile and its tests from this repository's profiles/ folder into the profiles folder your deployment mounts (default /etc/evidence-hound/profiles): sophos-central.yaml and sophos-central.tests/. Then add the collector, which asks for the profile's settings and secret:

$ hound add collector rest --name example-sophos --config hound.yaml --secrets-dir /etc/evidence-hound/secrets \
    --set profile=sophos-central

That writes:

collectors:
  - name: example-sophos
    type: rest
    schedule: "0 4 * * *"                       # daily, 04:00 in scheduler.time_zone
    settings:
      profile: sophos-central
      client_id: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000050d1
      supported_firewall_firmware: "21.5, 22.0"
      super_admin_max: "2"
    secrets:
      client_secret: file:/run/secrets/sophos_client_secret

The ID above is made up. Keep your real client ID in your private deployment config, never in this repo.

Setting Required Meaning profile yes sophos-central. profiles_path no The profiles folder, when it is not the default. client_id yes Client ID of the API credential. supported_firewall_firmware yes Comma-separated firewall firmware versions still in support, such as 21.5, 22.0. A firewall passes when its version is one of them or within one: 21.5.1 is within 21.5, and 21.0.1 is within 21 but not within 21.5. Check the Sophos Firewall OS lifecycle when Sophos announces an end of support, and update the list. firmware_update_days no Most days a firewall may have a firmware upgrade offered before network.firewall.firmware_current fails. Default 14, the two weeks ISM-1694 allows. super_admin_max no Most Sophos Central admins allowed to hold the Super Admin role. Default 2: one for daily work is too few to recover from a lost account, and more than two is rarely needed. include_identities no true keeps host names, firewall names, serial numbers, IP addresses and admins' names and email addresses in evidence. Default false: they are hashed. id_url no Sophos ID address that issues tokens. Default https://id.sophos.com/. Change it only for tests. api_url no Sophos Central global API address. Default https://api.central.sophos.com/. Change it only for tests. Secret Required Meaning client_secret yes Client secret of the API credential.

To check your copy of the profile offline against its recordings, run hound profile test sophos-central. After an update to this repository, hound profile diff sophos-central --library <checkout> shows how your copy differs from the library version.

docs.title: 3. Dry run
docs.text:
$ hound config validate --check-secrets hound.yaml
valid
$ hound run --config hound.yaml --only example-sophos --dry-run

The dry run signs in, reads the firewalls, admins and roles, stores the evidence locally and plans the updates to CISO Assistant without sending them. A first run that fails with rest.auth_failed means the client ID or secret is wrong, or the credential has expired. A list the credential's role cannot read makes the checks over it unable to assess, and the observation gives Sophos Central's answer.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check Pass Otherwise network.firewall.firmware_supported Every firewall managed in Sophos Central runs firmware in supported_firewall_firmware. fail, listing the firewalls (by ID) whose version is unsupported or missing. No firewalls is not applicable. network.firewall.firmware_current No firewall has had a firmware upgrade offered for more than firmware_update_days days (the sophos.firmware_upgrade_age code check over the firmware upgrade check, firewall/v1/firewalls/actions/firmware-upgrade-check, one call per firewall). fail with the counts and the longest age. unable to assess when the upgrade check is refused or does not answer for a firewall. No firewalls is not applicable. network.management.super_admin_count At most super_admin_max Sophos Central admins hold the predefined Super Admin role (the sophos.super_admin_count code check). fail with the count. unable to assess when Sophos Central lists no predefined role named Super Admin, so nothing could be counted.

The checks see only firewalls managed or reporting in Sophos Central. A firewall outside Sophos Central is not seen at all, so pair these checks with an asset inventory.

docs.title: What the API does not show
docs.text:
• Admins' MFA. The Common API's admin list (common/v1/admins) has each admin's profile and role assignments, but nothing about multi-factor authentication. Sophos Central itself requires every admin to sign in with MFA and walks them through setting it up the first time (Sophos Central help: Multi-factor authentication), so there is no setting to read. ISM-1173 for Sophos Central admins rests on that, not on a check: keep a copy of the help page, or a screenshot of the sign-in prompt with no names in it, as manual evidence in CISO Assistant.
  • When firmware was released. The firmware upgrade check lists the upgrades offered to each firewall with their size, fixed bugs and news, but no release date. hound counts an offer's age from its own earlier runs: the check is given the upgrade check's answers from every earlier run the evidence store still keeps (history: firmware_upgrades in the profile) and counts from the first run of the unbroken series that saw an offer. Counting starts with the first run, so for the first firmware_update_days days after you start collecting the check cannot fail, and retention (evidence.retention_days) must be longer than firmware_update_days. The 48-hour window for exploited vulnerabilities (ISM-1877) is not judged: Sophos does not say which upgrades fix an exploited vulnerability.
  • Whether the read-only role may call the upgrade check. It is a POST that changes nothing. If your credential's role is refused, the check is unable to assess; the other checks are not affected.
  • What a custom role can do. The check counts the predefined Super Admin role only. A custom role with Super Admin's permissions is not counted, so review custom roles when you review admins.

docs.title: Essential Eight
docs.text:
In mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml:

Requirement Checks Why ISM-1501 Operating systems that are no longer supported by vendors are replaced (Patch operating systems) network.firewall.firmware_supported, with the Microsoft 365 collector's endpoint.os.supported_versions A firewall's firmware is the operating system of an internet-facing network device. Every check must pass. ISM-1694 Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of internet-facing servers and internet-facing network devices are applied within two weeks of release (Patch operating systems) network.firewall.firmware_current For the firewalls Sophos Central manages. Internet-facing servers, and fixes for exploited vulnerabilities within 48 hours, need the scanner and patch records as well. ISM-1883 Privileged user accounts explicitly authorised to access online services are strictly limited to only what is required (Restrict administrative privileges) network.management.super_admin_count, with the Microsoft 365 collector's identity.privileged.global_admin_count and identity.privileged.pim_eligible_not_permanent Sophos Central is an online service, and its Super Admins can change every network device it manages. Every check must pass.

A requirement is not_assessed when any of its checks has no result. If you do not run the Microsoft 365 collector, remove its checks from ISM-1501 and ISM-1883 in your own copy of the mapping, and say in each comment what covers the rest.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
File Holds firewalls.json Every firewall (firewall/v1/firewalls, all pages): ID, model, firmware version, management and reporting status. firmware_upgrades.json The firmware upgrade check for each firewall (firewall/v1/firewalls/actions/firmware-upgrade-check): its firmware and the upgrades offered. firmware_upgrades.history.json The same answers from every earlier run the evidence store keeps, with when each was collected: what the firmware age was counted from. admins.json Every Sophos Central admin (common/v1/admins, all pages): ID, role assignments, when they were added and changed. roles.json Every role (common/v1/roles, all pages): ID, name, type (predefined or custom) and description. Role names identify no one, so they are never hashed.

Each file records the request, the pages read and the SHA-256 of what was read; the run's _manifest.json names the profile and its version. Unless include_identities is true, host names, firewall names, serial numbers, IP addresses, firewall locations and people's names and email addresses are replaced by sha256: and the first 16 hex characters of a SHA-256 hash. The same device gets the same hash in every run. IDs are kept, so a finding can be traced back in Sophos Central.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Code Meaning config.collector_type_retired The config still says type: sophos. Use type: rest with profile: sophos-central, as above. profile.parameter_missing, profile.parameter_invalid A setting the profile needs is missing or has a value it cannot use. profile.secret_missing client_secret is not set. profile.not_found sophos-central.yaml is not in the profiles folder. rest.auth_failed Sophos ID refused the credential: wrong client ID or secret, or an expired credential. rest.value_missing whoami gave no tenant ID or data region: the credential is a partner or organisation credential. rest.host_not_allowed Sophos Central named a data region that is not a Sophos Central host. Nothing was sent there. rest.unreachable Sophos ID or Sophos Central could not be reached (network, DNS or proxy).

docs.title: Infrastructure drift from your IaC pipeline
docs.text:
The terraform-drift profiles tell you whether the cloud infrastructure still matches its reviewed infrastructure code, as evidence like any other check. They are ordinary REST profiles: hound never runs Terraform, never reads Terraform state and never holds cloud credentials. Your IaC pipeline already has those. It makes the plan, publishes it as a build artefact, and hound reads the artefact through the GitHub Actions API.

Profile What it does Token terraform-drift Reads the newest completed run of the drift workflow, its artefact and the plan in it. Read only. The default. Fine-grained, on the IaC repository only, Actions: read. terraform-drift-trigger Starts the drift workflow (workflow_dispatch), polls the run until it completes, then reads its artefact. The one write any library profile makes, so it is opt-in twice: the profile marks the request write: true, and the collector instance must set allow_writes: true. Fine-grained, on the IaC repository only, Actions: read and write. Nothing else.

Both have one check:

  • infrastructure.drift.none: pass when the plan lists no drift (resource_drift) and no change (resource_changes other than no-op or read); fail naming each changed resource address and its actions, for example oci_core_instance.grc (update); unable to assess when there is no completed run, the newest run did not succeed, its plan is older than max_age, or it published no plan artefact, saying which. Every finding ends with where the plan came from: the repository, the commit SHA and the run ID, read from the run itself, not from the artefact's name.

docs.title: 1. The pipeline makes the plan
docs.text:
In the IaC repository, add a workflow that makes a refresh-only plan on a schedule and publishes it as plan.json in an artefact named drift-plan. A fictional example for Example Pty Ltd:

# .github/workflows/drift.yml in the IaC repository
name: Drift
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 22 * * *" }]
  workflow_dispatch: {}            # only needed for terraform-drift-trigger
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform plan -refresh-only -input=false -out=drift.tfplan
      - run: terraform show -json drift.tfplan > plan.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: drift-plan, path: plan.json, retention-days: 14 }

The cloud credentials stay in that pipeline, as they already do. Drift is the finding, not a pipeline failure: if you use -detailed-exitcode, treat exit code 2 (changes) as success so the run still publishes the plan, because a run that does not succeed is unable to assess. A normal terraform plan works too; its resource_changes are checked as well.

docs.title: 2. A collector instance
docs.text:
In hound.yaml of your GRC config repository:

collectors:
  - name: grc-infra-drift
    type: rest
    schedule: "0 23 * * *"                      # after the pipeline's nightly plan
    settings:
      profile: terraform-drift
      repository: example/grc-infra
      workflow: drift.yml
    secrets:
      token: file:/run/secrets/iac_actions_token
Parameter Default Meaning repository required The IaC repository, as owner/name. workflow required The workflow file that makes the plan, such as drift.yml. branch main The branch whose runs are read (or that the trigger runs on). artifact drift-plan The artefact holding plan.json. max_age P2D The oldest plan still trusted, as an ISO 8601 duration. Make it longer than the schedule's interval. api_url https://api.github.com/ The GitHub API; GitHub Enterprise Server has its own. Secret Meaning token The fine-grained token above, as a secret reference.

GitHub answers an artefact download with a redirect to signed storage. The profiles follow it only to the hosts in the query's redirect_hosts (*.actions.githubusercontent.com and *.blob.core.windows.net), with a plain GET that carries no token. If GitHub moves its artefact storage, the download is refused (rest.redirect_refused) naming the new host: add it to your copy of the profile.

To start the workflow first, use profile: terraform-drift-trigger and add allow_writes: true to the instance's settings. Without it the trigger is refused, nothing is sent, and the check is unable to assess. The trigger waits up to 30 minutes for the run.

docs.title: Where the Terraform lives
docs.text:
Recommended: separate repositories. The IaC repository holds the Terraform and its pipeline; the GRC config repository holds hound.yaml, the scope and the profiles. Each has its own reviewers and its own token, and the drift token reads only the IaC repository's Actions. Every finding names the IaC repository and commit, so it is clear which version was assessed.

A monorepo works too. Point repository at the one repository; the workflow and artefact are named the same way.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• GitHub Actions only, for now. GitLab and Azure DevOps need only new profiles in the same shape, with no code.
  • One plan per artefact, read as plan.json; the archive and the unzipped plan both count towards the query's max_bytes.

docs.title: Hosting controls proven by your infrastructure tests
docs.text:
The terraform-tests profile turns the tests in your infrastructure code into evidence. You write each hosting control as a terraform test run block, for example "the VM has no public IP address". Your IaC pipeline runs the tests on every change and publishes the JUnit report as a build artefact. hound reads the artefact through the GitHub Actions API. It is an ordinary REST profile: hound never runs Terraform, never reads state and never holds cloud credentials.

The tests use mock providers (mock_provider, Terraform 1.7 and later). Terraform plans your real code against a fake provider, so the tests need no cloud account and no credentials, create nothing and cost nothing. The same works for any provider: OCI, AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.

What a mock proves, and what it does not. A control test proves that the reviewed code declares the control. It does not prove that the live cloud looks like that, because someone could change the cloud by hand. The drift check covers that: it proves the live cloud still matches the code. Map a requirement to both (rule: all_pass), and it passes only when the code declares the control and the cloud still matches the code.

Profile What it does Token terraform-tests Reads the newest completed run of the tests workflow, its artefact and the JUnit report in it. Read only. Fine-grained, on the IaC repository only, Actions: read. The drift token will do.

Its check:

  • infrastructure.tests.pass: pass when every test in the report passed; fail when one failed or ended in error, naming each test with Terraform's message (the assertion's error_message); unable to assess when there is no completed run, the run was cancelled or timed out, the report is older than max_age, the run published no report, or tests were only skipped. A failing test fails the run as well, and that run still counts, because the failure is the finding. Every finding ends with the repository, the commit SHA and the run ID, read from the run itself.

The code check behind it, terraform.tests_pass, also takes test: <run block name> to judge one test alone. A named test missing from the report is unable to assess. That is how you give each control its own check, so a mapping can name it.

docs.title: 1. Write the controls as tests
docs.text:
In the IaC repository, add a test file with one run block per control, named after the control. A fictional example for Example Pty Ltd's GRC platform is in examples/onboarding-tutorial/infra/oci:

mock_provider "oci" {}

run "vm_has_no_public_ip" {
  command = plan
  assert {
    condition     = oci_core_instance.grc.create_vnic_details[0].assign_public_ip == "false"
    error_message = "vm_has_no_public_ip: the GRC platform's VM must not have a public IP address."
  }
}

Start each error_message with the control's name, so a failure reads well in CISO Assistant. Where the code itself can refuse a bad value, add a variable validation and a run with expect_failures that shows the refusal, for example an office range of 0.0.0.0/0. Run them locally with terraform test; in this repository, make test-terraform runs the example's.

docs.title: 2. The pipeline publishes the report
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/controls.yml in the IaC repository
name: Control tests
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request: {}
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 22 * * 0" }]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform init -backend=false -input=false
      - run: terraform test -junit-xml=controls.xml
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: control-tests, path: controls.xml, retention-days: 14 }

The job needs no cloud credentials. if: always() publishes the report when a test fails, so the failure reaches CISO Assistant.

docs.title: 3. One check per control
docs.text:
Copy the profile into your GRC config repository under a name of your own, and add one check per control with test: set to its run block. The tutorial's copy is grc-infra-controls.yaml:

  - id: infrastructure.controls.vm_has_no_public_ip
    title: The GRC platform's VM has no public IP address
    over: [run, tests]
    code: terraform.tests_pass
    with: { max_age: "${max_age}", repository: "${repository}", test: vm_has_no_public_ip }

Copy its tests folder too, and add a case to its expect: lists for each new check, so hound profile test keeps passing.

docs.title: 4. A collector instance and a mapping
docs.text:
collectors:
  - name: grc-infra-controls
    type: rest
    schedule: "30 23 * * *"
    settings:
      profile: grc-infra-controls
      repository: example/grc-infra
      workflow: controls.yml
    secrets:
      token: file:/run/secrets/iac_actions_token
Parameter Default Meaning repository required The IaC repository, as owner/name. workflow required The workflow file that runs the tests, such as controls.yml. branch main The branch whose runs are read. artifact control-tests The artefact holding controls.xml. max_age P8D The oldest report still trusted, as an ISO 8601 duration. Make it longer than the schedule's interval. api_url https://api.github.com/ The GitHub API; GitHub Enterprise Server has its own.

Then map each requirement to its control tests and to the drift check, as the tutorial's backup rows do:

  - ref: ISM-1814
    rule: all_pass
    checks:
      - infrastructure.controls.backups_retention_locked
      - infrastructure.drift.none

Controls with no row in your framework, such as "no SSH from the internet" for the Essential Eight, are still evidence: each run keeps their findings with its evidence. They answer rows of later frameworks too, such as boundary protection in NIST SP 800-171.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• GitHub Actions only, for now, as for the drift profiles. Any test tool that writes JUnit XML works the same way.
  • The report is read as controls.xml, one file per artefact; the archive and the unzipped report both count towards the query's max_bytes.
  • Why not an emulator such as LocalStack? It emulates AWS only, its free plan is for non-commercial use and needs an account, and on that plan VMs and VPNs are records only. Mock providers prove the same configuration for any cloud with nothing to run.

docs.title: Vulnerability scan collector
docs.text:
The vuln-scan collector reads the exports your vulnerability scanner already makes. You drop them in a folder, and it turns them into structured scan evidence. It works with any scanner, because it reads files and never calls the scanner. It reads two formats:

  • Nessus v2 (.nessus), as Nessus, Tenable.io and Tenable.sc export it.
  • CSV, from any scanner, through a column map. A Microsoft Defender vulnerability management export works with the map below.

Each instance covers one scope, the way the Essential Eight patching requirements group software:

Scope What its scans cover internet_facing Internet-facing services. common_apps Office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software and security products on workstations. other_apps Other applications on workstations, servers and network devices. operating_systems Operating systems of workstations, servers and network devices.

So a business that scans its internet-facing servers with Nessus and its laptops with Defender has two instances, one per scope. Internet-facing scans cover both the applications and the operating systems of internet-facing services, servers and network devices; operating_systems is for the rest.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Required Meaning drop_folder yes Folder the exports are dropped in. A relative path is resolved against the config file's folder. format yes nessus reads *.nessus files; csv reads *.csv files with the column settings below. scope yes One of internet_facing, common_apps, other_apps, operating_systems. owner yes Who owns the scans and fixes what they find. scan_interval_days no Most days between scans. Default, for maturity level 2: 1 for internet_facing, 7 for common_apps, 14 otherwise. patch_window_days no Most days a finding may stay open after its patch is published. Default: 14 for internet_facing and common_apps, 30 otherwise. exploited_patch_window_hours no Most hours a finding rated critical, or with a known exploit, may stay open. Default: 48 for internet_facing, otherwise the patch window. column_host for csv The column with the host name. column_finding_id for csv The column that identifies the finding, such as a plugin ID or a CVE. column_severity for csv The severity column: info, low, medium (or moderate), high, critical, or 0 to 4. column_name no The finding's title or the software's name. Default: the finding ID. column_cve no CVE IDs, separated by commas, semicolons or spaces. column_first_seen no When the finding was first seen. column_patch_published no When the vendor published the patch. column_exploit_available no Whether an exploit exists. Empty, false, no, n, 0, none, NoExploit and not available read as no; anything else as yes. column_unsupported no Whether the vendor no longer supports the software. Read as yes or no in the same way. column_scan_date no When the scan saw the finding; the latest value is the scan date. Default: when the export file was written.

Column names match the header ignoring case. Dates are ISO 8601 (2026-11-20, 2026-11-20T06:00:00Z) and read as UTC unless they carry an offset.

collectors:
  - name: internet-facing-scans
    type: vuln-scan
    schedule: "0 7 * * *"
    settings:
      drop_folder: ../scans/internet-facing
      format: nessus
      scope: internet_facing
      owner: Sam Example
  - name: laptop-vulnerabilities
    type: vuln-scan
    schedule: "0 7 * * *"
    settings:
      drop_folder: ../scans/defender
      format: csv
      scope: common_apps
      owner: Sam Example
      # A Microsoft Defender vulnerability management export.
      column_host: DeviceName
      column_finding_id: CveId
      column_severity: VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
      column_name: SoftwareName
      column_cve: CveId
      column_first_seen: FirstSeenTimestamp
      column_exploit_available: ExploitabilityLevel
      column_scan_date: LastSeenTimestamp

Defender's export has no patch publication date and no unsupported flag. Its ExploitabilityLevel is NoExploit, ExploitIsPublic, ExploitIsVerified or ExploitIsInKit, so every level except NoExploit counts as an exploit being available.

docs.title: Dropping an export
docs.text:
Copy the export into the drop folder yourself, or use hound manual upload, which works for scan sources too:

hound manual upload --config hound.yaml --source internet-facing-scans internet-facing-2026-11-16.nessus

It refuses a file that is not the source's format. If the same content is already in the folder, under any name, it copies nothing. It does not ask you to attest the file, because the scan itself is the evidence.

docs.title: Scheduling exports from common scanners
docs.text:
The collector never calls a scanner, so three things run on their own schedules: the scan, the export into the drop folder, and the collector. Set them up so that:

  • the scanner scans at least as often as the scope's scan_interval_days (daily for internet_facing, weekly for common_apps, fortnightly otherwise);
  • the export runs after the scan has finished, and writes into the source's drop_folder;
  • the collector's schedule runs after the export has landed. For example: scan at 01:00, export at 05:00, collector at 07:00.

Leave older exports in the folder. They are the history that gives a finding its age when the export has no first-seen date, and the collector never deletes them. Archive exports older than your longest patch window if the folder grows too large.

Any scanner credential the export job uses stays with that job, in an environment variable or a secret store on the machine that runs it. hound only reads files, so it holds no scanner credential.

The menus and API paths below are as the vendors document them at the time of writing; check your product's own documentation for the current names.

  • Nessus (Professional or Expert): set a schedule in the scan's settings. Export a finished scan in the Nessus format from the scan's Export menu, or have a scheduled job request it through the Nessus API (POST /scans/{scan_id}/export with format set to nessus, then download the file once it is ready) and save it in the drop folder. Use format: nessus.
  • Tenable Vulnerability Management (Tenable.io): schedule the scan in the scan's settings, then export its latest results in the Nessus format, from the scan's export menu or through the same API pattern (POST /scans/{scan_id}/export, format set to nessus). Use format: nessus.
  • Tenable Security Center (Tenable.sc): schedule the scan, then download the finished scan result as a .nessus file into the drop folder. Use format: nessus.
  • Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management: there is no scan to schedule, because Defender assesses onboarded devices continuously. Schedule an export instead, for example a daily job that reads the per-device software vulnerability assessment (the Defender API's SoftwareVulnerabilitiesByMachine export) and writes it as CSV with the columns in the example above. LastSeenTimestamp becomes the scan date, so a daily export keeps scanned_in_interval passing. Use format: csv with the column map above.
  • Any other scanner: export CSV and map its columns with the column_ settings. Only column_host, column_finding_id and column_severity are required; each optional column you map makes the checks fairer, column_patch_published most of all.

docs.title: How a run reads the folder
docs.text:
• Every export of the source's format is read. The same content dropped twice is read once, under its newest name.
  • The current scan is the export whose scan ran last. That is the scan date inside the export, not the file's date, so a copied old export never replaces a newer scan.
  • The older exports stay in the folder as history. Each run lists them all in scan-history.json.
  • If any export cannot be read, the run fails with vuln_scan.export_invalid, naming the file and line. Nothing is published from a partial read. Fix or remove the file and run again.

From a Nessus export:

  • Each ReportHost is a host, named by its host-fqdn tag when it has one.
  • Each ReportItem above severity 0 is a finding. Informational items are left out.
  • A finding's ID is its pluginID, and its title is its pluginName. It also reads the item's cve elements, exploit_available and patch_publication_date.
  • A finding is unsupported when it has unsupported_by_vendor set to true, or its plugin name says "Unsupported" or "SEoL".
  • The scan date is when the last host finished: HOST_END_TIMESTAMP, or else HOST_END, read as UTC.
  • .nessus files have no first-seen date.
  • Document type definitions are refused, so an export cannot pull in other files.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
File Contents The current export The export itself, unchanged. A Nessus export is stored as <name>.nessus.xml, because CISO Assistant refuses the .nessus extension. scan.json The current scan, parsed: scope, owner, file, SHA-256, scan date, hosts, and each finding with host, finding ID, name, severity, CVEs, first seen, patch published, exploit available and unsupported. scan-history.json Every export read, newest first: file, SHA-256, scan date, number of hosts and number of findings. patch-assessment.json The policy used, and every overdue finding (host, finding ID, name, severity, exploit, what its age counts from, since when, its age and window in hours) and every unsupported one. The checks name at most 20; this file has them all.

An empty drop folder gives only scan-history.json, with no exports.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Each instance reports the checks of its scope, judged from the current scan:

Check Pass when Otherwise vuln.<scope>.scanned_in_interval The current scan is at most scan_interval_days calendar days old. fail, with the scan's age and owner; fail when no export has been dropped yet. vuln.<scope>.patched_in_window No open finding is older than patch_window_days, or exploited_patch_window_hours when the finding is rated critical or an exploit is available. fail, naming up to 20 overdue findings and counting the rest; error with no scan yet. vuln.<scope>.unsupported_removed No finding is marked unsupported. fail, naming the hosts and up to 20 findings; error with no scan yet.

So there are eleven check IDs:

  • vuln.internet_facing.scanned_in_interval, vuln.internet_facing.patched_in_window, vuln.internet_facing.unsupported_removed
  • vuln.common_apps.scanned_in_interval, vuln.common_apps.patched_in_window, vuln.common_apps.unsupported_removed
  • vuln.other_apps.scanned_in_interval, vuln.other_apps.patched_in_window
  • vuln.operating_systems.scanned_in_interval, vuln.operating_systems.patched_in_window, vuln.operating_systems.unsupported_removed

other_apps has no unsupported check. Removing unsupported applications other than the common ones is a maturity level 3 requirement (ISM-0304), and Evidence Hound's Essential Eight mapping covers levels 1 and 2.

A finding's age is counted up to the scan date, from the first of these that is known:

  1. When its patch was published.
  2. When it was first seen.
  3. The earliest export in the folder that shows the same host and finding ID.

The Essential Eight counts from the patch's release, so a scanner that gives the publication date is judged most fairly. A .nessus file has no first-seen date, so keep older exports in the folder to give findings their age.

Every open finding counts, whatever its severity, because the Essential Eight windows do not depend on severity. Informational Nessus items are not findings.

docs.title: In the Essential Eight mapping
docs.text:
Check Requirements vuln.internet_facing.scanned_in_interval ISM-1698 (online services, daily), ISM-1701 (operating systems of internet-facing servers and network devices, daily) vuln.internet_facing.patched_in_window ISM-1690 and ISM-1876 (online services: two weeks, or 48 hours when the vendor rates it critical or an exploit exists), ISM-1877 (their operating systems, 48 hours when critical or exploited) vuln.internet_facing.unsupported_removed ISM-1905 (unsupported online services removed) vuln.common_apps.scanned_in_interval ISM-1699 (weekly) vuln.common_apps.patched_in_window ISM-1691 (two weeks) vuln.common_apps.unsupported_removed ISM-1704 vuln.other_apps.scanned_in_interval ISM-1700 (fortnightly) vuln.other_apps.patched_in_window ISM-1693 (one month) vuln.operating_systems.scanned_in_interval ISM-1702 (fortnightly) vuln.operating_systems.patched_in_window ISM-1695 (one month), with Intune compliance vuln.operating_systems.unsupported_removed ISM-1501, with the Microsoft 365 operating system check and the firewall firmware check

All the rows use all_pass. So a deployment that maps ISM-1695 or ISM-1501 needs an operating_systems scan source, or those rows stay not assessed. ISM-1694, the two-week window (48 hours when critical or exploited) for operating systems of internet-facing servers and network devices, needs both vuln.internet_facing.patched_in_window and the Sophos Central firewall check network.firewall.firmware_current.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Code Meaning vuln_scan.setting_missing, vuln_scan.setting_invalid A setting is missing or has a value the collector cannot use. All are reported at once. vuln_scan.drop_folder_missing The drop folder does not exist. vuln_scan.export_invalid An export cannot be read. The message names the file and line.

docs.title: Backups and restore tests
docs.text:
CISO Assistant is your system of record, so its data must survive a lost disk, a bad upgrade or ransomware on the host. The reference stack ships two scripts in deploy/compose:

Script What it does How often backup.sh Dumps CISO Assistant's PostgreSQL database and copies its data volume (attachments and evidence files) and the runner's data volume (evidence store, run history, manual drop folders) into one file, encrypted with age, in an off-host folder. Keeps the newest 30. Daily restore-test.sh Decrypts the newest backup, restores it into a separate, temporary Compose project, starts CISO Assistant on it, checks its health endpoint and that it holds as many audits as the backup did, then removes the temporary project. It drops the result into a manual source's drop folder, so the test becomes evidence. Quarterly, and after every upgrade

Nothing is written unencrypted outside a private temporary folder, and the live stack is never changed by a restore test.

docs.title: Set up once
docs.text:
1. Install age on the host: sudo apt install age.
  2. Make the key pair off the host, on the laptop of the person who looks after backups or in your password manager's secure notes, never on the VM:
$ age-keygen -o evidence-hound-backup.key
Public key: age1...

Keep evidence-hound-backup.key (the identity) in your password manager. Copy only the public key to the host: echo age1... | sudo tee /etc/evidence-hound/backup-recipients.txt. Add a second person's public key on another line, so one lost key does not lose the backups. 3. Make the backup folder off-host. Mount a share from another machine or a NAS (NFS or SMB) at, say, /mnt/backups/evidence-hound, or point it at a local folder that a sync tool (such as rclone or your backup agent) copies off the host every day. A backup on the same disk as the VM is not a backup. 4. Schedule it. As root, in /etc/cron.d/evidence-hound-backup:

# Daily at 01:30, before the collectors' runs (hound init and hound add schedule them at 03:00 by default).
30 1 * * * root cd /opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose && HOUND_BACKUP_DIR=/mnt/backups/evidence-hound HOUND_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS=/etc/evidence-hound/backup-recipients.txt ./backup.sh >>/var/log/evidence-hound-backup.log 2>&1

Check the log the next morning: the last line reads backup: wrote ciso-assistant-<time>.tar.age (<n> audits, sha256 ...).

docs.title: Run a restore test
docs.text:
Every quarter, and after every CISO Assistant upgrade:

  1. Bring the identity to the host for the test only: sudo install -m 0400 /dev/stdin /root/backup.key and paste it.
  2. Run the test, naming the manual source that records restore tests in your hound.yaml (the example config calls it example-backup-restore-test, with the check backup.restore_tested):
$ cd /opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose
$ sudo HOUND_BACKUP_DIR=/mnt/backups/evidence-hound HOUND_BACKUP_IDENTITY=/root/backup.key \
    HOUND_RESTORE_SOURCE=example-backup-restore-test ./restore-test.sh
...
Restore test: passed
Audits at backup: 3
Audits after restore: 3
restore-test: dropped restore-test-20261125T030000Z.txt into manual source example-backup-restore-test
  1. Remove the identity: sudo shred -u /root/backup.key.
  2. The next run collects the result file. Your agent proposes the result (skill "process-manual-evidence") and you attest it in the weekly review, like any other manual evidence. A test that stops part way still drops a result that says where it stopped (Failed at:). A failed test is evidence too: record it and open an action.

The test needs about 2 GB of free memory and disk for the temporary project, and takes 5 to 10 minutes, most of it CISO Assistant starting. It exits 0 when the test passed, 1 when it failed and 2 when it could not start.

docs.title: Restore for real
docs.text:
When the live stack is lost, on a new host with the stack installed but not started (deploy/compose):

  1. Decrypt the newest backup into a private folder: install -d -m 700 /root/restore, then age -d -i backup.key ciso-assistant-<time>.tar.age | tar -C /root/restore -xf -, then check it: (cd /root/restore && sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS).
  2. Start PostgreSQL only: docker compose up -d --wait postgres.
  3. Restore the database: docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c 'pg_restore -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" --no-owner --exit-on-error' </root/restore/ciso-assistant.dump.
  4. Create the other containers without starting them (docker compose up --no-start), then restore the two volumes:
docker run --rm -i -v evidence-hound_ca-data:/data --entrypoint tar postgres:16.11 --numeric-owner -C /data -xpf - </root/restore/ca-data.tar
docker run --rm -i -v evidence-hound_runner-data:/data --entrypoint tar postgres:16.11 --numeric-owner -C /data -xpf - </root/restore/runner-data.tar
  1. Start everything: docker compose up -d --wait, sign in, and check the audits. Use the same django_secret_key as before if you still have it; with a new one, everyone signs in again and the runner needs a new token (./runner-token.sh).

manifest.txt in the backup names the CISO Assistant version it came from. Restore into the same version, then upgrade.

docs.title: Harden the host
docs.text:
The reference stack (deploy/compose) is locked down inside Docker: only Caddy publishes a port, the database network is internal, secrets are files, and the runner is read-only with no capabilities. This guide covers the host around it. Work through it once when you build the VM, record the date in your private compliance repo, and check it again every year or after a rebuild. Each section says what to do and how to check it.

The commands are for Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS. Another distribution needs its own equivalents.

docs.title: 1. Patch the host
docs.text:
Install security updates every day, automatically, and reboot when a kernel update needs it.

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades
echo 'Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "03:30";' | sudo tee /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52evidence-hound

Pick a reboot time outside the backup (01:30) and the collectors' schedules. The stack's restart: unless-stopped brings it back.

Check: sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug lists the security origin; /var/log/unattended-upgrades/ has today's log.

docs.title: 2. Firewall
docs.text:
Allow HTTPS for people and the agent's read-only account, and SSH only from your admin network. Deny everything else inbound.

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow from 192.0.2.0/24 to any port 22 proto tcp   # your admin network
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp                                       # or CA_HTTPS_PORT
sudo ufw enable

Docker publishes ports through its own iptables rules, which bypass ufw. Only Caddy publishes a port in the reference stack, so this is safe as long as you add no other ports: in an override. If CISO Assistant should be reachable only inside your network, put the VM behind your network firewall or a VPN instead of opening 443 to the internet.

Check: from another machine, nmap -Pn <host> shows 443 open and 22 only from the admin network.

docs.title: 3. Encrypt the disks
docs.text:
CISO Assistant holds your audit results, evidence and supplier records: sensitive data, and for a defence supplier possibly CUI. Keep it encrypted at rest.

  • On a cloud VM, turn on the provider's disk encryption with a key you control (a customer-managed key), for the boot and data volumes.
  • On your own hardware, install Ubuntu with full-disk encryption (LUKS) and keep the recovery key in your password manager.
  • Backups are encrypted by backup.sh with age (backups); keep the private key off the host.

Check: lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT shows a crypt device under / (own hardware), or the provider's console shows the volumes encrypted with your key.

docs.title: 4. Docker daemon
docs.text:
Rotate container logs, keep containers running through a daemon restart, and stop containers gaining privileges. In /etc/docker/daemon.json:

{
  "log-driver": "local",
  "log-opts": { "max-size": "20m", "max-file": "5" },
  "live-restore": true,
  "no-new-privileges": true,
  "userland-proxy": false
}

Then sudo systemctl restart docker. Only administrators are in the docker group: membership is root on the host.

Check: docker info --format '{{.LoggingDriver}} {{.LiveRestoreEnabled}}' prints local true; getent group docker lists only administrators.

docs.title: 5. Forward the logs
docs.text:
Keep logs off the host, so an attacker on the VM cannot erase them and you can see the history after a failure.

  • Send the host's journal (SSH logins, sudo, Docker) to your log platform or SIEM with its agent, or with rsyslog to a central syslog server.
  • Send the containers' logs: docker compose logs covers CISO Assistant and the runner. With the local log driver, the platform's Docker integration reads them; or switch the driver to journald and forward the journal.
  • Keep them at least as long as your framework asks (the ISM asks for event logs to be retained for at least seven years for some systems; agree the period with your authorising official).

Check: sign in over SSH, then find that login in the central log within a few minutes.

docs.title: 6. Certificates and uptime
docs.text:
Know before people do when CISO Assistant is down or its certificate is about to expire.

  • Point an uptime monitor (your monitoring platform, or a hosted one) at https://<CA_HOSTNAME>/api/health/ every five minutes, with an alert to the GRC team and IT.
  • With Caddy's internal certificate authority, Caddy renews the site certificate itself; the root it issued is valid for ten years. With your own certificate, add a certificate-expiry check that alerts 30 days ahead.
  • hound status shows each collector's last run; the collectors' health control in CISO Assistant shows the same to the GRC team.

Check: stop the frontend (docker compose stop frontend) and see the alert arrive; start it again.

docs.title: 7. MFA for every CISO Assistant user
docs.text:
Every person who signs in to CISO Assistant uses multi-factor authentication. In CISO Assistant, each user turns on MFA (an authenticator app) under their profile's security settings; administrators check it for every account. If your CISO Assistant signs people in through your identity provider (SSO), enforce MFA there with a Conditional Access or equivalent policy.

Service accounts (the runner, an agent's read-only account) sign in with personal access tokens, not passwords, so MFA does not apply; section 8 covers them.

Check: the users list in CISO Assistant, or your identity provider's MFA report, shows every person enrolled.

docs.title: 8. A service account per integration
docs.text:
Give each integration its own account and token, with only the access it needs, so one leaked token can be revoked alone:

Integration Account Access The runner hound-runner@..., made by runner-token.sh Writes audits and evidence Your agent, for reports and questions A Reader user on the folders in scope (AI-assisted reporting) Reads only Each collector's source system The collector's own app registration or API key (collectors) Read-only roles listed per collector

Tokens expire: runner-token.sh issues one for 365 days by default. Put the renewal in your evidence plan, and rotate a token at once when someone who could read it leaves.

Check: CISO Assistant's users list has one service account per integration and no shared accounts; every token has an expiry.

docs.title: Record it
