docs.text: When you have worked through the guide, record the date, the VM and who did it in your private compliance repo (for example in deploy/hardening-record.md), and attach it as evidence to your system hardening control. Repeat the checks every year.

docs.title: Keep it up to date
docs.text: The stack has three things to update: the host (patched daily, see hardening), CISO Assistant (CA_VERSION) and the Evidence Hound runner (HOUND_RUNNER_IMAGE). Both images are pinned in your private compliance repo's deploy/deploy.env (or .env), so every update is a reviewed pull request and every version you ran is in git history.

docs.title: Get told about new versions
docs.text:
Let a bot open the pull request for you. In your private compliance repo:

  • Renovate reads versions out of any file with a custom manager. For example, in renovate.json:
{
  "extends": ["config:recommended"],
  "customManagers": [
    {
      "customType": "regex",
      "fileMatch": ["^deploy/deploy\\.env$"],
      "matchStrings": ["CA_VERSION=(?<currentValue>v\\S+)"],
      "depNameTemplate": "ghcr.io/intuitem/ciso-assistant-community/backend",
      "datasourceTemplate": "docker"
    },
    {
      "customType": "regex",
      "fileMatch": ["^deploy/deploy\\.env$"],
      "matchStrings": ["HOUND_RUNNER_IMAGE=ghcr\\.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:(?<currentValue>\\S+)"],
      "depNameTemplate": "ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound",
      "datasourceTemplate": "docker"
    }
  ],
  "schedule": ["before 9am on the first day of the month"]
}
  • Dependabot reads image tags from Compose files only, not from .env files. To use it, pin the two images in your deploy/compose.override.yml (image: for backend, worker, frontend and runner) and add a docker-compose entry for /deploy to .github/dependabot.yml.

Security releases of either project are announced on its GitHub releases page; watch both repositories for releases.

docs.title: Update once a month
docs.text:
Take updates in a monthly window, such as the first Tuesday morning, and sooner for a security release. For each update:

  1. Read the release notes of every version between yours and the new one. Look for breaking changes, database migrations and changed settings. For CISO Assistant, check that its API still has what hound uses: the release notes of the Evidence Hound version you run name the CISO Assistant versions it was tested with.
  2. Back up, and check the backup is there: HOUND_BACKUP_DIR=... HOUND_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS=... ./backup.sh (backups). Note its name: it is your rollback point.
  3. Merge the pull request that changes the version, then on the host:
cd /opt/compliance && git pull
cd /opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d --wait

CISO Assistant migrates its database on start; the backend can take a few minutes to become healthy. 4. Check it works: sign in, open an audit, then run the collectors once and check their status:

docker compose run --rm runner run --config /config/hound.yaml
docker compose run --rm runner status --config /config/hound.yaml
  1. Run a restore test of the backup from step 2 (backups). It proves the rollback point works, and it is evidence for your backup requirements.
  2. Record the update as evidence on your patching control: the pull request, the date and the result of step 4.

docs.title: Roll back
docs.text:
CISO Assistant's database migrations only go forward, so going back to an older version means going back to the backup taken before the update. Anything recorded since the update is lost and must be entered again, which is why the window is short and announced.

  1. Revert the version change in your private repo (git revert), and git pull on the host.
  2. Stop the stack: docker compose down (keep the volumes for now).
  3. Restore the pre-update backup as in restore for real, into fresh volumes: docker compose down --volumes, then steps 1 to 5 there.
  4. Run the checks in step 4 above, and tell the GRC team what must be entered again.

A runner-only update rolls back without a restore: revert HOUND_RUNNER_IMAGE and docker compose up -d runner. The runner's evidence store keeps working across versions.

docs.title: Design: onboarding driven by the person's own coding agent
docs.text: Status: Agreed (Nov 23). Approvals are gathered into one guided weekly session by one guided review a week (Proposed, Nov 24). Changes the onboarding assistant design: the model moves out of hound and into the coding agent the person already uses. The build is tasks s09-36 to s09-42 in the s09 sprint.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The first real onboarding (a Sophos XGS 88w against Essential Eight ML2, s09-25 evidence) worked end to end, and showed where the built-in model falls short:

  • It cannot do the research a good pass needs. It read only the text it was given: no PDFs (the vendor's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate), no response fields behind $ref in the API spec (so it missed firmwareVersion), no vendor documentation beyond what the person pasted. 46 of 107 requirements fell back to "manual", including MFA, admin accounts, logging and configuration backups that the firewall's own XML API can likely evidence.
  • It cannot iterate. Profile drafting stopped after 3 rounds with a profile that did not validate; an agent that can run hound profile validate and hound profile test itself would keep going.
  • It costs a second subscription. A small business needs an API key, a token budget and hound onboard config on top of the Claude Code or GitHub Copilot seat it already pays for.
  • The review was too weak. About 27 of 60 "not applicable" rows rest on another system ("a vulnerability scanner", "the SIEM") that no audit covers yet, so real gaps showed as closed.

The person running the trial asked for a best-effort pass that a small business can get from tools it already has, and is content for that agent to read their own audit workbook and evidence, then onboard, validate, plan and apply through hound.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The agent drafts; hound decides what is valid; a person approves. The person's coding agent (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or another that reads repo instructions) does the reading, mapping and drafting. hound stays deterministic: it validates every file, plans every change, and records every decision with its provenance. Approvals stay with people.
  2. hound grows an agent interface, non-interactive and JSON in and out, so an agent never has to script around prompts:
  3. hound onboard <system> pending --json: what is still undecided, with requirement text, the API summary and the skills that apply.
  4. hound onboard <system> decide <requirement> --kind <api_check|manual|not_applicable|other_system> --reasoning ... --source ...: records one decision, validated, marked "drafted by agent".
  5. hound supplier draft ..., hound scope import ... and the existing hound scope validate|plan --json, hound profile validate|test, hound explain --json.
  6. Approvals refuse an agent, and happen in VS Code, never in CISO Assistant. Everything a person must approve is written in config as a draft and approved with hound approve in a terminal (the VS Code one), which walks the person through every pending item in turn and refuses to run without a terminal: not-applicable decisions, a system's applicability, environment capabilities, supplier approval and the conclusion of a supplier review, and manual evidence attestations (hound manual approve is the same walk-through for evidence only). hound then writes the approved state to CISO Assistant through scope plan and apply (and run for evidence); the person never clicks a button there. A supplier review's conclusion (ok, warning or blocker, who, when) lives in the third-party file. (In the trial, Claude Code's own permission system blocked it from approving the supplier, and the review had to be concluded through CISO Assistant's API; both move into hound approve.)
  7. "Met by another system" is its own state, never not applicable. The row stays open in this audit, names the system, and closes only when that system's audit shows the requirement met. hound scope plan lists such rows as open dependencies.
  8. The agent drives every kind of onboarding, not only systems: the organisation (hound init), the environment and its capability map, third parties (vendors, resellers and managed service providers, with their assurance documents, PDFs included), systems, audits (from a framework, or imported from an existing audit workbook), and manual evidence sources. Each has its skill, and the same pattern: the agent drafts through hound commands, hound validates, the person approves.
  9. Imported decisions keep their provenance. An agent onboarding an existing audit workbook records each result as "imported from <workbook>, row <n>, approved by <who> on <date>" as the workbook says, never as approved by the agent. A row without an approver is imported as a draft.
  10. Skills ship for the agents people have. The existing skills (supplier assessment, applicability, reading an API specification, reviewing a config change, mapping) are packaged as Claude Code skills (.claude/skills/) and as AGENTS.md plus .github/copilot-instructions.md for Copilot, in the compliance repo template that hound init writes. A new skill, import an audit workbook, covers mapping an existing Excel audit of controls and evidence to scope files.
  11. A stronger review before apply. A review skill runs hound explain --json, compares each decision with the same ISM control under other strategies, and must clear every flag it raises (or the person accepts it) before the agent proposes hound scope apply.
  12. The built-in model is frozen, then removed. No new features use it from today. Once the agent path has onboarded the Sophos firewall again, one task removes the model calls, the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, hound onboard config, onboarding.yaml, the outbound guard and the token budget. Commands keep their deterministic parts (explain still prints the flags code finds; onboard still records decisions).
  13. Manual evidence: the agent proposes and records, the person attests. When a manual source's file arrives (an export, a restore-test record, a screenshot), the agent reads it and records a proposal with hound manual propose <source> <file> --result <pass|fail|partial> --observation <text> --supports <where in the file>. The proposal is pending: it is not evidence and reaches no audit. hound manual approve walks the person through every pending proposal (the file, the agent's result, observation and supporting extract), and the person attests, changes or rejects each one. Only an attested result is published by hound run, recorded as "proposed by agent, attested by <person> on <date>", with the file attached and its hash.
  14. hound agent setup writes the assistant files. It asks which assistant the person uses in VS Code and writes them into the compliance repo from one source of skills, and hound init offers it at the end. Re-running it updates hound's files and leaves the person's own untouched:
Assistant Files Claude Code CLAUDE.md; .claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md for each skill; .claude/agents/<agent>.md for the onboarding and review agents GitHub Copilot in VS Code Custom agents .github/agents/<agent>.agent.md (frontmatter name, description, tools, skills; tools by alias: read, search, edit, execute), and .github/copilot-instructions.md for the rules every agent follows Both All of the above, from the same skill text

Agents get only the tools their job needs: the review agent has read, search and execute (to run hound) but not edit, because VS Code warns that an instruction not to edit is no permission boundary. Approvals are enforced by hound, not by the agent files.

docs.title: Principle: one hound, two ways to drive it
docs.text:
Every command works for a person at the terminal and for an agent at the terminal, with nothing either can do that the other cannot (except approve):

  • A person gets prompts, with a hint and an example for each answer, and plain-text output.
  • An agent gives the same answers as options and reads --json output; nothing waits on a prompt.
  • Both go through the same validation, the same plan and the same records, so a decision reads the same however it was made, apart from saying who drafted it.
  • Approvals are the one exception: they need a person on a terminal, whoever drove the rest.

A task that adds or changes a command is done only when both ways work and are tested.

docs.title: Rules that do not change
docs.text:
• No model in evidence collection, and no evidence without a person. hound run, hound serve and every collector stay model-free. For manual evidence an agent may read the file and propose a result, but a result becomes evidence only when a person attests it with hound manual approve (decision 10). This rewords the rule of the onboarding assistant design, at the maintainer's request: the person attests, as before, with the agent's proposal in front of them.
  • Nothing reaches CISO Assistant except through hound scope plan and apply.
  • No organisation data in this repository. The person's workbook, evidence and outputs live only in their private compliance repo. Each skill says so first.

docs.title: What changes about data handling
docs.text: With the built-in model, hound's outbound guard decided what left the machine. With an agent, the agent reads the repository and the files it is given, so the person's agent provider sees them. The docs say so plainly. Secrets stay in files the agent has no need to read (secrets/, outside the repo), and the skills tell the agent not to open them.

docs.title: Proposed tasks
docs.text: Task What Agent interface and approvals (s09-37) pending, decide, supplier draft, --json on validate, plan and explain; hound approve walks through every pending approval on a terminal; supplier review conclusions in config. Agent-driven onboarding of everything (s09-41) Organisation, environment, third parties, systems, audits and workbook import, each with a skill and agent commands. Manual evidence with the agent (s09-42) hound manual propose and hound manual approve; attested results only. Another-system state Its own result and plan section; environment onboarding uses it instead of not applicable; skips rows the mapping computes. Skills for agents Package the skills for Claude Code and Copilot in the repo template; a driving skill ("onboard a system with hound") and the review skill. Import an audit workbook A skill, plus hound scope import for the structured part (requirement, result, evidence reference, approver, date), with provenance. Sophos firewall XML API A reader for the on-device XML API, read-only, so MFA, admin accounts, device access, syslog and backup schedules can become checks. To be checked against Sophos's XML API documentation first. Spec summaries Resolve $ref response schemas so read endpoints list their fields. Trial Onboard the Sophos firewall again, this time driven by Claude Code with the skills, and compare with the s09-25 run.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: • Can a person's approval be proved by a signed commit alone, or does hound also need an interactive confirmation?

docs.title: Design: one guided review a week
docs.text: Status: Agreed and built in s10-07 (Nov 24). Builds on onboarding driven by the person's own coding agent. The build is task s10-07 in the s10 sprint; later sprints add their own items to the same queue.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
The maintainer's direction (Nov 24): the Cyber GRC member at a small supplier has 2 to 8 hours a week for all of it. AI should help the team learn, mature, operationalise and sustain compliance, and come as close as it can to approving everything itself. Every human review and approval should be gathered into one simple, direct process: alert the person, then a batched session in which the agent guides them through each recommendation (read, understand, accept or challenge) and then applies what they accepted.

Today a person signs off in several places: hound approve for onboarding decisions and suppliers, hound manual approve for evidence, reading hound scope plan before apply, and, from later sprints, an SSP version, a risk acceptance and a report. Each is sound on its own, but together they ask the person to know where to look and when.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. One queue. hound review pending --json lists everything that waits on a person, from every source, in one shape: what it is, why it matters, the agent's recommendation with its reasons and sources, the effect of accepting it (the plan it would apply), the deadline it serves, and an estimate in minutes. Sources: undecided onboarding decisions and not-applicable rows, supplier approvals and review conclusions, manual evidence proposals, scope changes waiting to be applied, and later SSP versions (s11), POA&M items and risk acceptances (s15), and committee actions (s12).
  2. The agent prepares; the person decides once. Before the session the person's agent works the queue: it drafts each recommendation through the existing prompt-free commands (onboard decide, manual propose, supplier draft, scope plan), and attaches its reasons and the extract that supports it. Nothing it prepares takes effect.
  3. One session, in order. hound review (a terminal; an agent or a pipe is refused, as hound approve is) walks the queue most-urgent first and stops at the time the person gives (--for 60m). For each item it shows the recommendation in plain words and asks: accept, challenge (with a note the agent answers before the next session, the item stays queued), or skip. At the end it shows what will change and applies the accepted items in one batch: the same approved files, scope apply and the next run publish as today. One sign-off record names the person, the time and every item accepted.
  4. Alert, not chase. A recurring CISO Assistant task assigned to the GRC team ("Weekly compliance review", from the evidence plan in s10-04) emails the person before each session with the queue's size, the time it needs and anything due this week. Nothing else is emailed. Items past their deadline are listed in the committee report (s12-05), as overdue manual evidence is.
  5. Standing approvals shrink the queue. The person may approve a rule instead of each instance, for a year, in the same session: for example, "a manual source whose new export has the same checks and the same results as last time may be re-attested by its owner without review". The rule is written to the repo, shown in every session's summary, and expires. A rule can never cover a not-applicable decision, a risk acceptance or a first approval.
  6. Learning is part of the session. Each item carries a short "why this matters" from the requirement and the mapping, so the person learns the framework as they work through it, and a challenge teaches the agent. The session summary says what the team has now operationalised (sources automated, items that needed no change) so maturity is visible.

docs.title: Rules that do not change
docs.text:
• No model in evidence collection. Collectors stay deterministic; the agent proposes only after collection.
  • No evidence without a person: an attestation is accepted in the session (or by a standing approval the person signed), never by the agent alone.
  • "Met by another system" stays open, and a not-applicable decision is always reviewed one by one.
  • CISO Assistant stays the system of record; the queue is read from the repo and CISO Assistant, not a new store.

docs.title: Proposed tasks
docs.text:
• s10-07 Review queue and guided weekly session (this sprint): hound review pending --json, hound review, the sign-off record, the weekly task in the example evidence plan, and the skill that prepares the queue.
  • s11, s12, s15: each new kind of approval (SSP version, POA&M item, committee action, risk acceptance) joins the queue rather than adding its own command.
  • s12-03: the operating guide is built around the weekly session and the 2 to 8 hour budget.

docs.title: As built (s10-07)
docs.text:
• hound review pending --json lists what hound approve and hound manual approve would ask, in one shape. Items that become ready only once another is accepted (a system after its supplier and not-applicable decisions) are asked in the same session, marked "now ready", rather than listed beforehand.
  • The agent records its recommendation for any item with hound review recommend (kept in review/recommendations.json), and answers a challenge the same way. A supplier review joins the queue 14 days before it is due (s10-05).
  • The one standing rule is unchanged_reattestation, for 12 months, per manual source. It is offered after a person accepts an unchanged attestation.
  • Scope changes waiting to be applied are not items: the session ends by showing the plan and applying it after a confirmation.
  • The weekly task's email is CISO Assistant's own task reminder with the runbook; it does not yet carry the queue's size.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Who may sign a standing approval when the authorising official is not the GRC member.
  • Whether a challenge should reach the system owner as well as the agent.

docs.title: Design: a generic REST collector
docs.text: Status: Implemented (s09-09 to s09-14, Nov 22). The reference is docs/collectors/rest.md and the tutorial Write a profile. Changes made during the build are listed at the end, under "As built".

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Every collector today is hand-written C# for one API. For each system we write code that signs in, follows that vendor's paging, saves the lists as evidence, parses the JSON into typed records, and then evaluates checks over those records. Getting the evidence right means reading API docs, writing a parser, and only then writing the check that matters.

The shape is already good. The Sophos and Microsoft 365 collectors both read each list once per run, save it as evidence, and run pure check functions over the saved data (SophosSources and SophosChecks, GraphSources and M365Checks). Many checks already share one list. What is expensive is that every part of that shape is code, written again for each vendor:

Part Sophos today Generic? Sign in OAuth client credentials, then whoami for tenant and data region Yes, with a "bootstrap" step Paging page and pages.total Yes, one of a few styles Evidence and privacy Raw list, identities hashed by property name Yes, from a list of property names Parse to typed records SophosData.Parse Not needed if checks read JSON directly Checks Pure C# per check Most are "for each item, test a field"; some are not

So the question is not "should queries and checks be separate" (they already are), but "should queries and checks be configuration instead of code".

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Add a system by writing a profile (YAML), not a C# project, for the common case.
  2. Call each endpoint once per run, eagerly and with paging, and let many checks share one response. A 1 to 1 check is just a query with one check.
  3. Each check pulls fields out and tests them against the requirement, giving pass, fail, or unable to assess.
  4. A broken query, a missing field or a wrong path never shows as a control failure.
  5. Keep checks framework-neutral. Profiles emit check IDs; the mapping files stay as they are.
  6. Keep TDD: a profile is tested against recorded responses before it is trusted.

Not goals: a general workflow engine, writing to any API, or replacing the manual collector.

docs.title: A. Keep coded collectors, extract a shared HTTP kit
docs.text:
Move auth, paging, rate limiting, evidence saving and redaction into a reusable library. Each vendor is still a C# project, but much thinner.

  • Gains: smallest change; full power of C# for every check; nothing new to learn.
  • Costs: still a code change, review, release and new image for every system and every new check. The GRC team cannot read or adjust a check without reading C#. Does not address the person's main pain.

docs.title: B. Declarative REST collector with a code escape hatch (recommended)
docs.text:
One built-in collector type, rest, driven by a profile. The profile declares the connection, the queries and the checks. Checks use a small, fixed set of operators over JSON paths. Anything the operators cannot express is a code check: a named, pure C# function built into hound, with the same inputs as a declarative check.

  • Gains: most systems need no code; checks are readable by the GRC team and auditors; one tested engine for auth, paging, retries and redaction; fewer API calls; one consistent snapshot; profiles are testable against saved responses.
  • Costs: we design and maintain a small language; some logic still needs code; a wrong path has to be caught (see "Making failure visible").

docs.title: C. Declarative queries, checks in a general expression language
docs.text:
Like B, but each check is an expression in an existing language: JMESPath, JSONata, jq or CEL.

  • Gains: more expressive without code (filters, projections, some date maths in JSONata and CEL); someone else maintains the language.
  • Costs: expressions get dense and hard for non-developers to review; static validation of an expression is weaker; .NET support varies by language (JMESPath and JSONata have .NET ports; CEL and jq support in .NET would need checking before we rely on it); one more dependency in the core.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: B, with two guard rails: start with a deliberately small operator set, and keep the code-check hatch from day one. If, after converting Sophos and writing two or three new profiles, the operators keep falling short in the same way, add JMESPath as one more operator (expression:) rather than switching wholesale. That keeps the common case readable and leaves a path to C.

docs.title: Three phases: collect, extract, assess
docs.text:
Evidence for one control often spans two or more API calls: an admin's role comes from one endpoint, their MFA state from another, and the firmware they run from a third. So a run is three phases, each finished before the next starts:

 1. Collect                       2. Extract                          3. Assess
 every query, once                named evidence datasets             every check
 ------------------------         -----------------------------       ---------------------------
 token, whoami  (bootstrap)       admin_accounts =                    super_admin_count
 admins, roles, firewalls  --->     admins + roles (join on roleId)   ---> firmware_supported
 firmware_upgrades (per fw)       firewall_firmware =                 firmware_current
                                    firewalls + firmware_upgrades
 raw responses saved              datasets saved, with lineage        results cite datasets
  1. Collect. Run every query the profile needs, including dependent ones, as a graph: a query that needs an ID from another (whoami before anything, one call per firewall after firewalls) waits for it; independent ones can run in parallel within the rate limit. Each response is saved as raw evidence. No check runs until collection ends, so every check sees the same snapshot.
  2. Extract. Build named evidence datasets from one or more responses: pick the fields that matter, join responses on a key, filter to what is in scope. A dataset is the evidence a control is judged on, for example "admin accounts with their roles and MFA state". Each dataset is saved as its own evidence file, listing the raw files (and their hashes) it came from, so an auditor can trace a result back to the API responses.
  3. Assess. Each check reads one dataset and tests its fields against the requirement. Checks never call an API or join anything themselves.

This splits the hard parts. Collecting is about APIs (auth, paging, retries). Extracting is about data (which fields, which joins). Assessing is about the control (what good looks like). Each can be tested on its own: extraction against recorded responses, checks against a small hand-written dataset.

When one of several queries fails, only what depends on it is affected. A failed query makes every dataset built from it, and every check reading those datasets, unable to assess, naming the failed query. Checks that do not depend on it still run and report normally. A dataset is never built from a partial set of its inputs.

Evidence from two different systems (for example, a user list from an HR system checked against identity provider accounts):

  • Within one product family, one profile can declare more than one connection, and datasets can join across them.
  • Across separate collector instances, the first answer is the mapping file: the requirement needs both systems' checks to pass. A true join across instances (one dataset built from two collectors' responses) is a later step; it needs the runner to share snapshots between collectors, and we should wait for a real case before building it.

docs.title: Profile and instance
docs.text:
• A profile holds what is true for every customer of a product: endpoints, paging, which properties identify people, the checks. No profile is built into hound. Every profile loads the same way, from a profiles folder the organisation keeps in its own config repo, so a new system does not need a new release. This repo keeps a public library of profiles to copy from (for example profiles/sophos-central.yaml). See "Where profiles live".
  • A collector instance in the deployment config names the profile and gives the per-organisation parts: settings, secrets, thresholds.
# deployment config (fictional)
collectors:
  - name: sophos-example
    type: rest
    settings:
      profile: sophos-central
      client_id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
      supported_firewall_firmware: 20.0, 21.0
      super_admin_max: 2
    secrets:
      client_secret: env:SOPHOS_CLIENT_SECRET

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
profile: sophos-central
version: 1

parameters:                       # validated before anything is called
  client_id: { type: string, required: true }
  supported_firewall_firmware: { type: list, required: true }
  super_admin_max: { type: int, default: 2 }
secrets:
  client_secret: { required: true }

connection:
  base_url: https://api.central.sophos.com/
  allowed_hosts: ["*.central.sophos.com", id.sophos.com]   # secrets and tokens go nowhere else
  auth:
    type: oauth2_client_credentials
    token_url: https://id.sophos.com/api/v2/oauth2/token
    client_id: ${client_id}
    client_secret: ${secrets.client_secret}
    scope: token
  rate_limit: { per_second: 5, retry_after: honour, max_retries: 3 }

bootstrap:                        # runs first; its values feed later requests
  whoami:
    get: whoami/v1
    vars:
      tenant_id: $.id
      data_region: $.apiHosts.dataRegion

queries:
  firewalls:
    get: ${data_region}/firewall/v1/firewalls
    headers: { X-Tenant-ID: "${tenant_id}" }
    paging: { style: page_number, page: page, size: pageSize=100, total_pages: $.pages.total }
    items: $.items
    identities: [hostname, name, serialNumber, ipv4Addresses, macAddresses]
  admins:
    get: ${data_region}/common/v1/admins
    headers: { X-Tenant-ID: "${tenant_id}" }
    paging: { style: page_number, page: page, size: pageSize=100, total_pages: $.pages.total }
    items: $.items
    identities: [firstName, lastName, email]
  roles:
    get: ${data_region}/common/v1/roles
    headers: { X-Tenant-ID: "${tenant_id}" }
    items: $.items

The engine supports, at first:

  • Auth: OAuth 2.0 client credentials (secret or certificate), static API key (header or query), bearer token, basic, and mutual TLS. Tokens are refreshed on expiry.
  • Paging: next link in the body (Graph @odata.nextLink), page number with total, cursor or continuation token, offset and limit, and the HTTP Link header. A page cap per query stops endless paging, as SophosClient.MaxPages does today.
  • Rate limits: per-profile request rate, Retry-After on 429 and 503, bounded retries.
  • Bootstrap variables for flows like Sophos whoami that tell you where to read from.
  • Fan-out (for_each: firewalls) for APIs that need one call per item, capped, because it multiplies calls.
  • XML: converted to the same JSON tree at the edge (attributes as @name, text as #text), so checks use one path language. A profile lists paths that must always be arrays, which avoids the usual "one element is an object, two are an array" trap.

Each query is read once per run, before any check runs, and saved as one evidence file. Checks only ever see the saved snapshot, so every result can be reproduced from the evidence.

A dependent query names what it needs, and the engine orders the calls:

  firmware_upgrades:
    # Illustrative: s08-13 confirms the real endpoint and whether release dates are exposed.
    for_each: firewalls               # one call per firewall, after firewalls is read
    max_calls: 200
    post: ${data_region}/firewall/v1/firewalls/actions/firmware-upgrade-check
    body: { firewalls: ["${item.id}"] }
    items: $.firewalls

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
datasets:
  admin_accounts:
    from: admins
    join:
      - with: roles
        on: { left: $.roleAssignments[*].roleId, right: $.id }
        as: roles                     # each admin gains a list of its roles
    fields:
      id: $.id
      role_names: $.roles[*].name
      # identities stay hashed, as in the raw evidence
  firewall_firmware:
    from: firewalls
    join:
      - with: firmware_upgrades
        on: { left: $.id, right: $.id }
        as: upgrades
        optional: true                # no row means no upgrade is available
    fields:
      id: $.id
      version: $.firmwareVersion
      upgrade_released: $.upgrades[0].releasedAt

The first extraction operations, kept small on purpose: from (one query), join (on a key, one-to-many allowed, optional for a left join), where (filter), fields (pick and rename), and flatten (one row per element of a nested list). A join whose key matches nothing on a required side is reported, not silently dropped: the dataset records how many rows did not match, and a check can treat unmatched rows as unable to assess.

A one-to-one check needs no dataset: a check can read a query directly, and the engine treats it as a dataset of that query's items.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
checks:
  - id: network.firewall.firmware_supported
    over: firewall_firmware
    when_empty: not_applicable
    each:
      field: $.version
      version_in: ${supported_firewall_firmware}
    require: all
    describe: "{passed} of {total} firewalls run supported firmware. Supported: ${supported_firewall_firmware}."

  - id: network.management.super_admin_count
    over: admin_accounts
    where: { field: $.role_names, any_matches: "(?i)^super ?-?admin$" }
    require: { count_at_most: ${super_admin_max} }
    describe: "{matched} of {total} Sophos Central admins hold Super Admin; at most ${super_admin_max} allowed."

  - id: network.firewall.firmware_current
    over: firewall_firmware
    each:
      field: $.upgrade_released
      missing: pass                   # no upgrade available is up to date
      older_than: P14D
      negate: true
    require: all
    when_empty: not_applicable
    describe: "{failed} of {total} firewalls have had a firmware upgrade available for more than 14 days."

With the join done in extraction, "updated within 14 days of release" no longer needs code. Code checks stay for logic that is not "test a field of each row", such as conditional access policy coverage.

A declarative check has four parts:

  1. over: which dataset (or query) it reads. Many checks can name the same dataset.
  2. where (optional): which items are in scope, for example only enabled users, or only admins with a given role.
  3. each: the test applied to a field of each item in scope.
  4. require: how item results become the check result: all, any, none, count_at_most, count_at_least, or ratio_at_least with an optional partial band (for example pass at 95 %, partial from 80 %).

The first operator set, deliberately small: equals, not_equals, in, matches (regex), exists, version_in, version_at_least, within and older_than (a duration against the run's clock), at_least and at_most for numbers, and any_matches for lists. Each test can say what a missing field means (missing:) and can be negated. Joins are not a check operator: they belong to datasets.

describe is the observation written to CISO Assistant, with counts filled in. Offending items are listed in the observation (capped, as today) and in full in the evidence.

docs.title: Code checks
docs.text: A code check is a pure function built into hound under a name (a small library in the repo, reviewed and tested like any other code, not loaded at runtime): it receives the snapshots it names, its parameters and the clock, and returns a Finding. That is exactly the signature SophosChecks already has, so today's checks can move over unchanged and be replaced by declarative ones one at a time. Microsoft 365 conditional access coverage is expected to stay as code.

docs.title: Where profiles live
docs.text:
Kind Where How it gets to hound Who changes it Profile library profiles/ in this repo, each profile with fictional recordings and tests Not loaded by hound. Copied into an organisation's profiles folder; the interactive tutorial copies the ones it uses Pull request here; CI runs every library profile's tests Organisation profile A profiles/ folder in the organisation's private config repo, next to its deployment config Mounted read-only into the container (setting profiles_path, default /config/profiles); the only place hound reads profiles from Pull request in that private repo, same hound profile validate and hound profile test Code check src/ in this repo Compiled into hound Pull request here, test-first

Rules:

  • One way in. hound reads profiles only from the profiles folder, so there is nothing to override and the image stays the same size whatever profiles exist. A copied library profile keeps its source and version fields, so hound profile diff <name> can show how a local copy differs from the library version it came from.
  • Validated before use. Every profile passes the same schema and reference checks before any request is made. A profile that fails validation stops only its own collector instances, as unable to assess, not the whole run.
  • No code in profiles. A profile can only name built-in operators and built-in code checks. It cannot load a DLL, run a script or call a shell, so a profile cannot do more than make the read requests it declares.
  • Secrets stay on declared hosts. A profile's allowed_hosts bounds where its tokens and secrets can go; redirects to other hosts are refused.
  • Compatible versions. A profile declares the hound features it needs (requires: { hound: ">=1.2" }), so an older image refuses it clearly instead of half-running it.
  • Traceable. Each run's manifest records every profile's name, version and SHA-256, so evidence shows which rules judged it. A changed profile is visible in the next run's manifest.
  • Tests encouraged, optionally required. hound warns when a profile in the folder has no tests (library profiles bring theirs when copied); the deployment setting require_profile_tests: true makes that an error.

This replaces the earlier plan to load collector DLLs from a known folder at runtime. The folder still exists, but it holds YAML, not code. Runtime code plugins are not needed for release 1, and they are only worth revisiting if a system needs a protocol the REST engine cannot speak (see "Edge cases").

Alternatives considered:

  • Profiles built into the image: works without copying anything, but every new system or tweak waits for a release, the image grows with every vendor, and built-in and local profiles need override rules. Rejected in favour of one load path.
  • Built-in library plus organisation folder (the earlier draft): convenient for common vendors, at the cost of two load paths and a no-override rule. Replaced by the library-to-copy model.
  • Profiles fetched from a URL or registry: convenient, but a supply chain risk for a tool that holds API credentials. Rejected.
  • Profiles stored in CISO Assistant: keeps everything in the system of record, but CISO Assistant has no place for them and it would mix GRC records with collector code. Rejected.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: Case How it is handled Evidence across several endpoints of one API Datasets join the responses (see "Three phases"). Evidence across two collectors Mapping requires both checks; a cross-collector join waits for a real case. A query needs IDs from another Dependency graph and for_each, capped by max_calls. Sign-in reveals where to read (Sophos whoami) bootstrap variables. Paging styles Next link, page number and total, cursor, offset and limit, Link header; page cap. Rate limits, 429, 503 Per-profile rate, Retry-After, bounded retries; then unable to assess. Reports that run as a job (start, poll, download) async query: a start request, a status URL polled with a timeout, then the result download. CSV or XML responses Converted at the edge to the same tree as JSON; checks do not change. POST queries (search APIs, GraphQL, hunting queries) post: with a body; paging works the same. Licence missing for one endpoint optional_on: [403, 404] on the query; dependent checks become not applicable with the reason, as M365 does today. Very large lists Item and byte caps, keep: to hold only needed fields. Wrong path or renamed field Missing field is unable to assess; profile tests against recordings catch it before use. Empty lists when_empty is required on every check. Logic beyond "test a field of each row" Built-in code check, named in the profile. Non-REST systems (SNMP, SSH, LDAP, file shares) Out of scope. The manual collector covers them; a code collector only if one becomes important. Push-only systems (webhooks, syslog) Out of scope for a scheduled collector; use the system's export or the manual collector.

docs.title: Making failure visible
docs.text:
The biggest risk of configuration is that a wrong path quietly returns nothing and a check passes over an empty list. The design closes that off in five ways.

1. Three results, plus the two we already have. The core already has Error, and the mapping engine already turns any Error into not_assessed for the requirement (MappingEngine.Assess). So "unable to assess" exists in the domain; this design makes it the default whenever the engine cannot be sure, and renames it in user-facing text from "error" to unable to assess. The full set a check can return:

Result When pass Items in scope meet the requirement. fail Items in scope were read and some do not meet it. unable to assess A query the check depends on (directly or through a dataset) failed, paging stopped early, a page cap was hit, a required field was missing on any item in scope, or a value had the wrong type. The observation says which. not applicable The list was read successfully and was empty, and the check says when_empty: not_applicable. partial Only for ratio_at_least with a partial band.

2. No silent empties. Every check must say what an empty list means (when_empty: not_applicable, fail or unable_to_assess). There is no default, so "all of nothing passes" cannot happen by accident.

3. Missing is not false. If the field a check tests is absent on an item, the check is unable to assess, not failed. A profile can say missing: fail for a field whose absence genuinely means "not configured", but it has to say so.

4. Validate before calling. hound validates a profile and the instance before any request: parameters, secrets, path syntax, that every over names a query, that every code check is registered, and that every check ID is in the mapping (as for coded collectors today).

5. Profile tests. Each profile ships with recorded, fictional responses and the expected result per check, and hound profile test <profile> runs them offline. This is how strict TDD applies to profiles: write the recording and the expected outcome (red), then the check (green). CI runs every profile's tests.

docs.title: Evidence, privacy and secrets
docs.text:
• Each query is saved as one JSON file: the request (without headers), page count, item count, and the items.
  • Identities listed in the profile are hashed, as SophosEvidence does today, unless the instance sets include_identities. Profiles default to hashing.
  • Secrets never reach evidence. Request headers and the token exchange are never saved. A final scan rejects any saved file containing a value of a secret in use, and fails that query as unable to assess rather than saving it.
  • Secrets only go to allowed_hosts. Profiles are configuration that can make requests with your credentials, so a profile cannot send a token or secret to a host it did not declare, and cross-host redirects are refused. This is what stops a bad or edited profile from leaking a credential.
  • Size budgets. Each query has an item cap and a byte cap (defaults set by the engine, raised per query). Over the cap is unable to assess, with the cap named, rather than a run that eats the host's memory. A query can declare keep: to save and hold only the fields its checks use, for very large lists.

docs.title: Trade-offs in one place
docs.text: We gain It costs Profiles instead of code New systems and checks without a release; readable by the GRC team A small language to design, document and keep stable One query, many checks Fewer calls, fewer rate limit problems, one consistent snapshot Memory for big lists; budgets and keep: needed Collect, extract, assess as separate phases Evidence across several APIs without code; each phase tested alone; auditors see the dataset a control was judged on A third concept (datasets) to learn; one more evidence file per dataset Fixed operators Easy to read, easy to validate Hard logic needs code checks Code-check hatch Nothing is out of reach Two ways to write a check; a new code check needs a release Unable to assess by default Broken queries never show as control failures on the board report More results show "not assessed" until profiles are right, which is the honest answer Profiles loaded at runtime Systems added without a new image A profile is now security-relevant config; host allowlist and review needed

docs.title: How existing collectors move over
docs.text:
• Sophos is the proof. Write profiles/sophos-central.yaml in the library and run it beside the coded collector on the same recordings. A parity test requires the same check IDs, outcomes and evidence content. When it passes, the coded collector is removed; existing type: sophos instances move to type: rest with profile: sophos-central, and hound explains the change when it meets the old type. The interactive tutorial copies the profile into the trial's profiles folder.
  • Microsoft 365 follows only if Sophos goes well. Most of its reads fit; several checks (conditional access coverage, PIM) are likely to stay as code checks inside the profile.
  • Manual and vuln-scan are not REST and stay as they are.
  • New systems after that (the roughly 13 SaaS systems) start as profiles. Where an API is weak, the manual collector stays the answer.

docs.title: Decisions (all agreed Nov 22)
docs.text:
1. Option B with the code hatch, adding JMESPath later only if the operators keep falling short.
  2. XML converted to the JSON tree rather than a second path language (XPath).
  3. Evidence keeps the full response minus identities and secrets, rather than only the fields checks use. Fuller evidence for auditors, at the cost of size; keep: is there for very large lists.
  4. Missing fields mean unable to assess unless the profile says otherwise.
  5. No profiles built into hound. Every profile loads from the organisation's mounted profiles folder. This repo keeps a tested public library to copy from, and the interactive tutorial uses it. No runtime code plugins.
  6. Collect, extract, assess as three phases, with joins in named datasets rather than in checks, and joins across separate collector instances left until a real case needs one.

docs.title: s09 tasks
docs.text:
Added to s09 rather than a new sprint, ahead of s09-01 so new Microsoft 365 and Veeam work can be profile checks. Full acceptance criteria are in the sprint file:

  • s09-09 Profile model and validation. Profile and instance schema, parameters, secrets, allowed_hosts, hound profile validate. Pure; no HTTP yet.
  • s09-10 Query engine. Auth types, paging styles, rate limits and retries, a dependency graph for bootstrap variables and fan-out, XML conversion, budgets, snapshot evidence with identity hashing and the secret scan. Contract tests with WireMock.
  • s09-11 Datasets and declarative checks. Extraction (from, join, where, fields, flatten) with lineage and unmatched-row counts; failure propagation from queries to datasets to checks; check operators, where, require, when_empty, missing-field rules, observations; "unable to assess" wording in user-facing text. Property tests over the evaluator.
  • s09-12 Code checks and profile tests. Built-in code-check library with names profiles can use; profiles folder as the only load path, with validation, requires, source and manifest hashes; hound profile test and hound profile diff; the public profiles/ library with an example profile; CI runs every library profile's tests.
  • s09-13 Sophos as a profile. profiles/sophos-central.yaml in the library; parity test against the coded collector; then remove the coded collector, migrate type: sophos config, and have the interactive tutorial copy the profile.
  • s09-14 Documentation. docs/collectors/rest.md (reference) and a tutorial: write a profile for a fictional API, test-first.

docs.title: As built
docs.text:
What changed from this design while it was built:

  • Retries. rate_limit has per_second and max_retries only. Retry-After is always honoured, so there is no retry_after key.
  • Redirects are followed only on the same host, at most 5 times, and refused otherwise (rest.redirect_refused).
  • Identities are hashed before extraction, so datasets and checks see the hashed values, the same as the evidence.
  • Results. A check gives pass, fail, partial (only for a ratio with partial_at), not applicable or unable to assess. when_empty has no default.
  • Sophos as a profile. The sophos-central profile matched the coded collector on six recordings (same check IDs, outcomes and evidence items), so the coded collector was removed and type: sophos now fails validation, naming the replacement. The profile needed no datasets: its firmware check reads the firewalls query directly, and the Super Admin count is the sophos.super_admin_count code check over admins and roles. It supports tenant credentials only; partner and organisation credentials, which the coded collector also read, are not supported.
  • Profile tests are YAML cases in <profile>.tests/ with recordings beside them, run offline by hound profile test. A profile without tests runs with a warning, or is unable to assess when the instance sets require_profile_tests.
  • Adding a collector. hound add collector rest --set profile=<name> asks for the profile's required parameters and secrets.
  • Manifest. The run's _manifest.json lists each profile that ran, with its version, source and SHA-256.

docs.title: Drafting reports with AI
docs.text: hound writes every figure in the committee and board reports itself, from CISO Assistant, with fixed rules. An AI assistant can help with the words around them: the committee summary, the board's compliance statements, and the questions members will ask. This guide shows how to use your own agent (Claude Code or Copilot, set up with hound agent setup) safely.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text: Every figure comes from the generated report, not from the model. The assistant may reword, shorten, order and explain. It may not add, round, estimate or change a number, a result, a date or a name. If it says something the report does not, delete it.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
1. Give the agent the report and its snapshot, nothing else: the Markdown file from hound report committee or hound report board, and the snapshot JSON from the evidence store's reports/ folder.
  2. If you want it to look up detail in CISO Assistant, give it a read-only account: in CISO Assistant, create a user with the Reader role on the folders in scope, create its personal access token, and give the agent HOUND_CA_URL and that token. Never give it hound's own service-account token, which can write. If your CISO Assistant version offers an MCP server, connect it with the same read-only account.
  3. Keep the agent's work in the compliance repo or a scratch folder, not in CISO Assistant. You publish the final report yourself.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
The committee summary.

Read committee-2026-11.md. Rewrite section 1 (Summary) as at most five short sentences for busy managers: what got better, what got worse, and what the committee must decide. Use only facts and figures that appear in the report, and keep every figure exactly as written. After the summary, list each sentence with the report line it came from.

The board compliance positions.

Read board-2026-q4.md. For each programme in section 1, write two sentences the authorising official can read out: the position and the main reason, in plain English without acronyms. Do not change the position or any figure. Quote the report line for each fact.

Questions to expect.

Read the report. List the five questions a sceptical committee member is most likely to ask, and where in the report, or in CISO Assistant through the read-only account, the answer is. Do not answer from your own knowledge.

docs.title: Check before you send
docs.text:
• Every sentence has a report line behind it; the agent listed them, so tick them off.
  • Figures match the report exactly. The fastest check is to search the report for each number.
  • Nothing names a person who is not already in the report.
  • The final report is the one hound generated, with only the summary or positions replaced. Upload that file as the "Security reporting" evidence revision.

docs.title: Why it is done this way
docs.text: Reports go to people who make decisions on them. A model can write fluent text that is wrong. Keeping the figures deterministic, and the model to wording only, with every claim traced to a line, keeps the report true and makes the check quick. This is the same rule hound follows everywhere: no model in collection, no evidence without a person.

docs.title: Reporting to the board
docs.text: The board sets how much cyber risk the organisation will accept, and holds management to it. Once a quarter it reads a two-page report, hound report board, confirms each programme's compliance position, and endorses the risks management has accepted on its behalf.

docs.title: Risk appetite statement (template)
docs.text:
The board approves this once a year. The committee and the authorising official work within it.

[Organisation] holds [customer and defence contract data, some of it CUI] and relies on [Microsoft 365, the engineering file share]. We have a low appetite for risks to the confidentiality of customer and contract data, and to our ability to keep contracts that require [Essential Eight Maturity Level Two / CMMC Level 2].

  • We do not accept any risk rated high or above after treatment for longer than [3] months without the board's endorsement.
  • Exceptions and risk acceptances are time-limited. The committee may approve them for up to [12] months; anything longer, or without an expiry, needs the board's endorsement.
  • We aim to meet every requirement of our audits of record; a programme more than [25]% non-compliant is reported off track.
  • We have a moderate appetite for operational risk in internal systems where a failure would cause delay but no data loss.

Record the approved statement in CISO Assistant as a policy (an applied control in the policy category), with the board minutes as its evidence, and set the matching risk matrix levels so the board report's "above appetite" mark agrees with it.

docs.title: How the monthly reports roll up
docs.text:
Board report section Comes from 1. Compliance position The last month of the quarter, per programme, by fixed rules (reporting) 2. Posture and trend The snapshots of the last month of this quarter and the three before it 3. Key risks The top five risk scenarios by level against appetite, with owner, treatment and target date 4. Risk-acceptance decisions Acceptances and exceptions the committee made during the quarter, with who and when 5. Assurance Automated versus manual coverage, evidence freshness, independent review, supplier assurance 6. Decisions and asks The positions to confirm, endorsements and recovery plans, generated; the committee's escalations, added by hand

Nothing in the body is operational: no collector failure or task appears there. They stay in the committee reports and the appendix.

docs.title: Before the meeting
docs.text:
1. The agent drafts the report on the first working day of the quarter.
  2. The authorising official reads section 1 and confirms, or changes, each proposed position with a reason. A changed position is written into the report with the reason, never by editing a figure.
  3. The authorising official adds the committee's escalations of the quarter (actions with the board as owner in the committee reports) to section 6, and the chair of the security committee checks none is missing.
  4. The report goes to the board with its papers.

docs.title: Record the board's decisions in CISO Assistant
docs.text:
Decision Record it as Confirm a compliance position A comment on the audit of record, with the meeting date, and the report uploaded as a revision of the "Security reporting" evidence Endorse a risk acceptance or exception Add the board as approver in its description with the meeting date, and keep or shorten the expiry Decline one Set it to rejected, and add a remediation action with an owner and due date Change the risk appetite A new revision of the risk appetite policy's evidence, with the minutes Ask for an independent review A task in CISO Assistant for the authorising official, with a due date

Training for board members: board session.

docs.title: Continuous compliance procedure
docs.text: A generic procedure for keeping a compliance programme current between assessments, for a small organisation without a CISO. Adapt the bracketed values, approve it at the security committee, and keep it with your policies. It applies to every programme in scope/setup.yaml.

docs.title: 1. Roles
docs.text: Role Who (small team) Responsible for Authorising official [CTO or general manager] Accepting the residual risk of operating the systems in scope; confirming each programme's compliance position each quarter GRC member [one person, 2 to 8 hours a week] Running this procedure with an AI agent; the weekly review; preparing reports; recording decisions System owners [named per system] Providing manual evidence on time; fixing their systems' gaps Collector operator [IT lead] Keeping collectors running and credentials current Security committee [see its terms of reference] Monthly oversight, exceptions and risk acceptances within its authority Board Risk appetite, endorsement of long or large acceptances, quarterly oversight

docs.title: 2. Evidence and its freshness
docs.text:
Each requirement in an audit of record is answered by a collector, a manual source attested by a person, or a hand-written result in the audit file. Evidence counts only while it is fresh:

Evidence Freshness window Who refreshes it Collector checks [7 days]: the run schedule, at least weekly Runs on schedule; the operator fixes failures Manual evidence The source's interval in the evidence plan ([monthly], [quarterly], [annually]) The system owner, on CISO Assistant's reminder Supplier assurance [12 months], or the certificate's expiry if sooner The GRC member, with the agent's draft review Policies and plans [12 months] The owner, approved at committee

Evidence past its window is reported: a stale collector in the committee report, an overdue task in section 7. A requirement whose evidence is missing is not assessed, never assumed compliant.

docs.title: 3. The cycle
docs.text: When What Record Continuously Collectors run; changes are published to CISO Assistant Run records; audit history Weekly Guided review: attest manual evidence, approve drafts, answer challenges review/sign-offs/ in the repo Monthly Snapshot; committee report and meeting; decisions recorded Snapshot and report on the "Security reporting" control Quarterly Board report; authorising official confirms positions Board minutes; comment on the audit of record Annually Procedure, risk appetite and policies reviewed; independent assessment if required New revisions of each

docs.title: 4. Reassessment triggers
docs.text:
Outside the cycle, the GRC member reassesses the affected requirements, and tells the committee, when any of these happens:

  • A new system, supplier or AI feature enters scope, or one changes how it handles sensitive data (CUI, personal or export-controlled data). Onboard it before go-live (onboarding).
  • A significant change to identity, network boundary, backup or endpoint management.
  • An incident affecting a system in scope, or a supplier's incident that affects your data.
  • A framework or its library changes version, or a customer or prime changes the requirements they ask for.
  • A requirement becomes non-compliant and stays so for more than [one month].
  • An exception or risk acceptance expires.

docs.title: 5. Exceptions and risk acceptances
docs.text:
• Every exception or risk acceptance has an owner, a reason, the compensating controls, an approver with the authority, and an expiry. None is open-ended.
  • The committee may approve up to [12] months. Longer, open-ended, or above appetite needs the board's endorsement.
  • Each is recorded in CISO Assistant (security exception or risk acceptance), linked to the requirement, control or risk it covers.
  • Sixty days before expiry the committee report lists it. At expiry it is either renewed by a new decision or the gap is fixed.

docs.title: 6. AI assistance
docs.text: The GRC member's agent reads, drafts and recommends; a person approves. No model takes part in collection, and no evidence is recorded without a person's attestation (agent-driven onboarding). Report figures come from hound, not a model (AI-assisted reporting).

docs.title: 7. Records
docs.text: CISO Assistant is the system of record. The compliance repo holds the configuration and its history, so every change to scope, mapping or evidence plan is reviewed by pull request and can be traced.

docs.title: The security committee
docs.text: The security committee is where a small organisation without a CISO looks at its security every month, decides what to do and who does it, and escalates what it cannot fix. It reads one report, hound report committee, and records every decision back in CISO Assistant, so the next month's report shows whether it happened.

docs.title: Terms of reference (template)
docs.text:
Copy this into your policy set and fill in the brackets.

Purpose. The security committee oversees [Organisation]'s cyber security and compliance programmes ([Essential Eight Maturity Level Two], [AI6 Foundations], [others]) on behalf of [the CTO / the board]. It monitors posture each month, confirms remediation actions and owners, approves exceptions and risk acceptances within its authority, and escalates to the board what is outside it.

Members. The chair ([CTO or general manager]), the authorising official, the GRC member (secretary), the IT lead, and the owners of systems on the agenda. A quorum is the chair or authorising official, plus the GRC member.

Authority. The committee may accept a risk or approve an exception for up to [12] months. Anything longer, without an expiry, or above the risk appetite goes to the board (board reporting).

Meetings. Monthly, [45] minutes, within [10] working days of the month's end. The GRC member circulates the report two working days before.

Records. Decisions and actions are recorded in CISO Assistant within two working days. The report and minutes are kept as evidence on the "Security reporting" applied control.

Review. These terms are reviewed every year, or when a programme is added.

docs.title: Before the meeting (GRC member, about 30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Your agent takes the snapshot and drafts the report on the first working day of the month (reporting).
  2. Read the summary and section 8 (Actions). Check every proposed owner and due date is realistic; change them in the draft if not.
  3. Refine the summary wording with AI help, without changing a figure.
  4. Send it to the members.

docs.title: Agenda (45 minutes)
docs.text: Minutes Item Report section 0 to 5 Actions from last month: done, late or dropped Section 8 of last month's report 5 to 10 Summary and collector health 1 and 2 10 to 20 What changed and what is failing, per programme 3 20 to 30 Exceptions and risk acceptances: new, expiring, expired; decide renewals 4 30 to 35 Remediation and incidents 5 and 6 35 to 40 Overdue manual evidence and supplier reviews: owners overdue a second month are asked why 7 40 to 45 Confirm this month's actions, and anything for the board 8

docs.title: Record decisions in CISO Assistant
docs.text:
The committee's decisions only count once they are in CISO Assistant, because that is what the next report reads.

Decision Record it as A remediation action, with owner and due date An applied control's ETA and owner, or a finding in the audit's findings assessment Accept a risk A risk acceptance with approver, date and expiry, linked to the risk scenario Approve an exception to a requirement A security exception with expiry, linked to the requirement or control Renew an expiring exception Edit its expiry, and note the meeting date in its description Close an incident The incident's status, with the date Ask a system owner for overdue evidence Comment on the task in CISO Assistant; the next report lists it again if still overdue Escalate to the board An action in section 8 with the board as owner. The board report does not read actions, so the authorising official adds each escalation to section 6 of the quarter's draft

Then upload the minutes as a new revision of the "Security reporting" evidence, next to the month's snapshot.

docs.title: Who does what in a small team
docs.text:
Role Hours a month Does Chair 1 Runs the meeting, decides when the committee disagrees Authorising official 1 Accepts risks and approves exceptions within the committee's authority GRC member (secretary) 2 to 3 Prepares the report with the agent, records decisions in CISO Assistant IT lead 1 Answers for collectors, remediation and incidents System owners as needed Attend when their system or evidence is on the agenda

Training for members: committee session. A member's own guide: reading the committee report.

docs.title: Your system security plan
docs.text:
A system security plan (SSP) says what a system is, where its boundary is, who is responsible for it, and how each control the framework asks for is met. Assessors read it first. ISM-0041 asks for one for each system; CMMC Level 2 asks for one too (NIST SP 800-171 3.12.4).

hound builds most of the plan from what you already keep up to date: the records in CISO Assistant and the scope files in your repo. People write the parts that records cannot hold, and the authorising official signs each version. This guide walks through the whole cycle with the fictional example in examples/compliance-repo. The reference for every command and column is ssp.md.

docs.title: What the plan is built from
docs.text:
Part of the plan Comes from System name, version, classification, roles, documents scope/ssp.yaml Boundary The perimeter ssp.yaml names, and the systems in it (CISO Assistant assets) Inventory and owners CISO Assistant assets External services and suppliers CISO Assistant third parties (solutions and their entities) Each requirement's status The audit of record's results in CISO Assistant Implementation statements The descriptions of the applied controls linked to each requirement, then the row's observation Responsible party The owners of those controls Annex (section 13) The framework, in the ASD SSP annex template's columns, one row per control POA&M appendix Every requirement not yet met, with its control, owner and ETA

Every value carries its source (hound ssp build --json), so a reviewer can check where it came from. The layout is NIST SP 800-18 Rev 1, Appendix A, for every framework; for the Essential Eight (profile: ism) the annex lists ISM controls by strategy, and for CMMC Level 2 (profile: nist-800-171) it lists the NIST SP 800-171 requirements by family (below).

docs.title: What people write or draw
docs.text:
hound cannot generate these. They need someone who knows the business:

  • Sections of the plan, as Markdown files in your repo named under sections: in ssp.yaml: the system's purpose, its environment, how it is managed, and the laws and policies that apply. The example's are in examples/compliance-repo/ssp/.
  • Boundary and network diagrams, and data flows. Draw them yourself. A Mermaid diagram in the environment section, like the example's, stays readable as text and shows in GitHub; a picture exported from a drawing tool works too.
  • Policies and procedures. Name them under documents:; they are the documents your audits already list.
  • Physical and personnel arrangements: offices, access, vetting and training, in the sections where they apply.
  • Signatures. Only the authorising official approves a version, and does so in ssp.yaml by pull request (below).

A section file you have not written yet prints as "not written yet", so you can build a draft before everything is done.

docs.title: Build a draft
docs.text:
hound ssp build --programme essential-eight --strict

The draft says DRAFT in its title, in a banner and at the end. --strict exits non-zero while any gap remains: an implemented requirement with no statement, a requirement with nobody responsible, or one marked not applicable without a reason. The gaps are listed first. Close them in CISO Assistant or the scope, then build again.

--format docx --out ssp-essential-eight-0.1.docx also writes a Word file; every page of a draft carries a DRAFT header.

docs.title: Drafting descriptions with your own agent
docs.text:
When many controls have no description, your own coding agent can draft them. hound has no model; it only gives your agent the facts and writes its text where you review it:

hound ssp suggest --programme essential-eight            # JSON brief: controls to describe, and what they are for
hound ssp describe --control AC-BACKUP --text "..."      # writes the draft to scope/controls.yaml, marked "drafted with AI"

Read every drafted description in the pull request: accept it, edit it or delete it. Once merged, hound scope apply sends it to CISO Assistant, and the next build uses it.

docs.title: Review and approval
docs.text:
1. Build the draft with its snapshot, the record of exactly what it was built from:
hound ssp build --programme essential-eight --snapshot-out ssp-essential-eight-1.0.json > ssp-essential-eight-1.0.md

The log prints the draft's SHA-256 and the snapshot's. Keep both files out of the repo: the example's .gitignore ignores ssp-*. 2. The reviewers (the system owner and security contact) read the draft and fix what is wrong at its source, then rebuild. 3. The authorising official approves by adding a sign-off under the plan in scope/ssp.yaml, in a pull request:

sign_offs:
  - {version: "1.0", by: ceo@example.com, date: "2026-12-01", sha256: <draft SHA-256>, snapshot: <snapshot SHA-256>}

hound scope validate checks that by is the authorising official and that the hashes look right. 4. Rebuild the signed plan from the snapshot. It must give the same draft, or hound refuses:

hound ssp build --programme essential-eight --from-snapshot ssp-essential-eight-1.0.json
  1. Publish it to CISO Assistant, the system of record:
hound ssp publish --programme essential-eight --snapshot ssp-essential-eight-1.0.json

This uploads one zip (the signed plan, its POA&M, the snapshot and CISO Assistant's own Word audit report) as a new revision of the evidence SSP-ESSENTIAL-EIGHT. An unsigned version is refused.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Change version: in ssp.yaml for each new version: a minor version (1.1) for updated statuses and statements, a major version (2.0) when the boundary or the inventory changes. To see what a reviewer needs to read:

hound ssp diff ssp-essential-eight-1.0.json ssp-essential-eight-1.1.json

The diff lists boundary and inventory changes first, then suppliers, statuses, statements and sections. Review the plan at least once a year and whenever the boundary, a system or a supplier changes.

docs.title: NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC Level 2
docs.text:
For CMMC Level 2, the plan is the same layout with profile: nist-800-171. The example's second entry in examples/compliance-repo/scope/ssp.yaml is the CMMC plan for the programme cmmc-level-2 (audit EX-CMMC-2026, CISO Assistant's cmmc-2.0 framework at groups L1 and L2), with its own sections in examples/compliance-repo/ssp/cmmc/.

hound ssp build --programme cmmc-level-2 --strict

The profile changes three things.

CMMC asset categories. The inventory in section 10 gains a column for each system's category from 32 CFR 170.19: CUI asset, security protection asset, contractor risk managed asset, specialized asset or out-of-scope asset. Give each system a cmmc_asset_category tag in scope/setup.yaml:

systems:
  - name: Example 365
    tags:
      cmmc_asset_category: cui   # or security_protection, contractor_risk_managed, specialized, out_of_scope

It is a tag rather than a CISO Assistant field because asset custom fields are a CISO Assistant Enterprise feature. A system without a category is listed as a gap, and an unknown value fails hound scope validate. Out of scope is a claim an assessor will test: say in the environment section why the system never handles CUI.

External service providers. Section 11 lists the supplier solutions that provide systems in the boundary, as for every plan. For CMMC, a cloud service provider that stores, processes or sends CUI needs FedRAMP Moderate or equivalent assurance (DFARS 252.204-7012): record it on the supplier in CISO Assistant and name it in the environment section.

The annex and the POA&M. The annex lists all 110 requirements, grouped by family, each with its status, statement, responsible party, evidence and POA&M item. CMMC limits what a Conditional Level 2 status may leave on a POA&M (32 CFR 170.21(a)(2)):

  • only requirements worth 1 point in the DoD Assessment Methodology, except SC.L2-3.13.11 when encryption is used but is not FIPS-validated (3 points, which a person decides);
  • never AC.L2-3.1.20, AC.L2-3.1.22, CA.L2-3.12.4, PE.L2-3.10.3, PE.L2-3.10.4 or PE.L2-3.10.5;
  • the SPRS score must be at least 88 (0.8 of 110), and every item must close within 180 days.

hound reads the points from the bundled methodology that hound sprs score uses, marks each unmet requirement CMMC does not allow as "not allowed" in the annex, lists it under the POA&M and in the gaps, so --strict fails until it is met. Work those first: they decide whether you can claim a Conditional status at all. The CMMC Level 2 guide covers the score.

docs.title: Migrating from the Essential Eight to the ASD Essentials
docs.text:
ASD's Essentials for enterprise IT replaces the Essential Eight Maturity Model (November 2023). This plan covers how an Evidence Hound deployment moves its assessment from the Essential Eight to the Essentials without losing evidence or history. It also covers what Evidence Hound must change to support the Essentials.

The figures below come from the libraries that ship with CISO Assistant v4.3.4, the version in dev/ciso-assistant:

Library URN Framework URN From urn:intuitem:risk:library:essential-eight-2023 urn:intuitem:risk:framework:essential-eight-2023 To urn:intuitem:risk:library:asd-essentials-enterprise-it urn:intuitem:risk:framework:asd-essentials-enterprise-it Transition mapping urn:intuitem:risk:library:mapping-essential-eight-2023-and-asd-essentials-enterprise-it Essential Eight 2023 to Essentials

Do not use urn:intuitem:risk:library:essential-eight. CISO Assistant now marks it "legacy", and the 2023 library replaces it.

Always refer to libraries and frameworks by URN. The /stored-libraries/<uuid> address in the CISO Assistant UI is different on every instance.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
When Frameworks in use Evidence Hound needs Now Essential Eight 2023 at ML2 is the audit of record Requirement rows by URN and the ML2 mapping (s06) In a few months Essential Eight and the Essentials in parallel, then the Essentials alone Several audits per run (s06) and the Essentials mapping (s14, release 2) A few months later The Essentials and NIST SP 800-171 in parallel The 800-171 mapping, SSP and POA&M (s17, release 2)

The parallel run in stage 1 below uses the same mechanism as running the Essentials and 800-171 together later: one collection run, one evidence upload, several audits.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The requirements can be mapped, but only partly. ASD's mapping links 81 of the 87 Essential Eight ISM controls in scope at ML1 and ML2 to 32 of the 58 Essentials actions (35 counting ML3 controls). Every link is intersect, meaning the two requirements overlap but neither fully covers the other.
  • CISO Assistant cannot carry a "compliant" result across. For an intersect link it turns compliant into partially_compliant at most (RequirementAssessment.infer_result in v4.3.4). A mapped audit is a starting point to review, not an answer.
  • Evidence Hound can do better. Its checks are framework-neutral, so it can map the same checks straight onto Essentials actions with their own mapping file. Results then come from fresh evidence, with no cap.
  • About 40 % of the Essentials is new ground. 23 actions have no Essential Eight source, mostly governance, supplier assurance, training, content filtering and segmentation. They need new checks, or manual sources with attestations.
  • Evidence Hound has to change before either framework works. Both libraries reuse a requirement's ref_id in more than one place, but Evidence Hound selects requirement rows by ref_id alone. See Changes to Evidence Hound.

docs.title: How the frameworks differ
docs.text:
Essential Eight (Nov 2023) ASD Essentials for enterprise IT Structure 8 mitigation strategies, each with ISM controls 8 domains, then 28 principles, then 58 actions Assessable rows 152 (126 distinct ISM ref_ids) 212 (58 distinct action ref_ids, each rated in every domain it applies to) Scope selector (implementation groups) Maturity Level 1, 2 or 3 Priority phase 1, 2 or 3 What a group means How capable an adversary the controls resist Which parts of the environment are assessed first Rating Each control rated per strategy Each action rated per domain; a principle takes its lowest applicable action in that domain (weakest link)

The Essentials domains and their phases:
