Domain Priority phase Assessable rows Rows with an Essential Eight source Governance and culture 1, 2, 3 9 1 Visibility and response 1, 2, 3 12 8 Boundary services 1 37 26 Identity services 1 35 26 Critical processes and services 2 37 26 Privileged environments 2 35 26 Business systems 3 27 20 User devices 3 20 15

"Governance and culture" and "Visibility and response" are the capability domains, and they are assessed in every phase.

The Essentials' phases are not a new name for maturity levels. ML2 asked how strong the controls are everywhere. Phase 1 asks whether boundary and identity services are fully effective. A stable ML2 programme therefore maps to phase 1 first, then phase 2, rather than to "phases 1 and 2" in one step.

docs.title: The requirement mapping
docs.text: ASD's mapping, packaged by intuitem, has 975 links. Each one goes from an Essential Eight row to an Essentials row, for every domain the action applies to. All of them are intersect with functional rationale.

docs.title: Essential Eight controls with no Essentials target
docs.text:
Six ISM controls in scope at ML1 and ML2 are not mapped. They are not dropped by ASD as unimportant; the Essentials covers them under broader actions with no direct link. Assess them by judgement during the parallel run, and record where they now fit.

ISM-1704 Patch applications 1, 2, 3 Office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, Adobe Flash Player, and security… ISM-1705 Regular backups 2, 3 Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) cannot access backups belonging to other user accounts. ISM-1707 Regular backups 2, 3 Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) are prevented from modifying and deleting backups. docs.title: Essentials actions with no Essential Eight source
docs.text:
These are new work. Most are processes rather than technical settings, so a manual source (see configuration.md) with an owner and a due interval is the natural first step. Content filtering (PRO-09), legacy authentication (PRO-13.5) and secret scanning (PRO-13.3) are good candidates for automated collectors later.

The ciso-assistant profile (s16) evidences part of this ground from what CISO Assistant already holds: GOV-03.1 (risk studies reviewed, no approved exception past its expiry), GOV-11.1 and GOV-11.2 (supplier assessments and contracts current) and PRO-16.1 (suppliers assessed). Each keeps its manual source for the rest of the action. It also adds the business impact analysis's recovery tests to PRO-10.3.

docs.title: Changes to Evidence Hound
docs.text:
These are the changes Evidence Hound needed before it could publish to the Essentials. Changes 1, 2, 3 and 5 shipped in s06, and change 4 in s14, with the reference phase 1 mapping mappings/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml. Change 6 is still open.

  1. Address requirement rows by URN. Today hound publish selects a requirement assessment by audit ref_id and requirement ref_id (Selector.RequirementInAudit). In the Essentials, 37 of 58 action ref_ids appear in more than one domain. In the Essential Eight, 10 ISM ref_ids appear under more than one strategy, ISM-0123 under four. A mapping file must be able to name a requirement by its URN, such as urn:intuitem:risk:req_node:asd-essentials-enterprise-it:identity-services:pro-13:it.pro-13.4. For readability it could also use a domain-qualified form, such as identity-services/IT.PRO-13.4. This also blocks the Essential Eight 2023 mapping kept for the transition.
  2. Scope the mapping to the audit's groups. A mapping file covers the whole framework. The publisher should skip requirements outside the audit's selected implementation groups (maturity levels or phases), rather than writing results CISO Assistant hides.
  3. Fix the dev seed. dev/ciso-assistant/seed/seed.py imports the legacy essential-eight library. It should import essential-eight-2023, asd-essentials-enterprise-it and the transition mapping.
  4. Generate a draft mapping (done, s14). hound mapping derive reads an Essential Eight mapping file and the transition mapping, then writes a draft Essentials mapping file. Each action row gets the union of the checks of its source ISM controls, with rule: all_pass, and is marked draft: true. Runs do not publish a draft row until a person has reviewed it and removed the mark, because intersect means the checks may not cover the whole action (mapping-files.md).
  5. Publish to more than one audit. The config has one target. The parallel run needs two: the Essential Eight audit with its mapping, and the Essentials audit with its own.
  6. Systems know their Essentials domain. Essentials actions are rated per domain, so the scope file (see s06) should let each system say which Essentials domain it belongs to, such as boundary services or user devices. The mapping then rolls up only the evidence from systems in that domain.

docs.title: Stage 0: prepare (before any audit changes)
docs.text:
• Load essential-eight-2023, asd-essentials-enterprise-it and the transition mapping into CISO Assistant. Check that their URNs match the table at the top of this page.
  • If your current Essential Eight audit uses the legacy library, move it to essential-eight-2023 first. CISO Assistant ships mapping-essential-eight-and-essential-eight-2023 for that step.
  • Use an Evidence Hound release that has changes 1 to 5 above (every release from v1.0.0 does).

Exit: hound mapping validate passes for the Essential Eight mapping using URNs, and the current Essential Eight audit publishes as before.

docs.title: Stage 1: parallel run
docs.text:
• Keep the Essential Eight audit as the audit of record. Keep publishing to it.
  • Create an Essentials audit in the same perimeter with priority phase 1 selected. Use CISO Assistant's "create from another audit" with the transition mapping, to start every mapped row with a suggested partially_compliant or non_compliant.
  • Start from the reference mapping, mappings/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml, or generate your own draft from your own Essential Eight mapping (change 4):
$ hound mapping derive mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml --from frameworks/essential-eight-2023.json \
    --to frameworks/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.json \
    --links frameworks/mapping-essential-eight-2023-and-asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml --groups 1 --out mappings/asd-essentials-draft.yaml

Review every action row with the system owner and the assessor. Keep a check only if it evidences the action, add checks where the action asks for more, record the reason in the row's comment, and delete its draft: true line. derive never replaces an existing file unless you add --force, so the reference mapping stays as it is; runs publish no draft row, and hound mapping validate and hound mapping coverage count the rows still in draft. - Set up the manual sources for the new ground from examples/manual-sources/essentials/ (governance, supply chain, training, content filtering, segmentation, secure build and secrets, secure administration, incident learning, asset records), then check that no domain has an uncovered or draft row:

$ hound mapping coverage mappings/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.yaml --framework frameworks/asd-essentials-enterprise-it.json \
    --groups 1 --manual hound.yaml

--manual hound.yaml reads the manual sources configured in your repo; a check none of them gives counts as automated, so add the sources before you trust the count. - Add a second target for the Essentials audit (change 5), so one collection run publishes to both audits.

Exit: every phase 1 row in the Essentials audit has a result from Evidence Hound or a named manual source. No row's result depends only on mapping inference.

docs.title: Stage 2: close the gaps
docs.text:
• For each action with no Essential Eight source, either add a manual source with an owner and due interval, or plan a collector. Supplier assurance (GOV-11), supply chain security (PRO-16) and risk management (GOV-03) can be evidenced from CISO Assistant's own records by the governance collector (s16-01), once suppliers and risk studies are managed as configuration.
  • Place the six unmapped ISM controls under their Essentials actions, and record the decision in the mapping file's comments. The reference mapping already places the five that have checks (ISM-0123, ISM-1704, ISM-1705, ISM-1707 and ISM-1905 in the homes above); ISM-1687 has no check of its own.
  • Tag each system with its Essentials domain (change 6), and check the per-domain roll-up matches what an assessor would conclude.

Exit: phase 1 has no not_assessed rows, and the committee has accepted the Essentials results alongside the Essential Eight results for one reporting period.

docs.title: Stage 3: cut over
docs.text:
• Make the Essentials audit the audit of record. Report against it to the committee and board.
  • Stop publishing to the Essential Eight audit, then lock it in CISO Assistant. It stays as the historical record, with its evidence.
  • Add phase 2, then phase 3, as their own exit criteria are met.

Exit: one reporting cycle runs on the Essentials alone.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Until stage 3, the Essential Eight audit is untouched and still published to, so rolling back means removing the Essentials target from the config. After stage 3, unlock the Essential Eight audit and add its target back. Evidence collected meanwhile is still in the evidence store, and the next run publishes to both audits.

docs.title: To verify
docs.text:
• How CISO Assistant combines several source rows that map to one target row when it creates an audit from a mapping. Up to 28 Essential Eight rows map to one Essentials action.
  • Whether "create from another audit" also copies evidence and applied controls, or only results.
  • Whether the REST API can import the transition mapping library on an instance where it is not already stored.

docs.title: Operating guides
docs.text:
Short guides for each person who keeps the programme running. They assume the setup in the first deployment is done.

Guide For Time GRC member: your week, month and quarter The one person who runs compliance, 2 to 8 hours a week 2 to 8 hours a week System owner People who own a system and provide its manual evidence Minutes a month Collector operator Whoever runs hound's container: IT, often the GRC member An hour a month Committee member Members of the monthly security committee 30 minutes a month

Training outlines that go with them are in docs/training/.

docs.title: Collector operator
docs.text: You run hound's runner container next to CISO Assistant. It collects evidence on a schedule, so most months you do nothing. This guide covers the checks, the usual faults and credential rotation.

docs.title: Check it is healthy (5 minutes, weekly)
docs.text:
$ hound status --config hound.yaml

Every collector should have a run in the last day or two with outcome succeeded. hound status shows only the outcome and counts; the cause of a failure is in the output of hound run --only <name>. The committee report marks a collector stale after 7 days without a run, and that reaches managers. Details: running collectors.

docs.title: Run it by hand
docs.text:
$ hound run --config hound.yaml --dry-run      # collect and plan, send nothing
$ hound run --config hound.yaml --only <name>  # one collector

docs.title: Troubleshoot
docs.text:
Run hound run --config hound.yaml --only <name> and read its output:

What you see Likely cause Do An HTTP 401 or 403 from the service The collector's credential expired or lost a permission Rotate it (below); check the permissions in its collector guide under collectors A timeout The service was down or the network blocked it Run it again; check the firewall allows the host 0 sent in the PUBLISHED column for weeks Nothing changed; that is normal. Only changes are sent Nothing Publishing to CISO Assistant fails CISO Assistant is down, or hound's token expired hound config validate hound.yaml --check-secrets; renew the token in CISO Assistant A requirement flips between results Two sources write it, or someone edits it by hand hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml shows the drift; ask the GRC member which source is right

docs.title: Rotate a credential
docs.text:
Credentials are never in the repo: hound.yaml names a reference (env:NAME or file:/run/secrets/name), and the container reads it at run time (configuration).

  1. Create the new credential in the service (an app secret, an API key, a CISO Assistant token) with the same permissions.
  2. Replace the secret's value where the reference points: the Docker secret file or the environment variable of the runner.
  3. hound config validate hound.yaml --check-secrets resolves every reference without printing a value.
  4. hound run --config hound.yaml --only <name> and check it succeeds.
  5. Revoke the old credential in the service.

Rotate when a credential is about to expire, when someone who knew it leaves, and at least once a year.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text: Upgrade the runner image by tag, run hound run --config hound.yaml --dry-run first, then let the schedule carry on. A dry run collects and plans but does not prove CISO Assistant is reachable; hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml does. When you upgrade CISO Assistant, check the framework snapshots with the GRC member (mapping files).

docs.title: Reading the committee report
docs.text:
Each month you get one report, about five pages, the week before the security committee meets. Read it in 15 minutes this way.

  1. Summary first. Three to five lines: what changed and what you must decide.
  2. Section 8, Actions. These are proposed: an action, an owner and a due date. Be ready to agree, change or drop each one.
  3. Section 4, Exceptions and risk acceptances. Anything expiring within 60 days needs a renewal decision, or a plan to fix the underlying problem.
  4. Section 7, Overdue evidence. Owners overdue for a second month are listed first; the committee is where that is followed up.
  5. The rest when you have questions. Every figure links to its record in CISO Assistant, if you have a login.

docs.title: Words you will see
docs.text: Word Means Programme One framework you report against, such as the Essential Eight at Maturity Level Two Audit of record The CISO Assistant audit whose results count for that programme Compliant, partially, non compliant, not assessed The result of a requirement in that audit; not assessed means the evidence is missing or old Collector A program that reads a system (Microsoft 365, the firewall) and records evidence on a schedule Stale A collector with no run in the last 7 days of the month; its evidence may be out of date Manual evidence Evidence a person exports because no API shows it, attested by the GRC team Exception Approval not to meet a requirement for a time, with a reason and an expiry Risk acceptance Approval to live with a risk for a time, by someone with the authority to accept it

docs.title: In the meeting
docs.text: Decide, and make sure each decision has an owner and a date. The GRC member records it in CISO Assistant; next month's report shows whether it happened. Training: committee session.

docs.title: GRC member: your week, month and quarter
docs.text: You are the one person who runs compliance, with 2 to 8 hours a week and an AI agent that does most of the reading and drafting. hound is built so that everything waiting on you arrives in one queue, with a recommendation, and nothing reaches CISO Assistant without you.

docs.title: Every week (1 to 2 hours)
docs.text:
1. CISO Assistant's weekly task emails you the weekly review runbook.
  2. Ask your agent: "Prepare this week's review." It starts with hound next --json, one read-only list of everything that needs doing this week, most urgent first: the review queue, collectors that failed or missed their schedule, manual evidence due, exceptions expiring within 60 days, scope changes not yet applied and whether CISO Assistant accepts hound's token. Then it runs hound review prepare --json and records a recommendation, with reasons and sources, for each item (manual evidence, onboarding decisions, suppliers, drafted audits), and saves the scope plan your session applies.
  3. In your own terminal: hound review --for 60m. Read each item, then accept, challenge with a note, or skip. Challenged items come back next week with the agent's answer. Accepted items and the prepared plan are applied in one batch at the end, after one confirmation (guided review).
  4. Look at hound status --config hound.yaml --scope scope/. A collector that failed or has not run is the one thing to chase this week. The standing lines say how much of each programme is met and how many rows are still not assessed, from last month's snapshot.

What the agent does for you: reads every export and proposal, drafts the recommendations, answers your challenges, and keeps the queue in order of urgency. What only you can do: accept, approve and attest.

docs.title: Every month (2 to 3 hours, first working days)
docs.text:
1. Ask your agent: "Take last month's snapshot and draft the committee report" (reporting).
  2. Read the draft's summary and actions; fix owners and due dates; refine the wording (AI help).
  3. Send it out, run the committee meeting as secretary, and record its decisions in CISO Assistant.
  4. Close the month's manual evidence tasks in CISO Assistant whose results were published.

docs.title: Every quarter (half a day)
docs.text:
1. Ask your agent to draft the board report for the quarter; give it to the authorising official to confirm the positions (board reporting).
  2. Review exceptions and risk acceptances that expire next quarter; put renewals on the committee's agenda.
  3. Supplier reviews due this quarter: the agent drafts each one; you approve in the weekly review.
  4. If your audits run in periods, ask your agent to draft the next period's audit (hound audit draft); approve it in the review.

docs.title: Every year
docs.text:
• Re-read the continuous compliance procedure and the risk appetite with the board.
  • Renew standing approvals that expire (the review lists them).
  • Upgrade CISO Assistant and hound; snapshot new framework versions (mapping files).

docs.title: When a prime asks a questionnaire
docs.text: Use the crosswalk: one evidence set, many questionnaires.

docs.title: System owner
docs.text: You own a system (a file share, the laptops, the accounting service) and some of its evidence has no API, so a person has to export it. You do not need a CISO Assistant login. You need about ten minutes each time a reminder arrives.

docs.title: When the reminder arrives
docs.text:
CISO Assistant emails you before each due date, with a runbook: what to export, from where, and what the export must show.

  1. Follow the runbook. Export exactly what it asks for (a report, a screenshot of a setting, a list of accounts), dated today.
  2. Check it shows what the runbook says it must, for example every server in the backup report, not only the first page.
  3. Send it to the GRC team as the runbook says (usually by email or a shared folder). Do not paste it into chat tools.
  4. If you cannot do it by the due date, reply to the email with the reason and a date. Do not ignore it: at month end an open task is reported to the security committee with your name.

The GRC team's agent reads the export and proposes a result; a person in the GRC team attests it. You may be asked a question about it.

docs.title: Find your audit and your actions
docs.text:
If you have a CISO Assistant login (some owners do):

  • Your audit: Compliance, then Audits, then the audit of record (for example EX-E8-2026). Filter the requirements by your system's applied controls to see the rows your evidence answers.
  • Your actions: Applied controls with you as owner, sorted by ETA. Each one the committee assigned you has a due date.
  • Update an action: change its status and ETA, and add a note on what changed. Do not change results in the audit: the runs write those, and a hand edit is overwritten or reported as drift.

No login: ask the GRC member for the list of your actions; they are in each month's committee report under section 8.

docs.title: When something changes
docs.text: Tell the GRC team before you: add a new system or supplier, connect a new AI feature, move data to a new place, or change who can sign in as an administrator. Each of these changes your audit's scope, and some must be assessed before they go live.

docs.title: CISO review, November 2026
docs.text:
A CISO's review of Evidence Hound before release 3 (s19-07). It asks one question: does hound get a small business with one GRC member and two to eight hours a week to Essential Eight Maturity Level 2 or CMMC Level 2, and keep it there, and what will an assessor ask for that it does not give?

It walks the fictional Example Pty Ltd (examples/compliance-repo/) through a year, checks every automated claim the Essential Eight and CMMC mappings make against the code of the check behind it, and ranks what to cut and what is missing. Every gap that would fail an assessment is either fixed in s19 or written into the release notes as a known limitation.

Reviewed 2026-11-26 against the branch after s19-06.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
hound is fit for release 3 for its target: a small business whose estate is Microsoft 365, Intune-managed Windows laptops, a firewall managed in Sophos Central and a vulnerability scanner, working towards Essential Eight ML2, with CMMC Level 2 as a second programme from the same evidence. The year below takes the GRC member a little over 2 hours a week on average, inside the 2 to 8 hour budget. Collection, mapping, publishing and the reports are deterministic, and nothing is approved without a person.

Four mapping claims were wider than their checks (fixed below), and one guide and one cheat sheet line were out of date (fixed). What remains are limits of scope, not defects, and the release notes say each one plainly. The largest is that a CMMC assessor assesses the 320 objectives of NIST SP 800-171A, while hound records each of the 110 practices: the person answers the objectives in CISO Assistant.

docs.title: A year at Example Pty Ltd
docs.text:
Times are the GRC member's, from the procedure (docs/govern/continuous-compliance-procedure.md), the minutes hound next estimates for each item, and the walk-through below. Every hound command in the walk-through answered in under a second on the example repo.

Step What hound does What the person does Their time What an assessor asks for that hound does not give Onboarding (month 1) hound init writes the repo; hound agent setup the agent kit; the agent drafts suppliers, systems and each requirement's decision; scope plan and scope apply write CISO Assistant Approves each draft with hound approve or the guided review; sets owners; uploads the first manual evidence 12 to 20 hours over four weeks Evidence that each Essential Eight control was tested, such as an attempt to run a macro from the internet (the ASD assessment process rates configuration evidence below a test). hound reads configuration. Weekly review Collectors run on schedule; hound next and review prepare list what is due with a recommendation for each; accepted items are applied in one batch Reads and accepts or challenges each item in hound review --for 60m 30 to 60 minutes Nothing missing for the weekly cycle. Monthly committee report snapshot and report committee from CISO Assistant and the run store Presents the report; records decisions 1 hour Minutes of the committee's decisions are the person's to keep. Quarterly board report board from the last four quarter-end snapshots Presents it; the authorising official confirms positions 2 hours a quarter Nothing missing. An incident (INC-2026-01) incident obligations lists each report owed and its deadline; incident report-pack --dfars assembles the 72-hour DFARS report; irp build the plan Decides severity; makes the reports (DIBNet needs a medium assurance certificate); runs the lessons-learned review 2 to 6 hours The forensic image and the 90-day media preservation DFARS 252.204-7012 asks for are outside hound. A supplier change supplier draft, the supplier review and flow-down findings; supplier list --data cui answers the prime Approves the supplier before the system is registered; files the provider's authorisation (such as a FedRAMP Moderate equivalent) 1 to 2 hours Nothing missing once the authority and its evidence are recorded on the solution. Annual affirmation sprs score with each deduction; sprs affirmation-pack; ssp build and ssp poam Reviews the score; the affirming official affirms and posts the score in SPRS 4 hours hound does not post to SPRS; the person does. Assessment The audit of record in CISO Assistant with every result's evidence and history; the SSP, POA&M and IRP; scope export --with-files Walks the assessor through it; answers what is manual 2 to 3 days with the assessor For CMMC, the 320 assessment objectives: hound assesses the 110 practices, so each objective is the person's. For the Essential Eight, test evidence (above).

Across the year that is about 110 hours (onboarding 16, weekly reviews 39, committee 12, board 8, an incident 4, three supplier changes 5, the affirmation 4, the assessment 20), a little over 2 hours a week.

docs.title: Walk-through on the example repo
docs.text:
Run on a copy of examples/compliance-repo/ with HOUND_TODAY=2027-02-15, offline:

Command Result Time hound init <folder> --org "Example Pty Ltd" -y --json A new repo, no audit until a system is onboarded 0.4 s hound config validate hound.yaml valid 0.3 s hound scope validate scope --config hound.yaml 1 domain, 7 controls, 6 audits, 1 risk study, 2 metrics 0.6 s hound next --repo . --config hound.yaml --json The week's work, with the connection not checked offline 0.6 s hound review pending --repo . --json and review prepare Nothing waiting on the person 0.6 s each hound programme list --scope scope --json The programmes with their audits of record 0.5 s hound supplier list --data cui --repo . No solution lists CUI: the example records CUI on its systems' cmmc_asset_category tags, not on a supplier 0.3 s hound irp build --programme essential-eight The plan, gaps first 0.6 s

The steps that read CISO Assistant (incident obligations, incident report-pack, ssp poam, sprs score, the reports) could not run here: this environment's network policy blocks the CISO Assistant images. They run against a real instance in the functional suite in CI (IncidentFunctionalTests, SprsFunctionalTests, SspFunctionalTests, ReportFunctionalTests), and the sprint review records that run.

The walk-through found the cheat sheet listing --config and --format on hound irp build, which takes neither. It is fixed, and a test now checks every option the cheat sheet names against the command's help.

docs.title: The mappings' claims
docs.text: Every Essential Eight ML1 and ML2 requirement row whose checks come from a collector (60 rows across the two levels), and every CMMC row marked covers: part (32 practices), was read against the code of each check behind it.

docs.title: Fixed in s19
docs.text: Finding What an assessor would have found Fix ISM-1876 and ISM-1877 give 48 hours when the vendor rates a vulnerability critical or a working exploit exists. vuln.internet_facing.patched_in_window used the 48-hour window only for an exploit. A critical finding on an internet-facing service ten days old, published as compliant. Critical findings use the short window too (PatchChecksTests.Critical_finding_on_an_internet_facing_service_uses_hours_window). ISM-1667 to ISM-1673 apply to every workstation. endpoint.asr.office_rules_enabled passed when the blocking policy was assigned to any group. Office rules blocking on a pilot group only, published as compliant. It passes only when the rules block for all users or all devices, and is partial for some groups (OfficeChecksTests.Asr_rules_blocked_only_for_some_groups_partial). ISM-1657 lists compiled HTML, HTML applications and control panel applets beside executables, libraries, scripts and installers. The check reads the last four; the row's comment said the ruleset review covered the rest, but the row did not include it. Three file types nobody looked at, published as compliant. The row includes appcontrol.rulesets_validated, attested yearly (E8MappingTests.Application_control_file_types_include_the_ruleset_review_for_the_types_no_collector_reads). Every CMMC row is covers: part, and the published observation said "a person assesses the rest" without saying what the rest is. A partially compliant practice with no hint of what is missing. A row's rest: says what the person assesses, and the observation names it. All 32 rows have one (CmmcMappingTests.Every_row_covering_part_names_what_the_person_adds).

docs.title: Correct, with a limit the release notes state
docs.text:
• The collectors see only what they read. The Essential Eight rows for MFA, privileged access, patching and application control answer for Microsoft 365, Intune-managed Windows devices, Sophos Central firewalls and what the scanner reaches. Each row's comment says so. An organisation with servers, macOS or other online services must add a REST profile or a manual source for them, or the row overstates. The capability map (hound onboard environment) is where that is decided.
  • ISM-1883 is answered by counts. Few Global Administrators, roles activated only when needed, and few Sophos Central Super Admins show that privileged accounts are limited; they do not show that each is required. The yearly privileged access review (privileged.requests.validated) is where a person justifies each, and an assessor will ask for it.
  • endpoint.asr.office_rules_enabled stands for four requirements. When one Office rule is not blocking, all four rows are partial, even those whose own rule blocks. It understates, never overstates.
  • ISM-1695 uses Intune compliance. It stands for monthly operating system patching only when the compliance policy sets a minimum version that tracks monthly updates; the operating system scan in the same row shows what is still missing.

The checks for MFA (all users and all applications, no exclusions but documented break-glass accounts), application control (all devices or every listed group), unsupported software and the scan intervals (daily, weekly, fortnightly) match their requirements.

docs.title: Features a small business does not need
docs.text:
Ranked by how much they cost to keep against how few small businesses use them. Removals go to the maintainer in the s19-02 list; nothing here is removed without a yes.

  1. The retired model options (--no-model, --show-requests, the old --config on six commands): hidden, unused since s09. Remove in release 3 (engineering review E8).
  2. The step commands hound collect, hound plan and hound publish. hound run does all three, and the agent kit uses run. They are useful for debugging a failed publish, so keep them, but take them off the cheat sheet's first page.
  3. Two onboarding entry points (hound onboard <system> and hound onboard environment). Both are needed: the capability map decides what provides each mitigation, and system onboarding decides each requirement. Keep both; s19-08 puts them on one route.
  4. The older example configs (examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml, examples/example-essential-eight.yaml): many tests read them. Fold into the compliance repo later (s19-D4); nothing for a user to decide.

DISP readiness, the AI register and the ASD Essentials mapping were each asked for by the maintainer and serve a defence-industry small business; they stay.

docs.title: Features a small business needs that are missing
docs.text:
Ranked by what an assessor would fail first.

  1. CMMC assessment objectives. A C3PAO assesses each of the 320 objectives in NIST SP 800-171A; hound maps the 110 practices. Until objectives are mapped, the person records each objective's answer in CISO Assistant. Release notes: known limitation.
  2. Control tests for the Essential Eight. The ASD assessment process rates a test (try the macro, run the unapproved binary) above configuration. A manual source per mitigation for the test result, with its runbook, would lift the evidence. Planned work.
  3. Collectors beyond Microsoft 365 and Sophos. Servers, macOS and other SaaS need REST profiles; the profile tooling exists but no profile ships for them. Release notes: known limitation.
  4. The DFARS forensic image and media preservation (90 days after an incident report). hound tracks the report, not the image. The DFARS report pack reminds the person of both (incidents); keeping them is the person's.

docs.title: Part B: the document generators
docs.text: Verdict: reorder and cut; move after release 3. The documents an assessor of a small business asks for first already exist: the SSP (s11, s17), the POA&M (s11-03) and the IRP (s15-09). Of the rest, the ones hound's data largely fills and an assessor of a small business asks for are, in order: policy statements (s19b-04), the continuous monitoring plan (s19b-03), the change and configuration management plan (s19b-10) and the risk assessment report (s19b-05), with the catalogue (s19b-01) only once three of them exist. Cut the security assessment report (s19b-02, the assessor writes it), the authorisation package (s19b-09, a government authorisation a small business does not run), the business continuity summary (s19b-06, the BIA covers it) and the supplier report (s19b-07, supplier list covers it). The document register (s19b-08) and registers (s19b-11) follow the catalogue. The maintainer decides; the verdict is recorded in s19b-security-documents.md.

docs.title: Engineering review, November 2026
docs.text:
A principal engineer's review of Evidence Hound after s18 and before release 3 (s19-03). It asks one question of every part: is this the right code for a small team to understand, change and test for years? Less code is welcome where it gives the same behaviour, but the aim is code whose next change is obvious.

Measured with scripts/code-measures.sh on 2026-11-26, at the start of s19: 47,051 lines of production C# and 43,367 lines of tests, 2,195 unit tests in about 30 seconds, no analyser warnings.

docs.title: What is right, and stays
docs.text:
• Dependencies point inwards. EvidenceHound.Core references nothing. Collectors reference only EvidenceHound.Collectors.Abstractions. CisoAssistant, Core.Yaml and Onboarding reference only the core. The only I/O in the core is the IClock port and a publisher that takes its time from the run.
  • Results, not exceptions. Expected failures return Result<T> with a code; the CLI's global handler turns the rest into exit codes.
  • The contract with CISO Assistant is tested at every level: contract tests against recorded responses, a request budget for every read, and functional tests against a real instance in CI.
  • The agent kit is checked against the CLI (AgentFilesTests, AgentCommandTests), so guidance cannot drift from behaviour.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: Each finding has its cost (what it makes hard), the fix, an estimate and a priority. P1 findings are fixed in s19-04 to s19-06; the rest are under "Discovered work" in the sprint file.

docs.title: E1 (P1) Commands share helpers by reaching into each other
docs.text:
Cost. The CLI has no shared command infrastructure, so commands borrow it from whichever command wrote it first: ConfigCommands.LoadAsync is called from 19 places, OnboardAgentCommand.Indented (the JSON settings) from 17, ScopeCommands.ValidateAsync (load and check the scope) from 15 and PublishCommand.ConnectionAsync (connect to CISO Assistant) from 13. A change to how one command works can break another, and a new contributor cannot find the shared code by its name.

Fix. Move each helper to a class named for what it does: CommandJson (settings and writing --json answers), RepoScope (load and check a repo's scope), CisoAssistantConnection (resolve URL and token and connect), DeploymentConfig loading where config is loaded. Behaviour does not change. About half a day.

docs.title: E2 (P1) Every command declares the common options itself
docs.text:
Cost. --repo is declared 14 times and --json 17 times, each with its own wording ("The config repo to work in", "The config repo", "The compliance repo"), so help reads inconsistently, and a change to a default means 14 edits.

Fix. CommonOptions.Repo(), CommonOptions.Json() and CommonOptions.Config(), one description each. The command-reference skill regenerates from --help, so the agent kit follows. About two hours.

docs.title: E3 (P1) The largest command files mix several commands' work
docs.text:
Cost. ScopeCommands.cs (851 lines) builds the scope command tree and also holds scope loading and validation for the whole CLI, saved-plan fingerprints, the prepared review plan, exports, new-audit drafting and reporting obligations. OnboardSystemCommand.cs (767) and ReviewCommand.cs (551) are similar. Reading one behaviour means scrolling past five others.

Fix. One file per subcommand where the subcommand has logic of its own (scope plan, scope apply, scope export, scope validate), with the shared parts moved out by E1. No behaviour change, checked by golden files of the --json output of hound next, hound status, hound review pending and hound scope plan, written first. About a day.

docs.title: E4 (P1) ScopeStateReader reads every kind of object in one class
docs.text:
Cost. 886 lines: folders, users, frameworks, audits, evidence, risks, exceptions, BIA, metrics, third parties and settings are read and turned into ActualObjects in one class. Adding a kind touches it in three places, and its test file is 706 lines.

Fix. One small reader per kind of object behind a shared Reading (the list cache from s18-04), composed by ScopeStateReader. RequestBudgetTests must hold or shrink. ScopeLoader (699 lines) is split the same way. About a day; s19-05.

docs.title: E5 (P1) Tests repeat their setup
docs.text:
Cost. 24 test classes declare their own RunAsync around HoundCli.RunAsync, 111 tests make their own temporary folder, and ScopeTestInstance repeats helpers of ScopePlanCommandTests (s18-D5). A change to how the CLI is invoked in tests means editing dozens of files.

Fix. One Hound test driver (args, input, settings, terminal, returns exit, output and error) and one TempRepo that copies the example repo and cleans up, shared by the CLI tests; fold the scope test instance helpers together. No test is deleted without one that covers the same behaviour. About a day; s19-06.

docs.title: E6 (P2) HoundCli.RunAsync has 11 overloads
docs.text:
Cost. Every way a test or host wanted to call the CLI added an overload, so the composition root's entry point is 80 lines of forwarding, and it is not clear which one production uses.

Fix. One RunAsync(args, HoundIo io, HoundOptions? options, CancellationToken) and RunFromConsoleAsync, with the test driver of E5 building the options. Part of E5.

docs.title: E7 (P2) Runtime references every built-in collector
docs.text:
Cost. EvidenceHound.Runtime (runner, scheduler, config) references the Microsoft 365, manual, REST and scan collectors to build the registry. The runner therefore cannot be tested or packaged without them, and adding a collector touches the runtime.

Fix. Register the built-in collectors in the CLI's composition root, where the concrete types belong. About two hours.

docs.title: E8 (P2) Retired options are still parsed
docs.text:
Cost. Retired adds hidden --no-model, --show-requests and --config options to six commands so pre-s09 scripts keep working. Release 3 is the first release the maintainer treats as the product, and no script outside this repo used the built-in model.

Fix. Remove them in release 3, with a changelog line. Goes to the maintainer in the s19-02 list.

docs.title: E9 (P3) Two homes for agent guidance
docs.text:
Cost. agent/skills/ (workflow skills rendered by hound agent setup) and skills/ (reference skills embedded in hound and included by the workflow skills) both hold Markdown for agents. A contributor has to learn which is which.

Fix. Move skills/ to agent/reference/. It changes the Dockerfile, the embedded resource path and a compliance repo's own skills/ override folder, which people may rely on, so it waits for a release after 3 unless the maintainer wants it now.

docs.title: E10 (P3) Two older deployment configs beside the example compliance repo
docs.text:
Cost. examples/example-pty-ltd.yaml and examples/example-essential-eight.yaml predate examples/compliance-repo/hound.yaml. Thirty tests and guides read them, so the example deployment lives in three files.

Fix. Fold them into the compliance repo once E5's shared test repo exists. Later sprint.

docs.title: Not changed, on purpose
docs.text:
• One state read per audit per collector publish (s18-D4): a shared read would report drift that is not there.
  • System.CommandLine and the one global error handler: the right shape; the findings above are about what sits around it.
  • The dev servers: about 2,100 lines in four projects, but they are what lets the trial and functional tests run without a real tenant, which the maintainer asked for.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Short sessions, each run by the GRC member on the example deployment (make trial, then the local CISO Assistant), with exercises.

Session For Length Outline Providing evidence System owners 60 minutes system-owners.md The monthly committee Security committee members 30 minutes committee.md The quarterly board report Board members 20 minutes board.md Running the AI programme The Cyber GRC team 30 minutes ai-governance.md

docs.title: Training: running the AI programme (30 minutes)
docs.text:
A 30-minute session for the Cyber GRC team, built on the AI governance walkthrough. It assumes no AI knowledge. One person runs it on the local stack while the others watch and answer the screening questions; afterwards each person follows the walkthrough alone (45 minutes).

By the end, each person can: say what AI6 asks at Foundations, screen a proposed AI system with the National AI Centre's questions, register it by pull request, and read the AI6 rows and the register line the committee sees.

Before the session: the presenter runs steps 1 and 2 of the walkthrough, and everyone has read the primer (15 minutes).

Minutes Topic What happens Walkthrough 0 to 5 Why we do this The six AI6 practices in one sentence each, and what Foundations asks of a small team (the primer's "What you do not need to do at Foundations"). 5 to 8 The register today Show the register line from hound programme list and the assets labelled ai-system in CISO Assistant. Step 2 8 to 15 Screening The group answers the seven questions for the search assistant and agrees the outcome. Discuss: why does a general-purpose model make almost any assistant elevated, and what would make it unacceptable? Steps 3 and 4 15 to 20 Registering by pull request Add the ai block, validate, read the plan. Show one validation problem and its hint. Steps 5 and 6 20 to 25 Before go-live Impact assessment, risk scenarios, the test and the go-live date: who does each, and why the order matters. Steps 7 and 8 25 to 30 Results and the committee Run hound, read AI6-4.1 and AI6-5.1, and the new register line. Who fixes Example proposal assistant's missing test? Steps 9 and 10

Check understanding with three questions at the end:

  1. A supplier switches on an AI feature in a product you already use. What do you do first? (Screen it with the runbook, and check the supplier is approved.)
  2. A system is elevated. What must be true before in_use_from? (Its impact assessment is approved, and it has been tested.)
  3. AI6-5.1 is not compliant. Where do you look, and who fixes it? (Its observation names the system; the system's owner tests it and the GRC team records last_tested_on by pull request.)

Afterwards: each person follows the walkthrough alone and notes anything unclear for the GRC lead, who updates the walkthrough or the runbook.

docs.title: Training: the quarterly board report (20 minutes)
docs.text:
For board members. Built on reporting to the board.

By the end, each person can: read the board report's compliance positions and trends, understand the risks accepted on the board's behalf, and know what the board is asked to decide.

Before the session: on the local stack, the presenter takes a snapshot for the last month of this quarter and of the three quarters before (hound report snapshot --period YYYY-MM for each; they all read today's data, which is enough for training), then generates hound report board and prints it.

Minutes Topic What happens 0 to 5 What the board sets The risk appetite statement, and what the committee may decide without the board. 5 to 12 Reading the report Compliance position per programme and the fixed rules behind on track, on track with conditions and off track; the four-quarter trend; key risks against appetite. 12 to 17 Exercise Decide on one acceptance marked for board endorsement: endorse, shorten or decline, and say what that means for its owner. 17 to 20 Recording decisions How the decision is recorded in CISO Assistant and appears next quarter.

Check understanding:

  1. Why is a programme off track although most requirements are compliant? (A requirement got worse since last quarter, or more than a quarter are non-compliant.)
  2. What marks an acceptance for endorsement? (Valid for more than 12 months, or no expiry.)
  3. Who proposes the compliance position, and who confirms it? (Management proposes it by fixed rules; the authorising official confirms it; the board notes it.)

docs.title: Training: the monthly committee (30 minutes)
docs.text:
For security committee members. Built on reading the committee report and the security committee guide.

By the end, each person can: read a committee report in 15 minutes, decide on proposed actions and expiring exceptions, and say how each decision reaches CISO Assistant.

Before the session: the presenter takes two example snapshots and generates the report from the local stack (hound report snapshot --period <last month> and the month before, then hound report committee). Hand out the printed report.

Minutes Topic What happens 0 to 5 What the committee is for The terms of reference in two sentences; the committee's authority versus the board's. 5 to 15 Reading the report Summary, then actions, exceptions and overdue evidence, in the order of the reading guide. Words members will see. 15 to 25 Exercise In pairs: decide each proposed action (agree, change or drop), and one expiring exception (renew or fix). Each pair says who owns it and by when. 25 to 30 Closing the loop The presenter records one decision in CISO Assistant and shows where next month's report will show it.

Check understanding:

  1. A risk acceptance expires in 45 days. Where is it in the report, and what are the options? (Section 4, expiring within 60 days; renew by a new decision, or fix the gap.)
  2. An owner is overdue for a second month. What does the committee do? (Asks them why, and confirms an action with a date in section 8.)
  3. Someone wants to accept a risk for two years. Can the committee approve it? (No: longer than 12 months needs the board.)

docs.title: Training: providing evidence (60 minutes)
docs.text:
For system owners. Built on the system owner guide. The presenter runs the example deployment; owners watch, then do the exercises themselves.

By the end, each person can: follow a runbook from a reminder email, check an export is complete, send it the right way, say what happens to it next, and find and update their own actions.

Before the session: the presenter runs make trial and hound scope apply so the example tasks exist in the local CISO Assistant.

Minutes Topic What happens 0 to 10 Why your evidence matters One requirement of the example audit (ISM-1515, restoring backups): what it asks, why no API shows it, and what happens at month end if nobody provides it (the committee report's section 7). 10 to 25 A reminder arrives Open the example task's runbook (backup restore test). Walk through what to export and what the export must show. 25 to 35 Exercise 1 Each owner lists, from the runbook alone, what a complete export must show. The presenter then shows a restore report that leaves out one system; owners spot what is missing and say what they would send instead. 35 to 45 What happens next The presenter uploads it (hound manual upload), the agent proposes a result (hound manual propose), and shows the attested result in the audit after a run. Owners see that a person, not the AI, attests it. 45 to 55 Exercise 2 Each owner finds an applied control they own in CISO Assistant (or in the committee report's actions) and updates its ETA with a note. 55 to 60 When something changes New systems, suppliers, AI features, data moves and admin changes: tell the GRC team first.

Check understanding:

  1. The export is missing two servers. What do you do? (Export again with every server; if you cannot, reply to the reminder with why and when.)
  2. Who decides the result of your evidence? (The GRC team attests it, with the agent's proposal; you provide it.)
  3. You cannot meet the due date. What happens if you say nothing? (It is overdue at month end and listed by name in the committee report.)

docs.title: Walkthrough: run the AI programme on the local stack
docs.text:
This walkthrough takes one new AI system from "someone wants to use it" to results in the AI6 self-assessment, on your own machine. It uses the fictional Example Pty Ltd and a local CISO Assistant, so nothing you do reaches a real system. Allow 45 minutes. No AI knowledge is needed: the primer explains the words, and AI governance is the reference.

The scene. Example Pty Ltd's staff want a search assistant that answers questions from the company's own documents, including HR policies and staff records. The IT team will set it up on a model they configure themselves. You are the GRC team member who registers it, gets it screened and assessed, and shows the committee where the AI programme stands.

Each step starts with what it is for, then what to type. The dates below use 2026-11-24 as "today"; use your own today.

docs.title: 1. Start the local stack
docs.text:
What it is for: a CISO Assistant with Example Pty Ltd's scope already in it, including the AI6 framework, the AI6 audit EX-AI6-2026 and the two AI systems already registered.

From the dev container:

make ca-up
set -a && . .dev/ca.env && set +a      # HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN for the commands below
hound() { dotnet run --project src/EvidenceHound.Cli -- "$@"; }   # hound from your checkout

Open CISO Assistant at https://localhost:8443 and sign in as the admin user make ca-up printed.

Then work on a copy of the example compliance repo, so the example itself stays as it is:

mkdir -p .dev/ai-walkthrough && cp -R examples/compliance-repo .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo

docs.title: 2. Look at the register you already have
docs.text:
What it is for: knowing what is registered before you add to it, the way the committee sees it.

hound programme list --scope .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/scope

The AI programme's line ends with Register: 2 AI systems. screening: elevated 1, normal 1. use: built 1, customised 1. In CISO Assistant, open Assets and filter by the label ai-system: the same two systems, each with its screening outcome, use and oversight as labels and its register entry at the end of its description.

docs.title: 3. Decide whether it is an AI system, and who supplies it
docs.text:
What it is for: only AI systems go in the register, and a supplier must be approved before their system is registered.

Open the screening runbook (runbooks/ai-screening.md in the repo) and follow sections 1 and 2. The search assistant produces answers from data with some autonomy, so it is an AI system. The IT team sets it up on a model they configure, so its use is customised. Had it been a supplier's product, its use would be third_party and it would name the supplier's approved solution as solution (third parties).

docs.title: 4. Answer the screening questions
docs.text:
What it is for: the answers set the screening outcome, and the outcome decides how much assurance the system needs.

Answer the National AI Centre's seven questions in section 3 of the runbook. For the search assistant:

# Question, in short Answer 1 Personal, sensitive or confidential information? Yes: staff records 2 Talks to people without a person checking? No: staff read each answer before acting on it 3 Acts by itself at scale, or hard to stop? No: it only answers questions 4 Affects people in vulnerable circumstances? No 5 Regulated area or legal effects? No 6 Harm hard to undo? No 7 General purpose or easily repurposed? Yes: it is built on a general-purpose language model

Any yes makes it elevated; here, questions 1 and 7. Keep the answers for the pull request.

docs.title: 5. Register it
docs.text:
What it is for: the register entry is a reviewed change in the repo, and hound turns it into CISO Assistant labels.

Add the system to the Example Pty Ltd domain's systems in .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/scope/setup.yaml, after Example proposal assistant:

      - name: Example knowledge search
        ref_id: SYS-AI-SEARCH
        type: supporting
        description: Answers staff questions from company documents, including HR policies and staff records.
        owner: it@example.com
        ai:
          screening: elevated
          screening_yes: [1, 7]
          screened_on: "2026-11-24"
          registered_on: "2026-11-24"
          use: customised
          purpose: Help staff find answers in company documents without asking HR or IT.
          intended_uses: [Answer staff questions about company policies]
          limitations: Not for decisions about a person; answers about pay or leave must be checked with HR.
          misuse: Asking it about another staff member's records.
          data_sources: [Company policies (text), HR policies (text), Staff records (structured)]
          stakeholders: [All staff, HR team]
          oversight: human_in_the_loop
          oversight_note: Staff read every answer before acting on it; the IT lead can switch it off in its admin console.
          impact_assessment: not_started

Add it to the AI6 audit's systems in scope/audits/ex-ai6-2026.yaml:

systems: [Example ticket triage, Example proposal assistant, Example knowledge search]

Check the files:

hound scope validate .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/scope --config .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/hound.yaml

It reports no problems. To see a check at work, add impact_assessed_on: "2026-11-24" while impact_assessment is still not_started, validate again, and read ai.impact_date_without_approval; then take the line out again.

docs.title: 6. See what CISO Assistant will get, then apply it
docs.text:
What it is for: the plan is what reviewers approve on the pull request; applying writes exactly that.

hound scope plan .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/scope --config .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/hound.yaml
hound scope apply .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/scope --config .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/hound.yaml

The plan creates the asset Example knowledge search with the labels ai-system, ai-screening-elevated, ai-use-customised and ai-oversight-in-the-loop, and adds it to the audit. Filter Assets by ai-system again: there are three.

docs.title: 7. Record the impact assessment
docs.text:
What it is for: an elevated system needs an approved impact assessment before it goes live (AI6-2 and AI6-3).

The owner writes the impact assessment: who it affects, what could go wrong, and how they will know. For an elevated system, record its main risks as risk scenarios in CISO Assistant (Risk assessments, then a risk scenario linked to the asset Example knowledge search). The screening template says to consult senior leadership or your governance committee about an elevated system; here that is their approval of the impact assessment. Once they approve it, change the entry:

          impact_assessment: approved
          impact_assessed_on: "2026-11-24"

docs.title: 8. Test it, then put it in use
docs.text:
What it is for: AI6-5.1 asks for a test before go-live, and the date shows when it needs testing again.

The IT team tests that it answers correctly from the right documents and refuses what staff should not see, and keeps the result as evidence. Then record the test and the go-live date:

          last_tested_on: "2026-11-24"
          in_use_from: "2026-11-24"

Validate, plan and apply again, as in steps 5 and 6. Tell staff that the search assistant is AI and how to report a wrong answer (AI6-4).

docs.title: 9. Run hound and read the AI6 rows
docs.text:
What it is for: the ai-register collector checks every entry and turns the checks into AI6 results, so the self-assessment stays current without anyone filling it in.

Write a config that runs the collector and publishes to the AI6 audit:

cat > .dev/ai-walkthrough/run.yaml <<'EOF'
ciso_assistant:
  url: http://localhost:8000/api/        # HOUND_CA_URL overrides this
  token: env:HOUND_CA_TOKEN
evidence:
  root: evidence
collectors:
  - name: example-ai-register
    type: ai-register
    schedule: "0 6 * * *"
    settings:
      scope: repo/scope
target:
  mapping: repo/mappings/ai6.yaml
  compliance_assessment: EX-AI6-2026
EOF
hound run --config .dev/ai-walkthrough/run.yaml --dry-run
hound run --config .dev/ai-walkthrough/run.yaml

The dry run shows the updates without sending them. After the real run, open the audit AI6 Foundations 2026 in CISO Assistant:

  • AI6-4.1 (Maintain an AI register) is compliant: every AI system has the National AI Centre register template's columns, an impact assessment status and an owner.
  • AI6-5.1 (Pre-deployment testing) is not compliant, and its observation names Example proposal assistant, which went live with no last_tested_on. Your new system passes. The fix is the same as step 8, for that system.
  • AI6-3.2 (Assess AI system risks) shows whether each system in use was screened before it went live, and each elevated one had its impact assessment approved first.

The evidence store (.dev/ai-walkthrough/evidence/example-ai-register/<time>/, named by when the collector ran, to the millisecond) holds ai-register.json: every entry, whether it is in use, and the SHA-256 of the setup.yaml it read, so a result traces back to the reviewed file.

docs.title: 10. Show the committee
docs.text:
What it is for: the committee wants counts and what is not met, not the detail.

hound programme list --scope .dev/ai-walkthrough/repo/scope

The register line now reads Register: 3 AI systems. screening: elevated 2, normal 1. use: built 1, customised 2. Together with the AI6 rows that are not met, that is the AI part of the monthly report: hound report committee puts them in its section 3 (reporting).

docs.title: 11. Clean up
docs.text:
What it is for: leaving the local stack as the example describes it.

rm -rf .dev/ai-walkthrough
make ca-down ARGS=-v && make ca-up      # -v deletes the local CISO Assistant's data

docs.title: What next
docs.text:
• Put a third-party AI system through the same steps, with its supplier approved first (third parties).
  • Add the ciso-assistant profile with a read-only token, so the risk scenarios and supplier checks run too (the collectors).
  • Set up the yearly and quarterly AI records people attest (AI governance).

docs.title: First deployment: your private compliance repo and a scheduled run
docs.text:
This tutorial goes from an empty VM and an empty private repository to collectors running on a schedule and publishing to an Essential Eight audit in CISO Assistant. It uses the fictional Example Pty Ltd throughout; replace its names with yours as you go. Allow an afternoon, most of it waiting for CISO Assistant's first start and for approvals.

You need:

  • A VM with Docker Engine and the Compose plugin, 4 GB of memory or more, and a DNS name for it (here ciso.example.com).
  • A GitHub account or organisation where you can create private repositories.
  • For the Microsoft 365 collector, rights to register an app in your Microsoft Entra tenant.

Two repositories are involved. The public Evidence Hound repo provides the stack (deploy/compose) and the hound runner image. Your private compliance repo holds everything about your organisation: deployment settings, collector schedules, scope, access and settings. Secrets are in neither.

docs.title: 1. Create the private compliance repo
docs.text:
1. Copy the template, examples/compliance-repo, into a new folder and make it a repository:
git clone https://github.com/tnbozman/evidence-hound.git
cp -r evidence-hound/examples/compliance-repo ~/compliance
cd ~/compliance
git init -b main && git add . && git commit -m "Start from the Evidence Hound template"
gh repo create <owner>/compliance --private --source . --push
  1. In the new repository's settings:
  2. Turn on branch protection for main: require a pull request with at least one approving review, require the validate and secrets checks to pass, and block force pushes.
  3. Secret scanning with push protection turned on (Settings > Code security), so a token pushed by mistake is blocked before it lands.
  4. An environment named ciso-assistant with required reviewers, so every apply after a merge waits for a second approval.
  5. Replace Example Pty Ltd with your organisation in scope/setup.yaml, scope/controls.yaml, scope/access.yaml and hound.yaml. Each YAML file's first line links a schema with a relative path into the Evidence Hound repo; point it at the schema of the Evidence Hound version you run so your editor keeps checking the files.

To start from a smaller repo instead, hound init asks about your organisation and writes the config, scope and mapping (audits come per system, as you onboard each), and hound add adds systems, controls and collectors (guided setup). Copy the template's deploy/, scope/settings.yaml and .github/ into it. Keep the scope/access.yaml that hound init wrote: its GRC team is the one the evidence plan names, and the template's would replace it.

Commit each step on a branch and merge it through a pull request, so the repo's history starts as it will continue.

docs.title: 2. What goes in the repo, and what never does
docs.text:
In the repo Never in the repo deploy/deploy.env: the CISO Assistant release (CA_VERSION), host name, time zone, runner image tag and where things are on the host Passwords, including the Postgres password and Django secret key deploy/compose.override.yml: your additions to the stack API tokens, such as the runner's CISO Assistant token hound.yaml: collectors, their schedules and the target audit Certificates and private keys, such as the Microsoft 365 app's scope/: scope/setup.yaml, scope/controls.yaml, scope/audits/, scope/access.yaml and scope/settings.yaml Exported evidence, logs and screenshots mappings/, frameworks/, documents/ (policies and procedures) and manual-sources/README.md .env files

Secrets live on the VM as Docker secrets files in /etc/evidence-hound/secrets (or in a secret manager) and are named from the repo by reference only: file:/run/secrets/m365_client_certificate or env:HOUND_CA_TOKEN. The template's .gitignore excludes secrets, keys, certificates, .env files and evidence, and its workflow runs gitleaks on every change as a second line behind push protection.

docs.title: 3. Install the stack on the VM
docs.text:
1. Make the secrets folder and the two secrets CISO Assistant needs. The runner's token and the Microsoft 365 certificate start empty and are filled below.
sudo install -d -m 0700 /etc/evidence-hound/secrets
cd /etc/evidence-hound/secrets
sudo sh -c 'umask 022; openssl rand -hex 24 > postgres_password; openssl rand -hex 32 > django_secret_key; : > hound_ca_token; : > m365_client_certificate'
  1. Check out both repositories. Give the VM read-only access to your private repo with a deploy key.
sudo git clone https://github.com/tnbozman/evidence-hound.git /opt/evidence-hound
sudo git clone git@github.com:<owner>/compliance.git /opt/compliance
  1. Link your settings as the stack's .env. deploy/deploy.env sets COMPOSE_FILE, so every docker compose command in deploy/compose, and the stack's own scripts, also use your deploy/compose.override.yml.
sudo ln -s /opt/compliance/deploy/deploy.env /opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose/.env
cd /opt/evidence-hound/deploy/compose
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up -d --wait postgres backend worker frontend caddy

The first start migrates the database and loads CISO Assistant's libraries, which takes several minutes.

  1. Create the first administrator, who signs in to CISO Assistant as a person:
./manage.sh createsuperuser
  1. Sign in at https://ciso.example.com. Caddy signs the certificate with its own authority; install its root on your devices (see the stack's guide) or use your own certificate.
  2. Create the runner's service account and its token. The script writes the token straight into the secrets folder; it is never shown or copied.
sudo ./runner-token.sh hound-runner@example.com /etc/evidence-hound/secrets

runner-token.sh puts the account in the administrators group, so the first apply below can run with its token. Once the CI workflow applies with its own account, declare the runner in scope/access.yaml with service_account: publish and the analyst role on the domains it publishes to. The next apply narrows its groups to that, and scope plan's access review stops flagging it.

docs.title: 4. Register the Microsoft 365 app
docs.text:
Follow the Microsoft 365 collector guide (docs/collectors/m365.md): register the app, grant its read-only Graph permissions, and create its certificate on the VM. Store the PEM (certificate followed by its private key) as the m365_client_certificate secret, then delete the loose key file:

sudo install -m 0444 hound-m365.pem /etc/evidence-hound/secrets/m365_client_certificate
sudo rm hound-m365.pem hound-m365-private.pem

Put the tenant and client IDs (not secrets) in hound.yaml through a pull request, merge it, and pull it on the VM with git -C /opt/compliance pull. Check the config and that every secret resolves:

docker compose run --rm runner config validate /config/hound.yaml --check-secrets

docs.title: 5. Validate, plan and apply the scope
docs.text:
Do this in two pull requests, so the first apply is small and easy to check.

First: setup, settings and access. Move the audit files out of scope/audits/ for now and keep scope/setup.yaml, scope/controls.yaml, scope/access.yaml and scope/settings.yaml. The template's settings turn on enforce_mfa, so everyone must set up multi-factor authentication at their next sign-in, and leave the modules you do not use off. On your own machine, run hound from the runner image against your checkout:

hound() { docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/config:ro" -w /config ghcr.io/tnbozman/evidence-hound:1.0.0 "$@"; }
hound config validate hound.yaml
hound scope validate scope/ --config hound.yaml

Validation runs offline and reports every problem with its file, line, code and a hint. Then, on the VM, see what applying would do, and apply:

docker compose run --rm runner scope plan /config/scope --config /config/hound.yaml
docker compose run --rm runner scope apply /config/scope --config /config/hound.yaml

The plan lists every user (with the roles they will hold), team, flag and setting it will create or change. New users get CISO Assistant's invitation and set their own password; hound never handles one. The plan's access review lists anyone who has not turned on MFA yet.

Second: the Essential Eight audit. Put scope/audits/ex-e8-2026.yaml back (renamed for your audit; a repo from hound init has no audit until you onboard a system, or scope/audits/<code>-e8.yaml with --organisation-audit, and no scope/settings.yaml until you copy the template's), check the mapping, and repeat validate, plan and apply:

hound mapping validate mappings/essential-eight-2023.yaml
hound scope validate scope/ --config hound.yaml

After apply, the audit, its controls and documents are in CISO Assistant, and a second scope plan lists no changes.

docs.title: 6. Turn on the schedule and check the first run
docs.text:
Run the collectors once by hand, then start the runner, which runs each collector on its schedule in scheduler.time_zone:

docker compose run --rm runner run --config /config/hound.yaml
docker compose run --rm runner status --config /config/hound.yaml
docker compose up -d runner
docker compose logs runner

status shows each collector's latest run and the result it published; the logs show each collector's next run. In CISO Assistant, open the audit: requirements the collectors cover have results and evidence, and the AC-AUTO-EVIDENCE control shows that collection is healthy. Manual sources show as due until their owners drop an export into the folders manual-sources/README.md lists.

docs.title: 7. Day-2 changes
docs.text:
From now on, every change goes in as a pull request to the compliance repo, whoever makes it:

  • Access: a new starter, a leaver (removed from scope/access.yaml, then deactivated by scope apply --prune, never deleted) or a role change.
  • Settings: a feature flag or general setting in scope/settings.yaml.
  • Scope: systems, controls, audits, documents and sign-offs.
  • Schedules and collectors: hound.yaml.
  • Upgrades: CA_VERSION or HOUND_RUNNER_IMAGE in deploy/deploy.env; snapshot the VM first.

The repo's workflow, .github/workflows/compliance.yml, scans the change for secrets, validates it, comments the scope plan on the pull request so reviewers approve the change in CISO Assistant's terms, and applies it after merge once the ciso-assistant environment's reviewers approve. It needs a self-hosted runner that can reach CISO Assistant and the HOUND_CA_URL and HOUND_CA_TOKEN repository secrets. After a merge that changes deploy/ or hound.yaml, pull it on the VM and restart: git -C /opt/compliance pull && docker compose up -d.

The scope files guide covers every file in detail, and running collectors covers the schedule, status and health.

docs.title: The IaC pipeline dev server
docs.text:
A fictional Example Pty Ltd IaC pipeline that answers the terraform-tests and terraform-drift profiles (and your copies of them, such as the onboarding tutorial's grc-infra-controls) on your machine. It stands in for the GitHub Actions API of the repository example/grc-infra, which holds the GRC platform's Oracle Cloud Terraform from the onboarding tutorial. make trial uses it so the GRC platform's hosting controls are collected with no GitHub account and no token. Nothing leaves the machine.

make iac-dev                                                # every control in place, no drift, on port 5380
make iac-dev ARGS="--variant gaps"                          # every deviation below
make iac-dev ARGS="--deviation drift --port 5381"
make iac-dev ARGS="--controls-report /path/to/controls.xml" # serve the report your own terraform test wrote

The server prints the settings for each rest collector: profile, api_url (the server's address), repository and workflow. The secret token can be any text: the server checks none.

docs.title: What the pipeline holds
docs.text:
Workflow Run Artefact controls.yml One completed, successful run on main, finished a minute before the server started control-tests, holding controls.xml: the JUnit report of the tutorial's controls.tftest.hcl, one test case per run block, every one passing drift.yml The same drift-plan, holding plan.json: a refresh-only plan in which every resource of the tutorial's Terraform is a no-op and nothing drifted

It answers these addresses, and any other gets 404:

Address Answer GET /repos/example/grc-infra/actions/workflows/{workflow}/runs The newest run, dated from the server's start, so max_age never makes it stale. GET /repos/example/grc-infra/actions/runs/{run}/artifacts The run's artefact. GET /repos/example/grc-infra/actions/artifacts/{artifact}/zip The artefact's zip, served directly rather than through GitHub's redirect.

docs.title: A real report
docs.text:
With Terraform installed, run the tutorial's control tests and serve their real report:

cd examples/onboarding-tutorial/infra/oci && terraform init -backend=false && terraform test -junit-xml=/tmp/controls.xml
make iac-dev ARGS="--controls-report /tmp/controls.xml"

The tests use mock providers, so they need no Oracle account and create nothing. Change the Terraform (give the VM assign_public_ip = true, say), test again and collect again to watch a control fail. make trial does the first part for you when terraform is on the path.

docs.title: The variants
docs.text:
Deviation What changes Check and expected outcome public-ip The control test vm_has_no_public_ip fails: a change gave the VM a public address. infrastructure.controls.vm_has_no_public_ip and infrastructure.tests.pass: fail drift The nightly plan finds the backup bucket changed outside Terraform. infrastructure.drift.none: fail

IacDevServerTests runs the rest collector with the library profiles and the tutorial's grc-infra-controls against the compliant pipeline and each deviation, so this table and the pipeline cannot drift apart. A test also checks the report has one test case per run block of the tutorial's control tests.

docs.title: Adding a control test or a deviation
docs.text:
• The pipeline is described once, in src/EvidenceHound.IacDevServer/IacDevPipeline.cs; IacAnswers.cs turns it into GitHub Actions JSON, the JUnit report and the plan.
  • A new run block in controls.tftest.hcl adds a ControlTest (the test fails until it does).
  • A deviation is a name, a sentence, the checks it fails with their expected outcome, and a change to the pipeline. Add it to IacDevPipeline.Deviations and a row to the table above.

docs.title: What it cannot show
docs.text:
• GitHub itself: rate limits, the artefact download redirect, expired artefacts and token scopes. The profiles' recorded tests and a run against your own IaC repository cover those.
  • Your cloud: a mock-provider test proves what the code declares, and the drift plan stands in for a real refresh against Oracle Cloud.

docs.title: Local trial: Evidence Hound next to your CISO Assistant
docs.text:
This tutorial is interactive: make trial runs it step by step from the dev container. It sets a scene and walks it the way you would onboard for real, so you can explore CISO Assistant and Evidence Hound with little fuss.

The scene. The fictional Example Pty Ltd self-hosts its cyber GRC: CISO Assistant and Evidence Hound run in Docker Compose on one private Oracle Cloud (OCI) VM with no public IP address (GRC-PLATFORM). The office reaches it only over a site-to-site VPN through its Sophos XGS 88W firewall, managed in Sophos Central (OFFICE-FIREWALL). Staff sign in with Microsoft 365. The GRC team audits each system to the Essential Eight, maturity level 2. This is the onboarding tutorial's deployment, with its diagram.

The order. The organisation with hound init (guided setup), its third parties (Oracle, Sophos, and the CISO Assistant and Evidence Hound projects), then each system with its own audit and the controls it relies on, and last the collectors that gather evidence on a schedule: the IaC pipeline's control tests and drift check for GRC-PLATFORM (its dev server), Sophos Central for OFFICE-FIREWALL (its dev server) Microsoft 365 for identity and laptops (its dev server), and vulnerability scan exports for patching (fictional exports). Every collector reads a fictional tenant on your machine, so you need no account, API key or cloud; Sophos Central and Microsoft 365 can be your own tenants instead. From the third parties on, your coding agent drafts each stage with hound's skills and you approve it. Allow an hour or two; the first image build takes much of it.

make trial

Each step shows the hound command before it runs and asks before anything that changes CISO Assistant. Answer q to stop. Run make trial again to carry on: finished steps are skipped. make trial-clean removes the workspace and leaves CISO Assistant running.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• The dev container, with Docker answering inside it.
  • A CISO Assistant. The dev container starts its own, at http://backend:8000 in the dev container and https://localhost:8443 in your browser. A stack from make ca-up works too. If none is running, the trial offers to start one.
  • No account or key: each collector reads its dev server. Optionally Terraform (the dev container has it), so the trial runs the GRC platform's real control tests.
  • For your own Sophos Central tenant instead (step 13), an API credential with the Service Principal Read-Only role, created as the Sophos guide describes; for your own Microsoft 365 test tenant (step 14), section 14.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
Before it starts anything, the trial checks:

Check What happens Docker answers Stops with a hint if it does not. The dev container's CISO Assistant answers at http://backend:8000 Reused. Nothing new is started. A CISO Assistant backend container runs on the Docker daemon the dev container sees (make ca-up) Reused, on its Docker network. Something answers at http://localhost:8000 Reused. None of these, and ports 8000 and 8443 are free Offers make ca-up. None of these, and port 8000 or 8443 is taken Stops and names the container, or says it is a process outside Docker.

docs.title: 2. The runner image
docs.text:
The trial builds the runner image from your checkout (make image HOUND_IMAGE=evidence-hound-runner:trial), so it tests your branch, not a published release. Every hound command then runs as a throwaway container: docker run --rm with the workspace mounted at /trial.

How the container reaches CISO Assistant:

  • The dev container's CISO Assistant runs on the Docker daemon outside the dev container. The dev container uses Docker-in-Docker, so its containers cannot join that network. They share the dev container's network namespace (--network host) instead, where backend resolves.
  • A make ca-up stack runs on the dev container's own daemon. hound joins its network (hound-ciso-assistant_default).

In both cases the API is http://backend:8000/api/. The token is copied from .dev/ca.env to .dev/trial/secrets/ca_token (mode 600) and reaches the container as HOUND_CA_TOKEN_FILE. It is never printed or put on a command line.

docs.title: 3. The workspace
docs.text:
.dev/trial/ is git-ignored and holds everything the trial writes:

Path Holds repo/ The organisation's compliance repo, as hound init writes it secrets/ The API token and, later, the Sophos client secret (folder 700, files 600) profiles/ The profiles the collectors read, with their tests: grc-infra-controls and terraform-drift (step 12), sophos-central (step 13) iac/ The GRC platform's Terraform, copied to run its control tests, and their report controls.xml (step 12) manual/ Drop folders for manual evidence sources evidence/ Evidence and run records specs/ API specifications for the agent: the trial puts a fictional description of the Sophos Central API calls the dev server answers here inbox/ Vendor documents for the agent (the trial puts fictional notes on each of the four suppliers here), and the Microsoft 365 test certificate bin/hound hound for your coding agent: the trial's image, against the trial's CISO Assistant

docs.title: 4. A new organisation
