docs.text:
hound init /trial/repo --organisation-audit asks about the organisation: its name, a short code for ref IDs, the CISO Assistant address, the time zone, the Essential Eight maturity level, whether the audit runs by quarter or by month, and the compliance owner. Press Enter to take each default, the fictional Example Pty Ltd at maturity level 2, audited by quarter: the series EX-E8, whose open period on 23 November 2026 is EX-E8-Q2-2027FY. It writes the config, the scope (the domain, the health control and the audit) and the Essential Eight mapping, and checks them. The organisation gets its own audit because an organisation-wide source feeds it: Microsoft 365 covers every account and laptop (step 14). Each system still gets its own audit in the series; without such a source, leave --organisation-audit out. The trial then runs:

hound config validate hound.yaml
hound scope validate scope --config hound.yaml
hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml --out /trial/scope-plan.json
hound scope apply /trial/scope-plan.json

Read the plan before you answer: it lists every object and field the apply would create or change. The plan is saved outside the repo, and apply writes exactly that saved plan. If the scope or CISO Assistant changed in between, it refuses with scope.plan_stale (Saved plans). A second run plans nothing new.

It then runs hound agent setup --assistant both, which writes the skills and agent files for Claude Code and GitHub Copilot (onboarding), and links .dev/trial/bin/hound to scripts/trial-hound.sh: it runs the trial's runner image against the trial's CISO Assistant with the trial's token, in the folder you call it from. hound's container sees only .dev/trial, so it refuses a folder outside it. Start your agent in a second terminal and keep it open:

cd .dev/trial/repo && export PATH="$PWD/../bin:$PATH"
claude

Or open .dev/trial/repo in VS Code and pick the hound-onboarding agent in Copilot. The trial has already put fictional supplier notes in .dev/trial/inbox and a Sophos Central API description in .dev/trial/specs; add any other API specification or vendor document there.

docs.title: 5 to 11. Third parties, then each system, its audit and controls
docs.text:
Each of these stages works the same way. The trial says what the stage is and prints what to ask your agent, with the skills it uses. It waits until hound sees the draft in the repo; answer y when the agent has finished, or q to stop and carry on later. Where a person must approve, it runs hound approve --repo . in your terminal, which shows each draft one at a time (answer y, n or s). Then it validates, plans and applies, as in step 4, and says what to look at in CISO Assistant. Steps 6 to 8 are GRC-PLATFORM; steps 9 to 11 are the same for OFFICE-FIREWALL.

Stage The agent drafts (skills) You In CISO Assistant 5. Third parties Oracle (OCI hosting, SOL-OCI-HOSTING) and the CISO Assistant and Evidence Hound projects for GRC-PLATFORM; Sophos (the XGS 88W and Sophos Central, SOL-SOPHOS-FIREWALL) for OFFICE-FIREWALL, with hound supplier draft (onboard-a-third-party, assess-a-supplier) Approve each supplier and conclude its review with hound approve. A system is registered only once its supplier's review is concluded ok Third parties SUP-ORACLE, SUP-SOPHOS, SUP-CISO-ASSISTANT and SUP-EVIDENCE-HOUND, with their solutions, contracts and reviews 6 and 9. The system The session, with hound onboard <system> pending: owner, product, solution and maturity level (onboard-a-system-with-hound) Answer what it asks Nothing yet: the session waits in repo/onboarding/<system>/ 7 and 10. Its audit One decision per requirement with hound onboard <system> decide (read-an-api-specification), then the review (review-before-apply) Approve the decisions with hound approve, which writes the system and its audit The asset and the audit EX-E8-<period>-<system>, such as EX-E8-Q2-2027FY-GRC-PLATFORM, next to the organisation's EX-E8-Q2-2027FY 8 and 11. Controls The applied controls the audit's manual requirements rely on, with hound add control … --audit EX-E8-<system>: for GRC-PLATFORM patching (ISM-1695) and restore tests (ISM-1515), for OFFICE-FIREWALL a daily external scan (ISM-1701) Review them The applied controls, linked to the audit's requirements

A finished stage is skipped on the next run; remove its file in .dev/trial/state/ to do it again.

docs.title: 12. GRC-PLATFORM's evidence: its hosting controls and drift, from the IaC pipeline
docs.text:
The GRC platform's network, backups and hosting controls are Terraform (infra/oci). Its IaC pipeline proves each control with terraform test on every change and checks nightly that the cloud still matches the code (the tutorial, steps 5 and 6). hound only reads the pipeline's reports through the GitHub Actions API; it never runs Terraform against the cloud and holds no cloud credential. In the trial:

  1. If Terraform is installed, the trial copies the Terraform to .dev/trial/iac/oci and runs terraform init -backend=false and terraform test -junit-xml=controls.xml, as the pipeline would. The tests use mock providers: no Oracle account, nothing created.
  2. It starts the IaC pipeline dev server (make iac-dev on port 5380), which serves that report, or its own report of the same tests without Terraform, and a drift plan with no drift, as the fictional repository example/grc-infra.
  3. It copies the tutorial's mapping for the system, mappings/grc-platform-essential-eight-2023.yaml, and adds a target for EX-E8-GRC-PLATFORM to hound.yaml, so the results reach the system's own audit. No hound command writes these yet.
  4. It adds two rest collectors with a placeholder token, grc-infra-controls (the tutorial's per-control copy of terraform-tests) and grc-infra-drift (terraform-drift), then validates, dry-runs and, after asking, publishes each.

Each backup row (ISM-1811, ISM-1705, ISM-1812, ISM-1707, ISM-1814) needs its control test and no drift: the test proves the code declares the control, and the drift check proves the cloud still matches the code. The trial then offers to restart the dev server with the drift deviation and collect again: the backup rows now fail. The system's other rows stay manual, with the controls from step 8 and it@example.com as their owner.

docs.title: 13. OFFICE-FIREWALL's evidence: Sophos Central, a fictional tenant on this machine or your own
docs.text: The trial copies the sophos-central library profile and its tests into .dev/trial/profiles, then asks which tenant to read. Press Enter for the dev server; an unattended run takes it too.

docs.title: The dev server (default)
docs.text:
The trial starts the Sophos Central dev server in the background (make sophos-dev on port 5370, log in .dev/trial/sophos-dev.log, stopped when the trial ends). It serves the fictional Example Pty Ltd tenant: two XGS firewalls on supported firmware and five admins, two of them Super Admins. Nothing leaves the machine and no question asks for a credential:

hound add collector rest --name sophos --config hound.yaml --schedule "0 4 * * *" --secrets-dir /trial/secrets \
  --set profile=sophos-central --set profiles_path=/trial/profiles \
  --set client_id=00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000050d0001 \
  --set id_url=http://localhost:5370/ --set api_url=http://localhost:5370/ \
  --set "supported_firewall_firmware=21.0, 21.5" \
  --secret-file client_secret=/trial/inbox/sophos-dev-secret --yes

The secret is a placeholder the trial writes; the dev server checks no credential. The address is localhost on a make ca-up network too: hound sends credentials over plain http only to the machine it runs on, so while the config reads a dev server the trial runs hound on the host network and reaches CISO Assistant on its published port.

docs.title: Your own tenant
docs.text:
Answer n and hound add collector rest --name sophos --config hound.yaml --schedule "0 4 * * *" --secrets-dir /trial/secrets --set profile=sophos-central --set profiles_path=/trial/profiles asks for what the profile needs:

  1. The credential's client ID, and the firewall firmware versions still in support (see Sophos's firmware lifecycle), such as 21.5, 22.0. Other settings, such as super_admin_max, keep their defaults; add them with --set key=value. The credential must be the tenant's own: partner and organisation credentials are not supported.
  2. The client secret, which is not shown as you type. It is saved to .dev/trial/secrets/sophos_client_secret (mode 600), never in git, and the config references it as file:/trial/secrets/sophos_client_secret.

docs.title: Then, either way
docs.text:
The trial runs:

hound config validate hound.yaml --check-secrets
hound run --config hound.yaml --only sophos --dry-run
hound run --config hound.yaml --only sophos
hound status --config hound.yaml

Before it runs, the trial copies the tutorial's mappings/office-firewall-essential-eight-2023.yaml and targets EX-E8-OFFICE-FIREWALL, as in step 12. The dry run signs in, reads the firewalls, stores the evidence locally and plans the updates, and sends nothing. The real run publishes the firmware, firmware upgrade and Super Admin checks to OFFICE-FIREWALL's audit (ISM-1501, ISM-1694 and ISM-1883) and the firmware checks to the organisation's (ISM-1694, and ISM-1501 together with the Microsoft 365 collector's operating system check, so that row waits for step 14). Sophos Central is read for network devices only; evidence about endpoint protection comes from the endpoints' own antivirus, not from Sophos.

With the dev server, the trial then offers to restart it with the unsupported-firmware deviation (the branch firewall on SFOS 20.0.3) and run again: the firmware check now fails, and you can watch the result change in CISO Assistant. This is continual evidence collection in miniature: the schedule runs the same collector every day and CISO Assistant keeps each result.

If you share output for help, remove identifiers first: tenant IDs, host names, IP addresses and serial numbers.

docs.title: 14. Identity and laptops: Microsoft 365
docs.text:
The trial offers the Microsoft 365 dev server first: a fictional Example Pty Ltd tenant that answers Microsoft Graph on this machine, with no tenant, no sign-in and nothing leaving the machine. Choose the compliant tenant, which passes every check, or the gaps tenant, where each named check fails. The trial:

  1. Starts it (make m365-dev ARGS="--variant compliant"), with its output in .dev/trial/m365-dev.log, and waits until it answers on http://localhost:5365/.
  2. Adds the m365 collector with the settings the server prints, graph_url: http://localhost:5365/ and sign_in: none, so it asks for no certificate or secret. sign_in: none is refused for any address not on this machine (settings).
  3. Validates, dry-runs and, after asking, publishes, with hound's container on the host network so it reaches the server; then shows hound status and stops the server.

The checks publish to the open period of the organisation's audit, EX-E8-Q2-2027FY on 23 November 2026. A later make trial starts the server again and runs the same collector.

docs.title: Your own test tenant
docs.text:
Answer n to the dev server to use a tenant of your own instead.

Use a test tenant, never a work one: the collector only reads, but a trial is the place to make mistakes. Two ways to get one:

  • The Microsoft 365 Developer Program, if you qualify for its E5 sandbox (Microsoft limits who does). It has Entra ID P2 and Intune, so every check can run.
  • A Microsoft 365 Business Premium trial (one month). It has Entra ID P1 and Intune, which the Conditional Access and device checks need; the PIM check reports not_applicable without P2. Cancel the trial when you are done.

In the tenant, register the app as the Microsoft 365 guide says: the six read-only Graph application permissions, admin consent, and a certificate. The trial offers to make a test certificate with openssl in .dev/trial/inbox/ (valid 90 days): upload hound-m365.crt to the app, and the trial keeps hound-m365.pem (certificate and key). If you have your own, put it at .dev/trial/inbox/hound-m365.pem first.

Then hound add collector m365 --config hound.yaml --secrets-dir /trial/secrets --secret-file client_certificate=/trial/inbox/hound-m365.pem asks for the tenant ID, the app's client ID and the Windows builds still in support, such as 10.0.22631, 10.0.26100. The other settings keep their defaults; add any with --set key=value. The PEM is copied to .dev/trial/secrets/m365_client_certificate (mode 600) and the inbox copy is removed. As with Sophos, the trial then validates the secrets, runs a dry run and, after asking, a real run and hound status.

If you share output for help, remove identifiers first: tenant and client IDs, domains, user names and device names.

docs.title: 15. Patching evidence: vulnerability scans
docs.text:
Scanners export files instead of answering an API, so the vuln-scan collector reads exports dropped in a folder (its guide). The trial:

  1. Writes fictional scan exports for the Example Pty Ltd estate into .dev/trial/scans, dated from today. That is make scan-dev ARGS="--variant compliant --out ../scans", run from the workspace's repo folder, with its output in .dev/trial/scan-dev.log. There is one export per scope: Nessus for internet-facing services, other applications and operating systems, and a Defender CSV for the laptops.
  2. Adds one vuln-scan source per scope, named internet-facing-scans, laptops-scans, other-apps-scans and operating-systems-scans, with the settings the generator printed. Their drop folders are ../scans/<scope folder>, relative to hound.yaml.
  3. Runs each source dry, then publishes after asking. The eleven patching checks reach the Essential Eight rows they map to: scanning frequency, patch windows and unsupported software.
  4. Offers to write the gaps estate and collect again. That estate has a stale internet-facing scan, an exploited web flaw past 48 hours, an unsupported VPN appliance, an overdue browser patch, an overdue operating system update and an unsupported laptop operating system. The patching rows then fail, naming the hosts.

In a real deployment, each new export goes into the same folder, by hand or with hound manual upload --source <name>.

docs.title: 16. What CISO Assistant reads for each audit
docs.text:
The trial ends by reading each audit's compliance percentage the way CISO Assistant computes it on its Compliance pages: compliant rows, plus half of the partially compliant ones, over compliant, partially compliant and non-compliant rows. CISO Assistant leaves not-assessed and not-applicable rows out of that figure, so an audit with three passing checks and every manual row not assessed would read 100%. hound therefore sends a row with no evidence as non-compliant, its observation starting "No evidence yet: " (why), and the trial prints each audit's figure with those rows counted, for example EX-SYSTEM-2026: CISO Assistant reads 6% (3 compliant, 0 partially compliant, 43 non-compliant of which 43 have no evidence yet; it leaves out 61 not applicable and 0 not assessed). It stops if any audit reads 100% while a row is not assessed.

For each programme's standing (the maturity level met, and compliant of applicable with every open row counted), use hound report committee (reporting).

docs.title: Unattended
docs.text: HOUND_TRIAL_YES=1 make trial answers yes to every question and gives the wizards their answers as options (--yes). Stages 5 to 11 replay fictional answers through the same commands an agent uses: the four third parties with hound supplier draft, each system with hound onboard <system> pending, its decisions from the onboarding tutorial's answers (answers/) typed into hound onboard, and its controls with hound add control. Because hound approve refuses without a person at a terminal, approved copies of the four supplier files stand in for it (examples/trial/). Steps 12 to 15 use the three dev servers and the fictional scan exports, publish, and collect again with the drift and unsupported-firmware deviations and the gaps scan estate. No step needs a credential. CI uses it to check the trial against a fresh CISO Assistant, twice: the second run applies nothing new.

docs.title: The Microsoft 365 dev server
docs.text:
A fictional Example Pty Ltd tenant that answers Microsoft Graph on your machine, for building and testing Microsoft 365 checks without a test tenant. Nothing leaves the machine and nothing signs in.

make m365-dev                              # every control in place, on http://localhost:5365/
make m365-dev ARGS="--variant gaps"        # every deviation below
make m365-dev ARGS="--deviation synced-admin --port 5366"

The server prints the collector settings for the tenant (tenant_id, client_id, break_glass_accounts, supported_windows_builds and graph_url). Try curl http://localhost:5365/v1.0/users to see the first page.

docs.title: What the tenant holds
docs.text:
Part In the compliant tenant People 12 enabled members at example.com: two admins, two break-glass accounts and eight staff, all MFA-capable; one disabled leaver and one guest. All cloud-only. Roles The two break-glass accounts hold Global Administrator permanently; the two admins are eligible for Global Administrator through PIM, and for Exchange and Security Administrator. Devices Eight Windows laptops on 10.0.26100 or 10.0.22631, all compliant, and one iPhone. Conditional Access "USR - G - Require strong auth" (phishing-resistant MFA for all users and apps) and "USR - B - Block access via legacy auth", each excluding only the break-glass accounts. Intune "ASD Office Hardening Guidelines" (macros from the internet blocked, among 82 settings) and "ASD Windows Hardening Guidelines - Attack Surface Reduction" (19 rules in block mode), both assigned to all users; one Windows device restriction profile; an invented AppLocker custom profile enforcing the EXE, DLL, Script and MSI rule collections on all devices. Defender for Endpoint All eight laptops onboarded. Advanced hunting (POST v1.0/security/runHuntingQuery) answers the collector's three queries, told apart by their // evidence-hound: <name> first line, with application control events from three laptops (blocked and audited) and two blocked files. Any other query gets 404.

The same IDs appear in every collection, so a role holder is a user, a device's owner is a user, and a policy's exclusions are users. Every collection the m365 collector reads is served, in pages of five with @odata.nextLink, as Graph pages them. A path the server does not know gets 404.

docs.title: The two variants
docs.text:
The compliant tenant passes all fourteen m365 checks. The gaps tenant applies every deviation below, each expected to fail the checks it names and no other.

Deviation What changes Check and expected outcome staff-member-without-mfa One staff member has no MFA method (11 of 12). identity.mfa.registered_all_users: partial mfa-policy-report-only "Require strong auth" left in report-only mode, as the Blueprint ships it. identity.mfa.enforced_conditional_access and identity.mfa.phishing_resistant_admins: fail legacy-auth-excludes-a-group The legacy authentication block also excludes a group. identity.legacy_auth_blocked: fail permanent-global-admin A staff member holds Global Administrator permanently (five in all). identity.privileged.global_admin_count and identity.privileged.pim_eligible_not_permanent: fail synced-admin An admin account is synchronised from on-premises. identity.privileged.admins_cloud_only: fail unsupported-windows-build One laptop runs Windows 10 22H2 (10.0.19045). endpoint.os.supported_versions: fail noncompliant-laptop One of eight laptops is not compliant (87.5 %). endpoint.managed.compliant_ratio: partial office-hardening-unassigned The Office hardening policy is assigned to nobody. apps.office.macros_blocked_from_internet: fail asr-office-rule-in-audit "Block Win32 API calls from Office macros" in audit mode. endpoint.asr.office_rules_enabled: partial applocker-for-one-group The AppLocker profile is assigned to one group of kiosks, not all devices. endpoint.application_control.enforced: partial applocker-dll-rules-in-audit The AppLocker DLL rule collection is in audit mode. endpoint.application_control.file_types_covered: fail defender-missing-on-two-laptops Two of the eight laptops are not onboarded to Defender for Endpoint (75 %). endpoint.application_control.events_centrally_logged: partial

M365DevTenantTests runs the m365 collector against each variant and each deviation, so the table and the tenant cannot drift apart.

docs.title: Adding a setting or a deviation
docs.text:
• The tenant is described once, in src/EvidenceHound.M365DevServer/DevTenant.cs; GraphCollections.cs turns it into Graph JSON. Add people, devices, roles or policies there.
  • A deviation is a name, a sentence, the checks it fails with their expected outcome, and a change to the tenant. Add it to DevTenant.Deviations and a row to the table above; the tests then hold it to both.
  • A new check that reads a new collection adds the collection to GraphCollections.Paths and Render, and its settings to the compliant tenant.

docs.title: Where the settings come from
docs.text:
The Intune and Conditional Access settings follow the ASD Blueprint for Secure Cloud, pinned to commit a6e1e5f. © Commonwealth of Australia 2023, used under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence.

  • The Office hardening policy is the Blueprint's Graph export, embedded unchanged. The server adds the assignment and a description, which an export does not carry.
  • The attack surface reduction rules and the two Conditional Access policies are translated by hand from the Blueprint's Microsoft365DSC configurations. The Conditional Access policies are switched on (the Blueprint ships them in report-only mode), and the Blueprint's excluded group is replaced by the two break-glass accounts, because the m365 collector only accepts excluded accounts listed in break_glass_accounts.

src/EvidenceHound.M365DevServer/Blueprint/NOTICE.md lists each file, its source and every change. The people, devices, roles and the AppLocker profile are invented.

docs.title: What it cannot show
docs.text:
A recording of a real tenant (s09-27) and a trial against one (s09-18) still matter for:

  • throttling: the server never answers 429, and real Graph paces requests differently from one tenant to the next;
  • licences: what Graph answers without Entra ID P2 or Intune, beyond the cases the unit tests already stand in;
  • real data: odd values, very large collections and settings nobody wrote down.

The server answers Graph only, not sign-in. To collect from it with hound, add sign_in: none to the m365 collector's settings with graph_url: http://localhost:5365/: the collector then sends a placeholder token and asks for no certificate or secret. sign_in: none is refused for any address that is not on this machine, so real Graph always signs in (settings). The trial's Microsoft 365 step does this for you (local trial).

docs.title: Onboarding tutorial: a privately hosted GRC platform on Oracle Cloud
docs.text:
This tutorial onboards one realistic stack end to end for the fictional Example Pty Ltd. Its CISO Assistant and Evidence Hound run on one private virtual machine in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and the office reaches them over a site-to-site VPN through its Sophos XGS firewall. You onboard two systems with hound onboard: the GRC platform itself, because the compliance platform is in scope too, and the office firewall. Then you review, validate, plan and apply.

Everything here is made up apart from the public product names. Addresses come from the documentation ranges (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24) and stand in for your own; use private ranges that do not overlap between the office and the cloud. You start from a copy of the template compliance repo, examples/compliance-repo. Every file the tutorial writes is in examples/onboarding-tutorial, at the same paths, so you can compare your result with it. The template itself stays without them, so a new repo still starts empty.

It assumes you have read Onboarding and, for installing the stack, the first deployment tutorial. To try the whole deployment on your machine first, with fictional tenants for Sophos Central, Microsoft 365 and the IaC pipeline and no account or key, run make trial: it walks the same third parties, systems, audits, controls and collectors.

docs.title: The deployment
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph office[Office]
    staff[Staff laptops<br/>Example laptops]
    xgs[Sophos XGS firewall<br/>OFFICE-FIREWALL<br/>WAN 203.0.113.10]
  end
  subgraph oci[OCI tenancy, one region]
    drg[Dynamic routing gateway<br/>IPSec tunnels]
    bastion[OCI Bastion]
    subgraph vcn[VCN, private subnet, no public IP]
      vm[VM 192.0.2.10<br/>GRC-PLATFORM]
    end
    nat[NAT gateway]
    sgw[Service gateway]
    bucket[(Object Storage<br/>backups)]
  end
  central[Sophos Central API]
  github[GitHub Actions API<br/>IaC drift plan]
  idp[Example 365<br/>sign-in and MFA]
  staff -- HTTPS to CISO Assistant --> xgs
  xgs == Site-to-Site VPN ==> drg
  drg --> vm
  bastion -- SSH sessions --> vm
  vm -- outbound HTTPS --> nat
  nat --> central
  nat --> github
  vm -- backups --> sgw --> bucket
  staff -. single sign-on .-> idp

Inside the VM, the reference Compose stack runs Caddy, CISO Assistant's frontend, backend and worker, PostgreSQL and the hound runner (see the stack's guide).

Which traffic goes where

From To How Staff in the office (198.51.100.0/24) CISO Assistant HTTPS to Caddy on the VM, port 443, through the XGS and the Site-to-Site VPN. Nothing else reaches the VM. Staff Example 365 Single sign-on into CISO Assistant, with MFA enforced by the identity provider. Administrators The VM's shell SSH only through OCI Bastion sessions (time-limited, signed in to OCI), or over the VPN from the office. The hound runner CISO Assistant Inside the Compose network, to the backend; it never leaves the VM. The hound runner Sophos Central and GitHub's API Outbound HTTPS through the NAT gateway. No inbound port is opened for it. The VM Object Storage Nightly database dumps through the service gateway, never over the internet.

Each part, and what covers it

Part How it is protected Covered by The VM and its operating system Private subnet, no public IP, Ubuntu LTS with unattended security updates GRC-PLATFORM's audit: patching (ISM-1695, ISM-1501) as manual evidence CISO Assistant sign-in Single sign-on with Example 365 GRC-PLATFORM's audit: MFA rows provided by Example 365 TLS Caddy terminates HTTPS with its own certificate authority, or yours The first deployment tutorial PostgreSQL and its backups On the VM's encrypted boot volume; nightly dumps to an Object Storage bucket with a retention rule, weekly volume backups GRC-PLATFORM's audit: the bucket's rows (ISM-1811, ISM-1705, ISM-1812, ISM-1707, ISM-1814) from the control tests backups_private_and_in_another_region, backups_retention_locked, storage_encrypted and only_backup_admins_reach_backups with the drift check (step 6); taking backups and restore tests (ISM-1511, ISM-1810, ISM-1515) as manual evidence Secrets Files in /etc/evidence-hound/secrets on the VM, given to containers as Docker secrets under /run/secrets; never in the repo The first deployment tutorial The runner's schedule hound serve runs each collector in hound.yaml on its cron schedule, in scheduler.time_zone The collector health control AC-AUTO-EVIDENCE The network path Private subnet with no public IP, HTTPS only from the office, SSH only from the Bastion, the VPN carrying the office network only The control tests vm_has_no_public_ip, https_only_from_the_office, office_range_is_not_the_internet, no_ssh_from_the_internet, vpn_routes_only_the_office and vm_metadata_v2_only (step 6): evidence kept with each run; the Essential Eight has no row for them The cloud configuration Terraform in its own repository, with control tests on every change and a nightly refresh-only plan The grc-infra-controls and terraform-drift profiles (steps 5 and 6) The office firewall Firmware in support and upgraded within two weeks, few Super Admins in Sophos Central OFFICE-FIREWALL's audit: ISM-1501, ISM-1694 and ISM-1883 from the sophos-central profile

docs.title: 1. Build the platform on OCI
docs.text:
1. The shape. An x86 (AMD) VM, VM.Standard.E5.Flex, with 2 OCPUs (4 vCPUs), 16 GB of memory and a 100 GB balanced boot volume, runs CISO Assistant's Compose stack and the runner with room to spare. Oracle's price list, checked on 23 November 2026, gives USD 0.03 per OCPU per hour, USD 0.002 per GB of memory per hour, and USD 0.0255 per GB per month for block volume storage plus USD 0.0017 per performance unit per GB per month (10 units for balanced). That is about USD 44 for the OCPUs, USD 23 for the memory and USD 4 for the boot volume: about USD 71 per month, before backups in Object Storage and outbound data. Site-to-Site VPN and Bastion are free. Check the price list again before you commit to it.
  2. The network. Create a VCN with one private subnet. Turn off "Assign a public IPv4 address" for the VM, so it has no public IP. Its security list allows HTTPS (443) only from the office network, through the VPN, and SSH only from the Bastion. Add a NAT gateway for outbound HTTPS and a service gateway for Object Storage.
  3. The Site-to-Site VPN. Create a dynamic routing gateway (DRG) attached to the VCN, a customer-premises equipment object for the XGS's public address (203.0.113.10 here), and an IPSec connection with a static route to the office network. OCI gives two tunnel endpoints (203.0.113.101 and 203.0.113.102 here). On the XGS, add an IPsec site-to-site connection to each, with the shared secrets OCI shows, and a firewall rule that lets the office reach the VM on 443 only.
  4. The Bastion. Create an OCI Bastion for the private subnet. Administrators open a time-limited managed SSH session to the VM; no SSH port faces the internet.
  5. The stack. Install it as in the first deployment tutorial, from step 3, with CA_HOSTNAME=ciso.example.com resolved by the office's DNS to the VM's private address (192.0.2.10). The secrets folder stays on the VM; Docker gives each container only the secrets it needs.
  6. Backups. Schedule a nightly database dump to an Object Storage bucket in another region with a retention rule, and a weekly backup policy on the boot volume. Test a restore to a scratch VM each quarter; that test is the evidence for ISM-1515.
  7. The infrastructure code. Keep the VCN, VM, VPN and bucket as Terraform in a repository of its own, with a nightly plan workflow (see Infrastructure drift from your IaC pipeline) and control tests on every change (step 6). The cloud credentials stay in that pipeline. The tutorial's Terraform is in examples/onboarding-tutorial/infra/oci: steps 2 to 6 above as code, with fictional values.

On another cloud. Only the names change: a VM in a private subnet with no public address, the provider's site-to-site IPsec VPN, its bastion or session manager, a NAT gateway for outbound HTTPS and object storage for backups. The supplier is your provider instead of SUP-ORACLE, and the Essential Eight decisions below hold as they are.

docs.title: 2. Suppliers first
docs.text:
A system is registered in CISO Assistant only once its supplier is approved, so the supplier register comes first. The platform has four:

Supplier What it provides How it gets into the register SUP-ORACLE The VM, network, VPN, Bastion and storage that host the GRC platform Drafted by hound onboard GRC-PLATFORM (step 3), then reviewed SUP-SOPHOS The office firewall and Sophos Central, which manages it Drafted by hound onboard OFFICE-FIREWALL (step 4), then reviewed SUP-CISO-ASSISTANT The CISO Assistant community edition, run from its published images Written by hand: scope/third-parties/sup-ciso-assistant.yaml SUP-EVIDENCE-HOUND The hound runner and its profile library Written by hand: scope/third-parties/sup-evidence-hound.yaml

The open-source projects have no system of their own, since GRC-PLATFORM is registered under its host, so write their files by hand. Their contract is the licence, with no contract value, and each has a yearly review, like any supplier the platform depends on.

The commands below run from the root of this repository. Copy the template, and add the two open-source supplier files (write your own the same way):

cp -R examples/compliance-repo /tmp/grc-repo
mkdir -p /tmp/grc-repo/scope/third-parties
cp examples/onboarding-tutorial/scope/third-parties/sup-ciso-assistant.yaml examples/onboarding-tutorial/scope/third-parties/sup-evidence-hound.yaml /tmp/grc-repo/scope/third-parties/

docs.title: 3. Onboard the GRC platform
docs.text:
1. Start. You decide each level and decision yourself here. With a coding assistant set up by hound agent setup, it drafts them through hound and you approve with hound approve.
hound onboard GRC-PLATFORM --repo /tmp/grc-repo --group 1 --group 2

Groups 1 and 2 are Essential Eight maturity levels one and two: 107 requirements. Answer the first questions:

Question Answer Your name Sam Example System owner's email it@example.com Product CISO Assistant and Evidence Hound on an OCI Compute VM Supplier ref_id and name ORACLE after the SUP- the prompt shows, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Solution ref_id and name OCI-HOSTING after SOL-, OCI compute, networking and storage Contract ref_id and name OCI-2026 after CTR-, OCI pay-as-you-go 2026 What it provides The private VM, network, site-to-site VPN, bastion, block volumes, object storage, logging and vault that host the GRC platform A vendor document Enter, for none Each of the five levels Enter, to decide it in the file in the next step, or a number from the scale printed above it and a reason

Each question comes with a line saying what it is for and an example.

Oracle is a new supplier, so hound drafts scope/third-parties/sup-oracle.yaml with a draft contract and a review, EA-SUP-ORACLE, and stops.

  1. Review the supplier. Decide its four levels and the solution's criticality in the file, each with its reason. Compare yours with scope/third-parties/sup-oracle.yaml. Then approve it yourself, in a terminal:
hound approve --repo /tmp/grc-repo

It shows the supplier and makes the contract active when you approve it, then concludes the review EA-SUP-ORACLE (ok, warning or blocker), recorded under conclusions: in the file. It refuses to run without a person at a terminal, so an agent cannot approve for you.

  1. Decide applicability. Run the same command again, with the same groups. For each requirement type m (manual evidence), n (not applicable, with a justification and who approved it), o (another system meets it, naming that system) or c (an API check), each with your reasoning. Type s to stop; the next run carries on. The decisions for this VM:

  2. Not applicable (61): the platform has no public address and is not an online service, so the online-service patching and MFA rows do not apply. Application control, Microsoft Office macros and user application hardening at maturity level two cover workstations and internet-facing servers, and this is a private Linux container host with no office suite, browser or PDF software. Each has its justification and "Approved by Alex Example".

  3. Manual evidence (32): patching (OCI Vulnerability Scanning, unattended upgrades, pinned images updated through a pull request), taking backups and restore tests, privileged access reviews, logging to OCI Logging, and incident response.
  4. API check (5): the backup bucket's rows (ISM-1811, ISM-1705, ISM-1812, ISM-1707 and ISM-1814), from the control tests and the drift check (steps 5 and 6).
  5. Another system (9): MFA for the platform's users and administrators is provided by Example 365, through single sign-on; the privileged operating environment rows by the administrators' Example laptops.

To replay these decisions instead of typing them, give the tutorial's answers as input:

hound onboard GRC-PLATFORM --repo /tmp/grc-repo --group 1 --group 2 < examples/onboarding-tutorial/answers/grc-platform.decisions.txt

At the end, accept the default domain and perimeter. It writes the audit scope/audits/grc-platform-essential-eight-2023.yaml, adds GRC-PLATFORM to scope/setup.yaml with its solution, and records every decision in onboarding/grc-platform-essential-eight-2023-2026-11-23.md (dated the day you run it). The answers to step 1 are in examples/onboarding-tutorial/answers/grc-platform.supplier.txt.

docs.title: 4. Onboard the office firewall
docs.text:
1. Start and review the supplier as in step 3, with OFFICE-FIREWALL and the answers in examples/onboarding-tutorial/answers/office-firewall.supplier.txt: supplier SUP-SOPHOS, solution SOL-SOPHOS-FIREWALL, contract CTR-SOPHOS-2026. Review the drafted scope/third-parties/sup-sophos.yaml as you did Oracle's.
hound onboard OFFICE-FIREWALL --repo /tmp/grc-repo --group 1 --group 2
  1. Decide applicability. Three requirements become API checks, which the sophos-central profile answers: ISM-1501 (the firmware is still supported), ISM-1694 (no firmware upgrade offered for more than two weeks) and ISM-1883 (few Sophos Central admins hold Super Admin). The firewall is an internet-facing network device, so the daily scan and the two-week firmware window apply, and ISM-1695 (non-internet-facing devices) does not. Applications, application control, Office macros and user application hardening do not apply to an appliance.
hound onboard OFFICE-FIREWALL --repo /tmp/grc-repo --group 1 --group 2 < examples/onboarding-tutorial/answers/office-firewall.decisions.txt

The API check rows are left out of the audit file: the collector's results fill them.

  1. Collect them. Copy the library's profile and its tests into the repo's profiles folder, which the runner mounts read-only, and test them offline:
mkdir -p /tmp/grc-repo/profiles && cp -R profiles/sophos-central.yaml profiles/sophos-central.tests /tmp/grc-repo/profiles/
hound profile test sophos-central --profiles /tmp/grc-repo/profiles

Then take hound.yaml, mappings/office-firewall-essential-eight-2023.yaml and deploy/compose.override.yml from examples/onboarding-tutorial (compare them with the template's to see what changed):

cp examples/onboarding-tutorial/hound.yaml /tmp/grc-repo/
cp examples/onboarding-tutorial/mappings/office-firewall-essential-eight-2023.yaml /tmp/grc-repo/mappings/
cp examples/onboarding-tutorial/deploy/compose.override.yml /tmp/grc-repo/deploy/

The collector instance example-sophos in hound.yaml reads Sophos Central (see Sophos Central for the API credential), and a second target sends its results to the firewall's audit through mappings/office-firewall-essential-eight-2023.yaml. Its client secret is the Docker secret sophos_client_secret, added to the runner in deploy/compose.override.yml.

docs.title: 5. Check the platform for drift
docs.text:
The terraform-drift profile reads the IaC pipeline's nightly plan through the GitHub Actions API, read only, and reports whether the cloud still matches the reviewed code. hound never runs Terraform and never holds cloud credentials. Copy the profile and its tests as in step 4, then see the instance example-grc-infra-drift in hound.yaml: it runs at 23:00, after the pipeline's 22:00 plan, with a fine-grained token that reads only the IaC repository's Actions (the Docker secret iac_actions_token).

cp -R profiles/terraform-drift.yaml profiles/terraform-drift.tests /tmp/grc-repo/profiles/
hound profile test terraform-drift --profiles /tmp/grc-repo/profiles

Keep the Terraform in its own repository, as recommended in the drift guide: each finding names that repository and the commit the plan was made from. A monorepo works too.

docs.title: 6. Prove the hosting controls
docs.text:
The hosting controls are written as Terraform tests in the IaC repository, infra/oci/tests/controls.tftest.hcl: one run block per control, such as vm_has_no_public_ip or backups_retention_locked. They use mock providers, so they need no Oracle account and create nothing. Try them:

cd examples/onboarding-tutorial/infra/oci && terraform init -backend=false && terraform test

The IaC pipeline (controls.yml) runs them on every change and weekly, and publishes the JUnit report as the control-tests artefact. The grc-infra-controls profile, the tutorial's copy of terraform-tests with one check per control, reads it with the same Actions-read token (instance example-grc-infra-controls in hound.yaml). Copy it and its tests into the repo:

cp -R examples/onboarding-tutorial/profiles/grc-infra-controls.yaml examples/onboarding-tutorial/profiles/grc-infra-controls.tests /tmp/grc-repo/profiles/
hound profile test grc-infra-controls --profiles /tmp/grc-repo/profiles

The GRC platform's mapping, grc-platform-essential-eight-2023.yaml, needs a control test and the drift check for each backup row: the test proves the code declares the setting, and the drift check proves the live tenancy still matches the code. A mock alone proves only the code. See Hosting controls proven by your infrastructure tests.

docs.title: 7. Review, validate, plan and apply
docs.text:
1. Review the change as a pull request: the four supplier files, the two audits, the two systems in scope/setup.yaml, the onboarding records, hound.yaml, the two mappings and the grc-infra-controls profile. Each not applicable row carries its justification and approver, and each row met by another system names it.
  2. Validate offline:
cd /tmp/grc-repo && hound config validate hound.yaml && hound scope validate scope --config hound.yaml
  1. Suppliers, then systems. A plan that registers a system whose supplier's review is not concluded ok is refused (system.supplier_not_approved) and nothing is applied. hound approve recorded EA-SUP-ORACLE and EA-SUP-SOPHOS as concluded in the supplier files (steps 3 and 4), and the plan counts those conclusions, so one plan applies the suppliers, their conclusions, the systems and their audits. The two open-source projects' reviews are concluded the same way: run hound approve once more if it still lists them. Then:
cd /tmp/grc-repo && hound scope plan scope --config hound.yaml
cd /tmp/grc-repo && hound scope apply scope --config hound.yaml

The plan creates GRC-PLATFORM, OFFICE-FIREWALL and their audits, with every decided row. 4. Run the collectors once, then check their status:

cd /tmp/grc-repo && hound run --config hound.yaml --only example-sophos
cd /tmp/grc-repo && hound status --config hound.yaml

From then on, the runner's schedule keeps the firewall's two rows, the platform's five backup rows and the drift check current, and the manual rows wait for their evidence.

docs.title: What your repo holds now
docs.text:
File Written by scope/third-parties/ Oracle and Sophos drafted by onboarding and reviewed; the open-source projects by hand scope/setup.yaml Onboarding: the two systems, each with its solution scope/audits/grc-platform-essential-eight-2023.yaml Onboarding scope/audits/office-firewall-essential-eight-2023.yaml Onboarding onboarding/ Onboarding: one record per system, every decision and who accepted it hound.yaml By hand: the three collector instances and the two systems' targets mappings/office-firewall-essential-eight-2023.yaml By hand: the firewall's three API checks mappings/grc-platform-essential-eight-2023.yaml By hand: the platform's five backup rows, each from its control tests and the drift check profiles/grc-infra-controls.yaml By hand: a copy of terraform-tests with one check per control deploy/compose.override.yml By hand: the two collectors' secrets

The audits in examples/onboarding-tutorial also start with a schema comment line, so editors check them; onboarding does not write it.

docs.title: Fictional scan exports
docs.text:
make scan-dev writes vulnerability scan exports for a fictional Example Pty Ltd estate. You get one export per scope, dated from today, so the vuln-scan collector and its patching checks can be tried without a scanner. make trial uses them. You can also use them to work on the checks. Nothing leaves the machine.

make scan-dev                                          # the compliant estate, into .dev/scans
make scan-dev ARGS="--variant gaps"                    # every deviation below
make scan-dev ARGS="--deviation browser-patch-overdue --out /tmp/scans"
make scan-dev ARGS="--today 2026-11-23"                # date the exports from another day

It writes one folder per scope under --out, and replaces that folder's exports each time, so the export it just wrote is always the current scan. Then it prints the four vuln-scan sources' settings (a name, then key=value pairs) for a hound.yaml. See the collector's guide.

docs.title: What the estate holds
docs.text:
Scope Folder and format In the compliant estate internet_facing internet-facing, Nessus web-01, vpn and mail.example.com, scanned today. One medium web server flaw, patched upstream 3 days ago, with no known exploit. common_apps laptops, a Microsoft Defender vulnerability management CSV Four laptops, read today. One browser flaw on laptop-02, first seen 5 days ago. other_apps other-apps, Nessus app-01 and file-01, scanned 2 days ago. One backup agent flaw, patch out 10 days ago. operating_systems operating-systems, Nessus The four laptops, app-01 and file-01, scanned yesterday. One missing operating system update on file-01, out 12 days ago.

Hosts are *.example.com and addresses are documentation ranges (203.0.113.0/24 and 192.0.2.0/24). Every scan finishes at 02:00 UTC on its day.

docs.title: The two variants
docs.text:
The compliant estate passes all eleven vuln.* checks. The gaps estate applies every deviation below, and each one fails only the check it names.

Deviation What changes Check and expected outcome internet-facing-scan-stale The internet-facing scan last ran 3 days ago, where it must run daily. vuln.internet_facing.scanned_in_interval: fail exploited-web-flaw-unpatched The web server flaw has a public exploit, and its patch came out 6 days ago, past the 48 hours. vuln.internet_facing.patched_in_window: fail unsupported-vpn-appliance The VPN appliance runs a version its vendor no longer supports. vuln.internet_facing.unsupported_removed: fail browser-patch-overdue The laptop browser flaw was first seen 20 days ago, past the two weeks. vuln.common_apps.patched_in_window: fail os-update-overdue The file server's operating system update came out 45 days ago, past the month. vuln.operating_systems.patched_in_window: fail unsupported-laptop-os One laptop runs an operating system version its vendor no longer supports. vuln.operating_systems.unsupported_removed: fail

ScanDevEstateTests runs the vuln-scan collector over the exports for each variant and each deviation, so this table and the estate cannot drift apart.

docs.title: In the trial
docs.text:
make trial, step 15, does the following:

  1. Writes the compliant exports into the trial workspace's scans folder.
  2. Adds the four scan sources.
  3. Runs them dry, then publishes.
  4. Offers to write the gaps estate and collect again, so you can watch the patching rows change in CISO Assistant.

See the trial guide.

docs.title: Adding a host, a finding or a deviation
docs.text:
• The estate is described once, in src/EvidenceHound.ScanDev/ScanDevEstate.cs. ScanExports.cs turns it into Nessus XML and Defender CSV.
  • A deviation has a name, a sentence, the checks it fails with their expected outcome, and a change to the estate. Add it to ScanDevEstate.Deviations, and add a row to the table above.

docs.title: What it cannot show
docs.text:
• A real scanner's output. That means odd plugin output, very large exports, and Tenable.sc or Tenable.io exports with first-seen dates. The collector's parser tests and a run against your own exports cover those.
  • Defender's other export shapes. Only the software vulnerabilities export, through the column map, is covered.

docs.title: The Sophos Central dev server
docs.text:
A fictional Example Pty Ltd Sophos Central tenant that answers the sophos-central profile on your machine. make trial uses it so the trial needs no Sophos account and no API key; you can also use it to work on the profile or its checks. Nothing leaves the machine.

make sophos-dev                                   # every control in place, on port 5370
make sophos-dev ARGS="--variant gaps"             # every deviation below
make sophos-dev ARGS="--deviation third-super-admin --port 5371"

Run hound where the server is on localhost (in a container, with --network host): hound sends credentials over plain http only to the machine it runs on, so an address such as http://host.docker.internal:5370/ fails with rest.host_not_allowed.

The server prints the settings for a rest collector with the sophos-central profile: client_id, id_url and api_url (both the server's address) and supported_firewall_firmware. The secret client_secret can be any text.

docs.title: What the tenant holds
docs.text:
Part In the compliant tenant Firewalls Two XGS firewalls, fw-office.example.com on SFOS 21.0.1 and fw-branch.example.com on SFOS 21.5.0. Admins Five admins at example.com: two Super Admins, one Admin and two Read-only. Roles The four predefined roles: Super Admin, Admin, Read-only and Service Principal Read-Only.

It answers every address the profile reads, with the same IDs in every answer:

Address Answer POST /api/v2/oauth2/token Always the same token. The server checks no credential and has no sign-in logic; this is the same fixed answer the profile's recorded tests use. GET /whoami/v1 The tenant, with the server's own address as its global and data region host, so every later request comes back to it. GET /firewall/v1/firewalls, /common/v1/admins, /common/v1/roles The lists, in pages of two by page number with a page total, as Sophos Central pages them. POST /firewall/v1/firewalls/actions/firmware-upgrade-check The upgrades offered to the firewall the body names, as Sophos Central answers: versions and release notes, no date.

Any other address gets 404.

docs.title: The two variants
docs.text:
The compliant tenant passes the three checks of the sophos-central profile. The gaps tenant applies every deviation below.

Deviation What changes Check and expected outcome unsupported-firmware The branch firewall runs SFOS 20.0.3, out of support. network.firewall.firmware_supported: fail third-super-admin A Read-only admin is made Super Admin: three, where at most two are allowed. network.management.super_admin_count: fail firmware-upgrade-overdue SFOS 21.5 has been offered to the office firewall for 20 days, more than the 14 allowed. network.firewall.firmware_current: fail, once hound has 20 days of earlier runs

SophosDevTenantTests runs the rest collector with the library profile against each variant and each deviation, so this table and the tenant cannot drift apart.

Sophos Central gives no firmware release dates, so network.firewall.firmware_current counts an offer's age from hound's own earlier runs. The server cannot make that history: on a first run against firmware-upgrade-overdue the offer is 0 days old and the check passes, saying counting starts today. The tests give the collector the evidence twenty daily runs would have kept (SophosAnswers.EarlierUpgradeChecks), and so does a real deployment after twenty days of collecting.

docs.title: In the trial
docs.text: make trial, step 13, starts the server, adds the sophos collector pointed at it with a placeholder secret, runs it dry, publishes, and then offers to restart the server with unsupported-firmware and collect again, so you can watch the result change in CISO Assistant. See the trial guide.

docs.title: Adding a firewall, an admin or a deviation
docs.text:
• The tenant is described once, in src/EvidenceHound.SophosDevServer/SophosDevTenant.cs; SophosAnswers.cs turns it into Sophos Central JSON.
  • A deviation is a name, a sentence, the checks it fails with their expected outcome, and a change to the tenant. Add it to SophosDevTenant.Deviations and a row to the table above.
  • A new query in the profile adds its path to SophosAnswers.Paths and its items to SophosAnswers.Items.

docs.title: What it cannot show
docs.text:
• The firewall itself: the XGS firewall's own API waits on its specification (s09-15 and s09-16), so the dev server stands in for Sophos Central only.
  • Sophos Central's real behaviour: rate limits, expired tokens, partner credentials and data region moves. The profile's own recorded tests and a run against a real tenant cover those.

docs.title: Write a collector
docs.text:
Most systems need no code. If the system has a REST API, write a YAML profile for the built-in rest collector instead (write a profile): profiles load from your compliance repo, are tested offline with hound profile test, and need no new release of hound. Write a code collector only when a system needs something a profile cannot do, such as a protocol other than HTTP or a vendor's signing scheme.

A code collector is a small .NET library: it implements ICollector from EvidenceHound.Collectors.Abstractions, calls one system, and returns framework-neutral check results with evidence files. It never writes to the system it reads, and never talks to CISO Assistant: hound maps and publishes its results.

docs.title: 1. Make the project
docs.text:
Download the .nupkg files from the release into a folder, such as ~/hound-packages, unless the packages are on nuget.org. Then, with the release's version:

$ dotnet new install EvidenceHound.Templates@1.0.0 --add-source ~/hound-packages
$ dotnet new hound-collector -n Example.Widget
$ cd Example.Widget
$ dotnet restore --source ~/hound-packages --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json
$ dotnet test

dotnet restore needs both sources: the Evidence Hound packages from the folder, everything else from nuget.org. Once the packages are on nuget.org, dotnet new install EvidenceHound.Templates@1.0.0 and dotnet test are enough.

The template references the EvidenceHound.Collectors.Abstractions and EvidenceHound.Collectors.Testing packages of its own version. The generated README lists every file and the steps below in more detail.

docs.title: 2. Choose the checks
docs.text: Name each check by what it proves, in the system's own terms, such as widget.mfa.admins or widget.backup.daily. Never use a framework's control number: the mapping file of each framework (mapping files) says which checks answer which requirement, so one collector serves the Essential Eight, NIST SP 800-171 and whatever comes next.

docs.title: 3. Test first, from recorded responses
docs.text:
1. Save a synthetic response for each API call in recorded/: the shape of the real one, with made-up values (example.com, "Example Pty Ltd", no tokens). Never commit a real response.
  2. Write a failing test for each check in WidgetCollectorTests, then make it pass. Keep the evaluation pure: response in, CheckResult out.
  3. The contract tests (WidgetCollectorContractTests) run the shared kit from EvidenceHound.Collectors.Testing against your collector: it describes at least one check and emits only the checks it declares, its evidence files can be hashed, it honours cancellation, it returns a failed result rather than throwing when credentials are refused, and it never logs a secret. Read-only access is up to you: ask the system for read-only permissions and call only read endpoints. They must pass unchanged. The kit is documented in its README.

docs.title: 4. Bring it into hound
docs.text:
The runner loads no code at run time, so a code collector ships inside hound. When it is ready:

  1. Open a pull request that adds the project under src/Collectors/ and its tests under tests/, following CONTRIBUTING.md.
  2. Register it in src/EvidenceHound.Runtime/Collectors/BuiltInCollectorServiceCollectionExtensions.cs with AddCollector<WidgetCollector>(), or the extension method the template made.
  3. Add its checks to a mapping file, and a page under docs/collectors/ with the read-only permissions it needs.

make test-template (also a CI job) generates a collector from the template against freshly packed packages, and checks it builds and its tests pass unmodified.

docs.title: Write a profile
docs.text:
This tutorial writes a REST profile test-first, from recorded API answers to a green hound profile test. It uses the fictional Example Asset API of Example Pty Ltd (api.example.com), whose recorded answers are in this repository, so you need no account and no network. Allow 20 minutes.

You will write example-devices, a profile with one check: every device runs a supported operating system. The library's example profile is the finished, larger version; the REST collector reference explains every key used here.

Run the commands from a checkout of this repository, in the dev container, after make build. hound below stands for dotnet run --project src/EvidenceHound.Cli --, or the hound binary if you have one.

docs.title: 1. Look at what the API answers
docs.text:
A profile starts from real answers, not from the API's documentation alone. For a real system you record them yourself, with identities removed (see the Sophos and Microsoft 365 recordings in this repository for the shape). For this tutorial they are already recorded in profiles/example.tests/recordings:

File Is the answer to token.json POST https://login.example.com/oauth2/token: an access token. whoami.json GET /v1/whoami: the organisation the API client belongs to, org-0001. devices.json GET /v1/orgs/org-0001/devices: the first page of devices, with a next link to page 2. devices.2.json GET /v1/orgs/org-0001/devices?cursor=page-2: the last page.

Open devices.json. Each device has an id, a hostname, a serial, an owner and an os.version, and the list is under items. The next link uses {{api}}, which a profile test replaces with the address of the request, so the recording works wherever it is replayed.

Make a profiles folder for your work and copy the recordings into your profile's test folder:

$ mkdir -p my-profiles/example-devices.tests
$ cp -R profiles/example.tests/recordings my-profiles/example-devices.tests/

docs.title: 2. Write the first test
docs.text:
A test case gives the instance's settings and secrets, the recorded answer to each request, and the result each check must give. Write the case for a tenant where every device is supported:

# file: my-profiles/example-devices.tests/all-supported.yaml
description: Every device runs version 14 or 15, which are both supported.
now: 2026-11-22T02:00:00Z
settings:
  client_id: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000c1
  supported_os: "14, 15"
secrets:
  client_secret: example-test-client-secret
responses:
  - { post: /oauth2/token, file: recordings/token.json }
  - { get: /v1/whoami, file: recordings/whoami.json }
  - { get: /v1/orgs/org-0001/devices, file: recordings/devices.json }
  - { get: /v1/orgs/org-0001/devices, query: { cursor: page-2 }, file: recordings/devices.2.json }
expect:
  example.device.os_supported: pass

The secret is a made-up test value: a profile test never calls the real API.

Run it:

$ hound profile test example-devices --profiles my-profiles

It fails with profile.not_found: there is no profile yet. That is the red step.

docs.title: 3. Write the profile
docs.text:
Write the profile, part by part:

  • Parameters and secrets are what each organisation sets: its client ID, the versions it supports, and its client secret.
  • Connection says where the API is, which hosts may receive the credential, and how to sign in.
  • Bootstrap asks whoami for the organisation ID, which the devices address needs. It is not evidence.
  • Queries read the devices, following the next link, and hash the host name, serial and owner, which identify a device or a person.
  • Checks test every device's os.version against the supported list.
# file: my-profiles/example-devices.yaml
profile: example-devices
version: "0.1.0"
description: Devices of the fictional Example Asset API, and whether they run a supported operating system.
requires:
  hound: ">=0.1"

parameters:
  client_id:
    type: string
    required: true
    description: Client ID of the read-only API client.
  base_url:
    type: url
    default: https://api.example.com/
    description: Where the API is.
  token_url:
    type: url
    default: https://login.example.com/oauth2/token
    description: Where tokens are issued.
  supported_os:
    type: list
    required: true
    description: Operating system versions still in support, for example 14, 15.

secrets:
  client_secret:
    required: true
    description: Client secret of the read-only API client.

connection:
  base_url: ${base_url}
  allowed_hosts: [api.example.com, login.example.com, "${base_url}", "${token_url}"]
  auth:
    type: oauth2_client_credentials
    token_url: ${token_url}
    client_id: ${client_id}
    client_secret: ${secrets.client_secret}
    scope: read

bootstrap:
  whoami:
    get: v1/whoami
    vars:
      org_id: $.organisation.id

queries:
  devices:
    get: v1/orgs/${org_id}/devices
    paging:
      style: next_link
      next: $.next
    items: $.items
    identities: [hostname, serial, owner]

checks:
  - id: example.device.os_supported
    title: Devices run a supported operating system
    over: devices
    each: { field: $.os.version, version_in: "${supported_os}" }
    require: all
    when_empty: not_applicable
    describe: "{passed} of {total} devices run a supported operating system. Supported: ${supported_os}."

Check it, then run the test again:

$ hound profile validate example-devices --profiles my-profiles
$ hound profile test example-devices --profiles my-profiles

validate prints example-devices 0.1.0: valid (1 query, 0 datasets, 1 check), and the test prints example-devices/all-supported: passed (1 check). That is green.

docs.title: 4. Test the failure too
docs.text:
A check that has only been seen to pass has not been tested. Add a case where version 14 is no longer supported, so the device on 14.6 fails:

# file: my-profiles/example-devices.tests/old-version.yaml
description: Only version 15 is supported, so the device on 14.6 fails.
now: 2026-11-22T02:00:00Z
settings:
  client_id: 00000000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000c1
  supported_os: "15"
secrets:
  client_secret: example-test-client-secret
responses:
  - { post: /oauth2/token, file: recordings/token.json }
  - { get: /v1/whoami, file: recordings/whoami.json }
  - { get: /v1/orgs/org-0001/devices, file: recordings/devices.json }
  - { get: /v1/orgs/org-0001/devices, query: { cursor: page-2 }, file: recordings/devices.2.json }
expect:
  example.device.os_supported: fail

$ hound profile test example-devices --profiles my-profiles

Both cases pass. When a case fails, hound profile test prints the check, the result it expected, the result it got, and the observation, which names the devices that failed; a request with no recording is listed as no recording for ....

A case for a check with history (a code check given a query's earlier evidence) lists the earlier runs it stands in for under history, each the evidence file an earlier run saved: - { at: 2026-11-12T02:00:00Z, evidence: firmware_upgrades.json, file: recordings/history/firmware_upgrades-2026-11-12.json }. The sophos-central tests use it for firmware age.

docs.title: 5. Use it
docs.text:
Copy example-devices.yaml and example-devices.tests/ into your organisation's profiles folder, then add a collector for it, which asks for the client ID, the supported versions and the client secret:

$ hound add collector rest --name example-devices --set profile=example-devices --config hound.yaml

Before relying on a new profile, run it once with --dry-run against the real API and read the evidence it saved: every identity should be a sha256: hash, and the observation should say what you expect.

From here, the reference covers more paging styles, datasets that join lists, the other operators and require modes, and code checks. To share a profile with others, add it to this repository's profiles/ folder with its tests and recordings, scrubbed of anything that identifies your organisation.
